papers.abstract: We consider the problem of constructing knowledge bases for applications based on large language models, in which the structure of a knowledge base determines how an application can retrieve and connect the information needed to answer a question. We study Self-Structuring Learning, a setting in which questions and expected answers guide the construction of a persistent knowledge base whose editable structure can be a graph schema or the organization of linked knowledge documents. We propose Knowledge-Base Gradient Descent, which diagnoses discrepancies between expected answers and responses obtained through the current knowledge base. At each round, the method proposes a structural edit, rebuilds the knowledge base, and adopts the edit when the learning loss decreases. The retained structure is evaluated on other questions about the same sources. By randomizing over candidate edits, we express the loss change of an edit as a derivative with respect to the probability of selecting it, and we evaluate joint edits as single candidates because their changes interact. Schema Descent instantiates the method for graph schemas. In experiments on large documents, each a bundle of research papers, the updated knowledge cards and graph schemas obtain higher mean Answer F1 on held-out generated questions than their initial structures, with schema gains in every document. On human questions, mean F1 rises for schemas and falls for cards: the updated structures serve the kind of question they were learned from.
bullets: Targets self-structuring knowledge bases whose organization controls information retrieval and connections.
Diagnoses answer discrepancies, proposes structural edits, rebuilds the knowledge base, and retains edits that reduce learning loss.
Models candidate-edit loss changes via selection probabilities and evaluates interacting edits jointly.
On document-based experiments, updated cards and graph schemas improved mean Answer F1 on held-out generated questions.
Performance on human questions improved for schemas but declined for cards, indicating question-type-specific effects.

papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on external memory, yet they still hallucinate about what they remember. Often the correct memory is retrieved and placed in the prompt, but the answer contradicts it or the memory is applied to the wrong question. We call these use-time memory hallucinations. Across five open models, we find that they arise from the conflict between parametric knowledge and external memory and take three forms: memory-ignoring, where the model returns to a stale fact in its weights (up to 46% of queries); memory-misapplying, where it attributes the memory to unrelated entities (up to 24%, and 49% when retrieval is combined with weight editing); and version confusion, where 53% of answers about revised facts assert the superseded value when both versions remain stored. We propose TASK memory, which goes beyond text-only memory by combining a Text note with Activation Steering and Knowledge editing that share one in-model address. The text holds the content. A removable knowledge edit supplies the address through its subject key and supports multi-hop composition. A pair of steering vectors decides, query by query, whether the model adopts the memory or keeps its own answer; the vectors store no content and control how the text memory is used. On frozen models under a pre-registered, test-once protocol, TASK reduces memory-ignoring hallucinations to at most 1.5% in all ten model-dataset cells and cuts neighbour misuse from 39.2% to 7.5% (+10.8 pp composite on CounterFact). It improves a 300-memory library over BM25 RAG by 16.4 pp, an advantage that holds at 3,000 memories, resolves fact revisions without fact IDs, and adds 7.5 pp of multi-hop accuracy on MQuAKE. 21 of 23 cross-model comparisons (8B-27B, four families) are significant, and TASK beats three recent context-steering methods in 9 of 10 model-dataset cells.
bullets: Memory hallucinations stem from conflicts between parametric knowledge and external memory, causing memory-ignoring, misapplication, and version confusion.
TASK stores content in text, uses a knowledge edit as an in-model address, and applies query-dependent steering to control memory use.
On frozen models, it reduced memory-ignoring errors to at most 1.5% across all tested model-dataset cells.
It improved over BM25 RAG by 16.4 percentage points on a 300-memory library, with gains persisting at 3,000 memories, and added 7.5 points on multi-hop accuracy.
The method resolved revised facts without fact IDs and outperformed three context-steering methods in 9 of 10 model-dataset cells.

figures.caption: Figure 3: TASK memory overview. (a) Write. A visible observation (s, p, o∗) is compiled into a memory object bound to the model hash, scope and version. The object contains a text record T, an address key km at layer ℓE with a threshold τm calibrated at write time, a closed-form, low-rank and removable patch E keyed on the same address, and steering vectors S = (v+m, v−m) trained on the frozen model; these are kept in a text store, a patch library and a steering bank. (b) Read, against memory-ignoring (Type I) and memory-misapplying (Type II) hallucination. Candidates are retrieved by BM25 or semantic search, and one partial forward pass to layer ℓE computes each candidate’s address response rm. The shared gate gm = ⊮[rm ≥ τm] decides whether the note is shown, whether the patch is loaded as W +BA, and whether v+m or v−m is added at the decision positions of layer ℓS ; multi-hop composition uses v+ only. All hooks and patches are unloaded after generation. (c) Revise, against version confusion (Type III). A new observation is matched to the top-2 active records by BM25, checked with the address and judged by the agent’s own model. On UPDATE the old version’s T, E and S are retired together; on DIFFERENT the existing record stays active. No fact IDs are used.

Figure 1: Memory hallucination: the memory is correct, the answer is not. (a) Text-only memory or RAG puts the retrieved note into the prompt and leaves the rest to the frozen model, where the note in the context conflicts with the stale fact in the weights. On a question about the memory, the weights win and the model answers with the stale fact (Type I, memory-ignoring). On a question about another entity, the note wins and the model assigns the memory to the wrong entity (Type II, memory-misapplying). Across our five models these rates reach 46% and 24%, and Type II reaches 49% when retrieval is combined with weight editing. (b) TASK memory goes beyond text-only memory. Each memory object holds Text content, a Knowledge edit ∆Wm whose key ûm serves as the in-model address, and a pair of Activation-Steering vectors (v+, v−) that carry no content. For a query x, the address response rm(x) is compared with the threshold τm. A relevant query shows T, loads E and adds v+, so the model adopts the memory; an unrelated query leaves T and E off and adds v−, so the model keeps its own answer.

Figure 4: TASK reduces both types of use-time memory hallucination on five models and two datasets (test). (a) Type I, memoryignoring: reversion to the stale parametric answer on queries whose stale fact is in the weights. (b) Type II, memory-misapplying: misuse on neighbour questions that the no-memory model answers correctly. This subset is why the values differ from the misuse over all neighbours in Table 3 (e.g. 24.3% vs. 39.2% for Qwen3-8B with T). Bars give values in %. Per-cell bootstrap CIs are in Section A.

Figure 2: Use-time memory hallucinations caused by the conflict between parametric knowledge and external memory (test splits, text memory in context, greedy decoding). (a) Type I, memory-ignoring: adoption of the memory’s answer on paraphrased questions. Filled markers: queries on which the no-memory model states the stale fact, i.e. the old fact is in the weights. Hollow markers: all other queries. The gap is in percentage points; ∗ marks a paired world-level bootstrap 95% CI that excludes 0. (b) Type II, memory-misapplying: on neighbour questions (same relation, different subject) that the no-memory model answers correctly, the rate at which the model instead states the memory’s answer. Without memory this is ≤0.9%. With text memory it rises on every model, and with text memory plus a weight edit (T+E) it rises further on four of the five models. All numbers come from frozen predictions (Section A).

Figure 5: Scaling the library to 3,000 memories (CounterFact test queries; distractors are training-split memories written by the same writer). Dashed: BM25 retrieval; solid: address-verified reading. Colours follow the carriers as in Figures 2 and 4. At 300 memories, address-verified T and T +S have the same locality (96.9%), so their markers coincide in (b). The full configuration with gated E (address-verified T + gated E + S, Table 4) scores 0.946 / 0.928 / 0.916 and lies between the two upper curves in (a); it is omitted for legibility.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses use-time memory hallucinations in LLM agents via activation steering and knowledge editing; fits LLM memory.
papers.title: TASK Memory: Beyond Text-Only Memory with Activation Steering and Knowledge Editing against Memory Hallucination
papers.tldr: TASK memory combines text notes, removable knowledge edits, and activation steering to substantially reduce use-time memory hallucinations in LLM agents.

papers.abstract: The behavior of memory systems for long-running AI assistants is governed by a harness, which consists of the code, prompts, and configurations for memory construction, maintenance, retrieval, and answer generation. However, optimizing the harness of a memory system remains largely manual, and unrestricted editing alone does not ensure structural improvements. In this paper, we introduce HoMe, an evaluation-driven framework that iteratively evaluates candidate harnesses and derives each new candidate from any previously evaluated harness by editing any part of it. HoMe combines session-level memory versioning with execution traces to identify shared failure mechanisms across cases and localize them to the responsible sessions and harness components. It encourages early structural exploration through candidate gating and reduces evaluation cost through smoke tests, adaptive sampling, and the reuse of constructed memory. We validate HoMe with the open-source memory system ReMe on two large-scale long-horizon memory benchmarks, LongMemEval-S and BEAM. With six formal candidate evaluations per benchmark, after a full initial evaluation, HoMe discovers harnesses that improve end-task performance over the originally strong harness while consuming far fewer query-time tokens. The code is available at https://github.com/agentscope-ai/ReMe.
authors: Yifei Xu, Li Yu, Zhaoyang Liu, Ce Wang, Sen Huang, Yanyan Shen, Yun Lin, Linpeng Huang, Hong Mei
bullets: Targets the largely manual optimization of memory-system code, prompts, and configurations.
Iteratively evaluates and edits previously tested harnesses, using session-level memory versions and execution traces to localize shared failures.
Promotes structural exploration with candidate gating and lowers evaluation cost through smoke tests, adaptive sampling, and memory reuse.
Validated with ReMe on LongMemEval-S and BEAM; after six formal evaluations per benchmark, it found harnesses with better end-task performance and fewer query-time tokens than the original harness.

papers.abstract: Multi-session hiring assistants must infer evolving recruiter preferences and decision patterns across projects and time. We introduce Open Knowledge Format (OKF)-indexed episodic memory to organize interactions and retrieve related events through their lineage. We also introduce Procedure Memory, which learns reusable decision procedures from these episodes through prompted reflection or reinforcement learning. We compare these approaches with no memory, full-history context, and conversation search, and evaluate Jev-class models for index navigation and GPT-5.6 Luna as a lower-cost alternative to GPT-5.4. In our evaluation, OKF-indexed retrieval achieves low-priority preference F1 scores of 0.93-0.95 at medium and high preference overlap between hiring projects. It significantly outperforms full-history context and conversation search in both settings, and no memory at high overlap, while using 69% fewer context tokens than full history. Procedure Memory reduces conversational turns by up to 39% relative to no memory. Qualitative and long-horizon evaluations provide evidence of temporal reasoning, with RL-learned procedures achieving 60% on both correct abstention and exact-field identification. Jev-class models improve conversational efficiency but more frequently miss temporally relevant evidence, highlighting the importance of evidence selection. On PersonaMem-v2, Procedure Memory with OKF retrieval achieves 50.2% accuracy versus 48.6% for full-history context and 29.0% for no memory, using 90.5% fewer reader input tokens than full history. GPT-5.6 Luna performs comparably to GPT-5.4 at lower cost. These findings highlight the value of structured episodic memory and learned decision procedures for efficient personalization and temporal reasoning.
authors: Praveen Kumar Bodigutla, Yizhi Zhang, Sai Vivek Kanaparthy, Arup De
bullets: OKF-indexed memory organizes interactions by lineage to retrieve temporally and project-relevant episodes.
Procedure Memory learns reusable hiring decision procedures through prompted reflection or reinforcement learning.
OKF retrieval reaches 0.93–0.95 low-priority preference F1 and uses 69% fewer context tokens than full-history context.
Procedure Memory reduces conversational turns by up to 39%; on PersonaMem-v2, the combined approach reaches 50.2% accuracy with 90.5% fewer reader input tokens than full history.
Smaller Jev-class models improve efficiency but more often miss temporally relevant evidence, emphasizing evidence selection.

papers.abstract: We formalize Agentic Waterfall Feed, a new problem of personalized information discovery in which users actively direct recommendations and the system adapts to evolving needs inferred from both explicit requests and browsing behavior. We address this problem with the Agentic Waterfall framework, whose language-model controller maintains persistent user state and coordinates content retrieval, ranking, and state updates. To evaluate systems on this task, we contribute the Agentic Waterfall Dataset and a replay-based evaluation protocol. The dataset combines real content metadata with simulated interaction histories. The protocol compares systems under shared histories using relevance scores and blind judgments of how well recommendations satisfy current user goals and constraints. Agentic Waterfall remains competitive with strong baselines on conventional recommendation tasks across five public benchmarks. On the Agentic Waterfall Dataset, it outperforms the strongest baseline in both evaluations, with relative improvements of up to 16.1%.
authors: Yige Luo, Shining Zhang, Jikun Liu, Hongjiao Qiang, Ran Guan
bullets: Targets personalized discovery where users actively steer recommendations rather than passively receiving feeds.
Uses a language-model controller to coordinate retrieval, ranking, and updates to persistent user state.
Introduces the Agentic Waterfall Dataset and a replay-based evaluation protocol with relevance scores and blind goal-satisfaction judgments.
Remains competitive on conventional recommendation tasks across five public benchmarks.
Outperforms the strongest baseline on its dataset by up to 16.1% in the reported evaluations.

papers.tldr: Agentic Waterfall is an intent-driven recommendation framework that uses persistent user state and feedback from requests and browsing to adapt information discovery to evolving goals.

papers.abstract: Agent harnesses today manage context on the model's behalf: when the window fills, the harness triggers a compaction that summarizes the history. We study the alternative, \emph{model-driven} context management, in which the model itself decides when and what to compact through a context API. We gave models control over their own context in \nooa, NVIDIA's open source agent harness, and compared the two strategies on document research and machine learning engineering across context budgets from 8K to 512K tokens. Models that use the context API effectively reach higher accuracy, often with fewer input tokens, especially at tight budgets: \textbf{GPT 6.1 nearly triples its score at a 32K budget} on OfficeQA Pro v2 (21\%~$\rightarrow$~56\%), and \textbf{Kimi gains with up to 41\% fewer input tokens}. Models differ widely, however, in how often they use the API, how aggressively they compact, and when they start compacting, and prompt changes shift that timing. Finally, we show that \textbf{inference engines can make model-driven edits cheaper}: by reusing the KV cache of the unchanged suffix after an edit, \textbf{we cut prefill compute by up to 15\% per request with no measurable change in accuracy}. Together, these results point to a new co-design frontier: models trained to manage their own context, served by inference engines that support KV cache editing.
authors: Alessio Devoto, Avinash Vem, Tara Safavi, Sanjay Kariyappa, Yu-Hsuan Tseng, Paul Furgale, Ricardo Silveira Cabral
bullets: Replaces harness-triggered summarization with a context API that lets models decide when and what to compact.
Evaluated on document research and machine learning engineering across 8K–512K-token budgets.
Effective API use improves performance at tight budgets: GPT 6.1’s OfficeQA Pro v2 score rose from 21% to 56% at 32K tokens, while Kimi used up to 41% fewer input tokens.
Models vary widely in compaction frequency, aggressiveness, and timing; prompt changes also affect when compaction begins.
KV-cache reuse after context edits reduced prefill compute by up to 15% per request without measurable accuracy changes.

papers.tldr: Model-driven context management can substantially improve agent accuracy and token efficiency under tight context budgets, especially when inference engines support efficient KV-cache editing.

papers.abstract: Medical reasoning agents combine large language model (LLM) reasoning with clinical workflows and specialized neural tools. However, general-purpose LLMs receive limited training exposure to domain-specific medical tools, and the uncertainty and distributional shifts of neural tool outputs make selecting tools from simple descriptions significantly more challenging than in deterministic settings such as calculators or dictionary lookups. In this paper, we propose EATS, an experience-augmented tool selection strategy that leverages accumulated tool-use trajectories to improve tool selection in medical reasoning agents. EATS constructs a memory of past interactions, including queries, tool choices, arguments, and self-evaluated feedback, and retrieves relevant experiences to guide tool selection for new queries. As memory construction does not require ground-truth supervision, EATS scales naturally with test-time experience. We evaluate EATS on tool-augmented medical reasoning tasks, including closed-ended visual question answering and free-form report generation. Experiments on four public datasets, ChestAgentBench, CheXbench, MIMIC-CXR, and SLAKE-VQA, across three multimodal LLMs, Qwen3-VL 2B, Qwen3-VL 32B, and GPT-5.5, show consistent gains in tool selection behavior and downstream medical reasoning performance. Code is available at https://github.com/Limingyuan001/EATS.
authors: Mingyuan Li, Tong Jia, Haoran Wang, Wenbo Qi, Ziyuan Yang, Bowen Ma, Jie Gui, Baosheng Yu
bullets: Medical LLM agents struggle to select specialized tools because tool outputs are uncertain and distribution-shifted.
EATS stores queries, tool choices, arguments, and self-evaluated feedback from prior interactions.
Relevant experiences are retrieved to guide tool selection for new medical queries.
Evaluated on visual question answering and report generation across four public datasets and three multimodal LLMs.
The abstract reports consistent improvements in tool selection and downstream medical reasoning performance.

papers.abstract: Reusing past experience in long-horizon tasks requires more than storing successful procedures: Language agents must distinguish which procedures apply and what work remains as execution progresses. We introduce MetaDecomp, an in-context meta-learning framework for adaptive task decomposition that jointly learns a task-relative state space and reusable procedures. Its outer loop builds procedural memory from successful training executions, representing task progress as abstract states and procedures between states as directed acyclic graphs of operations and dependencies. As new progress distinctions are learned, MetaDecomp revisits historical execution evidence to reassess state assignments and reorganize the procedures they support. With memory fixed at test time, the inner loop refines an initial decomposition and revises it from environmental feedback, combining applicable procedure fragments with task-specific steps missing from memory. Evaluated on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld over three seeds, MetaDecomp achieves the highest mean performance among the compared methods in four of five settings, for example, an 86.3% success rate on ALFWorld with Qwen3-4B. Fixing the initial schema or omitting historical reprojection reduces performance in component ablations. MetaDecomp also uses fewer inference tokens than ReAct and AutoRefine in all five settings. Cross-benchmark analysis identifies a low-performance area where partial coverage degrades success relative to hidden memory; high coverage improves success, while low coverage changes little. Code will be released upon acceptance.
authors: Ziyi Wang, Yixiao He, Yichen Wu, Ruite Lu, Jiayu Wang, Ying Wei
bullets: Builds a task-relative state space and represents reusable procedures as directed acyclic graphs of operations and dependencies.
Revisits historical executions as new progress distinctions emerge, reorganizing state assignments and supported procedures.
At test time, refines initial decompositions using environmental feedback and fills memory gaps with task-specific steps.
Evaluated on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, it achieves the highest mean performance in four of five settings and uses fewer inference tokens than ReAct and AutoRefine.
Partial procedural coverage can hurt performance relative to hidden memory; high coverage helps, while low coverage has little effect.

papers.abstract: Standard attention's key-value cache grows linearly with context length. Bounding it raises the question of what a sequence model should retain for long-context reasoning. We argue this choice should be learned, and introduce State Space Attention (SSA), which learns to keep a bounded set of past representations and reads them with standard attention. A learned scorer rescores every chunk against newly arriving context and the rest of memory. A fixed-context Transformer is then the special case that always keeps the most recent tokens. We train the scorer and reader jointly, either moving gradually from a differentiable soft weighting of memories to hard retention, or with hard retention from the start. To produce signal for the scorer, we generate supervised samples during training, a technique we call recovery. We compare SSA with recurrent models, bounded-memory attention methods, and full-attention Transformers across retrieval, variable tracking, multi-hop reasoning, and language modeling. On our retrieval and reasoning benchmarks, SSA matches or comes within a few points of full attention on most tasks, far outperforms a Transformer with the same readable budget on every long-context retrieval task we evaluate, and matches or outperforms one with about 4 times that budget, while using constant inference memory. The largest remaining gap to full attention at small language model scale is on RULER. SSA makes a fixed number of tokens useful over a longer context, and since it reads memory with standard attention, we propose that it can be stacked with KV cache eviction methods. We also pretrain and post-train 400M-parameter models and measure how SSA's training and inference costs scale with context length and model size. Together, these experiments examine the capabilities and limitations of learned memory retention for long-context sequence modeling.
bullets: Addresses the linear growth of standard attention’s key-value cache by learning context-dependent memory retention.
Uses a learned scorer to rescore memory chunks as new context arrives, while a standard attention reader accesses retained representations.
Trains retention jointly with reading using either gradual soft-to-hard selection or hard retention from the outset, aided by generated recovery supervision.

Across retrieval, variable tracking, reasoning, and language modeling, SSA substantially outperforms equal-budget bounded attention and can match or exceed attention with roughly four times its readable budget on retrieval tasks.
Its main remaining gap to full attention at small model scale is on RULER; the approach is evaluated across different training and inference context/model scales.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents can self-improve over time by utilizing procedural memory derived from prior task trajectories, yet the distinct utilities of memories derived from local successes and failures remain underexplored. This work studies this question in a realistic setting with heterogeneous streams of multi-domain tool-use tasks and various environment constraints common in real-world scenarios. We develop \emph{Dual-Polarity Memory with Periodic Maintenance} (DualPM), a simple, retrieval-free memory workflow characterized by (1) customizable reflection and procedural memory generation from both local successes and failures within each trajectory, and (2) periodic memory consolidation over long task streams under a given memory capacity, preventing memory explosion. Online prequential evaluation with fine-grained metrics reveals that failure memory more strongly broadens coverage, success memory better streamlines execution, while combining both polarities effectively integrates both benefits. Further studies demonstrate that DualPM enables cross-domain memory generalization and continual memory adaptation, while external evaluation on EvoMemBench reveals the portability and effectiveness of DualPM as a general long-term procedural memory method.
authors: Tianmai M. Zhang, Hoda Shajari, Amr Hendy, Xiaohu Liu, Piyush Behre, Omar Zia Khan, Ankur Gupta
bullets: Studies how success- and failure-derived procedural memories support continual adaptation across heterogeneous, multi-domain tool-use tasks.
Introduces a retrieval-free workflow with customizable reflection, memory generation from both outcome types, and periodic consolidation under fixed capacity.
Online evaluation finds failure memory broadens coverage, success memory improves execution efficiency, and combining both captures both benefits.
Shows cross-domain memory generalization and continual adaptation over long task streams.
External evaluation on EvoMemBench supports DualPM’s portability as a general long-term procedural memory method.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for biomedical question answering, but plausible incorrect answers remain a safety risk in clinical settings. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can ground responses in medical literature, while confidence-based adaptive RAG retrieves only when the model appears uncertain. We evaluate this routing strategy on three biomedical QA benchmarks of increasing difficulty and compare models across a broad range of parameter scales. The results reveal a paradox: confidence is well calibrated (AUROC 0.78--0.89) on standard medical exam questions where retrieval adds little value (+2.4\% to -1.4\%), yet becomes \emph{near-random} (AUROC 0.506) on specialist-level questions where retrieval helps most (+11.2\%). Five uncertainty signals---first-token probability, margin, entropy, consistency-based sampling, and verbalized confidence---show the same failure pattern. Five post-hoc calibration correction strategies, including density-ratio reweighting and rank-preserving transformation, do not recover a useful routing signal on hard questions (best AUROC: 0.507). Cross-model comparison shows that larger parameter scale and higher base accuracy do not guarantee reliable confidence-based routing under specialist-domain difficulty shift. These findings challenge the premise of confidence-based adaptive RAG: in high-stakes biomedical settings, defaulting to always-retrieve is safer and more accurate than confidence-based routing when calibration on the target domain is unknown.
authors: Chengying She, Siyu Deng, Haiyan Ge, Lizhuang Liu
bullets: Evaluates confidence-based retrieval routing across three biomedical QA benchmarks with increasing difficulty and models of varied parameter scales.
On standard exam questions, confidence is well calibrated (AUROC 0.78–0.89), but retrieval offers little benefit (+2.4% to −1.4%).
On specialist-level questions, routing becomes near-random (AUROC 0.506) even though retrieval improves performance by 11.2%.
Five uncertainty signals and five post-hoc calibration methods show the same failure pattern; the best corrected AUROC is 0.507.
Larger models and higher base accuracy do not ensure reliable routing under specialist-domain difficulty shifts.

papers.abstract: Long-term conversational memory requires retrieving complementary facts scattered across dialogue sessions, including intermediate evidence with limited similarity to the original question. Existing approaches often rely on derived memory representations or persistent relational structures, introducing construction costs and potentially losing source details. We present SAG-Mem, a conversational memory framework that preserves complete dialogue messages in non-overlapping chunks and discovers complementary evidence through query-time lexical expansion. Memory construction requires no model inference, using a lexical index without LLM-based extraction, summarization, or semantic relation construction. At query time, BM25 retrieves initial candidates, an evidence evaluator identifies useful chunks, and lexical cues from selected evidence guide an additional retrieval round. Retrieved dialogue is further annotated with calendar interpretations of supported relative-time expressions, preserving the original wording and temporal granularity. We also introduce SAG-Mem-Lite, an alternative configuration that replaces evidence scoring with embedding-based candidate scoring, achieving lower operational cost than Full Context and all memory-based baselines across both benchmarks with low query latency. On LoCoMo and LongMemEval, SAG-Mem achieves overall scores of 83.08 and 80.20, respectively, the highest among the evaluated methods on both benchmarks. On LongMemEval, it exceeds the strongest compared baseline by 7.20 points. SAG-Mem-Lite achieves scores of 77.09 and 77.20, respectively. These results support dialogue preservation and evidence-guided retrieval expansion as an effective design for long-term conversational memory.
authors: Yuchao Wu, XingCheng Liang, Xuanze Wang, Yini Huang, Yue Wu
bullets: Addresses retrieval of complementary facts scattered across sessions, including evidence with limited query similarity.

Annotates supported relative-time expressions with calendar interpretations while preserving original wording and temporal granularity.
Achieves the highest reported scores among evaluated methods on LoCoMo (83.08) and LongMemEval (80.20); SAG-Mem-Lite offers lower operational cost with scores of 77.09 and 77.20.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate parallel programs, but their correctness and performance depend strongly on the instructions that guide generation. We present \textsc{MetaFORGE}, an execution-grounded meta-learning framework that iteratively optimizes persistent natural-language skill specifications for MPI C code generation. \textsc{MetaFORGE} combines correctness testing, compiler diagnostics, static-analysis findings, runtime measurements, and rank-level load-imbalance profiles into a scalar reward that drives textual-gradient refinement, while an external memory distills and retrieves reward-supported optimization knowledge across runs. Across six MPI tasks and three workload sizes, \textsc{MetaFORGE} improves static-analysis quality, runtime, and load balance relative to zero-shot generation and generally exceeds the evaluated \textsc{TextGrad} iterative baseline. A model-matched refinement ablation shows that the MetaFORGE advantage persists when its refinement model is reduced to \texttt{gpt-4o}. An expanded retrieval ablation across all 18 task--workload configurations shows consistent runtime benefit and broad static-analysis and load-balance benefit from retrieved context. Leakage-controlled held-out and zero-update experiments further provide evidence that optimization knowledge persists in both the transferred skill and external memory under the evaluated protocol.
authors: Scott Piersall, Yang Gao, Shenyang Liu, Liqiang Wang
bullets: Targets the strong dependence of LLM-generated parallel code on generation guidance.
Combines correctness tests, compiler and static-analysis feedback, runtime data, and load-imbalance profiles into a reward for textual refinement.
Uses external memory to retrieve and accumulate optimization knowledge across runs.
Across six MPI tasks and three workload sizes, improves runtime, static-analysis quality, and load balance over zero-shot generation and generally over TextGrad.
Ablations and leakage-controlled tests indicate benefits persist with a matched refinement model and transferred knowledge in both skills and memory.

figures.caption: Figure 1: MetaFORGE: An automated meta-learning skill-refinement architecture. MetaFORGE optimizes LLM coding skills through execution-grounded feedback. The held-out task is excluded from all Phase 1 skill updates and memory construction.

papers.abstract: Recent work proposes hypernetworks that convert a document into a low-rank parameter update (LoRA) in a single forward pass, enabling fast injection of new knowledge into a frozen LLM. However, storing separate LoRA adapters for each document can be unsustainable in streaming settings. In this paper, we study the problem of composing hypernetwork-generated LoRAs using two representative systems, Doc-to-LoRA and SHINE. We show that hypernetwork-generated LoRAs have a geometry sharply different from directly fine-tuned LoRAs. They exhibit greater spectral concentration and stronger cross-document alignment than next-token prediction and QA fine-tuned adapters, which are diffuse and nearly orthogonal across documents. Guided by this observation, we propose latent-space LoRA merging. We compose the intermediate hypernetwork latents and then decode the merged latent through the frozen LoRA-generation head. We show that latent-space merging techniques consistently improve over weight-space and factor-space baselines while preserving a single fixed-rank adapter. These results support latent-space composition as a promising mechanism for combining hypernetwork-generated LoRAs under a fixed output-rank budget.
authors: Yanlai Yang, Minki Kang, Divyam Madaan, Sung Ju Hwang, Mengye Ren
bullets: Addresses the storage challenge of keeping separate LoRA adapters for many streaming documents.
Finds that hypernetwork-generated LoRAs are more spectrally concentrated and cross-document aligned than directly fine-tuned LoRAs.
Composes intermediate hypernetwork latents, then decodes the merged latent into a LoRA using the frozen generation head.
Evaluated with Doc-to-LoRA and SHINE; latent-space merging consistently improves over weight-space and factor-space methods.
Scope: combines hypernetwork-generated adapters under a fixed output-rank budget.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Latent Merger overview. A shared, frozen hypernetwork encoder maps each document to a latent. The trainable merger adds a gated, permutation-invariant residual to the latent mean. The frozen LoRAgeneration head decodes the merged latent into one fixed-rank adapter for the frozen language model.

Figure 1: Hypernetwork-generated LoRAs occupy a qualitatively different region of adapter space. We visualize pairwise distances between unit-Frobenius-normalized adapters using metric MDS, with 500 passages per method sampled from the SQuAD validation set. In the two-dimensional MDS embedding, directly fine-tuned NTP-FT and QA-SFT adapters form broad shells, while D2L and SHINE adapters concentrate in compact regions. This structural difference motivates latent merging methods that respect the hypernetworkinduced adapter geometry.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents rely on external memory to retain and reuse information across interactions. Existing memory systems treat memory as a record of the past and evaluate it by fidelity to the conversation. However, the value of memory lies in whether it improves the agent's response. A memory system decides what to memorize and what to serve before that response exists, and fidelity checks neither decision against it. Faithful memory can therefore fail to improve the response. We instead view memory as a prediction problem and present \textbf{\emph{\leto{}}}, a memory system for LLM agents that focuses on the utility of memory to the future rather than on its fidelity to the past. Because future requests are unknown, \emph{\leto{}} preserves access to conversation details through memory indexing, allowing information to remain available through its sources. When a request arrives, memory replay draws on this index to anticipate and supply the context the agent needs beyond what the request explicitly states. The utility of the served context remains uncertain until the response is generated, motivating a utility loop that uses response outcomes to refine future memory selection. We evaluate our system against six memory systems on five benchmarks across three scenarios. In personalization, it outperforms the strongest compared memory system by 16.3 percentage points in accuracy on PrefEval and by 3.1 points in task completion on PERMA. For long-horizon tasks, it achieves the best overall performance on MemoryArena averaged over five environments with a gain that increases with the chain depth. In long-context understanding, it is on par with retrieval over the raw history while serving fewer context tokens.
bullets: Preserves conversation details through an index instead of permanently compressing or discarding them.
Uses memory replay to anticipate unstated context needs when a request arrives.
Applies a utility loop that learns from response outcomes to improve future memory selection.
Outperforms the strongest compared system in personalization and performs best overall on MemoryArena across five environments.

papers.tldr: Leto treats agent memory as a utility-driven prediction problem, selecting context based on its expected impact on future responses rather than fidelity to past conversations.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory retrieval often returns query-relevant records, but relevance does not guarantee sufficient evidence: answering requires a set of records that jointly satisfies a question's factual, relational, temporal, and state constraints. We study this demand--evidence misalignment through MemPath, an interventional framework that diagnoses failures in memory access, demand coverage, and evidence utilization. Guided by this diagnosis, we propose BiDE-Mem, which represents questions as typed demands and uses them to guide retrieval and evidence organization. We formalize demand--evidence support; in the evaluated compact path, it is conveyed through provenance-aware evidence organization and Reader guidance rather than a separate generative four-state verification step. On LoCoMo, BiDE-Mem improves accuracy by 6.23 percentage points over Mnemis; on LongMemEval, it achieves 91.80%, with strong multi-hop and temporal performance. Supplementary Qwen-Reader evaluations place it first among seven systems on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S under two judging protocols. Ablations and evidence-level analyses show that demand representation, retrieval, and evidence presentation each contribute to answer quality.
authors: Shiyao Liu, Yixing Fan, Ruqing Zhang, Xiaohui Yan, Jiafeng Guo, Xueqi Cheng
bullets: The paper identifies demand–evidence misalignment across factual, relational, temporal, and state constraints.
MemPath diagnoses whether failures arise from memory access, demand coverage, or evidence utilization.
BiDE-Mem represents questions as typed demands to guide retrieval and provenance-aware evidence organization.
It improves accuracy by 6.23 percentage points over Mnemis on LoCoMo and reaches 91.80% on LongMemEval.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon large language model (LLM) agents distill past trajectories into reusable experiences. Misleading or adversarial guidance in source trajectories can corrupt these experiences, allowing harmful instructions to persist across tasks and influence future agent actions. Assessing the risks of potentially corrupted experiences poses three challenges: (1) modeling provenance and execution dependencies before experience reuse, (2) learning task-conditioned risk from trajectory outcomes, and (3) repairing risky experiences at online inference. To address these challenges, we present ExpGuard, a framework for retrieval-triggered experience risk assessment and online repair. Specifically, to tackle challenge (1), ExpGuard integrates experience semantics with provenance and execution dependencies in a task-conditioned heterogeneous graph to predict attack and task-failure risks before experience reuse. To enable task-conditioned risk supervision and tackle challenge (2), we conduct matched counterfactual replays of each original experience and its minimally neutralized counterpart from the same task and environment checkpoint, deriving separate risk labels from differences in attack success and legitimate task completion. To tackle challenge (3) at inference time, ExpGuard repairs candidate experiences flagged as high-risk by the graph-based predictor at retrieval and re-predicts their risks before they enter the agent's active experience context. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of ExpGuard in identifying risky experiences and defending agents against experience corruption.
authors: Yuzhou Chen, Licheng Pan, Zhixuan Chu, Yunsheng Lu, Yichen Sun, Han Zheng, Yan Wang, Bingyu Zhu, Haiwen Hong, Longtao Huang, Kui Ren
bullets: Targets persistent harmful or misleading guidance distilled from past agent trajectories.
Uses a task-conditioned heterogeneous graph combining experience semantics, provenance, and execution dependencies to predict attack and task-failure risk.
Learns risk labels through matched counterfactual replays of original and minimally neutralized experiences.
Repairs high-risk experiences during retrieval, then re-evaluates them before adding them to the agent’s active context.
Experiments show effectiveness in identifying risky experiences and defending against experience corruption.

papers.abstract: Conversational assistants compact older messages into short notes and evict the originals. When the note's language requires a distinction that English leaves open, such as Spanish adjective gender (agotado vs. agotada), messages that omit or explicitly state that attribute can yield the same note. After eviction, later turns cannot tell them apart: taking the inflected form literally asserts an attribute the user never gave, whereas discounting it as routine grammar discards one the user did give. We propose a training-free repair across writing, pre-eviction verification and reading. The writer marks unstated attributes with paired forms (e.g., agotado/a), a likelihood check before eviction rewrites unsupported single forms into paired ones, and the reader trusts remaining single forms as stated facts. On five Qwen3.5 and Gemma-4 models, eviction cuts recall of stated attributes from 90% to 34% in question answering (QA); our repair raises F1 (which penalizes both errors) on every model, by 9-53 points in QA and 12-40 points in agent handovers.
authors: Ian Miao, Fangrui Zhu, Bowen Jiang
bullets: Problem: Compacted notes can conflate omitted and explicitly stated attributes when the target language encodes distinctions English leaves ambiguous.
Method: Writers mark unsupported attributes with paired forms, pre-eviction checks repair unsupported single forms, and readers treat remaining single forms as stated facts.
Result: Eviction reduced stated-attribute recall from 90% to 34% in QA; repair improved F1 across all evaluated models.
Scope: Evaluated on five Qwen3.5 and Gemma-4 models in question answering and agent handovers.
Contribution: A training-free repair spanning note writing, pre-eviction verification, and reading.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) ranks memory chunks by semantic similarity to the query. Many methods improve on this by learning from feedback on what was retrieved, but each is a separate heuristic, with no account of when it is the right choice. We introduce BRAG, a generative model of retrieval with use. Each chunk generates the queries it answers from a mixture of von Mises-Fisher components anchored at its original embedding, and each chunk has a latent utility that drifts over time. The model gives the optimal inference, a closed-form filter that stores a few keys and two scalars per chunk and updates them online from the labels of a curator, and it frames retrieval as a control problem. It also shows when existing methods are optimal. Query averaging, Rocchio-style feedback and frequency reranking are special cases with fixed parameters, NUDGE is the case of one key per chunk with no dynamics, and LADER the limit of one key per past query. On two public long-term memory benchmarks, BRAG matches these methods on queries asked before, as expected, because when nothing changes over time the assumptions behind these special cases hold. On harder problems, where a new chunk makes an old one obsolete, BRAG outscores them. They all stay at plain-search level (Recall@5 0.67-0.71), while BRAG retrieves the new chunk 0.80-0.86 of the time. We also ran BRAG on three of NUDGE's seven text benchmarks, and it matches or beats NUDGE on all three. On nine months of a personal agent's memory (20,640 chunks), BRAG raises Recall@5 on held-out queries from 0.75 to 0.98 and Recall@1 from 0.44 to 0.97, with little change on chunks never queried.
authors: Javier Movellan, Manjot Bilkhu, Young-mok Jung, Sirajul Salekin, Henry Tran, Zhao Huang
bullets: Models each chunk’s answered queries with a mixture of von Mises–Fisher components anchored at its embedding, plus a time-varying latent utility.
Provides a closed-form online filter that stores a few keys and two scalars per chunk and updates from curator feedback.
Unifies several existing retrieval-feedback methods as special cases under fixed or simplified assumptions.
Matches prior methods on unchanged-query settings but outperforms them when new chunks make old ones obsolete.
On a nine-month personal-agent memory, improves Recall@5 from 0.75 to 0.98 and Recall@1 from 0.44 to 0.97, with little effect on never-queried chunks.

papers.abstract: Recent Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) increasingly use shared memory to store and reuse successful collaboration records, enabling teams to improve across tasks. However, this memory introduces a new attack surface for malicious insiders. Unlike existing insider attacks that inject misleading information directly into the current collaboration, misinformation stored in shared memory can later appear as successful team experience and gain greater credibility and influence. We propose MIMPA (Multi-Agent Insider Memory Poisoning Attack), which exploits this vulnerability using only normal participation privileges, without direct memory access. During an earlier task, the malicious agent embeds a target-specific payload while helping the team answer correctly, allowing the payload to be retained in a successful collaboration record. When retrieved for a later target task, this poisoned record can steer benign agents toward a designated wrong answer, further amplified by malicious triggering. Across three benchmarks and two LLM backbones, MIMPA substantially outperforms existing insider attacks and remains effective under hierarchical memory management, while auditing only partially mitigates it. These results reveal that shared memory intended to accumulate team experience can become a persistent channel for insider attacks. Our code is available at https://github.com/ahnji0520/MIMPA-code.
bullets: Shared memory makes successful collaboration records a persistent attack surface because stored misinformation gains credibility when reused.
MIMPA embeds a target-specific payload during an earlier task while still helping the team answer correctly.
The poisoned record is later retrieved for a target task and amplified through malicious triggering to influence benign agents.
Across three benchmarks and two LLM backbones, MIMPA outperforms existing insider attacks and remains effective with hierarchical memory.
Auditing only partially mitigates the attack, highlighting the need for stronger defenses against persistent memory poisoning.

(c) Triggering: when this poisoned record is retrieved for the target task, the attacker invokes it to steer the team toward the designated wrong answer.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as persistent services that must reason over large volumes of external knowledge. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds model responses in relevant documents, but the retrieved content must still be encoded and stored in the key-value (KV) cache. As this content accumulates, the cache grows linearly, increasing memory consumption and inference cost. Existing memory-compression methods address this problem either by retaining a subset of cached states or by learning context compressors that map documents to compact latent representations. Despite these advances, consolidating information under tight memory budgets while preserving its usefulness for future queries remains challenging. We investigate how the model's native KV states can be selectively consolidated into a fixed-size working memory without access to future queries. To this end, we introduce SD-Cache (State-guided and Dynamically updated Cache), a query-agnostic KV-memory consolidation framework that operates alongside a frozen generator LLM. SD-Cache learns to consolidate layer-wise KV states into fixed-size memory through selective anchor-based pooling and state-guided refinement, processing new contexts in a single forward pass without context-specific optimisation. Experiments on retrieval-augmented question answering and synthetic long-context benchmarks show that SD-Cache maintains competitive downstream performance under constrained memory budgets.
authors: Yuanhong Chen, Yiping Ji, Cameron Gordon, Emily Hackett-Jones, Hemanth Saratchandran, Anton van den Hengel
bullets: Addresses the rising memory and inference costs of accumulating retrieved content in RAG KV caches.
Learns to selectively consolidate layer-wise native KV states without access to future queries.
Uses anchor-based pooling and state-guided refinement alongside a frozen generator LLM.
Processes new contexts in a single forward pass without context-specific optimization.
Maintains competitive performance on retrieval-augmented QA and synthetic long-context benchmarks under constrained memory.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Illustration of our SD-Cache method. The right panel details the memory update mechanism: OAPM performs noveltyguided pooling and gated slot updates, while OSGC refines the pooled KV representations using an associative state accumulated from the original KV stream.

papers.abstract: Context compaction enables large language model agents to tackle long-horizon tasks within limited context budgets by replacing interaction histories with compressed summaries. However, learning effective compaction jointly with the agent policy remains challenging, as summaries affect task success over many subsequent interactions. We introduce RECAP, a reinforcement learning (RL) framework based on the principle that a summary should preserve the behavior induced by the original interaction history. We formalize this principle with a behavior distortion objective that measures the divergence between the agent's subsequent behavior under compressed and original contexts. We show that the gradient of the distortion objective decomposes into two complementary learning signals: distortion-based reward for summary generation and self-distillation for subsequent actions. Experiments on Qwen3.5-4B show that RECAP consistently outperforms the task-reward-only RL baselines on both environments, leading to an absolute improvement of 4.6% and 4.3% on BrowseComp-plus and SWE-bench Verified, respectively. Ablations further highlight the value of jointly supervising summary generation and post-compaction behavior for RECAP.
authors: Yulun Jiang, Maria Brbic, Michael Moor
bullets: Addresses the challenge of learning context summaries jointly with agent policies under limited context budgets.
Uses a behavior-distortion objective to measure divergence between actions from compressed versus original histories.
Derives two learning signals: distortion-based rewards for summary generation and self-distillation for later actions.
On Qwen3.5-4B, outperforms task-reward-only RL baselines on BrowseComp-plus and SWE-bench Verified, with absolute gains of 4.6% and 4.3%.
Ablations show benefits from jointly supervising summary generation and post-compaction behavior.

papers.abstract: Generative agents are game characters whose plans, conversations, and memories are written on the fly by a large language model (LLM). The original Generative Agents demonstration used cloud inference in a custom simulation. We present GARP, a platform for real-time generative agents inside Godot, and describe the Character Behavior System used in GARP 2. The complete loop runs on local hardware using a 3B-parameter open-weight model and no cloud service. Alongside the original planning, memory, and reflection, GARP gives each agent an emotion system driven by LLM appraisal, four graded personality axes drawn from the Big Five that set simulation parameters as well as prompt text, six needs whose urgency grows over time, and pairwise relationships updated after every conversation. The system narrows 50+ candidate actions to typically 3-8, constrains model responses with JSON schemas, and surfaces important memories in decision prompts. A layered optimization strategy (an adjustable game clock, decisions taken ahead of need, multi-tier caching, prompt compression, and fully asynchronous execution) keeps the game responsive while the model thinks. In a nine-scenario evaluation, 25 of 27 runs passed log-based checks. Both failures occurred in the birthday party scenario, where one guest omitted the event from their daily plan.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of running planning, memory, conversation, and reflection for generative agents without cloud inference.
Adds emotion appraisal, Big Five-inspired personality traits, time-based needs, and conversation-updated relationships.
Improves decision-making with action filtering, JSON-constrained outputs, salient-memory prompts, and ahead-of-need planning.
Maintains responsiveness through adjustable game timing, caching, prompt compression, and asynchronous execution.
In nine scenarios, 25 of 27 runs passed log-based checks; both failures involved a guest omitting a birthday party from their daily plan.

papers.abstract: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) leverages centralized knowledge graphs to enhance large language models with structured knowledge retrieval. However, real-world knowledge is inherently distributed across multiple organizations rather than being centrally accessible. Privacy constraints further prohibit sharing entire local knowledge graphs, preventing GraphRAG from effectively retrieving and utilizing distributed knowledge. To this end, we propose Federated GraphRAG (FedGRAG), a unified framework for distributed graph retrieval and knowledge-enhanced generation over multiple clients with knowledge graphs. Specifically, we address two fundamental challenges in federated GraphRAG. First, the absence of a global knowledge graph makes unified retrieval impossible. To address this, we develop a Federated Knowledge Routing mechanism that efficiently identifies relevant clients through lightweight knowledge indices without exposing local graph structures. Second, local graph memory cannot be shared directly because it contains sensitive entities and knowledge information. We therefore propose a controlled-disclosure evidence construction method. It extracts retrieved evidence subgraphs and converts them into an evidence abstract, enabling evidence conversion and reconstruction on the server. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Federated GraphRAG consistently outperforms existing baselines in both retrieval and downstream generation tasks, establishing a new paradigm for deploying GraphRAG in federated environments.
bullets: Addresses distributed knowledge and privacy barriers that limit centralized GraphRAG.
Uses lightweight knowledge indices for federated routing to relevant clients without exposing graph structures.
Constructs controlled-disclosure evidence abstracts from retrieved subgraphs for server-side reconstruction.
Experiments show consistent improvements over existing baselines in retrieval and downstream generation tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The architecture of FedGRAG. This process consists of a pre-process and a query phase. During the pre-process phase, the client and server perform collaborative training to extract lowdimensional graph embeddings; the client then uploads prototypes to the server to construct a prototype graph. In the query phase, the server routes the query to the appropriate semantic cluster on the client. Subsequently, an evidence subgraph is constructed within the cluster, and the server aggregates these reconstructed evidence facts to generate retrieval results.

papers.abstract: Doc-to-LoRA (D2L) compiles documents into low-rank adapters, allowing language models to use their contents without repeatedly processing the original text. We investigate its suitability for internalizing user memories through factual question answering, controlled interventions, and a production MidBrain memory pipeline. Across Gemma-2-2B and Qwen3-4B, D2L loses accuracy relative to in-context learning, with additional documents introducing substantial interference. Single-document errors frequently match answers to other questions about the same passage, suggesting unreliable question-answer attribution. Layer-wise interventions show that interference accumulates across depth, with more concentrated early damage at larger bank sizes on Gemma. With eight documents, applying the full bank in the initial layers gives similar accuracy to withholding all document contributions there. Source membership is detectable in intermediate states, but trained readers do not reliably resolve the interference. On PersonaMem-v2, joint compilation and normalized adapter composition achieve accuracy close to consolidated text memory when retrieved episodes remain text, but the resulting token savings are modest. Measured throughput gains also depend on model and batch size despite substantial reductions in analytical compute. Together, these findings limit the practical case for D2L as a replacement for text-based memory and motivate investigating online-learning methods that acquire personalized behavior from interactions in which memory is used.
bullets: Across Gemma-2-2B and Qwen3-4B, D2L underperforms in-context learning for factual question answering.
Adding documents causes substantial interference; errors often retrieve facts from other questions about the same passage.
Layer-wise analysis suggests interference accumulates through depth, with source information present but not reliably resolved by trained readers.
On PersonaMem-v2, joint compilation and adapter composition approach consolidated text-memory accuracy when episodes remain text, but token savings are modest.
Throughput benefits vary by model and batch size, despite lower analytical compute; the study motivates online-learning approaches for personalized memory.

papers.abstract: An assistant that summarizes old conversations may later need a detail from the original exchange. It can score archived passages against the question, but only passages that fit in the prompt reach the answering model. We tested whether a BM25 filter saves input tokens once that limit is taken into account. We calibrated the filter on passages that individually corrected an answer the model got wrong from the summaries alone. Across 75 LongMemEval questions, filtering changed one prompt and saved 0.096% of input tokens. With and without the filter, the model answered the same questions correctly under a second automated grading. On a random sample, two human graders' settled judgments agreed with the automated grades in 92.9% of definite comparisons (Cohen's kappa = 0.805). Building on earlier work that distinguishes retrieved evidence from delivered evidence, we give an exact test for packers that try whole passages in a fixed order and skip any that do not fit. Run the packer without the filter. The prompt changes exactly when an admitted passage scores below the cutoff. Code and data: https://github.com/KurbanIntelligenceLab/Certfold
authors: John Knight, Erchin Serpedin, Hasan Kurban
bullets: Across 75 questions, filtering changed only one prompt and saved 0.096% of input tokens.

papers.abstract: AI agents accumulate conversations, images, and documents through long-term interactions with users. Answering later questions often requires connecting evidence across these records, yet the resulting understanding is rarely retained, allowing mistakes to recur on related questions. Existing multimodal memory methods largely focus on storing and retrieving records, with limited mechanisms for learning from completed tasks and consolidating task-specific experience. We therefore propose MMMem, a task-aware multimodal memory framework that extracts and consolidates experience from completed tasks through four complementary strategies. First, source-linked multi-view memory organizes original text, images, and rendered pages alongside generated scene images that combine clues across records for retrieval. Second, source-generated tasks support knowledge alignment at two levels: warm-up consolidates source knowledge into task-relevant experiences in external memory, while self-training adapts the model's parametric knowledge to task demands. Third, the same vision-language model distills completed tasks into experiences that record the task context, conclusion, and support links. Finally, task-aware retrieval recalls source views and relevant experiences for answering and verification, while source-supported reuse guides long-term retention. Across three memory benchmarks and two vision-language readers, MMMem outperforms eight baselines. With Qwen3.5-9B, MMMem achieves relative gains of 36.9%, 17.6%, and 15.2% over the best-performing baselines on LoCoMo, Mem-Gallery, and LooGLE v2, respectively. Ablations show consistent gains from training and memory warm-up, while case studies illustrate how individual components work in practice.
authors: Yuxuan Chen, Changwei Lv, Yunfei Li, Zhongjing Du, Kehui Tan, Zijun Liao, Ruochong Zheng, Hao Chen, Can Deng, Zheni Zeng, Chang Liu, Jie Chen
bullets: Addresses the problem of agents storing multimodal records without retaining task-level understanding, causing repeated mistakes.
Uses source-linked multi-view memory for text, images, rendered pages, and cross-record scene images.
Combines source-generated task warm-up, self-training, and task distillation into experiences containing context, conclusions, and supporting links.
Task-aware retrieval supports answering, verification, and evidence-backed long-term reuse.
Outperforms eight baselines across LoCoMo, Mem-Gallery, and LooGLE v2; ablations show benefits from training and memory warm-up.

Figure 2. MMMem framework. (a) Each memory node holds text, image, page, and generated views of its source records. (b) Tasks generated from the source memory are used to train the reader offline and to warm up the memory. (c) For the current question, text and image retrieval followed by reranking selects the evidence. The agent answers with its sources, writes a note, and may generate an image; the resulting experience moves from staged to retained after repeated, source-supported reuse.

papers.abstract: Long-lived Web assistants require effective memory and retrieval mechanisms to access information from past user interactions. While these capabilities can be learned through specialized policies, it remains unclear whether specialists trained independently in different environments can be effectively composed without joint optimization. This paper investigates compositional transfer through policy distillation. Memory-writing and sequential retrieval policies are independently distilled from frontier-model action trajectories into 3B models and combined with a fixed answer generator without downstream training. On a LongMemEval-based benchmark, the distilled composition achieves 73.1% accuracy, compared with 36.2% for a composition of existing RL-trained specialists, and also outperforms the evaluated RL-trained compositions on PersonaMem-v2. Component ablations reveal that improvements in individual policies depend on their composition, highlighting the importance of cross-specialist compatibility. Further task-specific adaptation improves accuracy to 75.2% on LongMemEval through RL and 48.9% on PersonaMem-v2 through supervised distillation. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of independent specialist distillation for modular multi-agent systems. Source code and datasets of teacher-generated memory-editing and retrieval trajectories are released to facilitate reproducibility and further research.

papers.abstract: Traffic forecasting is essential for intelligent transportation systems. However, traditional deep-learning models often rely heavily on high-quality observations. Recent LLM-based approaches incorporate pretrained knowledge to improve forecasting, but they remain sensitive to input perturbations and struggle to preserve long-term patterns. To address this, we propose STMemoLLM, a spatial-temporal memory-augmented LLM for robust traffic forecasting. STMemoLLM introduces memory prototypes to compress inputs into compact summary tokens while extracting reliable dynamics from residual signals, achieving a balance between stability and variability. Specifically, a memory-enhanced tokenizer encodes prototypes and sensor characteristics into attention biases to guide adaptive compression of correlated sensors into semantic summary tokens. A memory-calibrated router further evaluates contextual deviation, compression deficiency, and prototype alignment to identify reliable residual signals, which complement the summaries while suppressing noise. Extensive experiments on eight real-world datasets show that STMemoLLM achieves state-of-the-art performance. Additional experiments examine point masking, additive Gaussian noise, structured missingness, and limited training data, demonstrating strong robustness. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/STMemoLLM-70BF.
authors: Jian Zhou, Binqing Wu, Zongjiang Shang, Wanghui Qiu, Dongliang Cui, Chenxi Jin, Yue Yu, Xinyi Fu, Ling Chen
bullets: Targets LLM-based forecasting sensitivity to input perturbations and difficulty preserving long-term traffic patterns.
Uses memory prototypes to compress correlated sensor inputs into semantic summary tokens while retaining reliable dynamics from residual signals.
A memory-enhanced tokenizer guides compression through prototype- and sensor-informed attention biases.
A memory-calibrated router evaluates deviation, compression deficiency, and prototype alignment to suppress noisy residuals.
Experiments across eight real-world datasets report state-of-the-art performance and robustness to masking, Gaussian noise, structured missingness, and limited training data.

papers.abstract: A transformer language model computes a deep hidden state for every token but uses it only to sample that token. Existing latent-feedback designs, which feed hidden states back across tokens, are mostly built in during pretraining and gain little when added to a pretrained model. We introduce the temporal residual, a second residual stream that every sublayer reads and writes and that is carried from each token to the next. It adds 2,752 parameters to a 4.2B-parameter model and starts exactly at the pretrained network. Retrofitted onto Qwen3.5-4B-Base with 5B tokens of training, it beats a standard model trained on the same data by 7, 13 and 5 points on AIME 2024, AIME 2025 and AMC 2023, writes shorter solutions, and stays ahead at matched training compute. The separate stream matters: prior designs that feed state into the existing stream recover at most 40% of the gain when retrofitted. Validation loss can mislead: the recipe with the lowest loss gains nothing at decoding. Trained with filler tokens in place of reasoning, the model reasons in its hidden state: its GSM8K accuracy with no visible reasoning rises from 21% to 40%, and falls back when the carried state is zeroed.
authors: Ziyang Cai, Xingyu Zhu, Sanjeev Arora
bullets: Addresses the limited effectiveness of adding latent feedback after pretraining.
Adds a separate residual stream that each sublayer reads, writes, and carries across tokens.
Retrofitting Qwen3.5-4B-Base with 5B training tokens improved AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and AMC 2023 performance by 7, 13, and 5 points, respectively, versus a same-data standard model.
The approach supports hidden-state reasoning: GSM8K accuracy without visible reasoning increased from 21% to 40%, but dropped when the carried state was removed.
Separate-stream design and decoding evaluations matter; validation loss alone did not predict gains, and prior retrofits recovered at most 40% of the improvement.

papers.abstract: Effective long-horizon persuasion in recurring goal-oriented settings requires more than factual memory: it must track how a user's trust, negotiation behavior, and strategic receptiveness evolve across interactions. Existing persuasive dialogue systems are largely single-session, static, and unimodal, while cross-session memory systems, though temporally aware, retain only factual content and overlook persuasion-specific dynamics. We propose MERIT (Memory-augmented Experience-Rationale for Iterative Temporal persuasion), which pairs a graph-based memory of four persuasion-specific memory types with a per-persona experience rationale library that records which strategies succeed for each user and why. Together they enable adaptive persuasion through prompt composition alone, with no parameter updates. To support this setting, we introduce PERSIST (PERSona-driven InSurance Interactions over Time), a dataset of 60 curated personas spanning 10+ years of motor insurance renewal interactions, with probabilistic life events that shift negotiation behavior and receptiveness across sessions, verified through strict human-in-the-loop annotation. MERIT surpasses memory and experience-based baselines on every metric across two policy backbones, reaching persuasive-appeal scores of 4.10 and 4.74 (out of 5).
authors: Rohan Kirti, Akash Ghosh, Pratik Amrit, Aryan Vats, Niladri Ghosh, Sriparna Saha
bullets: Targets recurring persuasion settings where trust, negotiation behavior, and receptiveness evolve across sessions.
Uses a graph-based memory with four persuasion-specific memory types plus a per-persona library of successful strategies and rationales.
Introduces PERSIST, a human-verified dataset of 60 personas across 10+ years of motor-insurance renewal interactions and changing life events.
Evaluated with two policy backbones, MERIT outperforms memory and experience-based baselines on every reported metric, achieving persuasive-appeal scores of 4.10 and 4.74 out of 5.

papers.abstract: Conversation history is infrastructure: deployed language models rely on application layers to store and reinject prior turns, and that stored state is writable. We formalize session-level contamination by attack layer, state a coverage theorem, and measure its scope: each deployment-layer verification tier covers exactly its layer and is sound with respect to the others; instruction overrides are not detectable without false positives; and composite vectors evade per-fragment verification. A standardized harness applied to eight mechanism families across 3,249 sessions and three model families makes these claims checkable. First, pattern-based detection pays a measured false-positive price: the classic defenses flag 35 to 50 percent of benign sessions, and the naive refusal floor reaches only 2.4 percent attack-cell adoption while destroying 33 to 100 percent of benign turns, whereas provenance-gated channel separation achieves adoption at or below 1.2 percent with zero false positives and zero utility loss. Second, in the exploratory instruction-override extension, the gates' boundary is a cliff: directives rephrased without shape markers bypass them at control-equivalent rates, 47.7 to 49.5 percent against 0.0 percent for the shaped class, placing that class in the model-internal lane. Third, the deterministic core is storage-layer detection at 126 of 126 per model with zero false positives. External anchors reproduce published attack pressure, with PoisonedRAG falling from 70 to 0 percent under the full stack. For practitioners: authenticate stored history and content provenance with deterministic tiers, scope instruction-layer mitigation to provenance-gated designs whose measured benign cost is zero, and monitor composition at the trajectory level rather than per fragment. All protocols and acceptance criteria are pre-registered; the stack and harness are released.
authors: Fahrell Giovanny, Geby Bayuningtyas, Sahrul Mukharom
bullets: Defines attack layers and proves that each deployment-layer verification tier covers only its own layer; composite vectors can evade per-fragment checks.
Evaluates eight mechanism families across 3,249 sessions and three model families using a preregistered, released harness.

Instruction overrides without recognizable markers bypassed gates at 47.7–49.5% control-equivalent rates, identifying a model-internal detection boundary.
Storage-layer detection was deterministic across 126/126 cases per model with zero false positives; PoisonedRAG pressure fell from 70% to 0% under the full stack.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses integrity of conversation history as external memory for LLMs.
papers.title: Detectable Epistemic Attack Layers: A Coverage Theorem and Standardized Harness for Conversation-History Integrity
papers.tldr: The paper formalizes conversation-history contamination and shows that layer-specific, provenance-gated verification detects storage attacks without false positives, while instruction overrides and composite attacks require broader safeguards.

papers.abstract: Agents built on large language models must maintain continuity across repeated interactions with users. However, long-term conversations scatter facts across turns and sessions, making it difficult to retrieve the right evidence with enough context. Memory for such conversations must therefore preserve facts with their context while keeping evidence selectively accessible. We first study how memory construction and retrieval-unit boundaries affect answerability and evidence access. Reading the entire memory bank reveals gaps that cannot be resolved by retrieval selection alone, showing that some context must be preserved during memory construction. Adjacent-turn grouping improves evidence access at matched unique-turn budgets, while wider windows do not consistently help. This motivates keeping fact-specific context local while organizing cross-session evidence separately. We propose ContextFact, which links context-preserving fact memories with source-grounded entity representations. Within sessions, it gathers the context needed to interpret each fact. Across sessions, it aligns recurring referents and revisits the source dialogue to reconstruct coherent entity representations linked to the supporting facts. At query time, ContextFact retrieves fact and entity views, reranks them independently, and uses entity-linked expansion to surface related facts; complete entity representations then provide organized cross-session evidence. With Qwen3.5-27B as the backbone, ContextFact achieves state-of-the-art performance while using only $21\%$ of the evidence tokens consumed by the strongest evaluated baseline, obtaining $86.49\%$ overall judge accuracy on LoCoMo and $91.00\%$ on LongMemEval-S. Controlled ablations support context-preserving fact boundaries and source-grounded entity reconstruction, while entity readout improves multi-hop accuracy beyond adding more facts.
authors: Jiayu Huang, Yichao Cai, Xinyu Li, Zhen Zhang, Javen Qinfeng Shi
bullets: Long-term conversations scatter facts across turns and sessions, making context-aware evidence retrieval difficult.
Studies show memory construction and retrieval-unit boundaries affect answerability; adjacent-turn grouping improves access, while wider windows do not consistently help.
ContextFact links context-preserving fact memories with source-grounded entity representations across sessions.
At query time, it independently reranks fact and entity views and expands retrieval through entity links.

Using Qwen3.5-27B, it reports 86.49% judge accuracy on LoCoMo and 91.00% on LongMemEval-S while consuming 21% of the evidence tokens used by the strongest baseline; entity readout particularly helps multi-hop questions.
