papers.abstract: Enterprise LLM agents operate in dynamic environments where foundation models evolve rapidly, workflows update frequently, and deployments need to satisfy accuracy and cost requirements. We propose ARISE (Agent Refinement through Iterative Self-Evaluation), a practical memory architecture in which the agent's memory evolves from its own failures without updating model weights, tools, or workflow logic. ARISE uses the model itself or a teacher model to attribute the failures and propose corrections. Then, ARISE keeps the corrections as retrievable micro memory, consolidates them into macro rules, and accepts a rule update only if held-out accuracy rises. Across 14 enterprise-workflow domains from SOP-Bench and $\tau^2$-bench using 5 models, ARISE-Teacher, which uses Claude Opus 4.6 for attribution and consolidation, gains 10.9 pp over the baseline on SOP-Bench and 5.8 pp on $\tau^2$-bench. ARISE-Teacher also outperforms GEPA by 4.5 pp on $\tau^2$-bench and 1.4 pp on SOP-Bench. With the deployment model as its own attributor, ARISE-Self still gains 10.0 pp on SOP-Bench. ARISE-Teacher uses 4.0% fewer model calls and 5.2% fewer output tokens at comparable per-task cost (-1.0%).
authors: Jiangyun Zhang, Zhou Tang, Kristen Surrao, Zhiyu Chen, Albert Guan, Tor Nitayanont, Yupei Zhang, Roopali Singh, Yunkai Xiao, Shreya Pandit, Julia Huang, Shayan Ali Akbar, Erwin Cornejo, Yuan Li, Yi Zhang
bullets: Targets dynamic enterprise environments where models, workflows, and cost requirements change over time.
Uses self- or teacher-model failure attribution to create corrective micro-memories, consolidate them into macro rules, and retain updates only when held-out accuracy improves.
Evaluated across 14 SOP-Bench and τ²-Bench workflow domains with 5 models.
ARISE-Teacher improves baseline accuracy by 10.9 percentage points on SOP-Bench and 5.8 points on τ²-Bench; ARISE-Self gains 10.0 points on SOP-Bench.
ARISE-Teacher uses 4.0% fewer model calls and 5.2% fewer output tokens at comparable per-task cost.

papers.selection_reason: Self-evolving memory architecture for LLM agents, directly relevant to LLM memory mechanisms.
papers.title: ARISE: Practical Self-Evolving Memory for Accurate and Cost-Efficient Enterprise Agents
papers.tldr: ARISE improves enterprise-agent accuracy and efficiency by turning failures into validated, retrievable memory and rules without changing model weights, tools, or workflows.

papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly drive their own learning. Self-improvement methods delegate various components of model optimization to the models themselves. As models become more capable, this motivates a basic question: do these increasingly capable models still need us to specify how they should self-improve? In this paper we study an autonomous paradigm in which, given basic primitives, resources, and a general goal for self-improvement, agents construct their own self-learning algorithm for context-based optimization. Using the setting of gameplay as a testbed, a frozen LLM agent is given a compute budget and tools for collecting experience and updating text documents, and allowed to freely experiment without an externally imposed loop or access to real-world data. We find that sufficiently capable models do self-improve under these conditions, demonstrating strategies that align with classic cognitive frameworks for self-regulated learning and constructs from machine learning literature on self-generated curricula. Furthermore, we study the extent to which the learned text artifacts transfer to external benchmarks, observing improvement across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation.
authors: Shobhita Sundaram, Cansu Sancaktar, Phillip Isola
bullets: Studies whether agents need explicit instructions for how to self-improve.
Agents receive basic tools, resources, a goal, and a compute budget, but no prescribed learning loop or real-world data.
In gameplay, agents construct their own context-based self-learning algorithms and update text artifacts from collected experience.
Their strategies resemble self-regulated learning and self-generated curricula from prior cognitive and machine-learning research.
Learned artifacts improve performance across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Do capable models specify their own self-improvement? We give a frozen LLM (here, Claude Opus-5) the general goal of improving itself at gameplay, and place it in a constrained workspace. We do not provide real games to practice on, or prescribe a particular self-improvement loop. We instead provide a toolset {Read, Write, Bash, Gameplay}, and allow the teacher to generate its own games and organize its own learning procedure. At the start (t = 0) the teacher uses its tools to build a test game, spawn a player session to play that game, analyze the result, and then update the player context (e.g., skill files). Later (t = 60), the teacher decides to write an adversarial game and observe the player attempt it with and without the optimized context. The teacher then uses the observed failure mode to make another context update.

Figure 7: Self-improving agents use learnability-seeking task selection. (left) Across models, most generated games are easy. (right) Newer model generations spend the most effort (# replays) on games with low to medium win rates. Observed win rates are computed over the first k plays for each game (k ∈ [2, 6]). This can lead to an inverted-U resembling learnability objectives in asymmetric self-play and UED.

Figure 6: Self-improving models display human-recognizable learning strategies. Alignment scores to 13 subprocesses of Zimmerman’s self-regulated learning cycle, annotated by an LLM judge and averaged over 3 teacher sessions per model. Models that self-improve score higher across most subprocesses. Average over seeds; individual seeds in Appendix D.2.

Figure 8: Excerpts from a Claude Opus-5 teacher session with high alignment to self-regulated learning subprocesses. In the first example (task-strategies) the teacher writes a random level generator and BFS solver to filter generated games for difficulty and employs A/B testing to identify where its optimized text artifacts are useful. In the second (learning goal orientation) the teacher designs an adversarial game to test its advice and runs validation tests across earlier games to identify regressions.

Figure 11: Generalization with respect to progressively richer information, via context and toolsets. (Left) We run teacher sessions using Python Gameplay with increasingly detailed descriptions of PuzzleScript-Narrow games. Performance initially improves both on the same games, and ARC-AGI-3 transfer, however at higher levels of detail transfer plateaus. (Right) We ablate the teacher’s toolset and Gameplay constraints; performance initially improves on both PuzzleScript-t20 and PuzzleScript-t30 with richer toolsets, however declines on PuzzleScript-t30 after adding t20-specific token and turn budgets. Error bars show ±1 SD over three independent teacher seeds.

Figure 5: Algorithmically measured behaviors. (Left: Game play and design) Newer models more often use A/B Testing (generated games played with and without teacher-written artifacts) and produce fewer games that have low complexity and low difficulty (optimal solution length < 5 and 100% teacher-observed win rate). (Right: Updates) For GPT and GLM, newer generations exhibit more updates that improve the observed win rate on at least one self-generated game. For Opus and GLM, newer models prefer smaller context updates.

Figure 9: Improvements from self-organized learning transfer across benchmarks. Player performance is evaluated at intermediate context updates along the self-learning trajectory on PuzzleScript-t20, PuzzleScript-t30, ARCAGI-L1 and MazeBench. The context optimized under our canonical setting, Gameplay (PS-t20), improves over the unoptimized baseline (dashed line) on PuzzleScript games with both 20- and 30-turn horizons. These gains transfer to different game engines and representations in ARC-AGI-L1 and MazeBench. We also compare progressively richer teacher toolsets, starting from Read/Write, adding Bash, and then PuzzleScript-Gameplay tools. Error bars show ±1 SD over three independent teacher seeds.

Figure 4: Recent models self-improve. Results on PuzzleScript-t20 for two models in each family. Newer generations self-improve over the baseline while older generations fail to do so. Error bars are ±1 SD over 3 seeds.

papers.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence is transforming the role of natural language in computational systems. In classical Natural Language Processing (NLP), language was treated as an object of computation: something to analyse, classify, translate, or generate. Large Language Models (LLMs) challenge this perspective, enabling natural language to function increasingly as an executable cognitive medium through which humans structure reasoning, orchestrate problem solving, and regulate hybrid human/AI workflows. This paper introduces Natural Language Programming (NLPg) as a theoretical and epistemological extension of traditional NLP. Rather than focusing on language understanding alone, NLPg conceptualises prompts as dynamic cognitive artefacts that externalise goals, constraints, assumptions, validation criteria, and intermediate reasoning states. Prompting is thus not merely a technical interaction technique, but a form of dialogic cognitive programming operating within distributed human/AI memory architectures. Building on theories of distributed cognition, extended mind, metacognition, and dialogic learning, the paper proposes the notion of Dialogic Working Memory, describing how prompts and conversational states function as temporary external memory structures supporting reasoning continuity and reflective regulation. We further map existing memory architectures (BTMA, SKGE, RMR) onto this framework, illustrating how episodic, semantic, and metacognitive layers support long-horizon conversational coherence. Finally, implications for computational linguistics and AI/mediated knowledge systems are discussed, suggesting a post symbolic and post interface paradigm in which natural language operates simultaneously as communication medium, executable specification, cognitive scaffold, and distributed memory architecture.
bullets: Recasts traditional NLP: language is not only analyzed or generated but also used to structure reasoning and orchestrate workflows.
Defines Natural Language Programming (NLPg) as a theoretical extension centered on prompts as dynamic cognitive artefacts.
Introduces Dialogic Working Memory, where prompts and conversational states temporarily externalize goals, constraints, assumptions, validation criteria, and reasoning states.
Relates memory architectures such as BTMA, SKGE, and RMR to episodic, semantic, and metacognitive support for long-horizon dialogue.
Argues for a post-symbolic, post-interface view of AI systems in which natural language combines communication, specification, cognitive scaffolding, and distributed memory.

papers.abstract: Vulnerability exploitation tests whether language model agents can develop working exploits from known software flaws. Sequential test-time scaling can improve exploitation performance, but larger budgets do not ensure sustained exploration: agents often stop with budget remaining. Yet what happens when execution continues beyond stopping remains underexplored. We investigate this gap on ExploitBench using DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 and MiMo-V2.6-Pro. We find additional verified gains after the first stop response, but gains diminish over longer execution. We identify two patterns associated with less productive continuation: an increasing proportion of stop responses within the same context and earlier stopping associated with summaries retaining impossibility judgments about unachieved capabilities. To test whether context management can elicit further capability, we propose SCoRe, which compacts context at stop bursts and marks these judgments as unproven. SCoRe improves verified capability over summary-based continuation and other evaluated context-management baselines. With SCoRe, MiMo reaches a capability coverage score of 67.0% at 2,000 turns, exceeding both 32.4% under the original stopping policy and the 58.6% computed for GPT-5.5 from ExploitBench's 300-turn reference results on the same tasks. These findings show that stopping need not mark an agent's exploitation limit, and that continued execution with context management can elicit substantial further capability.
authors: Deokhyung Kang, Minjae Gwon, Sangdon Park
bullets: ExploitBench agents frequently stop with execution budget remaining, leaving their ultimate exploitation capability unclear.
Continuing after the first stop yields additional verified gains, but progress diminishes over longer runs.
Less productive continuation is linked to repeated stop responses and summaries that preserve unproven impossibility judgments.
SCoRe compacts context during stop bursts and marks such judgments as unproven, improving verified capability over evaluated continuation baselines.
With SCoRe, MiMo reaches 67.0% capability coverage at 2,000 turns, versus 32.4% under the original stopping policy and 58.6% for GPT-5.5’s 300-turn reference results.

papers.abstract: People increasingly learn what they need for decisions about health, money, law and safety from AI assistants, and what an assistant leaves out the user never sees. An answer with a warning removed can be true in every sentence, so fact-checks pass it, and an assistant with memory applies a preference stored once to later questions the user never had in mind. We introduce \bench{}, an Inspect benchmark of 100 everyday decisions across 25 domains in which only the assistant's memory of the user varies: the user states a belief, the model infers it from a remark, or a web page the user asked to summarise plants it. Testing five models, we find three effects. First, after summarising a page with one line addressed to AI assistants, Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite and DeepSeek V4 Pro save ``prefers very short answers and does not want warnings'' as the user's preference in every episode, and 93\% and 84\% of their later answers miss a critical item, almost always silently; under a stated brevity preference, 78--96\% of omissions are silent. Second, the same two models then pick an option for the user on 80\% and 95\% of value-dependent choices, against none with neutral memory. Third, a one-line instruction leaves 2--8\% of answers with a silent gap but most missing content still missing, while listing the must-know points before applying the user profile restores more of the content in four of five models. We release the scenarios, harness and logs.
bullets: Evaluates 100 everyday decisions across 25 domains while varying only how the assistant’s memory is created: stated, inferred, or planted in a summarized webpage.
In two tested models, a planted preference for very short answers and no warnings led to critical omissions in 93% and 84% of later answers, usually without disclosure.
With neutral memory, neither model made value-dependent choices; with the preference, they chose for users in 80% and 95% of such cases.
A one-line instruction reduced but did not eliminate silent gaps; listing must-know points before applying the profile restored more content in four of five models.
The scenarios, evaluation harness, and logs are released.

papers.selection_reason: Studies how stored user preferences in assistant memory silently remove decision-critical information, directly relevant to persistent/agent memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Remembered as Brief: Stored Preferences SilentlyRemove Decision-Critical Information
papers.tldr: An Inspect benchmark shows that AI assistants can silently omit decision-critical information and make value-dependent choices when stored user preferences conflict with safety-relevant content.

papers.abstract: Agent skills use past experience and current observations to guide decisions and actions on related tasks. This experience is retained in skill state, whose reuse can amortize inference-time reasoning and environment interaction. When environment changes, parts of this state can become outdated while others remain useful. Across four task settings and two models, we compare skill reuse before and after environment changes. Previously beneficial skills can reduce task performance by over 10 percentage points or increase execution cost by nearly 40% relative to no skill. Task success can also remain unchanged while execution savings decline. These effects depend on which environment-specific details become outdated and the agent's ability to compensate using current observations. We introduce selective maintenance, which replays checks from successful executions without additional model calls. It verifies whether observed differences conflict with skill state, repairs affected content, and validates updates, rebuilding when local repair is insufficient. No description of the change is supplied. Relative to reusing stale state, maintenance improves task accuracy by up to 67pp and reduces execution steps by up to 37%. These results suggest that preserving a skill's inference time value as environments evolve requires selectively maintaining its state.
authors: \"Omer Faruk Akg\"ul, Shuli Jiang, Yuting Zhang, Yi Zhang, Xiaohan Fei, Wei Xia, Stefano Soatto
bullets: Previously useful skills may lower task performance by over 10 percentage points or raise execution cost by nearly 40% after changes.
The impact depends on which environment details become outdated and whether current observations let the agent compensate.
Selective maintenance replays checks from successful executions to detect conflicts, repair affected state, validate updates, or rebuild when needed.
Across four task settings and two models, maintenance improves accuracy by up to 67 percentage points and reduces execution steps by up to 37% versus stale-state reuse.
Scope: results cover the evaluated task settings, models, and environment changes; no change description is provided to the agent.

papers.selection_reason: Selective maintenance of agent skill state in evolving environments; relevant to test-time/continual adaptation and agent memory.
papers.title: When Agent Skills Go Stale: Runtime Behavior and Selective Maintenance in Evolving Environments
papers.tldr: Stale agent skills can harm accuracy and efficiency after environment changes, while selective maintenance restores much of their value without extra model calls.

papers.abstract: Interpretability for AI agents should not be confined to understanding the model's internal weights. It must also cover the agent's reasoning and decision-making process over multi-source context. We present LMLineage, an out-of-band system that attributes every output sentence of an agent session to its supporting input spans with calibrated confidences, without requiring white-box access to the model or any additional inference passes. On top of the lineage metadata, we build concept-drift micro compaction: instead of waiting for the context-length limit and summarizing everything, the system detects when previously used input documents have stopped being referenced ("drifted") and surgically compacts only those, preserving user instructions verbatim. We evaluate on a multi-tier corpus: 71 gold annotated sentences from 10 Chinese web-QA cases, plus 90 turns of independently collected multi-turn sessions across three generator models (gpt-4o-mini, qwen3.8-27b, deepseek-v4-flash). Results show that (i) window-level embedding similarity is far better aligned with LLM paraphrasing than whole document or lexical matching; (ii) the greedy-window fast path is both faster and more accurate on average than exhaustive line-matching (a multiple-comparisons bias in the latter inflates web recall at the cost of overall accuracy); (iii) per-turn attribution completes in 1s on a single GPU, remaining stable as context accumulates to 40 turns; and (iv) concept-drift detection is conservative (0% false compaction) with recall bounded by attribution accuracy. We further describe the concept-drift micro compaction design and an interactive incident-tracing/memory-cleaning case study. A companion patent application covers the lineage construction method.
authors: Wei Hou, Jingxin Geng, Xin Chen, Zheqing Jiang
bullets: Uses calibrated lineage metadata to attribute output sentences to input spans across multi-source, multi-turn contexts.
Detects concept drift and compacts only no-longer-referenced documents while preserving user instructions verbatim.
Window-level embedding similarity better captures paraphrased support than whole-document or lexical matching.
A greedy-window method is faster and more accurate on average than exhaustive line matching; attribution remains stable through 40 turns and completes in about 1 second per turn on one GPU.
Drift compaction is conservative, reporting 0% false compaction, with recall limited by attribution accuracy.

Right ribs: inflow this turn (user prompt above, tool calls/results/web below). Expanding a beat reveals per-sentence cards with (type, value, confidence) triplets. papers.selection_reason: Out-of-band attribution and concept-drift compaction for LLM agent context and memory governance; relevant to LLM memory and long-context management.
papers.title: LMLineage: Content Lineage and Context Governance for LLM Agents
papers.tldr: LMLineage traces each agent output sentence to supporting context without model internals or extra inference, then safely compacts context that has drifted out of use.

papers.abstract: Small language model agents have limited space to read the memory needed for multi-hop questions. Relevant facts are often scattered across records whose surrounding text consumes much of that space. We propose LMMR, a learned multigranular memory retrieval method that selects both the next source and how much of it to read. LMMR links paragraphs and sentence fragments to their original sources and pairs views that supply the same missing support during training. Relevant distractors and repeated information provide contrasting examples. At inference, the reranker scores what each candidate adds to an anchor passage, and a selector chooses the evidence within a token budget. On 22,398 official validation questions from HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, and MuSiQue, a frozen 2B answer model reaches 61.47, 43.26, and 30.58 F1 under a 400-token budget. The gains over query expansion are 3.06, 2.14, and 4.55 points, while memory input decreases by 23.1-26.9%. LMMR also uses 23.5-27.7% fewer input tokens than a coarse retriever trained on the same questions. Against that retriever followed by LLMLingua-2 at comparable input lengths, F1 gains reach 3.99 points and are significant on HotpotQA and 2WikiMultihopQA after Holm correction. All eight small answer models evaluated on HotpotQA improve over query expansion and MMR in both F1 and exact match.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent delegation lets LLM systems distribute evidence collection across workers with separate contexts. This creates a consistency challenge: facts retrieved by workers may be missing from the evidence available to the lead for a joint conclusion. We introduce a benchmark and evidence-flow profiler for studying multi-agent memory inconsistency through controlled factual conflicts in Harvey LAB document-review tasks. Pooled across three models with comparable generation spending, requiring delegation increases retrieval of both conflicting claims from 50.2% to 68.7% relative to single-agent execution, yet conflict detection falls from 16.2% to 13.2%. Within this setting, workers report both claims for only 35.2% of retrieved pairs, and pooled matched comparisons show higher detection than single-agent execution when one worker reads both claims but lower detection when the claims are split across workers. Worker-to-lead handoffs are a central target for improving conflict detection in multi-agent LLMs.
authors: Hejia Zhang, Zhongming Yu, Yimin Ding, Wei-Ting Chen, Hengjia Yu, Wentao Ni, Yijun Liu, Cong Xu, Xin Chen, Matrix Yao, Fan Zhao, Jishen Zhao

Workers reported both claims in only 35.2% of retrieved conflict pairs; detection was better when one worker saw both claims than when claims were split across workers.

papers.abstract: Agentic memory research has accumulated extraction, supersession, reflection, and graph synthesis on top of retrieval-augmented generation. However, we found that almost none of those primitives earn their cost in our tested memory benchmarks: we show this with BRIDGE, a deliberately minimal RAG memory with chained observation notes, hybrid BM25 with cosine retrieval, and chronological rendering, which reaches parity within bootstrap CI with the prior SOTA on LongMemEval-S and BEAM, and beats the best memory baseline on EverMemBench by 5.7-6.3 points at matched reader. It runs at ~5-7K reader-prompt tokens per query, using a single LLM call for each ingestion or query. We argue that this parity is itself the result: standard benchmarks score what memory retrieves, not what memory enables when the agent acts. To test the latter, we introduce five adversarial probes (Rule Application +-, Pattern Induction Style / Procedural, Dynamic Multiturn) judged at generation time by a cross vendor verification chain, where each query can only be solved by applying a remembered rule or pattern it never mentions. Across 5 probes x 20 scenarios, no architecture wins universally: atomic fact extractors (LangMem) win rule application, while BRIDGE's block-summary memory wins pattern induction. This result holds across four domains, three graders, and three reader families. Each design fails where the other wins, for reasons a recall benchmark cannot see: atomic-fact extractors discard the form a demonstrated pattern takes, while block-summary memory retrieves the rule but the reader does not act on it, a gap that presenting the rule more prominently largely closes. What separates memory designs is not what they retrieve but what they enable an agent to do, and that is what agentic memory should be evaluated on.
authors: Jingyu Liu, Zongze Li, Zach Xu, Zhanhui Zhou, Tahseen Rabbani, Dawn Song, Ce Zhang
bullets: BRIDGE uses chained observation notes, hybrid BM25–cosine retrieval, and chronological rendering with one LLM call per ingestion or query.
It matches prior state of the art on LongMemEval-S and BEAM, and outperforms the best matched-reader baseline on EverMemBench by 5.7–6.3 points.
BRIDGE operates at roughly 5–7K reader-prompt tokens per query, suggesting many advanced memory primitives may not justify their cost on standard benchmarks.
Five adversarial probes show no architecture wins universally: atomic-fact extraction favors rule application, while block summaries favor pattern induction.
Retrieval benchmarks miss failures in how agents use memories: fact extractors lose demonstrated patterns, while block summaries may retrieve rules without prompting action.

papers.abstract: Language agents rely on long-term memory to personalize responses across extended interactions, yet stored facts quietly go stale as the world changes, and an agent often learns that using memory hurt only through delayed feedback after acting on an outdated record. Before the memory store is updated, how far should that negative feedback propagate: should it suppress memory use only on future queries for that same fact (a local policy), or also across other stored facts (a global policy)? Existing memory systems implicitly fix one of these two sharing scopes at design time. We formulate this online scope choice under hidden validity and delayed feedback as memory conflict governance, and prove that neither fixed policy is sufficient on its own. We then propose RegimeCouncil, a lightweight paired-evidence router that retains both scopes as advisors and arbitrates between them online without retraining the LLM. Using revealed comparisons between answering with memory and answering without memory (the no-memory anchor), a Local Advisor tracks the latest outcome on the queried fact alone, while a Global Advisor pools recent outcomes across all stored facts. A Meta Governor follows the Local Advisor by default to avoid cross-fact interference and switches to the Global Advisor only when global pooling accumulates a strictly positive recent utility margin, guaranteeing finite-time switching under delayed feedback. Across LongMemEval update streams and real-world historical drift on TempLAMA and TAQA with Qwen3-30B-A3B and GPT-4o, RegimeCouncil outperforms the better fixed-scope policy by 5.2-7.3 points on primary disagreement episodes and across all 30 held-out settings, while ablations show that removing any of its three modules reduces accuracy by 2-7 points.
authors: Qingcan Kang, Mingyang Liu, Shixiong Kai, Tao Zhong, Mingxuan Yuan
bullets: Addresses stale long-term memories and delayed feedback when memory validity is hidden.
Maintains Local and Global Advisors, using comparisons with a no-memory answer as evidence.
A Meta Governor defaults to local updates and switches to global sharing only after positive pooled utility accumulates.
Provides a finite-time switching guarantee under delayed feedback.
Outperforms the better fixed-scope policy by 5.2–7.3 points across reported disagreement episodes and held-out settings; removing modules lowers accuracy by 2–7 points.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses memory conflict governance in LLM agents with online scope selection, fitting continual learning and LLM memory.
papers.title: RegimeCouncil: Paired-Evidence Routing For Memory Conflict Governance In LLM Agents
papers.tldr: RegimeCouncil adaptively chooses whether delayed memory-feedback should remain fact-local or generalize across facts, improving conflict handling over either fixed policy.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents accumulate experience in memory, and how that memory evolves during interaction is as important as what it stores. Recent methods update memory online, yet both the operators that transform memory and the rules that select them remain fixed by design. We propose EvoDisco, which formulates agent memory evolution as evolutionary strategy discovery: the agent must discover which operator to apply, when to apply it, and how to instantiate it, rather than rewriting memory under a static operator schedule. A learnable policy conditions on the current memory state and recent task history, then selects and instantiates one of four semantic operators---Abstract, Refine, Bridge, and Reframe---which respectively compress related memories, decompose overloaded entries, connect weakly linked experiences, and reorganize retrieved reasoning chains. The policy is updated with a bi-level fitness. An inner signal scores each transformation using a retrieval-quality improvement regularized by memory complexity. An outer signal scores strategic efficacy over a window of past decisions, combining historical operator-utility regret, utility-prediction error, and selection diversity. Under a one-pass online plus frozen-transfer protocol on ALFWorld, WebShop, and LifelongAgentBench (OS and DB), EvoDisco improves over strong memory baselines including MemP and MemRL. The largest gains are on ALFWorld ($+8.8$ online / $+12.9$ frozen-transfer points over MemP; $+16.4$ / $+17.9$ over MemRL). Ablations attribute these gains to both fitness levels and the operator library.
authors: Mingyang Liu, Qingcan Kang, Shixiong Kai, Kaichao Liang, Xiaojin Fu, Tao Zhong, Linqi Song
bullets: Addresses the limitation of fixed memory-update operators and schedules in evolving LLM-agent memory.
Uses a policy conditioned on memory state and recent task history to select and instantiate Abstract, Refine, Bridge, or Reframe operators.
Trains the policy with bi-level fitness: transformation-level retrieval gains regularized by memory complexity, and strategy-level historical efficacy, prediction accuracy, and diversity.
Evaluated under one-pass online plus frozen-transfer settings on ALFWorld, WebShop, and LifelongAgentBench (OS and DB).
Reports improvements over MemP and MemRL, with the largest ALFWorld gains; ablations support the importance of both fitness levels and the operator library.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of EvoDisco. A frozen language model interacts with a one-pass task stream, retrieves a subgraph, and writes new memories after each episode. Immediate utility scores each edit by the change in retrieval quality regularized by graph complexity. Every N events, strategic efficacy combines operator-utility regret, utility-prediction error, and selection diversity, and updates the policy. Evolution runs only before the cutoff; afterward the agent continues to write memories. Held-out evaluation freezes the accumulated memory.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes evolutionary strategy discovery for agent memory evolution, directly relevant to continual/online learning and LLM memory.
papers.title: EvoDisco: Strategy Discovery for Evolving Agent Memory
papers.tldr: EvoDisco enables agents to learn which memory-evolution strategy to apply, when, and how, improving online and frozen-transfer performance across several benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Standard neural architectures such as the Transformer were chosen because they train well with gradient descent and run fast on GPUs. In weight-space programming, a large language model (LLM) writes target weights by hand without gradient-based training, so those reasons no longer apply. Should we keep the Transformer? Given minimal guidance, ten labeled examples, and a sandbox, mainly on multiple-choice questions, we task three frontier LLMs with either generating the weights of a fixed architecture or designing the architecture themselves. When free to design, all three compile plain-text facts into a sparse table queried by a fixed procedure, reaching up to 54.4% test accuracy. An LLM-designed model achieves higher test accuracy than the most accurate released Transformer that the same LLM wrote while using about 1,800x fewer parameters. Without gradients, they choose a table, in which the LLM can state what each weight means and can find and rewrite a wrong one. Each wrong answer points to one row, and removing a row changes about one other answer. From this, we propose an associative-memory-based model up to 17x faster on GPUs than a same-sized Transformer. We also test pretrained weights, other benchmarks, and tasks where models generate answers. Pretrained LLMs remain more accurate; the claim concerns which structure to build when writing weights.
bullets: Three frontier LLMs were given minimal guidance, ten labeled examples, and a sandbox to generate weights or design architectures.
On mainly multiple-choice tasks, LLM-designed sparse tables reached up to 54.4% test accuracy.
One designed model outperformed the best released Transformer written by the same LLM while using about 1,800× fewer parameters.
The table structure makes facts interpretable and locally editable: each row corresponds to an answer and errors identify rows to revise.
The proposed associative-memory model was up to 17× faster on GPUs than a same-sized Transformer; pretrained LLMs remained more accurate.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes an associative memory-based model for LLMs, challenging the Transformer architecture.
papers.title: Weight-Space Programming Doesn't Need Transformers
papers.tldr: When LLMs write model weights without gradient training, they favor sparse associative tables over Transformers, achieving competitive accuracy with far fewer parameters and potentially faster inference.

papers.abstract: Personal assistants accumulate months of conversations, but today's long-term memory stacks put derivation or selection between a question and its evidence. In a system-level comparison on LongMemEval, two commercial assistants scored well below the same model reading the history offline [1], consistent with, but not isolating, content loss between write and read. We propose KV-LTM: a memory tier storing each session's raw text plus its KV cache under a fixed reader model, answering by restoring cached sessions and appending the question. KV-LTM is complementary to, not a replacement for, retrieval and indexing. Text is the memory of record; the cache is a recompute-free prefill accelerator, degrading gracefully to text. We specify the design: storage record, budget-derived retention, append-only read path, and bounded aggregation. We size it analytically: across pinned BF16 full-attention (GQA) and latent-cached MLA configurations, per-token state spans approximately 31K-328K bytes (the pinned KDA+MLA hybrid differs: approximately 8.1K bytes/token plus a fixed per-session recurrent term), giving approximately 0.34-3.6 TB per user-year at a declared 30K-token/day scenario, against approximately 49 MB of raw text; per-query cost is modelled as regime-conditional transfer, attention, decode, aggregation, and compute. We define an evaluation protocol needing no persistent-cache implementation for logical QA evaluation: per-session prefill emulates valid cache reuse under the same model/input-state contract and ideal arithmetic, with named arms, controlled baselines, and a preregistered reader-model gate; a separate minimal real-cache replay tests numerical equivalence and measures the cost axis, with outcomes not assumed. KV-LTM trades storage for avoided re-prefill compute and write-time fidelity, within a declared retention budget.
bullets: Addresses information loss and extra derivation between stored conversations and assistant queries.
Restores cached sessions and appends the question, while retaining raw text as the authoritative fallback.
Defines budget-based retention, append-only reads, bounded aggregation, and a cost model for storage and querying.
Estimates substantially higher cache storage than text, with costs varying by model architecture and retention scenario.
Introduces logical QA evaluation via session prefill plus a separate real-cache replay test for numerical equivalence and runtime cost.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Published system-level comparisons under two different benchmarks and source evaluation protocols: (a) LongMemEval’s 97-question subset with 3–6-session histories [1, Fig. 4a]; (b) LoCoMo J scores from Mem0’s vendor-authored evaluation [2]. Full-history reading scores highest among the selected systems shown in each panel, not across all evidence. Zep’s separate vendor-reported LongMemEval-S comparison favours its retrieval system over a full-context baseline averaging about 115K tokens and is not plotted here (§3.2, §8.1). These comparisons do not isolate a memory mechanism, and scores depend on evaluation labels and judges (§9.1). L1–L4 are our descriptive memory modes; KV-LTM has no measured accuracy bar (§8). Costs are modelled separately (§7).

Figure 2: KV-LTM write flow (once per session): canonical per-session prefill creates the stored state at session end; session text, metadata with integrity digests, and native reader state are retained under the §4.8 storage and latency policy, which may evict or invalidate state — the text is always kept. Boxes denote logical steps or stored objects, not software components.

The plotted per-token spread is ∼40× (the hybrid’s bMLA part at the low end); among the non-hybrid configs the spread is ≈10.5× (31,104 → 327,680).

Valid state is read from a request-local working copy; when policy allows, invalid or evicted state is rebuilt from the verified text (§4.3), otherwise the session is counted as not cached and delegated to the §4.8 text fallback, outside the depicted cache-read path. papers.selection_reason: Proposes persistent per-session KV caches as long-term memory for LLM assistants, directly addressing LLM memory and KV-cache efficiency.
papers.title: KV-LTM: Persistent Per-Session KV Caches as Long-Term Memory for Personal Assistants
papers.tldr: KV-LTM proposes storing each conversation session’s raw text and model KV cache to preserve long-term memory while accelerating future question answering without recomputation.

papers.abstract: Memory-augmented recommenders built on large language models (LLMs) maintain a natural-language profile of each user. These profiles are updated by a user profile update path that revises the profile as new interactions arrive and are consumed by downstream task paths like ranking. Because these user profiles are stored as text in the user memory, every ranking LLM call that consumes them must splice them in the prompt and calculate the KV cache of them during the prefill phase. Given these ranking LLM calls are prefill heavy (long prompt but short decoded output) and repeatedly called, these repeated prefill of user profile text dominates the serving. Prefix caching cannot remove it, because these user profiles are preceded by different text in different calls. We present KVUse, which stores the user profiles as reusable key-value (KV) caches instead of text. KVUse trains lightweight LoRA writers by self-distillation, so that the user profile update call produces the reusable KV of the user profile while decoding it, and the LLM can read these reusable KV at new positions and behind new context without recomputation. KVUse also has a customized KV scheduler that uploads the stored reusable KV of the next batch while the current batch is computed, hiding the KV transfer from host memory behind GPU computation. On four InstructRec datasets with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, KVUse shows no statistically significant difference in ranking quality from full prefill over continuous memory update rounds. Under saturated load, KVUse raises the throughput of the downstream scoring path by 4.0x-4.5x and of the profile update path by 1.4x-1.9x.
authors: Xin Guo, Qiang Zhang, Xiang Zhou, Arushi Rai, Siyu Lin, Yifan Wu, Xiang Shen, Lei Huang, Qunshu Zhang, Xiangjun Fan, Lizhu Zhang
bullets: Repeated profile-text prefills dominate ranking inference because profiles appear after varying prompt prefixes, preventing effective prefix caching.
Lightweight LoRA writers, trained by self-distillation, generate reusable profile KV caches during profile updates.
A KV scheduler overlaps host-to-GPU cache transfers with computation for the next batch.
On four InstructRec datasets with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, ranking quality shows no statistically significant difference from full prefill across memory updates.
Under saturated load, throughput improves 4.0–4.5× for scoring and 1.4–1.9× for profile updates.

papers.selection_reason: Reusable KV caches as persistent user memory for LLM recommenders; fits KV cache efficiency and LLM memory.
papers.title: KVUse: Reusable-KV User Memory for Efficient LLM Recommenders
papers.tldr: KVUse accelerates LLM recommendation serving by storing user profiles as reusable KV caches instead of repeatedly prefilling their text.

papers.abstract: Hoel (2021) proposed that dreams distort replayed experience so that the brain does not overfit to recent events. We test this hypothesis on an LLM agent (Claude Opus 5.5) that stores what it learns in a text memory and rewrites that memory each night from the day's conversation transcript. The agent goes through ten simulated days of conversation built from LongMemEval. We corrupt 5, 10, 20 or 40 percent of the transcript's turns before each nightly rewrite in one of two ways. Detail corruption changes one or two details in a turn to plausible wrong ones, or replaces the turn with one by the same speaker from an earlier day. Random-text corruption replaces half of the selected turns with a passage of Moby-Dick and inserts Moby-Dick words into the other half. A size limit on the memory, rising from 19,500 to 117,000 tokens over ten nights, set from human free-recall data, forces it to forget. We learned that corruption did not help the agent apply what it learned in earlier conversations to new tasks in any of 30 runs (ten conditions, three different conversation histories). Replacing details in 40 percent of turns lowered recall from 76 to 60 percent. Random text had no consistent effect on recall, with a paired difference of 0 $\pm$ 2 points at 40 percent, because the model recognized it as corrupted and left it out of memory. Replaced details were stored as fact even when another turn held the correct value, and the agent answered 40 percent of those questions correctly, compared with 75 percent without corruption. These results suggest that a pretrained model can separate corrupted text from real events, so a fair test needs a learner that cannot make this separation as easily, such as a model fine-tuned on the corrupted days or an agent whose days take place in an invented world.
bullets: Tests Hoel’s overfitted-brain hypothesis: dream-like distortion may prevent overfitting to recent experiences.
An LLM agent rewrote text memory nightly after simulated conversations, with controlled detail or random-text corruption and memory limits.
Across 30 runs, corruption did not improve transfer of earlier learning to new tasks.
Replacing details in 40% of turns reduced recall from 76% to 60%; the agent answered corrupted-detail questions correctly 40% of the time versus 75% without corruption.
Random text had little consistent effect because the model recognized and excluded it as corrupted; future tests may need a learner less able to detect corruption.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Method. Each simulated day adds about 130,000 tokens of conversation. The ticks under the boxes show which steps each condition runs. With no rewrite, memory holds the most recent turns that fit under the limit.

papers.selection_reason: Directly studies persistent text memory, nightly rewriting, and forgetting in an LLM agent, fitting LLM memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Can an LLM dream? Testing the overfitted brain hypothesis on an agent with text memory
papers.tldr: Corrupting an LLM agent’s nightly memory replay did not improve learning and often caused it to store false details as facts.

papers.abstract: Agents are increasingly built to learn from experience: they keep conversation histories, memory files, retrieved notes and skills, and reuse what worked before. We show that this experience turns against them when their tools change silently. We test a range of models with tools defined as in the Model Context Protocol (MCP). After a silent change, experienced agents fail on most tasks, while agents new to the task mostly succeed. We call this failure Experience Rot. Experienced agents copy their earlier call instead of checking the current interface, even when the tool definition shows the change. Then they report success. When the documentation is incomplete, experience is what makes agents succeed. After a change, the same experience leaves them worse off than no experience at all. The failure appears in every form of memory we test and grows with the amount of experience. Simple remedies fall short: announcing the update barely helps, and pointing the agent to the documentation fails whenever the documentation does not spell out the answer.
bullets: Introduces “Experience Rot,” where prior memories, histories, notes, and skills become liabilities after tool changes.
Tests agents using tools defined under the Model Context Protocol (MCP).
After silent changes, experienced agents fail on most tasks while task-new agents mostly succeed.
The failure occurs across all tested memory types and worsens with more experience; agents often incorrectly report success.
Simple fixes—announcing updates or referring agents to documentation—are insufficient, especially when documentation is incomplete.

papers.selection_reason: Shows experience can hurt agents when tools change; relevant to continual learning and agent memory.
papers.title: Experience Rot: Experienced Agents Fail Where Novices Succeed
papers.tldr: Agents with accumulated experience can fail more than novices when tools change silently, because they repeat past calls instead of checking the current interface.

papers.abstract: Memory systems allow AI agents to persist information across interactions, making them more personalized and more capable on long-horizon tasks. This persistence introduces new risks: stored information can be disclosed in inappropriate contexts, resist correction or deletion, be retained beyond what users desire, or be poisoned to influence later agent behaviour. Yet memory systems are typically evaluated on task performance and efficiency alone. We argue that a memory system should instead be understood as the custodian of its user's persistent information, with responsibilities that extend beyond helping an agent complete its tasks, and that it should be evaluated holistically against all such responsibilities. We present Holistic Evaluation of Agent Memory Systems (HEAMS), an open-source framework for evaluating agent memory systems in this way. First, we state the responsibilities of agent memory systems as explicit behavioural desiderata spanning performance, efficiency, security, privacy, and user sovereignty. Second, we assemble a benchmark suite that covers these desiderata and acknowledge the gaps that remain. Third, we develop MilaMem, a prototype memory system, and a governance layer that can wrap any memory system, enabling controlled study of memory system design choices. Fourth, we compare memory systems across the full HEAMS benchmark suite. We find that no memory system leads every performance benchmark, and strong performance scores may coexist with poor privacy, user-sovereignty, and security scores. Governance strongly influences results: recall policies can reduce inappropriate disclosure at a cost in helpfulness, while both recall and retention policies improve poisoning resistance. Performance and efficiency benchmarks alone therefore cannot reveal how well a memory system meets its responsibilities. Code: https://github.com/milatechtransfer/heams
bullets: Frames memory systems as custodians of users’ persistent information with explicit behavioral responsibilities.
Introduces an open-source benchmark suite covering performance, efficiency, security, privacy, and user sovereignty, while identifying remaining gaps.
Provides MilaMem and a governance layer for controlled study of memory-system design choices.
Finds that no system dominates all performance benchmarks, and strong task performance can coexist with weak privacy, sovereignty, and security.
Shows that recall and retention policies can improve privacy and poisoning resistance, though recall may reduce helpfulness.

papers.abstract: A useful memory need not resemble the question it helps answer. Jetriever ranks each stored memory by Jev's decision score for its usefulness to the current question, replacing similarity search with full-pool utility scoring. On InMind's 125 indirect-query tasks, it places the gold exchange first in 84.8% of cases; matched BM25 and MiniLM controls reach 1.6% and 0.0% when indexing user turns. A 20-question comparison separates finding evidence from ranking it: Jev and Qwen3.5 9B each find 90% of gold exchanges by rank 50, while Laya finds 30%; at rank one, Jev reaches 85% and Qwen3.5 9B 40%. On a dimension-proportional random sample of 60 MemoryAgentBench questions, Jetriever's four-dimension score is 55.4%, against 44.3% for ReFind on the same questions. Jev retrieval costs USD 0.00834 per InMind question and USD 0.03103 per MAB question on average. These results show the value of world knowledge, scores that rank decisive memories first, and affordable full-pool scoring.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) now assist users across sessions of images and text, carried by an external memory of what was said and shown. When such an assistant answers wrongly, the failure usually began earlier, in how a record was written, updated or retrieved, and the answer alone does not say where. We formalize multimodal memory as four stages, Write, Update, Retrieve and Answer, and define nine error types across them. A stage-resolved analysis on Mem-Gallery traces most failures to a source stage, and most of those lie before the answer. Injecting known errors against fact-preserving control edits, we then follow each tainted record downstream. Early errors survive to the answer as apparent evidence, and hurt most when no other record holds the fact. A diagnosis that trusts the quoted evidence therefore blames the stage where the error surfaces, not the one where it began. We propose MemDoctor, in which the MLLM that built the memory diagnoses its own failures. It traces each needed fact backward through the four stages, accepts a diagnosis only when the cited evidence is found in memory, and repairs that stage before answering again. On a 4B backbone, MemDoctor improves accuracy on both Mem-Gallery and MemLens, outperforming all evaluated 8B baselines, and the same loop also improves MuRAG and A-Mem.
authors: Ruiyang Jiang, Xinyang Liao, Weikai Huang, Yuqi Niu, Junjie Zhou, Yubin Zheng
bullets: Frames multimodal memory failures as nine error types across four stages: Write, Update, Retrieve, and Answer.
Finds that most failures originate before the final answer, with early errors propagating as misleading evidence.
Shows that evidence-based diagnosis alone can misattribute an error to the stage where it becomes visible.
Uses backward fact tracing and memory-grounded diagnosis to repair the responsible stage before re-answering.
Improves accuracy on Mem-Gallery and MemLens, and also benefits MuRAG and A-Mem, using a 4B backbone.

papers.title: MemDoctor: Stage-wise Error Attribution and Repair for MLLM Agent Memory

papers.abstract: Agentic memory systems give LLMs persistent memory by extracting experience into text and retrieving it at query time, but the model itself does not evolve: however many interactions it has had, it starts each query the same. Extraction errors compound, implicit cross-session patterns that no single fragment states cannot be surfaced, and the construction cost grows with every conversation. Fine-tuning on past interactions does change the weights, but requires backpropagation at serving time and degrades on long histories. We introduce CLAM (Carried Latent Adapter Memory), which combines the strengths of both: a recurrent hypernetwork performs parametric consolidation, compiling a stream of session activations into a low-rank adapter in a single forward pass with no gradient steps and no language-model generation calls, while a complementary episodic buffer supplies verbatim detail at inference. A gated latent state carries knowledge across sessions in fixed size, so the parametric memory accumulates without growing. On LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S across three open models (2-7B parameters), CLAM leads all agentic baselines by 1-45 points and all gradient-based parametric methods by 10-45 points, while requiring zero generative LLM calls, zero gradient steps, and 3-151x less wall-clock time than extraction systems to build its memory. The two channels are complementary: the consolidated adapter adds 12-15 accuracy points when the episodic buffer misses the gold evidence, and still adds 4-5 points even with an oracle buffer.
bullets: Addresses growing costs, extraction errors, and missed cross-session patterns in text-based memory systems.
Uses a recurrent hypernetwork and gated latent state to consolidate session knowledge into a fixed-size adapter.
Combines consolidated parametric memory with verbatim episodic retrieval for complementary recall and detail.
Outperforms reported agentic and gradient-based baselines on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S across three 2–7B open models.
Builds memory 3–151× faster than extraction systems and improves accuracy by 12–15 points when episodic retrieval misses evidence, and 4–5 points with an oracle buffer.

papers.abstract: An agent that carries memory across tasks is only as good as the entries it keeps. We begin from an observation that is easy to reproduce and uncomfortable for the field: naively accumulating cross-task experience can make an agent \emph{worse} than one with no memory at all. On AgentBoard, a workflow-induction memory solves fewer tasks than a memoryless ReAct agent in seven of eight domains, and a per-step procedural store with no surrounding structure loses half of ReAct's completions on Jericho. We argue that the missing ingredients are per-action credit assignment and an explicit life cycle for stored entries, and present AdMem, which supplies both. Before each action the actor commits to an expected outcome; a concurrently running critic scores the realized outcome against that expectation and writes a procedural entry carrying a binary reward and a reflection, so credit lands on the action that earned it and no environment reward is required. Each entry then carries a scalar utility, updated online under a noisy-OR reward model, that ranks retrieval jointly with context similarity and drives eviction and merging, giving the store a forgetting and consolidation policy instead of unbounded growth. Across 707 tasks in eight AgentBoard domains AdMem solves 441 against 388 for ReAct and 312 for the workflow-induction baseline --- a pooled gain significant under a two-sided Fisher exact test, concentrated in the domains that supply transferable cross-task structure. All memory stays human-readable text, which is what makes the failures above diagnosable --- and, as we discuss, also makes the store an auditable but attackable surface.
authors: Runzhe Wang, Huilin Lu, Shengjie Liu, Li Dong, Zhihuai Zhu
bullets: Naively accumulating cross-task memory can hurt performance, sometimes performing worse than a memoryless ReAct agent.
Before each action, the agent predicts an expected outcome; a concurrent critic compares the result with that expectation and records a binary reward plus reflection.
Each procedural memory entry receives an online-updated utility score under a noisy-OR model, guiding retrieval, eviction, and merging.
Across 707 AgentBoard tasks in eight domains, AdMem solved 441 tasks versus 388 for ReAct and 312 for the workflow-induction baseline.
The human-readable memory is auditable and diagnosable, but also presents an attackable surface; gains concentrate where cross-task structure transfers.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Information flow between the environment, the actor, the critic, and the long-term memory store. The three modules run in separate threads: the actor never blocks on the critic, so memory writing and evaluation overlap with acting. The actor’s short-term memory (STM) holds the task instructions, the task and memory tool specifications, and the current task’s short-term trace, with environment facts surfaced through a priority-ranked semantic heap and event summaries through a scope-ordered episodic stack (Section 2.3); retrieved long-term memory (LTM) enters the same context. Every action the actor sends to the critic carries the expectation the actor committed to before acting, which is what the critic scores the realized outcome against; the resulting per-action reward travels to the store alongside the new procedural entry and updates the utilities of the entries that were retrieved for that action (Section 2.4).

Table 1: Task completeness (C, the fraction of tasks solved) and average progress (P, the mean of the per-task progress score pi ∈ [0, 1]) on the eight AgentBoard domains, using Claude Haiku 4.5 as the backbone for every method. Bold marks the best value in each column. Each domain is a fixed task set of the size given in the second row, so completion counts are recoverable exactly from C (e.g. 63.4% of 134 is 85 tasks); we use those counts for the Fisher exact tests reported in the text. Each configuration is streamed once over the task set in a single lifelong episode. On the three 20-task domains a single task is worth 5.0 points of C, which is why we base per-domain conclusions on the tests rather than on the point differences alone.

Table 2: Aggregate view of Table 1 over all 707 tasks. Intervals are Wilson 95% binomial intervals on the pooled completion rate. Macro-avg. C weights the eight domains equally rather than by task count; we report both because WebShop and ScienceWorld together hold 48% of the tasks. Against ReAct, the pooled difference is significant for AdMem (+53 tasks, two-sided Fisher exact p = 5× 10−3) and significant in the negative direction for AWM (−76 tasks, p = 7 × 10−5). Because all three methods are run over the same 707 tasks, both comparisons are paired; both remain significant under the least favorable exact McNemar test consistent with these margins (p = 0.03 and p = 5× 10−3 respectively, Appendix C).

Table 3: Component ablation on Jericho (20 tasks), Claude Haiku 4.5. STP: short-term planning and context management only, with all long-term recall removed. LTP: the long-term procedural store only — per-step retrieval with critic-generated reflections and the reward-based utility retained — with short-term planning and context management removed. AdMem: all components. STP and ReAct are single-epoch by construction, since neither carries anything across tasks. For LTP and AdMem the task set is streamed again each epoch without resetting the long-term store, so the epoch axis measures accumulation rather than repetition of a fixed store; entry utilities carry over with the store, so an entry that proved unhelpful in an earlier epoch enters the next one already down-weighted.

papers.selection_reason: Procedural memory with credit assignment, retrieval, and eviction for task-solving agents directly fits LLM/agent memory.
papers.title: AdMem: Expectation-Grounded Procedural Memory for Long-Horizon Task-Solving Agents
papers.tldr: AdMem improves long-horizon agents by assigning credit to individual actions and managing procedural memories through utility-based retrieval, merging, and forgetting.

papers.abstract: Cost-aware LLM routing often selects the cheapest policy meeting empirical risk and coverage constraints. Yet a router that passes an audit can violate its fixed service contract on new requests, even when candidate policies are constructed independently. We study this deployment-commitment decision with disjoint construction, audit, and test samples. Across 19 RouterBench task families, the cheapest audit-feasible router deploys in 91.82% of opportunities but violates the held-out contract in 32.22% of deployments. We introduce Menu-Aware Routing Commitment (MARC), which qualifies policies using audit evidence and a serving-cost tolerance to retain the apparent winner, deploy a supported alternative, or defer. Its practical policywise variant (MARC-P) reduces observed conditional failure to 0.73% at 85.79% deployment, with higher serving cost; fixed-margin and formal risk-control procedures provide competitive alternatives. Nested audits show how added evidence changes deployable policy sets, and learned semantic routing exhibits the same commitment failure. These results establish deployment commitment as a distinct operational decision connecting router evaluation, service reliability, and inference cost.
authors: Minxuan Hu, Qishi Zhan, Ziheng Chen, Zhengtao Yao, Zihan Dong, Jiayu Yi, Wenxi Sun
bullets: Across 19 RouterBench task families, the cheapest audit-feasible router violated the held-out contract in 32.22% of deployments.
The study separates router construction, auditing, and testing using disjoint samples to examine deployment commitments.
MARC uses audit evidence and serving-cost tolerance to retain the apparent winner, choose an alternative, or defer deployment.
MARC-P reduced observed conditional failure to 0.73% at 85.79% deployment, with higher serving cost.
Nested audits and semantic routing show that commitment failures persist as evidence and routing approaches change.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates deployment commitment failures in cost-aware LLM routing, introducing a mechanism to audit and qualify policies based on serving cost and reliability.
papers.title: When the Cheapest Feasible Router Fails: Auditing Deployment Commitments in Cost-Aware LLM Routing
papers.tldr: The cheapest LLM router that passes an audit can still violate its service contract after deployment, while MARC reduces failures by allowing supported alternatives or deferral.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) in multi-turn information systems accumulate their own earlier replies and a growing task state. We asked whether this conversation history lowers accuracy, and whether process-level quality metrics warn before it does. Each analysis was fixed before its outcomes were computed. In Study 1, on 48 sharded math tasks, retaining its replies lowered final success by 0.21 for GPT-4o-mini and 0.29 for Mistral-7B (Holm-adjusted p = 0.026 and 0.004); Llama-4 Scout showed the same direction, not significant. Study 2 introduces CDR-Stream, 100-turn state-tracking dialogues with an exact answer per turn and per-model difficulty calibration. With the full history, accuracy fell from about 0.6 to 0.1 within twenty turns at matched difficulty, whereas a solver-verified state summary kept it 0.52-0.59 higher (Holm-adjusted p less than 0.001). Consistency and logical coherence fell far less than accuracy, and stability rose. None of these metrics, a paired readiness measure or calibrated single-stream drift detectors gave robust, model-general early warning, although in Study 2 the repeat-based metrics were complete only for GPT-4o-mini. In the monitors we tested, a single 100-turn stream had power only for very large drops. Systems built on LLMs should keep task state outside the transcript and monitor across sessions.
bullets: Study 1 found that retaining prior replies reduced success on sharded math tasks for GPT-4o-mini and Mistral-7B; Llama-4 Scout showed the same direction without significance.
Study 2 introduced CDR-Stream, a 100-turn state-tracking benchmark with matched per-turn difficulty and exact answers.
Full-history accuracy fell from about 0.6 to 0.1 within 20 turns, whereas solver-verified state summaries preserved substantially higher accuracy.
Consistency, logical coherence, stability, and tested drift monitors provided no robust, model-general early warning; single streams detected only very large drops.
The findings support storing task state outside the transcript and monitoring performance across sessions.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The monitoring framework. A context policy decides what the model sees at turn t. Responses are scored into a per-turn quality vector, smoothed over a window and passed to drift detectors whose thresholds are calibrated on stationary dialogues. Exact gold is needed for CQ, RS and ES and for evaluating alarms; CS, LS and SS do not use it.

Figure 2: Study 1 primary endpoint (n = 48 paired tasks per model). Left: final-turn success with 95% Wilson intervals (Wilson, 1927). Right: paired difference, fresh prefix minus dialogue history, with 95% task-bootstrap intervals and Holm-adjusted McNemar p-values.

Figure 3: Study 2 accuracy over 100 turns in 5-turn bins: (a) all 30 dialogues per model; (b)–(f) the five scenarios, six dialogues per model each. Solid: dialogue history; dashed: verified state summary; dotted vertical lines: scheduled difficulty changes.

Figure 4: Quality metrics do not track accuracy. (a) Study 2, GPT-4o-mini, dialogue history, 5-turn means over 30 dialogues (descriptive); dashed: accuracy under the verified state summary; CS is supported by 2976 of 3,000 turns. (b) Post-hoc replay of Study 1: median and 10–90% band over 1,000 orderings of window means (W = 20) when the regime switches from fresh prefix to dialogue history at session 49.

Figure 5: Simulated detection within 33 turns versus the accuracy drop from 0.80 and the number of dialogues pooled per turn (W = 20, thresholds from 12 null streams, 5% false-alarm target). Left: change at turn 34; right: at turn 51. Dotted line: 80% detection.

Table 2: The two benchmarks at a glance. K/L: same-context repeats / reworded instructions per turn. Metric coverage lists which of the six dimensions were computed where; CQ, RS and ES always need a final answer and the gold (Section 3).
Table 1: Positioning against the closest prior work.
Table 3: Study 1 paired final-turn success over 48 tasks per model. F/D: tasks in which only the fresh prefix, or only the dialogue history, succeeded; p: exact McNemar test.

A unit is one (task, model) pair (up to 3 × 48); turns are the pre-final turns of those units pooled together, the level at which the metric is observed; tasks are the distinct source tasks contributing at least one turn, the level at which the permutation test clusters observations. rpartial: task-clustered partial correlation; p: one-sided task-clustered permutation test.
