papers.abstract: Language models evolve, but the observations, revisions, and context accumulated through user interactions should remain usable. Each new model must be able to retrieve past evidence, track revisions, and add new observations. We present MIGRO, a decoupled long-term memory system that treats experience as a persistent state shared across successive language models. MIGRO follows a simple principle: preserve historical evidence exactly, organize it approximately, and decide what to retrieve only when the question is known. We call this asymmetric fidelity with deferred selectivity. A shared semantic index supports retrieval, while exact records retain observations and their historical relationships. Because models differ in vocabulary and tokenization, host-specific interfaces convert selected evidence into inputs the receiving model can use. Reversible encoding reduces archival storage while enabling exact recovery. The shared state and its access interfaces let successive hosts read and extend the accumulated experience. On matched LoCoMo states, MIGRO scores 7.3% higher and uses 99.3% less private memory than the strongest quality baseline. After handoff, continued writing retains 99.9% of full-history rebuilding quality by extending the inherited state. On million-token BEAM histories, MIGRO uses 57.5% less private storage on average than the most compact baseline. MIGRO combines high answer quality, continued memory growth across hosts, and low storage cost. Code is available at https://github.com/zOUMINGXI/MIGRO.

papers.abstract: Tool-using language-model agents accumulate histories of their own mistakes, and a system that compacts, repairs or hands off such a history decides what it says about those mistakes while their effects stay in the world. Prior work cleans the history at a fixed world, where showing a corrected step and saying it is done move together. We ask whether the same correct content helps or hurts depending on how the history states it and what the world holds. We freeze an agent mid-task with its exact world state, edit the history or the world, and let a receiver model continue. On AgentCE-Bench, after the agent commits a wrong value, we hold the world fixed and add the correct value by two natural edits: a truthful note beside the preserved error or the agent's own completed action. The note raises recovery, the share of remaining targets the receiver gets right, from 51% under a matched neutral note to 66%. The completed action lowers it below the unedited history, from 50% to 44%, so the value's presence alone does not predict the effect. On AppWorld, after a database write, we vary whether its receipt reports success or failure and whether its effect is present. A success receipt lowers whole-task success from 45% to 28% while the effect is absent and raises it from 38% to 49% once present. The two effects differ by 27 points pooled over two receivers, a difference positive in six of eight receivers at 97.5% and seven at 95%. A history edit's effect thus depends on the world it describes, and a history made to look clean while the world still holds the error can leave an agent worse off than no edit at all.
authors: Egor Pakhomov, Anurag Koul, Hongjun Liu, Bo Pang, Shafiq Joty, Erik Nijkamp
bullets: The study tests whether identical information helps differently depending on how it is represented in history and whether the world reflects it.
With the world fixed after a wrong value, a truthful note improved recovery from 51% to 66%, while presenting the correction as a completed action reduced it from 50% to 44%.
In AppWorld, success receipts helped when their effects were present (38% to 49%) but hurt when effects were absent (45% to 28%).
History edits and world state interacted across receivers, showing that the value alone does not determine recovery.
Scope: results concern mid-task, tool-using agents and history/world edits evaluated on AgentCE-Bench and AppWorld.

papers.abstract: Recurrent sequence models must decide how strongly to overwrite their memory at each token. Read as Bayesian filtering, this write is the gain of a Kalman update, set by uncertainty from two sources that pull it in opposite directions: volatility, how quickly the underlying associations change, and stochasticity, how noisy each observation of them is. First, we show that the update of gated delta-rule memories is the form this filter takes under isotropic uncertainty. Next, we introduce Voltic, a recurrent memory that keeps the covariance anisotropic and makes both noise variances input-dependent, so the write is vector-valued and carries uncertainty accumulated over the sequence. A dense covariance would have to be propagated token by token, ruling out the parallel training these models depend on. We therefore give two assumed-density approximations, diagonal and quasi-diagonal, both of which leave the memory update in delta-rule form and reuse its chunked kernels. On controlled recall tasks in which associations change and observations are corrupted, Voltic leads all baselines. On the task combining volatility and stochasticity, its margin over the strongest baseline is larger at both extrapolation sizes than at the training sizes. In 45M-parameter language models it leads an eight-task reasoning average and achieves higher retrieval accuracy beyond the training context length than gated baselines, at throughput close to those baselines. Deriving the write from an uncertainty recursion therefore makes memory more responsive to change.
bullets: Recasts gated memory writes as Kalman-style updates driven by uncertainty.
Introduces input-dependent volatility and stochasticity with anisotropic covariance, producing vector-valued writes.
Uses diagonal and quasi-diagonal approximations to preserve parallel, chunked training.
Leads baselines on controlled recall, combined volatility–stochasticity, reasoning, and long-context retrieval tasks.
Scope: approximations trade full covariance modeling for computational efficiency.

papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly operate in long-horizon, verifier-rich environments, but current self-improvement mechanisms often write episode-derived lessons directly into memory, making local success an unreliable signal for reusable and safe knowledge. This paper addresses the core question of when an experience-derived behavioral update should be admitted into persistent agent state. We propose Falsification-Gated Self-Evolution (FGSE), a verifier-grounded framework that represents each candidate lesson as a structured hypothesis with an explicit precondition, behavior change, expected effect, and verifier. FGSE applies the hypothesis only in a temporary state, tests it on target-transfer, falsification, and archived-regression probes, and then commits, refines, or rejects it according to measured gain and risk. Across web, app, tool-use, and long-term memory benchmarks, FGSE achieves strong task performance, including 39.8 WebArena success rate, 78.8 AppWorld average completion, and 0.724/0.487 Pass$^1$ on $\tau$-Retail/$\tau$-Airline, while reducing falsification failures to 5.0%, regression damage to 1.3%, and harmful committed updates to 3.6%. These results suggest that testing memory updates as hypotheses supports more reliable long-term adaptation.
authors: Runxuan Tang, Haoyu Gao, Yuyan Ding, Junyi Yao, Zihao Zheng, Zecheng Sheng, Liwei Hou
bullets: Addresses the risk that local episode success leads agents to store unsafe or non-transferable lessons.
Represents each candidate update with a precondition, behavior change, expected effect, and verifier.
Tests updates temporarily using transfer, falsification, and archived-regression probes, then commits, refines, or rejects them based on gain and risk.
Reports strong performance across web, app, tool-use, and long-term memory benchmarks.
Reduces falsification failures to 5.0%, regression damage to 1.3%, and harmful committed updates to 3.6%.

The right-side annotation reports the sign-consistency score C(h). Figure 10: Memory-growth Pareto analysis. We vary the retention budget and evaluate longhorizon self-evolving agents under different memory policies. Left: task success rate versus committed memory size. Right: violation rate versus committed memory size. The x-axis is update gain ∆upd, and the y-axis is either harmful update rate H (left) or regression damage R (right). Point size indicates verifier cost C (average verifier calls per candidate update), and color denotes the update-selection strategy. The black dashed line shows the empirical Pareto frontier, where larger gain and smaller harm are jointly preferred. The left panel shows bad-update detection rate D(K), and the right panel shows harmful update avoided A(K). papers.abstract: External memory enables LLM agents to improve from experience by distilling trajectories of past tasks into concise lessons for new tasks. However, memory can also lead to memory-induced degradation, where an agent fails on tasks it would solve without memory, often because it follows a lesson that is incorrect, or misapplies or misreads a valid one. This is because lessons are inferred from trajectories labeled only with task success or failure, yet are typically provided without the trajectories they came from, leaving the agent no way to check them. To address this, we introduce WikiTrace, an evidence-linked memory system designed to let agents check each lesson against its original trajectory. Specifically, motivated by the finding that a trajectory often still holds the evidence needed to catch an erroneous lesson, WikiTrace stores each lesson as a concise insight linked to a summary of why its trajectory succeeded or failed and to the raw trajectory itself. Then, on a new task, the agent starts from all insights and, whenever one lacks details needed to act, conflicts with another, or comes from a failed task, descends through its links with terminal tools to fill in missing details or correct the insight before acting. We validate WikiTrace on five agentic benchmarks, showing that it consistently outperforms existing memory approaches and a baseline given the same insights alone, while also reducing memory-induced degradation. Our code is available at https://github.com/yukyeongleee/wikitrace
authors: Yukyeong Lee, Yumin Choi, Jinheon Baek, Sung Ju Hwang
bullets: External memory can hurt performance when lessons are incorrect, misapplied, or misread.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon personalized agents maintain an evolving memory by continuously deciding what to add, modify, or discard. However, learning an optimal update policy remains challenging. Conventional training relies solely on terminal question-answering accuracy, yielding a coarse feedback signal that treats all intermediate updates identically. Furthermore, update utility is inherently user-specific, as identical memory actions may yield opposite effects across different user personas. Existing methods fail to address this heterogeneity, relying on globally shared evaluation standards with at most a single scalar intermediate reward. To address these challenges, we propose \textbf{Personalized Memory Rubrics} (\textbf{PMR}), a framework that translates terminal feedback into fine-grained, per-step, and per-user credit assignment. PMR decomposes evaluation into a universal layer capturing cross-persona failure patterns and a per-user adaptive layer modeling individual traits as a specialized delta over the universal baseline. Through \textbf{Rubric-Guided Credit Assignment}, PMR redistributes credit at the token level, selectively amplifying validated decisions on successful trajectories while falling back to standard policy optimization on failed ones to avoid unreliable attribution. The rubric and memory policy \textbf{co-evolve} in a closed loop with anti-circularity guarantees. Crucially, PMR incurs zero inference overhead, operating without any rubric or external judge during deployment. Extensive experiments across four benchmarks demonstrate consistent gains over strong memory-augmented baselines.
authors: Yupeng Han, Kai Zhang, Shuochen Liu, Ze Liu, Xianquan Wang, Zhihong Pan, Xiangyu Zhao, Qi Liu, Enhong Chen
bullets: Addresses coarse terminal-only feedback and the fact that memory actions can help one user but harm another.
Uses a universal rubric for cross-user failure patterns plus an adaptive per-user layer capturing individual traits.
Redistributes credit at the token level, reinforcing validated decisions on successful trajectories and using standard policy optimization on failed ones.
Co-evolves the rubric and memory policy with anti-circularity safeguards.
Shows consistent gains over strong memory-augmented baselines across four benchmarks, with zero inference overhead.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of PMR. PMR first induces a personalized rubric 𝑅𝑢 from shared cross-user patterns and residual per-user failures, and then uses it to shape direction-safe, per-step credit while preserving the trajectory-level update direction. A co-evolution loop iteratively updates the student, rubric, and credit assignment, with standard GRPO used as a fallback for failures. At inference, only the student model is required.

Figure 1: Long-horizon memory learning involves multiple updates but only a terminal QA reward, making fine-grained credit assignment difficult. Hand-crafted methods use fixed, non-personalized rules, while RL-based methods rely on sparse scalar feedback with ambiguous step/token attribution. PMR decouples direction from magnitude: the QA advantage determines the learning direction, while personalized rubric evidence modulates credit magnitude through direction-safe gating.

PMR selectively adapts rubric dimensions to user behavior: Malia emphasizes timeliness and conciseness, Maria largely retains universal criteria, and Alex strengthens completeness and conciseness. papers.abstract: Language-model agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks whose interaction histories exceed the model's active context. They must therefore decide what to write down and what to read back, and when to do either. Recent work has begun to use on-policy distillation (OPD) to make memory control part of the policy, relying on memory tools and compaction protocols that lie outside either model's pre-training. However, this weakens the distillation on both sides: the teacher cannot give useful guidance on an interface it has never used, and the student samples too few meaningful memory actions for that guidance to take effect. To study this problem, we introduce Coding Agent Memory Gym II (CAMG-II), a suite of long-horizon agentic-RL environments spanning Shop, Coding, AutoResearch, General, and Visual. Alongside each environment's native task interface, CAMG-II provides ordinary Bash access and an episode-persistent workspace, enabling the policy to create, revise, search, and reuse files as memory across context replacements. We also introduce Coding Agent Memory Post-Training II (CAMP-II), which trains a single policy jointly across all five environments with fully asynchronous OPD to learn this file-based memory behavior directly from a frozen teacher with a prior for file operations. On CAMG-II, CAMP-II obtains 2.97 times the gain of the strongest OPD baseline. The memory behavior CAMP-II learns generalizes to two external benchmarks, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2, with improved success rates.
authors: Lirui Luo, Kelong Mao, Xinwei Yang, Rongqing Li, Luyu Chen, Kieran Wong, Yudong Guo, Xinrui Wang, Jiayin Zhu, Gu Simiu, Sulong Xu, Cong Fang
bullets: Long-horizon agents need to decide what information to save, retrieve, and when, as histories exceed active context.
CAMG-II evaluates memory behavior across Shop, Coding, AutoResearch, General, and Visual environments using Bash and persistent workspaces.
CAMP-II jointly trains one policy across all five environments with a frozen teacher that already understands file operations.
The learned file-based memory behavior transfers to Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2 with improved success rates.

papers.abstract: Practical Web applications increasingly require agents to interpret long conversations or documents. For inputs exceeding the context windows of large language models (LLMs), memory agents process segments sequentially and retain past information in bounded memory. However, they typically divide inputs into flat token segments without preserving structure or hierarchy, causing three limitations for structured data such as API responses or HTML documents. First, fixed-length segmentation can split fields of the same record, breaking their relationships. Second, segments lack hierarchical information, obscuring their structural context and positions. Third, successive memory updates may discard details of earlier sibling records needed for reasoning on later segments. To address these limitations, we propose TreeAgent, a structure-aware agent that uses the input hierarchy to guide both segment-wise context processing and access to past information. Specifically, TreeAgent constructs segments from complete subtrees and groups of adjacent sibling subtrees to preserve local structural relationships. We provide theoretical guarantees on segment counts to guide token budget selection toward matching the segment count of fixed-length segmentation. We further attach structural paths to the segments for the agent to identify their ancestors and hierarchical positions. We also introduce residual memory links from the segments of low-level children to the segments of high-level parents, enabling direct information flows beyond successive memory updates. We evaluate TreeAgent with four representative memory agents on eight retrieval and aggregation tasks. The inputs are derived from real-world application data in JSON, HTML, YAML, and JavaScript and range from 8K to 1M tokens. TreeAgent improves the average score across the four datasets for all four agents, with 3.61% performance gain on average.
authors: Wei Gu, Weiwei Qi, Jiajun Tang, Tianhang Zheng, Bo Chen, Zhibo Zhang, Jinfei Liu, Kui Ren
bullets: Targets flat, fixed-length segmentation that breaks relationships, loses hierarchy, and forgets earlier sibling details.
Builds segments from complete subtrees or adjacent sibling subtrees to preserve local structure.
Attaches structural paths to expose each segment’s ancestors and position.
Adds residual links from low-level child segments to high-level parent segments for direct information flow.
Evaluated on retrieval and aggregation tasks over JSON, HTML, YAML, and JavaScript inputs spanning 8K–1M tokens; improved all four tested memory agents on average.

The memory-agent block represents the agent’s original workflow, including its internal actions and stopping behavior. After processing each section, TreeAgent saves the updated memory. Parent–child relations determine which saved states are linked and accessed by later updates.

papers.tldr: TreeAgent improves long hierarchical-data processing by preserving structure during segmentation and memory access, yielding an average 3.61% gain across evaluated memory agents.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems provide a convenient framework for the massive deployment of agents based on Large Language Models (LLMs). It provides a sound framework where agents can interact with existing software to perform actions in an autonomous way. Agentic AI is the new term to denote these AI-based autonomous systems. In real multi-agent systems, agents need to deal with malicious agents some of which can exploit security vulnerabilities to do harm. A memory poisoning attack is an example of exploiting a vulnerability to modify agents knowledge and, thus, affect its behavior. In an agent, there are different types of memory systems (semantic, episodic, and short-term) which have their own characteristics and for which different memory poisoning attacks may be developed. In this paper we focus on semantic memory, we discuss its attack, and mitigation strategies. We introduce private knowledge retrieval and private inference. We propose a signature system in the knowledge base to prevent from undesired manipulation. This should avoid memory poisoning attacks by introducing security by design in the construction of the semantic memory. In our architecture, an agent contains a local Prolog-like inference system (i.e., using Horn clauses to represent knowledge) which accesses an external knowledge base to get the required knowledge. This externally signed knowledge base is accessed privately. We provide different implementations in Python using different privacy levels including k-anonymity and information-theoretical privacy (IT-PIR).
bullets: Focuses on attacks that manipulate agents’ semantic memory and alter their behavior.
Uses signed knowledge-base entries to prevent unauthorized or malicious knowledge manipulation.
Combines a local Prolog-like Horn-clause inference system with private access to an external knowledge base.
Describes Python implementations offering privacy levels including k-anonymity and information-theoretical privacy via IT-PIR.
Scope is semantic memory; episodic and short-term memory attacks are not addressed.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents reuse execution experience to improve reliability on complex tool-based tasks. Systems such as Sentry call large models to generate failure diagnoses before retrieving advice, adding inference cost to experience reuse. We present Synapse-Control, an agent runtime whose lightweight control plane selects advice and determines when to send it to the task-executing model. Rules shortlist relevant advice, and a lightweight 1.7B classifier fine-tuned on teacher-labeled state-suggestion pairs scores those candidates instead of generating a diagnosis. Micro-contracts encode reusable interface checks, such as required arguments or valid options, without prescribing complete task programs. A Prompt Value Table records earlier guidance and feedback to limit repeated suggestions through cooldown and token-budget checks. Across 1,308 attempts per method in AppWorld and WebShop, Synapse-Control achieves 270 successes (29.8% more than Base), replaces 4,987 generative diagnosis calls, and reduces auxiliary control time relative to Sentry by 50.2% and 51.0%, respectively.
authors: Zhiyuan Huang, Shengan Zheng, Chenghu Yang, Song Zhang, Lingyun Li, Chen Yu, Weiquan Huang, Linpeng Huang

Uses rules to shortlist advice and a fine-tuned 1.7B classifier to score candidate suggestions.

In AppWorld and WebShop, it achieved 270 successes—29.8% more than Base—and replaced 4,987 diagnosis calls.
Reduced auxiliary control time versus Sentry by 50.2% and 51.0% across the two environments.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated considerable potential in biomedical applications, while agentic memory systems have emerged as a promising approach to preserving and utilizing information across tasks and interactions. However, a fundamental question remains: how effectively and reliably do these systems retain, retrieve, update, and utilize biomedical information? In this study, we systematically investigate agentic memory in the biomedical domain, focusing on task effectiveness, retrieval quality, information fidelity, and long-term robustness. We evaluate five memory approaches across four LLMs in three representative settings: biomedical knowledge reasoning, clinical prediction, and long-term conversational memory. Our analyses reveal how memory construction, evidence relevance, and conversational history shape downstream biomedical performance, highlighting the distinct challenges of retrieving relevant information, preserving its fidelity, and effectively utilizing it for reasoning. Building on these findings, we introduce Hybrid Memory Retrieval and Utilization (HMRU), a training-free framework that jointly enhances evidence accessibility and task-aware utilization to improve biomedical reasoning and long-term conversational memory. HMRU achieves an average relative improvement of 8.6% across biomedical question-answering and conversational memory benchmarks, with additional gains in selected clinical prediction tasks. It further reduces conversational answer errors by 24.9% and closes 48.0% of the performance gap to full-context inference. Our findings provide a systematic characterization of biomedical agentic memory and practical insights into developing more effective and reliable memory-augmented LLM systems.
authors: Mingchen Li, Yongkang Xiao, Rumeng Li, Rui Zhang, Hong Yu
bullets: Evaluates five memory approaches across four LLMs in biomedical reasoning, clinical prediction, and long-term conversation settings.

Finds that memory construction, evidence relevance, and conversational history strongly affect downstream performance.
HMRU improves results by an average of 8.6%, reduces conversational answer errors by 24.9%, and closes 48.0% of the gap to full-context inference.
The study highlights persistent challenges in retrieving relevant information, preserving fidelity, and using memory effectively for biomedical reasoning.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented language model systems generally select context by query-conditioned relevance. We argue that long-lived AI systems require a second operator: activation-conditioned memory availability. We specify an architecture in which request and goal cues seed an authorized memory graph, activation and fan attenuation allocate a bounded traversal frontier, retrieved entities recursively emit cues, and a typed evidence graph is reconstructed before generation. The specification yields five architectural consequences about candidate selection, traversal control, graph regularization, evidence reconstruction, and reinforcement. We derive implementation-level cost estimates and define ablations, failure conditions, and a reproducible evaluation protocol. The central claim is narrowed or falsified if a simpler graph reranker matches full traversal on causal and temporal recovery under equal budgets. This architecture-and-analysis preprint reports no benchmark measurements. If the claim holds, retrieval returns the evidence path that makes a memory available, not only a ranked list.
bullets: Motivation: Query relevance alone may be insufficient for long-lived AI systems that must recover causally and temporally linked memories.
Method: Request and goal cues seed a memory graph; activation and fan attenuation bound traversal, while retrieved entities recursively emit cues.
Output: A typed evidence graph is reconstructed before language-model generation.
Analysis: The work specifies architectural consequences, cost estimates, ablations, failure conditions, and a reproducible evaluation protocol.
Scope: This is a preprint with no benchmark measurements; the claim is testable against a simpler graph reranker under equal budgets.

papers.abstract: We propose SciMARS, a framework for recursive task-local adaptation of multi-agent harnesses in closed-loop scientific discovery. Multi-agent systems coordinate analysis, experimental design, and verification as scientific evidence evolves. However, two problems limit their effectiveness: (i) without shared memory, agents lose observations and repeat work; (ii) fixed role procedures, handoffs, and memory policies perpetuate mistakes despite retained evidence. We address these problems with a shared evidence graph and separate component editors. SciMARS adapts roles and coordination; SciMARS + Memory adds a third editor for how agents record, retrieve, and receive evidence. Candidate probes guide composition and selection of the next harness. We evaluate scientific discovery through experimental-data replay and a digital twin. SciMARS + Memory resolves 12/18 GPT-6-Astra and 2/18 GLM-5.3 attempts on Autonomous Science Bench, compared with 8/18 and 1/18 for the base multi-agent team. On ScienceAgentBench and AppWorld, it solves 14/38 and 11/20 tasks, compared with 11/38 and 5/20 for the base team. These results support combining shared memory with harness adaptation across scientific and interactive tasks.
bullets: Targets repeated work caused by missing shared memory and persistent errors from fixed agent procedures.
Uses a shared evidence graph and separate editors for roles/coordination and, in SciMARS + Memory, evidence recording and retrieval.
Candidate probes guide composition and selection of the next multi-agent harness.
Evaluated with experimental-data replay, a digital twin, Autonomous Science Bench, ScienceAgentBench, and AppWorld.
SciMARS + Memory outperformed the base team across the reported benchmarks, though results varied by model and task.

papers.abstract: Correlation Matrix Memories (CMMs) store associations as sums of rank-one outer products, providing closed-form addressability, exact deletion, and linear attribution. While classical analyses assume random, orthogonal keys, semantic encoders produce correlated representations. We analyse CMMs under correlated keys using frame-theoretic coherence: (i) capacity bounds yielding an encoder-independent limit $n \le d(1+\varepsilon^2)$ for mean squared crosstalk $\varepsilon^2$; (ii) an exact characterisation of the collateral effect of deleting an association, guaranteeing that deletion never invalidates certified associations; and (iii) a geometric transparency bound demonstrating why attribution requires candidate sets of centred keys. On this basis, we introduce Topology-Aware Neuro-Symbolic Associative Retrieval (TANSAR). TANSAR traverses a directed acyclic association graph, prunes invalid paths via sound ground Horn constraints, and injects a representation derived strictly from the verified path into the residual stream of a frozen language model, guarded by a Clopper--Pearson selective-risk gate. Controlled experiments confirm all theoretical bounds. In multi-hop knowledge editing, Horn pruning reduces answer contradictions from 25.1% to 0.5%, whereas Hopfield retrieval incurs 24% contradictions when stale associations remain stored (and 0% if stale associations are removed). An end-to-end edit transaction requires 13.6 ms on a standard CPU and 2.37 ms on GPU. The symbolic component matches gold labels across all 600 ProofWriter theories and achieves 94.0% agreement on FOLIO, demonstrating sound and efficient multi-hop associative retrieval with exact unlearning.
bullets: Analyzes CMMs with correlated keys, deriving capacity, deletion-collateral, and attribution-transparency guarantees.
Traverses directed acyclic association graphs and prunes invalid paths using sound ground Horn constraints.
Injects only verified-path representations into a frozen language model, with a Clopper–Pearson selective-risk gate.
Reports reductions in multi-hop answer contradictions from 25.1% to 0.5% with Horn pruning, plus millisecond-scale edit transactions.
Matches gold labels on 600 ProofWriter theories and reaches 94.0% agreement on FOLIO.

papers.abstract: During reinforcement learning, experience can be both internalized in LLM parameters and retained externally as reusable textual skills. Parameter updates alter the model's behavior and the interaction experience from which new skills are extracted. These skills, in turn, guide the model's subsequent interactions and parameter updates. As the model's capabilities evolve, previously beneficial skills may become redundant or detrimental. We present SkillDuet, a framework that coordinates parameter updates and skill evolution through model response feedback. Skills extracted from on-policy trajectories guide parameter updates through OPD at every step. A response-based score, Strength, ranks candidate skills by the magnitude of the shift they induce in the current model's responses, and the highest-scoring skills are periodically consolidated into a persistent global skill set (Global). The updated model and Global jointly guide subsequent interactions, generating experience for further parameter and skill updates. With Qwen3-4B, SkillDuet achieves success rates of 98.57% on ALFWorld and 92.97% on WebShop, exceeding the matched SEED-API baseline by 2.86 and 5.47 percentage points, respectively. Ablations show that response-based skill selection and Global consolidation improve task performance. Further experiments show that the benefits of retained skills depend on both their content and their compatibility with the model. SkillDuet provides a concrete mechanism for model-skill co-evolution and skill-level recursive self-improvement.
bullets: Addresses the challenge that skills can become redundant or harmful as the model changes during reinforcement learning.
Uses on-policy skills to guide parameter updates through OPD, while a response-based Strength score ranks candidate skills.
Periodically consolidates high-impact skills into a persistent Global skill set that guides future interactions and updates.
With Qwen3-4B, reports 98.57% success on ALFWorld and 92.97% on WebShop, outperforming the matched SEED-API baseline.
Ablations indicate that response-based selection and Global consolidation improve performance; retained-skill benefits depend on content and model compatibility.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory lets LLM agents personalize, stay consistent, and reuse what worked before. Parametric memories need training, consolidation can lose details for good, and keeping every record leaves a growing store to search. We present MIRIX-2.0, a multi-agent memory system designed to be practical, accurate, and efficient at once. It is the most accurate of the compared systems on four of five QA benchmarks. It reaches 91.4% on LoCoMo and 72.6% on LongMemEval-S, where it leads the strongest baseline by 14.3 points, and with AutoDream disabled it gains 31.0 and 22.0 points over HyperMem on single-hop and multi-hop document QA. As procedural memory, it yields the highest mean success among the compared memory methods on ALFWorld and WebShop and reaches 49.2% on MetaClaw-Bench, against 44.0% for MetaClaw's skill library. Six typed memory agents keep complete records as the system of record, and a provenance hypergraph indexes episodic and semantic records with n-ary frames that cite their rows. Retrieval runs under explicit budgets, so the evidence a question inspects does not grow with the history. AutoDream merges duplicate anchors outside the write path without rewriting any record, and it distills task sessions into skills. With AutoDream disabled, MIRIX-2.0 answers faster than HyperMem on all five timed benchmarks. It needs no fine-tuning, runs with closed and open models, and its code is public.
bullets: Addresses memory loss, unbounded storage, and inefficient retrieval in long-running LLM agents.
Uses six typed memory agents, a provenance hypergraph with n-ary frames, explicit retrieval budgets, and optional AutoDream consolidation and skill distillation.
Leads compared systems on four of five QA benchmarks, including 91.4% on LoCoMo and 72.6% on LongMemEval-S.
Achieves the highest mean success among compared memory methods on ALFWorld and WebShop, and 49.2% on MetaClaw-Bench.
Runs with closed or open models, requires no fine-tuning, and is faster than HyperMem across five timed benchmarks when AutoDream is disabled.

papers.abstract: Large language models offer a promising technique for translating natural-language optimization problems into solver code, but their reliability remains constrained by the quality of template retrieval. While recent structured methods improve over flat prompting through hierarchical taxonomy search, their traversal rules remain fixed or LLM-driven at inference time, leaving retrieval unable to improve from past successes and failures. This motivates treating template retrieval as a policy that can be learned from modeling experience, rather than as a static inference-time rule. We propose COMPASS, a policy-amortized framework for retrieving optimization templates in LLM-based solver modeling, which represents the template library as a directed acyclic graph and formulates retrieval as a sequential decision process over template nodes. A deep Q-network learns a reusable traversal policy from template-level judgments and execution feedback, reducing reliance on fixed heuristic traversal through feedback-driven graph navigation. To support extensible retrieval, COMPASS embeds problem descriptions and template nodes in a shared semantic space, allowing newly inserted templates to be scored from their text descriptions without redefining the action space. Experiments across multiple LLM backbones and optimization-modeling benchmarks demonstrate that COMPASS consistently improves over heuristic structured retrieval, with the largest gains on complex and mixed-category problems.
bullets: Targets unreliable template retrieval in LLM-based optimization modeling.
Models templates as a directed acyclic graph and retrieval as sequential graph navigation.
Trains a deep Q-network using template judgments and execution feedback.
Uses shared semantic embeddings to score newly added templates without changing the action space.
Improves over heuristic structured retrieval across LLM backbones and benchmarks, especially on complex and mixed-category problems.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents increasingly rely on reusable natural-language skills, yet growing skill collections remain accumulations of isolated text artifacts that are difficult to compare, deduplicate, and compose. We argue that the reusable content of a skill lies not in its surface wording but in its procedural transitions: which operation to execute under a given state and which observable outcome to produce. Based on this observation, we propose State-Move-Outcome (SMO), a compilation-like framework that decomposes raw skills into reusable procedural bricks and organizes admitted bricks as an externalized symbolic structure. When compiling a skill, SMO first retrieves and composes existing bricks, dynamically connects them through Outcome-to-State conditions, and creates a candidate brick only for an uncovered procedure; the candidate becomes reusable only after validation and admission. Experiments on SkillsBench v1.1 demonstrate that SMO represents 232 rawSkills from 87 underlying tasks with 95 shared bricks, reducing the corresponding skill representations from 366,472 to 149,154 tokens--a $\mathbf{59.3}\times$ reduction and $\mathbf{2.46}\times$ compression. Across 232 skill-conditioned evaluation instances, SMO raises the average task score from $\mathbf{0.6379}$ to $\mathbf{0.7478}$ and increases 5/5 Pass instances from $\mathbf{138}$ to $\mathbf{164}$, while matching or outperforming rawSkill on $\mathbf{208}$ of $\mathbf{232}$ instances. It also reduces average runtime token consumption by $\mathbf{38.38\%}$. These results show that compiling natural-language skills into shared procedural units can jointly improve skill reuse, representation efficiency, and downstream execution.
bullets: Addresses skill collections that are difficult to compare, deduplicate, and compose because they remain isolated text artifacts.
Decomposes skills into procedural bricks linked by Outcome-to-State conditions, reusing validated bricks and creating new ones only for uncovered procedures.
On SkillsBench v1.1, represents 232 skills from 87 tasks with 95 shared bricks and reduces representation tokens by 59.3%.
Improves average task score from 0.6379 to 0.7478, raises 5/5 Pass instances from 138 to 164, and matches or beats raw skills on 208/232 instances.
Reduces average runtime token consumption by 38.38%, though the abstract does not specify broader limitations or scope beyond the reported benchmark.

papers.title: SMO: Compiling Natural Language Skills into Graphs of Reusable State-Move-Outcome Bricks
papers.tldr: SMO compiles natural-language skills into reusable state–move–outcome bricks, improving reuse, compactness, and task execution.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning a deployed language model on one task after another can change behaviour that should stay fixed, such as earlier skills, general chat or refusals. Today, such forgetting is found only after training, on the benchmarks someone chose to run. This work bounds, before training, how often its outputs change on chosen prompt distributions. FireGate places each task's update, such as a new LoRA, behind a gate, which is a classifier on the model's frozen lower layers that decides for each prompt whether the update is used. Where no gate fires, the model computes exactly what the old one computes. As a result, on any prompt distribution, every bounded behaviour score changes by at most the gates' firing rate there over a whole task stream. Calibrating each gate on unlabeled prompts of what must not change fixes that rate before training, with a PAC guarantee, whatever weights training produces. Forgetting is thus bounded by the gate's false-alarm rate, and its price is the gate's power: no update, gated or not, that changes as few protected outputs can change new-task outputs more often than the best test of that level tells new-task prompts from protected ones. On reinforcement-learning streams of up to five tasks, gated training keeps the earlier tasks and changes 3.3% of held-out chat responses, whereas ungated training changes 91.8%. Across seven models, the gain kept behind the gate follows its firing rate on new-task prompts, measured before training. The certificate covers the gated model as deployed, on the prompt distributions sampled for calibration, not against an adversary who searches for prompts that fire the gate.
bullets: Addresses forgetting of earlier skills, general chat, and refusals that is typically detected only after training.
Places each task update behind a classifier over frozen lower-layer features; when it does not fire, the original model is unchanged.
PAC calibration on unlabeled protected prompts bounds any protected-behaviour score change by the gate’s firing rate over a task stream.
On streams of up to five RL tasks, gated training changed 3.3% of held-out chat responses versus 91.8% for ungated training.
The guarantee applies to calibrated prompt distributions, not adversarially selected prompts; new-task gains depend on gate firing there.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses continual learning and forgetting in LLMs using a gating mechanism to bound behavior change, directly relevant to Adaptation and Memory and Language Foundation Models.
papers.title: FireGate: Bounding Behaviour Change Before Training in Continual RL Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: FireGate uses pre-training prompt gates to certify and limit behavioural changes during continual RL fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: In most LLM agents, weights are fixed after deployment, so new information must be retained in external memory. Existing approaches often rely on predefined records and fixed organizational rules, which cannot readily accommodate evolving tasks and interactions. This raises the question: can LLM agents organize their own memory using ordinary documents? We introduce self-organized memory (SoMem), a framework that stores memory in linked documents. The agent decides what to summarize, how to group related information, and when to revise existing topics, and every summary it produces stays linked to the original interactions as evidence. The runtime validates updates and automatically derives temporal, relational, and recent-memory views from the organized content. At query time, the agent chooses what to search and read, following document links and inspecting original evidence as needed. On LoCoMo, BEAM-100K, and LongMemEval-S, SoMem outperforms the strongest baseline by 2.66, 3.10, and 2.00 percentage points, respectively. The constructed memory can be reused across models, and additional reasoning effort can further improve answer quality. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of agents organizing and using their own persistent memory through ordinary documents. Code is available at: https://github.com/Qi202/SoMem.
bullets: Fixed model weights require agents to store new information in external memory, but predefined records and rules struggle with evolving tasks.
The agent decides what to summarize, how to group information, and when to revise topics, while linking summaries to original interactions as evidence.
Runtime validation and automatically derived temporal, relational, and recent-memory views support flexible retrieval and inspection.
SoMem outperforms the strongest baseline by 2.66, 3.10, and 2.00 percentage points on LoCoMo, BEAM-100K, and LongMemEval-S, respectively.
Organized memory can be reused across models, and additional reasoning effort can improve answer quality.

papers.selection_reason: Self-organized persistent memory for LLM agents using linked documents; directly fits LLM memory.
papers.title: Can LLM Agents Organize Their Own Memory?

papers.abstract: An answer can match the reference for a complete agent history even when the reader's visible history does not determine it. We study this distinction using executable device logs. Our protocol separates reference agreement, certified evidence sufficiency, and context-appropriate behavior. Insufficiency requires two legal histories yielding byte-identical visible contexts but different answers; public chronology and query cutoffs certify sufficient prefixes. On 80 confirmation histories, Qwen3-32B matches 87 hidden references among 203 insufficient raw-prefix instances, with only seven appropriate abstentions. A fixed-input DeepSeek-V4-Flash replication matches 85 and abstains on 21 of the same 203 instances. Each reader makes 1,600 requests. Compact CSV's estimated appropriateness effects remain inconclusive: +3.16 percentage points, clustered 95% interval [0.00,6.57], for Qwen and +2.46, [-1.84,6.94], for DeepSeek. A separate held-out judge study achieves 99.38% correctness but retains support errors and truncations; a deterministic baseline solves all constructed cases. These results support an evaluation diagnosis across two hosted reader configurations, not gains for a general memory system or natural-language evidence assessment.
bullets: Using executable device logs, the protocol tests whether visible histories uniquely determine the reference answer.
Insufficiency is certified by finding two legal histories with identical visible contexts but different answers; public chronology certifies sufficient prefixes.
On 203 insufficient raw-prefix instances, Qwen3-32B matched 87 hidden references and abstained appropriately only seven times; DeepSeek-V4-Flash matched 85 and abstained 21 times.
Compact CSV’s estimated appropriateness effects were inconclusive for both readers, and a separate judge study still showed support errors and truncations.
The findings diagnose evaluation issues across two hosted configurations, not improvements to a general memory system or natural-language evidence assessment.

papers.selection_reason: Controlled evaluation of agent memory sufficiency; directly relevant to LLM/agent memory research.
papers.title: Correct Answers from Insufficient Histories: A Controlled Study of Agent Memory Evaluation
papers.tldr: The study shows that correct answers can be unsupported by an agent’s visible history, motivating evaluations that separately measure answer agreement, evidence sufficiency, and appropriate abstention.

papers.abstract: Continual instruction tuning often preserves old skills with task-private modules. Inference still requires selecting the right module from the prompt alone. We introduce Task-Isolated Latent Adapter Continual Training (TILA-CT), a replay-free method that makes each task module self-indexing. Each task receives a latent memory and adapter bank in a frozen LLM. During adaptation, the memory gathers causal-prefix information and injects task-conditioned context. For access, its persistent state provides the routing prototype used by a shared prompt-only router. On the 8-task CT-Pipeline stream, TILA-CT achieves 65.19 acquisition and 63.98 final macro score, with 1.38 points of average forgetting. A middle-reversed order gives 65.38 acquisition and 64.17 final macro score. Across 6 backbones, final scores remain within 1.5 points of acquisition. Ablations support memory-derived routing keys and causal gathering. Final macro routing accuracy is 93.9\%, and oracle routing recovers 1.21 final macro points. These results separate preserved task computation from learned access to it.
bullets: Targets the access problem in continual instruction tuning: selecting the correct task module from a prompt alone.
Uses a frozen LLM with task-isolated latent memories and adapter banks; memories gather causal-prefix information and inject task-conditioned context.
The memories’ persistent states serve as routing prototypes for a shared prompt-only router.
On an 8-task CT-Pipeline stream, it reports 65.19 acquisition, 63.98 final macro score, and 1.38 average forgetting; results are similar under reversed task order.
Final macro routing accuracy is 93.9%, while oracle routing adds 1.21 final macro points, highlighting routing as a remaining limitation.

papers.selection_reason: Continual instruction tuning with self-indexing latent memories and prompt-only routing; fits continual learning and LLM memory.
papers.title: Self-Indexing Latent Memories for Access-Aware Continual Instruction Tuning of LLMs
papers.tldr: TILA-CT gives continual-learning task modules persistent latent memories that both preserve task-specific computation and enable prompt-only routing without replay.

papers.abstract: A deployed language model does not merely answer questions. It spends computation, consumes time, consults evidence, exposes memory, invites or avoids human review, and sometimes makes mistakes whose consequences are radically unequal. Yet LLM systems are still commonly compared as if the relevant object were a single model and the relevant outcome were a single benchmark score. This paper argues that the unit of analysis should instead be the deployment policy: the mechanism that decides when to retrieve, when to remember, when to call a larger model, when to verify, and when not to answer at all. We introduce risk-adjusted deployment efficiency (RADE), a system-level objective that scores the utility a deployment delivers net of inference, retry, oversight, and priced expected failure cost, while treating harms that cannot be priced as hard budgets alongside constraints on latency, privacy, and resources. The framework brings selective routing, retrieval and governed memory, efficient specialization, uncertainty estimation, abstention, and human escalation into a common account. We then examine five deployment regimes in which the same nominal LLM capability leads to different rational architectures, and propose a reporting protocol based on risk-coverage behavior, end-to-end cost, update drift, memory exposure, evidence quality, and escalation load. The central claim is modest but consequential: frontier capability should be treated as a resource to allocate, not a default state to maintain. A safe and sustainable system is not the one that always uses the strongest model; it is the one that spends capability where the reduction in risk or increase in utility justifies the cost.
bullets: Argues that deployment policy—not a standalone model or benchmark score—is the proper unit of analysis.
Defines risk-adjusted deployment efficiency as utility minus inference, retry, oversight, and priced expected-failure costs.
Treats unpriced harms, latency, privacy, and resource use as constraints or hard budgets.
Unifies routing, retrieval, governed memory, specialization, uncertainty estimation, abstention, and escalation.
Proposes reporting risk-coverage, end-to-end cost, update drift, memory exposure, evidence quality, and escalation load across five deployment regimes.

The figure is architectural rather than an empirical benchmark result.

papers.selection_reason: Framework for LLM deployment policies involving governed memory and routing aligns with LLM memory.
papers.title: RADE: Risk-Adjusted Deployment Efficiency, A Framework for Routing, Memory, and Escalation in Safe LLM Systems
papers.tldr: RADE evaluates LLM deployments as risk-aware policies that allocate computation, memory, retrieval, verification, and human review rather than always using the strongest model.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents acting across web applications and online services often need multi-turn corrections to align their work with users' underspecified goals and preferences. In practice, users may identify problems in the current outcome without specifying the desired result, so learning user intentions requires interpreting each correction against the agent's preceding and revised outcomes. These expectations are often connected to a particular context, making it hard to know when they apply and how to ensure the agent later acts as the user expects. To this end, we propose LiveAsset, an intent harness that learns reusable intent assets from corrective interactions and uses them for runtime control of agent execution. LiveAsset jointly interprets each correction with the agent's original and revised results to infer user intent, incrementally updating the assets while preserving earlier requirements that remain applicable. The learned requirements guide agent execution from task entry and provide criteria for runtime verification, which uses the explanations to assess applicability before each reply is delivered and directs the agent to revise the result to address unmet requirements while preserving those already satisfied. Following a learning phase in which simulated users progressively reveal requirements through multi-turn corrections, we evaluate LiveAsset using same-task replay of the original requests on π-Bench, PERMA, and Vita and cross-task transfer on PAST-Bench and SkillEvolBench. Experiments show that LiveAsset better fulfills requirements learned from corrective interactions and improves performance on these benchmarks compared with memory, skill, and rule-based harness baselines. Code is available at github.com/landian60/LiveAsset.
bullets: Addresses underspecified goals where users correct outcomes without explicitly stating the desired result.
Interprets each correction alongside the agent’s original and revised outputs to infer and incrementally update intent assets.
Guides execution from task entry and verifies each response, prompting revisions while preserving already satisfied requirements.
Evaluated through same-task replay and cross-task transfer across five benchmarks after simulated multi-turn requirement learning.
Outperforms memory-, skill-, and rule-based harness baselines in fulfilling requirements learned from corrections.

papers.abstract: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) improves multi-hop question answering, but deployed systems pay costs that research comparisons rarely measure: model calls at query time, building the graph, and removing documents correctly. We present Lightfoot, a GraphRAG system in which every entity, link, fact and synonym edge is a deterministic function of per-passage extractions that carry chunk-level provenance. Retrieval makes no language-model call, indexing makes one per passage, and deleting a document is a database transaction with no model calls: 14 seconds for 10% of an 11,402-passage corpus, after which the graph is identical to a fresh index of the surviving documents. On a corpus of near-duplicate names, HippoRAG 2's capped synonym lists leave 565 fewer edges than a rebuild, while Lightfoot remains exact. Under identical extraction, embedding and answer models on held-out questions of MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA, Lightfoot is competitive with HippoRAG 2: with Holm-corrected paired tests it is better on MuSiQue at recall@5 and recall@10 (+4.8 and +5.5 points) and on 2WikiMultiHopQA at recall@10 (+3.4), and tied on HotpotQA, while HippoRAG 2 keeps a non-significant 3.0-point edge at 2WikiMultiHopQA recall@2. Seeding the walk from entities named in the question accounts for most of the 2WikiMultiHopQA gain. Answers tie on all three datasets, and the retrieval pattern holds with three larger embedders, up to Qwen3-Embedding-8B. The gain is not the reranker's: with the same cross-encoder, dense retrieval trails Lightfoot by 9.3 and 17.8 points recall@5 on the two multi-hop sets. Lightfoot also builds the cheapest index, 26-31% below HippoRAG 2; LightRAG needed 2,187 model calls and 3.7 hours for the same deletion, and fast-graphrag cannot delete.
bullets: Targets deployment costs and correctness issues in graph construction, query-time model calls, and document deletion.
Builds graph entities, links, facts, and synonym edges deterministically from passage-level extractions with chunk provenance.
Uses no language-model calls during retrieval; indexing requires one call per passage, and deletion exactly reproduces a fresh index of remaining documents.
Competitive or better recall than HippoRAG 2 on MuSiQue and 2WikiMultiHopQA, tied on HotpotQA; answer performance ties across all three datasets.
Builds indexes 26–31% more cheaply than HippoRAG 2 and avoids deletion limitations or repeated model calls of alternatives.

papers.title: Lightfoot: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Exact, Model-Free Document Deletion

papers.abstract: Agents built on reasoning models resend their growing transcript at every call. Two transacting parties, not the model, decide what that costs: the client keeps or edits messages; the server decides whether earlier reasoning returns in the prompt and what its cache reuses. We define a cost model whose counts match an instrumented engine exactly; the architecture charges $c$ per token processed and $β$ per pair attended. Their ratio $P^*=c/β$ is an exchange rate between thinking and remembering: per token, processing dominates below this context length, a thinking regime, and attention above it, a memory regime. A policy change has a mechanical cost, incurred even if the agent writes the same tokens, and a behavioral one: it writes different tokens, changing cost and outcome. Serving alone can flip which policy is cheaper: on recorded Qwen3-8B ScienceWorld runs, dropping earlier reasoning costs 1.74 times keeping it when the server reuses generated states and 0.34 times when it reuses nothing. In live reruns, dropping it cuts correct HotpotQA answers by 9-23 percentage points on four models, at lower point-estimate cost. Comparing context policies means comparing systems: architecture and serving set the cost of the history kept and the work it induces.
bullets: Defines an exact cost model charging for processed tokens and attended token pairs, with an exchange rate separating thinking- and memory-dominated regimes.
Separates mechanical costs of a context policy from behavioral costs caused by the agent generating different reasoning and outcomes.
On recorded Qwen3-8B ScienceWorld runs, dropping earlier reasoning costs 1.74× as much with generated-state reuse but 0.34× as much without reuse.
Live reruns show that dropping earlier reasoning reduces correct HotpotQA answers by 9–23 percentage points across four models, despite lower point-estimate cost.
Context-policy comparisons must include the serving architecture because it determines the cost of retained history and induced computation.

papers.abstract: Long-term personalized agents are increasingly expected to answer queries over user histories in which preferences, goals, and constraints evolve across interleaved conversations. Existing retrieval-based and structured-memory systems can surface relevant facts, but often return isolated memory units that do not explain which earlier preference was refined, contradicted, or superseded by later evidence. We introduce TransMem, a transition-aware memory retrieval framework that stores preference updates as explicit retrieval units alongside ordinary factual memories. During memory construction, TransMem routes user interaction history into topic-structured memory graphs, detects shift events, and grounds them as transition records. At inference time, TransMem first retrieves factual anchors and then adaptively expands over transition records, producing a compact context of factual anchors and accepted transition records. Experiments on PersonaMem and PersonaBench across two Qwen backbones show that TransMem outperforms representative retrieval-based and structured-memory baselines. Controlled analyses further show that transition records and adaptive expansion contribute beyond factual anchoring, chronological expansion, flat transition retrieval, and fixed-hop traversal. These results suggest that preference-update records are useful retrieval units for long-term personalization.
bullets: Addresses the problem of evolving preferences, goals, and constraints that isolated memory retrieval fails to contextualize.
Builds topic-structured memory graphs and records detected preference shifts as explicit transition units.
Retrieves factual anchors first, then adaptively expands to relevant transition records for compact context.
Outperforms representative retrieval and structured-memory baselines on PersonaMem and PersonaBench across two Qwen backbones.
Analyses indicate benefits from transition records and adaptive expansion beyond several alternative retrieval strategies.

papers.abstract: Driven by increasingly complex real-world applications, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has evolved from textual pipelines to multimodal settings, comprising two complementary dimensions: knowledge organization and retrieval enhancement. However, existing methods still face challenges of high construction cost, context window limitations, and the lack of unified training across offline and online knowledge sources. To address these challenges, we propose MMGraph-Agent, a unified multimodal RAG framework based on cache-inspired multimodal knowledge hypergraphs. MMGraph-Agent enables extremely lightweight hypergraph construction with zero API cost and dynamic memory-based retrieval that alleviates long-context issues. Experiments across offline, online, and joint retrieval settings demonstrate consistent improvements in performance, efficiency, and architectural unification. Our software and data are publicly available at https://github.com/LHRLAB/MMGraph-Agent.
bullets: Targets multimodal RAG limitations in knowledge construction cost, context-window constraints, and disconnected offline/online knowledge handling.
Builds lightweight multimodal knowledge hypergraphs with zero API cost.
Uses dynamic, memory-based retrieval to alleviate long-context issues.
Supports offline, online, and joint retrieval within one unified architecture.
Experiments report consistent gains in performance and efficiency across these settings; software and data are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement-learning-trained agents for retrieval-augmented generation retrieve content (passages, knowledge-graph fragments, or hyperedges) and supervise training with outcome rewards on the final answer. Across these paradigms the reasoning route through retrieved content never leaves the language model's hidden state, conflating declarative knowledge with the procedural knowledge that recurs across queries of the same logical type; content-only methods consequently plateau as reasoning depth grows. We introduce PatternBloom, an agentic RAG framework that shifts the unit of retrieval from content (what to read) to logic (how to reason). A first RL stage scores the agent's constructed evidence graph by a frozen oracle's information gain through the Information-Density Reward (IDR), a size-normalized mutual-information surrogate. High-reward trajectories are distilled into a Graph Pattern Memory (GPM) of type-abstracted reasoning skeletons, and a second RL stage uses the Pattern-Augmented Reward (PAR) to couple policy to memory, turning procedural reasoning into a learnable, externalized structural prior. A 7B PatternBloom outperforms $27$ baselines by $+15.0$ Avg-OOD EM, with the gain compounding with reasoning depth precisely because procedural knowledge, once distilled, is reused rather than re-derived at every query. We release our code at https://github.com/EllenYiGe/PatternBloom.
bullets: Content-only retrieval conflates factual knowledge with recurring procedural reasoning, limiting performance on deeper reasoning tasks.
The framework retrieves abstract logic patterns rather than only passages, graph fragments, or hyperedges.
An RL stage builds evidence graphs scored by the Information-Density Reward, then distills high-reward trajectories into a Graph Pattern Memory.
A second RL stage uses the Pattern-Augmented Reward to integrate these procedural patterns into the agent’s policy.
A 7B model outperforms 27 baselines by 15.0 Avg-OOD EM, with gains increasing at greater reasoning depths.

papers.abstract: Model editing provides an efficient way to update factual knowledge in transformer models. Recent approaches reverse edits by modifying, masking, or decomposing model weights, but make recovery dependent on weight-space interventions. We instead show that pre-edit knowledge can be recovered through input-space interventions alone, without modifying the edited model's weights. We introduce Memento, a prompt-space mechanism for auditing residual knowledge that learns a reusable recovery signal to steer an edited model toward its pre-edit response. Memento supports both continuous recovery prefixes and discrete textual prompts for standard text interfaces. Across three LLMs and five editing techniques, Memento recovers 80.07% of held-out edited facts, achieving a 9.58% relative improvement over baselines, suggesting that editing may suppress the facts without fully eliminating their recoverability. We further investigate whether prompt-space recovery extends beyond model editing. On pristine, unedited LLMs, Memento improves average factual recall by 53.9% relative to standard inference. These results demonstrate the potential of prompt-space recovery for auditing residual knowledge in edited models and investigating the gap between factual knowledge and its accessibility during inference. We will release our source code.
bullets: Model-editing audits typically rely on modifying or analyzing model weights; this work uses input-space interventions instead.
Memento learns reusable recovery signals that steer edited models toward their pre-edit responses, via continuous prefixes or discrete prompts.
Across three LLMs and five editing methods, it recovered 80.07% of held-out edited facts, with a 9.58% relative improvement over baselines.
On unedited models, Memento improved average factual recall by 53.9% relative to standard inference.
The findings suggest editing can suppress factual accessibility without fully removing the underlying knowledge.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of MEMENTO’s continuous prompt-space recovery. The objective combines supervised recovery (Lrec), preference optimization (Lpref ), fluency preservation (Lflu), and distillation from the pre-edit model (Ldist). Gradients update only Π; the pre-edit model supplies distillation targets during training and is not needed at inference. Without the prefix, the edited LLM answers the edited object (o∗ = midfielder); with it, the LLM produces the original object (o = quarterback).

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can surface passages that support a claim, contradict it, or fail to address it, yet existing calibrated grounding methods are typically one-sided and model only supporting evidence. We introduce Conformal Evidence Sets (CES), a two-sided framework that returns separate support and refutation sets with finite-sample inclusion coverage of at least $1-α$ on each side under exchangeability; a Bonferroni union yields joint coverage of at least $1-2α$. On labeled candidate pools from the contrastive VitaminC benchmark, CES closely tracks nominal coverage across $α\!\in\!\{0.05,0.10,0.15,0.20,0.30\}$, with maximum deviations of $3.0$ percentage points for support and $5.4$ for refutation, and reaches essentially the same empirical coverage--size frontier as a test-tuned fixed-threshold heuristic without any test exposure. Stress tests mark the boundary of that guarantee: under FEVER distribution shift both sides under-cover, by up to $12.7$ percentage points, and support-side group-stratified recalibration substantially reduces the support gap. Scorer swaps, hard-negative retrieval, cross-dataset transfer, and a live end-to-end pilot expose a clear separation: when exchangeability holds and relevant evidence is retrieved, evidence inclusion remains calibrated even with an imperfect scorer, whereas the support/refute verdict tracks scorer quality directly. Calibrated evidence coverage and reliable verdicts are therefore distinct properties and should be reported separately.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of one-sided grounding methods that model only supporting evidence.
Returns separate support and refutation sets with at least 1−α finite-sample inclusion coverage per side; joint coverage is at least 1−2α via Bonferroni.
On VitaminC, empirical coverage closely follows nominal levels, with maximum deviations of 3.0 percentage points for support and 5.4 for refutation.
Under FEVER distribution shift, both sides under-cover by up to 12.7 percentage points; group-stratified support recalibration reduces the gap.
Evidence inclusion can remain calibrated despite imperfect scoring, while support/refute verdict quality depends directly on scorer quality.

papers.abstract: External state should become more valuable as a reader becomes more capable, yet long-context evaluations measure memory utility at a single model scale. This paper formulates scale complementarity: the absolute gain from external state increases when reader capacity and a compact state budget are jointly scaled. ASCENT realizes this principle with a target-blind causal writer, nested typed state, and a bounded query-conditioned readout; every language model remains frozen. Under log loss, the value of a nested refinement equals its target-relevant conditional information; a full factorial makes the reader-by-state interaction identifiable. Official 16K BABILong experiments show Qwen2.5 accuracy gains of 10.50, 78.88, and 82.63 percentage points at 0.5B, 1.5B, and 3B parameters, with both adjacent directional contrasts significant after family-wise correction. At 7B, Foundation accuracy rises to 33.25% while four-slot ASCENT answers every question, which caps the gain at 66.75 points; the 3B-to-7B accuracy increment is -15.88 points [-20.55, -11.20]. The accuracy-side claim is therefore established from 0.5B to 3B; the 7B conclusion rests on the non-saturated negative-log-likelihood factorial. A three-model by three-state factorial yields co-scaled negative log-likelihood gains of 0.388, 2.099, and 7.406 nats at 1.5B, 3B, and 7B; all interaction and gain contrasts retain positive simultaneous lower bounds. Five public 7B-8B readers obtain 66.75-85.63 point gains, and ASCENT exceeds task-trained retrieval checkpoints at the two larger shared scales. Controls, baselines, systems accounting, matched-hardware reproduction, and a cross-architecture sensitivity analysis accompany the experiments. The results establish scale-complementary external state under the evaluated benchmarks, metrics, and state schema.
bullets: Addresses the lack of scale-sensitive measurements of external-memory utility in long-context models.
Uses a target-blind causal writer, nested typed state, and bounded query-conditioned readout while keeping readers frozen.
Formalizes scale complementarity through conditional information and factorial reader-by-state interaction analysis.
On 16K BABILong, Qwen2.5 accuracy gains were 10.50, 78.88, and 82.63 percentage points at 0.5B, 1.5B, and 3B parameters.
Results support the claim from 0.5B–3B on accuracy and across 1.5B–7B on negative log likelihood, under the evaluated benchmarks, metrics, and state schema.

papers.abstract: Long-term conversational question answering can require several separated dialogue turns that support an answer only together. We introduce EviCover, a retrieval approach designed to retain this complementary evidence. It converts questions into observable evidence requirements, checks requirement coverage using retrieved source identifiers, and selects turns jointly. We track annotated support sets - the benchmark-labeled dialogue turns associated with each question - through retrieval, reranking, and final answer-generation context. We evaluate the baseline memory pipeline on generated, human-verified LoCoMo conversations and human-written REALTALK conversations, and examine EviCover on REALTALK's 108 multi-hop questions. Compared with the hybrid lexical/dense baseline, support-turn recall among 60 candidate turns rises from 0.526 to 0.575, and recall in the final ten-turn context rises from 0.349 to 0.379. The evidence funnel identifies separate discovery and selection failures, while paired answer evaluation shows that greater evidence recall does not yet establish a correctness gain. This analysis locates where complementary evidence is lost and distinguishes evidence retrieval from its use in answer generation.
bullets: Long-term conversational questions may require multiple separated dialogue turns jointly.
EviCover converts questions into evidence requirements, checks source coverage, and jointly selects turns.
Tracking annotated support sets reveals distinct evidence losses during retrieval, reranking, and context construction.
On REALTALK’s multi-hop questions, support-turn recall improves from 0.526 to 0.575 among candidates and from 0.349 to 0.379 in the final context.
Paired evaluation finds that better evidence recall alone does not establish more correct answers.

papers.abstract: Since large language model (LLM) agents rely on long-term memory, what they store now shapes what they do later. A memory manager decides how each input changes this memory and which records the agent acts on. It can fail in two ways: keeping a fact that has since changed (outdated memory), or storing a planted passage or injected instruction (memory poisoning). Most prior work studies them separately, yet they call for opposite write decisions, so no fixed write rule handles both. We therefore formalize memory robustness as handling both without doing worse on other inputs. Since accuracy checks only the answer, we measure robustness with evidence-conditioned accuracy (ECA), which also checks that the records the manager selects include all the evidence the answer needs, updated and free of attacks. However, existing memory systems and defenses are not more robust than an untuned manager on our test sets. We improve robustness with a simple one-shot recipe that fine-tunes the manager on episodes synthesized around a single conversation with inserted changes and attacks. On three backbones, it improves every category score on our test sets and more than doubles the untuned manager's overall ECA, though robustness remains incomplete.
bullets: LLM memory managers must handle two conflicting failures: retaining changed facts and storing injected or malicious content.
The paper introduces evidence-conditioned accuracy (ECA), which evaluates both answer correctness and whether selected memory contains complete, updated, attack-free evidence.
Existing memory systems and defenses are no more robust than an untuned manager on the authors’ test sets.
Fine-tuning on synthesized episodes built from a single conversation with inserted changes and attacks improves every tested category across three backbones.
The method more than doubles overall ECA versus the untuned manager, but robustness remains incomplete.

papers.selection_reason: Robust memory management for LLM agents addressing outdated and poisoned memory; fits LLM memory.
papers.title: Accept Changes, Reject Attacks: Robust Memory Management for LLM Agents
papers.tldr: A one-shot, episode-based fine-tuning recipe makes LLM-agent memory managers more robust to both outdated facts and memory-poisoning attacks, substantially improving evidence-conditioned accuracy while leaving room for improvement.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory enables large language model (LLM) agents to maintain personalized and temporally coherent interactions, but repeated LLM inference for memory admission, extraction, and organization introduces substantial cost and latency. We present SLICE-Mem, a lightweight memory framework that combines salience-guided admission and predicate-centered information extraction. A compact classifier identifies user turns worth retaining, and a semantic-dependency-based extractor converts admitted turns into concise memory entries. This online pipeline requires no generative LLM calls, while cross-entry reconciliation is deferred to an offline consolidation stage. We evaluate SLICE-Mem on the weekly subset of Memora and LongMemEval-S using 8B and 30B Qwen backbones for memory construction and consolidation on both benchmarks. Compared with the generative-memory baseline MemOS under the Qwen3-30B configuration, SLICE-Mem's online pipeline achieves 46.60 versus 46.68 FAMA (Forgetting-Aware Memory Accuracy) on Memora Weekly and 56.8% versus 59.3% accuracy on LongMemEval-S, while reducing total LLM token consumption by 92.4% and 99.5%, respectively. These results demonstrate that SLICE-Mem can preserve useful evidence for long-term memory with substantially less reliance on LLM-based memory construction.
bullets: Targets the cost and latency of repeated LLM inference for memory admission, extraction, and organization.
Uses a compact salience classifier to select user turns and a semantic-dependency extractor to create concise memory entries.
Runs online memory construction without generative LLM calls, deferring cross-entry reconciliation to offline consolidation.
On Memora Weekly and LongMemEval-S, it achieved near-baseline quality while reducing total LLM token consumption by 92.4% and 99.5%, respectively.
Quality was slightly below MemOS under Qwen3-30B: 46.60 vs. 46.68 FAMA on Memora Weekly and 56.8% vs. 59.3% accuracy on LongMemEval-S.
