papers.abstract: Language-model systems can separate contextual computation, persistent storage, and exact execution instead of updating all capabilities through one shared parameter system. We investigate FEM-ASM, a finite-element-method-inspired organization in which independently constructed document states and deterministic executable skills contribute typed proposals to a shared language-model state. An explicit residual operator reconciles proposals attached to common interface nodes. We evaluate this organization through controlled experiments and negative results rather than claiming a physical finite-element formulation of language. An attention-free Multi-Mesh prototype learns causal language modeling but does not establish competitive general capability. A versioned store contains 52,809 reconstructive memory elements near a 1.7-billion-floating-value budget; reconstruction is incomplete, with approximately 75\% token accuracy. Support-aware lexical indices make these elements addressable under provenance-controlled query construction. For executable arithmetic, positional result observations substantially improve neural rendering relative to a repeated global result vector, and output substitutions change the model's preferred answer. A bounded attachment demonstration further measures the effect of making selected evidence available, without establishing the utility of loading an entire multi-billion-value store. The results support a separation of storage, execution, and neural coordination, while identifying unresolved limitations in question-only retrieval, unrestricted answer generation, and end-to-end efficiency.
bullets: Uses independently constructed document states and deterministic executable skills that submit typed proposals to a shared model state.
An explicit residual operator reconciles proposals attached to common interface nodes.
An attention-free Multi-Mesh prototype supports causal language modeling, but does not demonstrate competitive general performance.
Reconstructive memory contains 52,809 elements with about 75% token accuracy; support-aware lexical indices enable provenance-controlled addressing.
Positional arithmetic-result observations improve neural rendering, while unresolved issues include incomplete retrieval, unrestricted generation, and end-to-end efficiency.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes separating persistent storage and executable skills in language-model systems, relevant to LLM memory and architecture.
papers.title: Beyond the Parameter Monolith: Reconstructive Memories, Executable Skills, and Residual Assembly for Language Models
papers.tldr: FEM-ASM explores separating language-model storage, execution, and coordination through reconstructive memories, executable skills, and residual proposal assembly, with promising component-level findings but no evidence of competitive general capability.

papers.abstract: Large language models reinvent the wheel all the time. They conflate task-solving with the execution of the solutions, which forces them to solve every problem from scratch. We show that once a task has been reasoned through, the application of its solution to a new problem instance can be done very efficiently and with little involvement from language models. We introduce agentic reasoning caching, a method for constructing robust CPU-executable agentic reasoning caches (ARCs) from LLM reasoning traces. ARCs show on-par performance with frontier LLMs across a range of difficult mathematical and scientific tasks, are fully explainable, continually trainable, robust to input perturbations, and 16-291x cheaper to invoke than the source model.
authors: Peter Belcak, Greg Heinrich, Saurav Muralidharan, Shizhe Diao, Pavlo Molchanov
bullets: Separates task-solving from applying a previously derived solution to new instances.
Constructs agentic reasoning caches (ARCs) from LLM reasoning traces for CPU execution.
Matches frontier LLM performance across difficult mathematical and scientific tasks.
ARCs are explainable, continually trainable, and robust to input perturbations.
Reported invocation cost is 16–291× lower than the source model.

papers.title: CPU-ARC: Agentic Reasoning Caching for on-CPU Reasoning Reuse
papers.tldr: CPU-ARC reuses LLM-derived reasoning through explainable, CPU-executable caches, achieving frontier-level performance at 16–291× lower invocation cost.

papers.abstract: A conversational agent that remembers has to decide what to keep. Retrieval-augmented generation keeps the transcript and searches it; the alternative is to compact each turn into atomic facts and search those. We compare the two on LoCoMo, with both arms answering all 1,985 questions in one window, against the same stores, with the same generator and judge, and both predictions on one row, which licenses McNemar's exact test on the 512 questions where they disagree. On the four categories comparable work reports, compaction scores 71.4 per cent against 64.6, a lead of 6.8 points (p = 5.5e-08) at 34 per cent fewer prompt tokens. On all five, including the adversarial set comparable work drops, the lead falls to 2.0 and stops being significant, because the baseline leads adversarial by 14.6. That loss has a structure. Our lead falls as the reference answer demands more source wording, 9.6 points ahead at one or two reference words and 3.1 behind past eight, with token overlap moving the same way, so the judge is not the cause. Compaction keeps what a fact asserts and discards how it was said, so it wins where the answer is a value and loses where it is a phrasing. We also report four negative results with their power calculations.
authors: Osamudiamen Edogun, Joshua Obigwe, Irfan Mehmood
bullets: On four comparable LoCoMo categories, compaction scored 71.4% versus 64.6% for retrieval-augmented generation, using 34% fewer prompt tokens.
Across all five categories, the advantage fell to 2.0 points and was not significant because retrieval performed better on the adversarial set.
Compaction’s lead declined as answers required more source wording: from 9.6 points for one or two reference words to 3.1 points behind beyond eight.
The paired evaluation used identical stores, generator, and judge, with McNemar’s exact test on 512 disagreements.
The approach preserves asserted facts but loses the original phrasing, limiting performance on wording-sensitive questions.

papers.selection_reason: Directly studies persistent conversational memory for LLMs against retrieval-augmented generation.
papers.title: Compaction, decay and reinforcement in a two-tier conversational memory: a paired evaluation against retrieval-augmented generation
papers.tldr: Compacting conversational turns into atomic facts improves answers and reduces prompt length for value-based questions, but retrieval of the original transcript is better when exact wording matters.

papers.abstract: LLM agents benefit from using memory systems to improve performance on long-horizon, multi-session tasks. However, memory introduces a critical attack surface. Malicious instructions encountered in one session may be stored and propagated through memory before being retrieved and acted upon in later sessions. Because memory systems differ in how they process and retrieve information, the downstream effects of poisoning can vary significantly across systems. To quantify the effects of poisoning across different memory architectures, we introduce MemoryDojo, a benchmark for tracing the lifecycle of poisoned information through agent memory and measuring its influence on subsequent agent behavior. MemoryDojo is easily extensible, consists of 155 multi-session long-horizon trajectories covering four domains, and supports five different memory systems. Through our evaluation, we find that all memory systems are susceptible to memory poisoning, with substantial variation in downstream effects. We further propose a memory-aware poison optimization process that increases the poisoning efficacy, highlighting differences between memory architectures. We hope that MemoryDojo will support research on understanding and mitigating agentic memory risks.
authors: David H. Yang, Blake Bullwinkel, Amanda Minnich, Mohammad Mohammadi Amiri, Giorgio Severi
bullets: Targets memory poisoning in long-horizon, multi-session LLM agents.
Provides 155 trajectories across four domains and supports five memory systems.
Traces poisoned information from storage through retrieval to downstream agent behavior.
Finds all evaluated memory systems are susceptible, with substantial variation in impact.
Introduces memory-aware poison optimization that increases poisoning efficacy.￼

figures.caption: Figure 1: MemoryDojo overview. Task trajectories are generated from 4 different domains and user-AI conversations are optionally added. Execution is done through a repeated retrieve-interactwrite cycle. Poison enters one tool result at the marked session t0, and can be written into memory. Different metrics capture the lifecycle effects of the poisoning.

Figure 4: Memory-aware poison optimization. An LLM optimizer revises candidate payloads p using a memory-system description, an attack objective ψ, and feedback from auxiliary runs. Behavioral outcomes, coarse memory evidence, and failure summaries guide subsequent revisions.

papers.abstract: Existing time series language models predominantly follow an offline, one-shot paradigm: they process fixed-length inputs independently and do not retain past states. This static approach fundamentally misaligns with the continuous nature of real-world streaming applications and fails to maintain the historical context necessary for cross-window reasoning. To bridge this gap, we introduce Continuous & Live Time Series Understanding (CL-TSU), a novel paradigm that shifts the focus toward maintaining a persistent, stateful understanding over open-ended data streams. To systematically evaluate this paradigm, we present LiveTS-Suite, the first comprehensive data suite tailored for CL-TSU, supporting data generation, model training, and systematic evaluation across 18 tasks spanning six core capabilities. It comprises over 5K streams totaling 2.2B timesteps, annotated with 15K specific response events. We further design an evaluation protocol that jointly assesses response timeliness, content accuracy, and computational efficiency. Building on this foundation, we propose TimeOmni-Live, the first live time series understanding model. It integrates a hybrid time series encoding for natively temporal input, a stream-persistent hybrid memory mechanism to effectively preserve exact historical evidence and long-term task states, and an elastic stream-inference synchronization strategy to reduce processing lag. Evaluations show that TimeOmni-Live establishes a strong baseline for CL-TSU, outperforming frontier LLMs (90.0 vs. 79.3 for Opus 5) with only 4B parameters and achieving 206$\times$ lower p95 latency than its backbone. Deployment on a Jetson edge device further shows its ability to support real-time continuous temporal understanding locally at the edge.
authors: Tong Guan, Alexander Chemeris, Yiqing Guo, Warren Jin, Zhao Li, Shirui Pan, Ming Jin
bullets: Introduces Continuous & Live Time Series Understanding (CL-TSU), replacing offline one-shot processing with persistent stateful reasoning over open-ended streams.
Presents LiveTS-Suite: 18 tasks across six capabilities, covering over 5K streams, 2.2B timesteps, and 15K response events.
Combines hybrid temporal encoding, persistent memory for historical evidence and task states, and elastic inference synchronization to reduce lag.
Reports a score of 90.0 versus 79.3 for Opus 5, with 206× lower p95 latency than its backbone using a 4B-parameter model.
Demonstrates real-time continuous understanding on a Jetson edge device.

papers.abstract: Language-model agents use experience through external retrieval and parameter learning. Consolidating stored experience into model weights requires deciding both which experience to train on and when its external records can leave retrieval. Admission based solely on student mastery can exclude useful teacher demonstrations, while removal immediately after training can discard guidance that the model still needs. We introduce ENGRAM, a framework that separates training admission from memory release. A demonstration-aware gate admits skills based on student mastery or sufficient successful teacher demonstrations. The student learns from selected action traces with context from an Engram Trace Graph (ETG). A verification gate then compares the updated model without episodic retrieval against the base model with retrieval on reserved probes. Release requires valid training participation and scores meeting both relative and absolute criteria; records for skills that fail verification remain retrievable. Experiments across interactive and reasoning benchmarks show consistent gains over frozen-weight ETG controls, with ablations supporting demonstration-aware admission and selective adapter activation. A controlled held-out comparison shows that verified release substantially reduces the retrievable footprint while remaining close to retain-all performance and outperforming immediate and budget-matched random release. ENGRAM also improves task performance while reducing input-token usage and model calls. Skill-level verification further reduces retrievable experience through selective archival, retaining external guidance for skills that do not meet the release criteria. Code is available in anonymous.4open.science/r/engram-anonymous.
authors: Ruiyi Yang, Zechen Li, Lihuan Li, Du Yin, Hao Xue, Flora D. Salim
bullets: Separates training admission from memory release to avoid discarding useful demonstrations or guidance prematurely.
Uses a demonstration-aware gate, Engram Trace Graph context, and selected action traces for training.
Releases records only after reserved-probe verification meets relative and absolute criteria; failed skills remain retrievable.
Reduces the retrievable-memory footprint while staying close to retain-all performance and outperforming immediate or random release.
Improves task performance while reducing input-token usage and model calls across interactive and reasoning benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Knowledge Graphs (KGs) and Large Language Models (LLMs) represent two approaches for knowledge representation and reasoning over heterogeneous data. Recent research has explored their integration through Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) systems, which use KGs to provide structured context to LLMs. However, existing GraphRAG approaches treat KGs as homogeneous graphs and rely on textual similarity between the input prompt and the context, rather than using it as a source of deterministic knowledge. This work proposes an agent-based GraphRAG system that introduces a symbolic layer to integrate deterministic reasoning alongside text similarities. This approach is based on the definition of typed centralities for KGs, where centrality measures are computed separately for each specific KG's class. This information is used to construct a symbolic representation that is provided to the LLM as a deterministic source. The proposed system was mathematically validated and evaluated on a real-world POLE (Person, Object, Location, Event) dataset, comparing reasoning and information retrieval with and without the symbolic layer. The results indicate that the our approach leads to responses that are more consistent with the context, improving the generated outputs.
authors: Rosario Napoli, Antonio Celesti, Massimo Villari, Maria Fazio
bullets: Addresses the limitation of treating knowledge graphs as homogeneous and relying mainly on text similarity.
Computes centrality measures separately for each knowledge-graph class, such as Person, Object, Location, and Event.
Provides the resulting symbolic representation to an LLM alongside retrieved context.
Mathematically validates the approach and evaluates it on a real-world POLE dataset.
Reports improved consistency with context for reasoning and information-retrieval outputs when using the symbolic layer.

papers.abstract: Persistent-memory systems choose not only which records are retrieved but which prior information can alter current inference. We propose Jacobian-causal memory control (JCMC), which represents each authorized memory intervention by a predicted influence signature in a shared behavioral measurement space, selects interventions against a target effect and side-effect budget, and compares predicted with observed effects before retaining or rolling back the intervention. Under explicit smoothness and bounded-estimation assumptions, we prove a quadratic local-approximation bound, characterize the target effects reachable by a set of signatures, bound selection regret under signature error, and bound non-additive interactions between simultaneous memories. The paper reports no benchmark measurements; it defines a paired counterfactual estimator and an evaluation protocol comparing JCMC with relevance, graph, and policy-filtered retrieval baselines. The central claim is narrowed or falsified if those simpler baselines match effect targeting, side-effect control, and rollback utility under equal model, memory, policy, and cost budgets.
bullets: Addresses the problem of deciding which authorized memories should alter current language-model inference, beyond simple retrieval.
Predicts each memory’s influence signature in a shared behavioral measurement space and selects interventions under target-effect and side-effect constraints.
Uses paired counterfactual estimates to compare predicted and observed effects, retaining or rolling back interventions accordingly.
Provides theoretical bounds for local approximation error, reachable target effects, selection regret, and interactions among simultaneous memories.
No benchmark results are reported; the proposed evaluation compares JCMC with relevance-, graph-, and policy-filtered retrieval under matched budgets.

papers.abstract: Conversational recommender systems often treat user sessions in isolation, limiting their ability to capture how user intent evolves over time. While large language models (LLMs) have improved semantic understanding, they are typically used as isolated components, without addressing how memory, retrieval, and decision-making should be integrated at the system level. In this work, we propose a memory-aware multi-agent architecture for conversational recommendation, in which LLMs act as orchestration layers that coordinate intent refinement, query construction, and interaction flow. A key design principle is the integration of long-term memory as a first-class component, influencing both routing decisions and semantic query formation. We evaluate the system through cross-session memory experiments, multi-turn conversational simulations, and supervisor-driven interaction studies on the Amazon Reviews dataset. Results show that memory-enabled interactions recover up to 63\% of the gap toward explicit-query scenarios and prevent semantic degradation in extended dialogues. In addition, supervisory orchestration increases user acceptance by +28.9 percentage points, highlighting the importance of structured orchestration in guiding interaction and output quality. We also observe an exposure bottleneck between retrieved candidates and displayed recommendations. While LLM-reranking does not improve Hit@K, it consistently enhances semantic consistency and diversity. To capture these effects, we introduce the Semantic Consistency Score (SCS), a complementary evaluation measure. Overall, the results emphasize the importance of system-level design choices, suggesting that effective conversational recommendation benefits from explicit memory integration, orchestration, and evaluation beyond traditional ranking metrics.
authors: Emilly Pitman de Castro, Vanessa Silva, Gustavo Kanno, Marcus Santos, Bruno Ferraz do Amaral, Marcelo Nogueira, Lucas Francisco Pellicer, Lucas Lanaro, Pedro Augusto Luiz, Jo\~ao Renato Ribeiro Manesco, Giovanni Carbinatti, Isabela de Lima Santos, Lucas Oliveira Jeronymo, Jeison Fappi, Raul Rotilli Aguirre, Fabio Andr\'e Frantz, Renata De Paris, Fabiana Marucci, Lohan Silva, Vinicius Diniz Reolon, Wandemberg Gibaut
bullets: Targets session-isolated recommenders that fail to track evolving user intent and lack system-level integration of memory, retrieval, and decision-making.
Uses LLMs to orchestrate intent refinement, query construction, routing, and interaction flow, with long-term memory informing these processes.
Evaluated on Amazon Reviews through cross-session memory experiments, multi-turn simulations, and supervisor-driven interactions.
Memory recovers up to 63% of the gap toward explicit-query scenarios, while supervisory orchestration raises user acceptance by 28.9 percentage points.
LLM reranking does not improve Hit@K but improves semantic consistency and diversity; the proposed Semantic Consistency Score captures these effects and exposes an exposure bottleneck.

papers.abstract: LLM agents do not learn from corrections across sessions. A user fixes the same mistake at the start of every conversation. Existing agent memory systems primarily handle facts, such as preferences, entities, and conversational history, rather than procedural knowledge. We present Forge Decision Context (forge_dc), a system that captures behavioral signals from human corrections and self-assessed tool-call failures, compiles them into imperative RULE directives, and injects them at the decision points where they apply. We evaluate forge_dc alongside four predecessor approaches on DC-Bench, a new benchmark of 71 scenarios across nine behavioral dimensions, built from real executed agent traces in a deterministic mocked-tool environment. forge_dc reaches 95% compliance, up from 55% with naive retrieval, while injecting approximately 10 times fewer tokens per query. Across the five-stage progression, the strongest systems represent behavioral memory as explicit directives and deliver it at the decision points where it applies. The results identify representation, activation, and placement as central design choices for persistent behavioral learning.
bullets: Targets persistent procedural learning, addressing repeated user corrections that existing fact-focused memory systems fail to retain.
Captures human corrections and self-identified tool-call failures, then compiles them into imperative RULE directives.
Evaluated on DC-Bench: 71 scenarios spanning nine behavioral dimensions in a deterministic mocked-tool environment.
Achieves 95% compliance versus 55% for naive retrieval while using roughly 10× fewer tokens per query.
Finds that behavioral-memory representation, activation, and placement are key design choices.

papers.abstract: Financial institutions construct knowledge graphs (KGs) from shared SEC 10-Ks to serve risk analysis, portfolio management, and investment research, whose analytical needs differ. Extraction must adapt without fragmenting shared grounding, typing, and temporal rules. Hand-authored persona prompts and fine-tuning add cost. Weight-free prompt optimization offers an alternative, but unconstrained evolution of a monolithic prompt can rewrite shared rules alongside persona guidance, obscuring changes and complicating review. We introduce FinEvolveKG, a KG-construction harness separating reusable general and persona-policy blocks and mechanically confining GEPA, a reflective prompt optimizer, to the designated block. During persona adaptation, the approved general block remains byte-stable and every optimizer edit is localized to a separately versioned persona policy. A dual objective balances generic temporal-KG quality with persona-relevant facts, motifs, and multi-hop connectivity. We evaluate five mutation scopes on ticker-disjoint 10-K splits, with three seeds for the persona-conditioned arms (v3-v5) across three personas. On the three-seed mean, the complete two-stage block-constrained workflow (v4) improves over the frozen prompt baseline (v1) by 19.4-30.9% and over the tested unconstrained full-prompt workflow (v5) by 2.2-6.4%, leading v5 on both objective components and winning all nine paired-seed comparisons with the lowest seed variance in every persona. Without further optimization, v4 also exceeds v5 across all evaluated out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts. An SME audit supports using the generated triplets as ground truth; a blinded two-SME audit favors v4 over v5 in 70.1% of contrast-enriched judgments. These results show that mechanically attributable evolution can coexist with strong empirical performance, without attributing the gains causally to the boundary.
authors: Abhinav Arun, Jayita Bhattacharyya, Fabrizio Dimino, Bhaskarjit Sarmah, Stefano Pasquali
bullets: Addresses the need to adapt KG extraction to different financial personas without changing shared grounding, typing, and temporal rules.
Separates general and persona-policy prompt blocks, mechanically confines GEPA edits to the persona block, and versions each change.
Optimizes a dual objective covering generic temporal-KG quality and persona-specific facts, motifs, and multi-hop connectivity.
Across three personas and ticker-disjoint 10-K splits, the complete workflow improves over the frozen baseline by 19.4–30.9% and over the unconstrained workflow by 2.2–6.4%.
It also shows lower seed variance, wins all nine paired-seed comparisons, and remains stronger under evaluated OOD shifts; the authors do not claim the boundary itself caused the gains.

papers.abstract: Longitudinal relational agents rely on memory for continuity, but remembering can lead to intrusion, clinical overconfidence, emotional manipulation, and opacity. We present Relic, a governance architecture for diegetic relational agents, and Gumi, a subject-specific companion agent initialized and governed through Relic. The architecture separates what the system can observe, what researchers can review, what Gumi can remember, and what Gumi can say. We describe three mechanisms. Relic represents sensitive safety signals as researcher-facing governance objects rather than user-facing explanations or agent memories. Shared Continuity Memory organizes relational markers around subject-confirmed wording, corrections, explicit follow-up permissions, and recall limits. We specify a runtime mediation layer for delivery, proactivity, session identity, output transformation, and platform allowlists; adoption across live paths remains partial. These mechanisms aim to preserve relational continuity without turning Gumi into a clinical assistant, mood tracker, general-purpose assistant, or opaque profiling system. We contribute the architecture, object model, researcher workbench design, and a proposed evaluation framework for governed relational memory. An exploratory pilot involved the author as P1 and one external participant as P2. Weekly self-reports from P1 and researcher-led interviews with P2 provide descriptive observations of early use and perceived naturalness. The pilot does not support claims about clinical efficacy, diagnosis, therapeutic outcomes, general usability, or deployment safety. Relic provides research infrastructure intended to make relational memory, safety constraints, and agent behavior inspectable and testable.
bullets: Addresses risks of longitudinal memory, including intrusion, emotional manipulation, clinical overconfidence, and opacity.
Introduces Gumi, a subject-specific companion governed by Relic, with separate layers for observation, researcher review, agent memory, and user-facing speech.
Uses researcher-facing safety objects, consent- and correction-centered continuity memory, and runtime mediation for delivery, proactivity, identity, output, and platform access.
Provides an architecture, object model, researcher workbench, and proposed evaluation framework; adoption across live paths remains partial.
An exploratory pilot with two participants offers descriptive observations only and does not establish clinical efficacy, general usability, or deployment safety.

papers.abstract: The vast amount of information available in lengthy, distributed documents makes finding relevant answers difficult, especially when the answer requires connecting evidence from multiple sources. Standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems often struggle with this type of "multi-hop" reasoning and frequently face issues with context fragmentation. In this paper, we propose a hybrid RAG framework that integrates the structured reasoning of knowledge graphs with the broad semantic coverage of dense vector retrieval. Our approach employs a multi-stage pipeline using transformer-based summarization and semantic chunking to improve context retention. We construct a dynamic knowledge graph to capture explicit relationships between entities while simultaneously maintaining a dense vector index. During inference, the system uses a hierarchical mechanism that prioritizes graph traversal for precision and falls back to vector retrieval when necessary. We evaluated our framework on the MultiHop-RAG dataset. The results show that this hybrid approach outperforms standalone vector and graph-based baselines, achieving higher Exact Match scores and improved retrieval accuracy for complex queries. This confirms that merging structured reasoning with standard vector retrieval creates a more robust system for handling complex knowledge-intensive questions.
bullets: Addresses context fragmentation and difficulty linking evidence across distributed, lengthy documents.
Uses transformer-based summarization and semantic chunking to retain relevant context.
Builds a dynamic knowledge graph alongside a dense vector index.
Prioritizes graph traversal for precise retrieval, with vector search as a fallback.
Outperforms standalone graph- and vector-based baselines on MultiHop-RAG in Exact Match and retrieval accuracy.

papers.abstract: Reusable skills guide large language model (LLM) agents through recurring requests, but each invocation still requires the model to interpret the skill and reconstruct its orchestration. Can agents automatically compile this orchestration into an executable fast path without human intervention? We first study zero-shot skill specialization, which compiles without execution evidence, and find that despite the skill's procedural guidance, incorrect assumptions about runtime bindings can make generated plans brittle and recovery costly. This motivates SkillCache, a one-trace skill specialization method that compiles a completed invocation into a parameterized capsule of programs and natural-language steps, replays it before reuse, and drives it with a plan executor that returns control to the model only when needed, keeping the source skill for recovery. With the Claude Code harness, warm execution of the same request reduces tokens on 87 SkillsBench tasks by 81% with Claude Sonnet 4.6 and by 74% with Claude Opus 4.8 at comparable reward, and capsules stay effective under controlled request changes. Capsules also transfer across models, raising three open-weight models' mean reward by 12-25 percentage points while reducing their tokens by 72-81%, suggesting that execution-grounded compilation is a promising approach to efficient repeated skill use and cross-model transfer.
bullets: Zero-shot skill specialization can be brittle because it may misjudge runtime bindings, making recovery costly.
SkillCache uses one completed trace to create a parameterized capsule combining programs and natural-language steps.
A plan executor replays capsules and returns control to the model only when needed, while retaining the original skill for recovery.
Across 87 SkillsBench tasks, warm execution reduced token use by 81% with Claude Sonnet 4.6 and 74% with Claude Opus 4.8 at comparable reward.
Capsules remained effective under controlled request changes and transferred across models, improving mean reward while reducing token use.

papers.abstract: LLM-based medical assistants that follow a patient across visits need a memory that keeps the patient's clinical state correct as it changes. We examine the errors of five memory systems on longitudinal medical dialogue and find three recurring causes: the retrieved evidence gives an outdated state, includes another person's health facts, or lacks a safety fact the answer depends on. We present MedGraph, a graph memory built for these three cases. Construction extracts dated facts from each session, attributes each fact to the person it describes, and links medication, diagnosis, and measurement records into chains that keep earlier states. Retrieval ranks the patient's chains as units, reads each chain at the time the question asks about, and adds the original dialogue text; a patient profile lists every recorded safety fact with every question. On MedMemoryBench, MedGraph has the highest overall accuracy with both a GPT and a Qwen backbone, 10.5 and 10.4 points above the strongest of five baselines, with efficient memory construction and answering in the GPT setting.
bullets: Existing memory failures stem from outdated evidence, mixing patients’ facts, and missing safety-critical information.
MedGraph extracts dated facts, assigns them to the correct person, and links diagnoses, medications, and measurements into state chains.
Retrieval selects the relevant patient chains at the time asked about, supplements them with original dialogue, and checks recorded safety facts.
On MedMemoryBench, it achieved the highest accuracy with both GPT and Qwen backbones, outperforming the strongest baseline by 10.5 and 10.4 points.
The study focuses on longitudinal medical dialogue and reports efficient construction and answering in the GPT setting.

(b) Retrieval: the system ranks the patient’s records, treating each chain as one unit and each fact outside a chain as an individual unit. For selected chains, it includes the matched fact, the state at the requested time, and the preceding record. It also adds causally linked facts, records from any explicitly requested date window, and original dialogue excerpts. The answer model receives the question, the assembled evidence, and the patient profile (L3), then generates an answer in one LLM call.

papers.abstract: AI agents store text as embedding vectors and compress them at scale. A compression is accepted when each item's nearest neighbors survive, but agents also consolidate, delete, and compare memories, tasks that depend on which items lie far apart. We evaluate both ends with two label-free fidelities from our prior work: the local fidelity $L$ at 10 neighbors and the global fidelity $G$ at 30 to 50 percent of the memory. At 96 bytes per passage, rescored binary codes reach an $L$ of 0.97 yet move 10.1 percent of passages to another theme; PCA with 8-bit codes, at an $L$ of 0.77, moves 1.7 percent. Rescoring leaves the stored codes, and thus $G$, unchanged. We prove that across the $G$ band, $1-ν_k$ is at most 2 to 2.18 times the square root of the near-far rank-violation rate, and that this rate follows the distance noise of the compression (correlation 0.979). Our locality-aware quantization (LAQ) turns the bound into a hinge objective on the codebooks of an OPQ index, keeping its bytes, rotation, and search. To our knowledge, LAQ is the first quantizer whose objective comes from a proven bound on the far end. Reconstruction alone raises $G$ in 0 of 52 held-out runs; the far hinge raises it in all 52. LAQ raises $G$ in all 52 ($p=8.5\times 10^{-4}$ over 13 memory-encoder groups), including the external FinDER memory, has the highest $G$ of seven equal-size quantizers in all 12 Multi-Doc-2025 runs, scales to a million passages, and keeps evidence recall.
bullets: Nearest-neighbor preservation alone can miss large-scale structural errors: high local fidelity may still move many passages between themes.
The study evaluates local fidelity at 10 neighbors and global fidelity across 30–50% of the memory.
A bound links global fidelity to near–far rank violations, which closely track compression distance noise.
Locality-aware quantization (LAQ) adds a far-end hinge objective to OPQ codebooks while preserving bytes, rotation, and search.
LAQ improved global fidelity in all 52 held-out runs, led seven equal-size quantizers in all 12 Multi-Doc-2025 runs, scaled to one million passages, and preserved evidence recall.

papers.selection_reason: Compression of AI agent memory with local/global fidelity guarantees; relevant to LLM/agent memory and adaptation.
papers.title: Enhancing Local and Global Structure in Compressed AI Agent Memory
papers.tldr: LAQ improves global as well as local fidelity in compressed AI-agent memory by optimizing quantization against a proven far-rank bound, without increasing storage or changing search.

papers.abstract: Much of human culture is tacit and is typically learned through situated social interaction. As LLMs are deployed as interactive agents across diverse communities, assessing their cultural competence demands moving beyond existing question-answering approaches, shifting from what they know to how they adapt. In this work, we broaden the scope of cultural adaptation in NLP by investigating whether LLMs can adapt through repeated interactions via a sandbox environment. By reframing cultural adaptation as a continuous process of norm assimilation through social interaction, our work demonstrates that memory mechanisms foster longitudinal learning across repeated interactions, facilitate transfer to different social settings, and enable multilingual norm assimilation across five languages. Together, our findings lay the groundwork for continuous, interaction-driven cultural adaptation in LLMs.
bullets: Frames cultural adaptation as continuous norm assimilation through situated interaction.
Uses a sandbox environment to study adaptation over repeated interactions.
Finds that memory mechanisms support longitudinal learning and transfer across social settings.
Demonstrates multilingual norm assimilation across five languages.
Establishes a foundation for continuous, interaction-driven cultural adaptation in LLMs.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a standard approach to enhance the reliability of large language model (LLM) outputs by retrieving documents relevant to a query and supplying them in the LLM prompt. Today's RAG systems collect, index, and serve these documents from centralized stores. In practice, however, documents are owned by organizations, devices, and individuals who cannot or will not surrender custody of them to a central party, e.g., because of privacy, copyright or regulatory compliance. Existing modern decentralized retrieval techniques either reintroduce a coordinating authority, or rely on a global data structure that requires continuous network-wide coordination (e.g., DHTs). We present ZeroRAG, a decentralized routing layer for document retrieval in RAG that performs semantic query routing across an overlay of peers with- out global data structures or centralized orchestration. Documents remain with the peers that own them, and each peer keeps only lightweight local state: a bounded set of neighbor advertisements and a cache of recently routed queries. Using these, ZeroRAG steers each query through a best-first walk that progressively rewires the overlay toward semantically relevant neighbors, so recall improves over time as the network self-organizes. We evaluate ZeroRAG using three real-world workloads and two decentralized baselines. We find that ZeroRAG outperforms baselines in terms of recall and required network messages, approaches the recall and LLM answer accuracy of a centralized document store, self-heals after catastrophic peer failures, and scales to 100 000 peers.
bullets: Addresses privacy, copyright, and compliance constraints that prevent centralizing document ownership.
Uses lightweight neighbor advertisements and cached query history for semantic peer routing.
A best-first walk progressively rewires the overlay toward relevant peers, improving recall through self-organization.
Across three real-world workloads, ZeroRAG outperforms decentralized baselines on recall and network-message cost.
It approaches centralized-store recall and LLM answer accuracy, self-heals after catastrophic failures, and scales to 100,000 peers.

papers.abstract: Memory summaries, prompts and steering vectors set a language model's beliefs and are judged by the prediction they produce. A prediction does not say how firmly it is held. We separate a belief's content, what it predicts now, from its weight, the number of new observations it is worth: for an ideal observer, the amount of evidence behind it. In Bernoulli inference we set beliefs in nine open-weight models of 8 to 397B parameters and follow each belief with the same new observations. We argue that these models hold an answer without its evidence and recover its weight from the text they re-read. Weight therefore follows the form of the evidence and the question asked more than its amount: matched on their current estimate, a record of observations and a summary of its counts usually move apart under the same new observations, in either direction. Scale does not close the gap. Across the nine models 64 observations are worth 20 to 53 as a record and 9 to 151 as a summary, no closer to 64 at 397B than at 8B. Where no text stands behind a belief there is little to re-read: a steering vector can install a record's answer, and sixteen observations undo it where a neutral passage leaves it in place. Where reasoning first writes the counts into the context the weight returns, and the same 64 observations are worth 58 to 67 in either form. A matched answer is not a matched belief, and methods that set beliefs should be judged by the futures they produce.
bullets: The study separates belief content—what a model predicts—from belief weight—how much new evidence should change that prediction.
Across nine open-weight models, beliefs with matched current estimates diverge under identical Bernoulli observations when represented as raw records versus summaries.
Models often recover evidential weight from text they reread, rather than retaining it intrinsically with the answer.
Steering vectors can install a belief’s answer without its supporting evidence, making it easier to overturn; reasoning that writes counts into context restores the weight.
The findings suggest belief-setting methods should be evaluated by the futures they produce, not only by immediate predictions.

papers.selection_reason: Separates belief content from evidence weight in LLM memory and steering; relevant to LLM memory and reasoning.
papers.title: Same Answer, Different Future: Dissociating Belief Content and Evidence Weight in Language Models
papers.tldr: Language models can produce the same answer while assigning different evidential weight to it, and this hidden weight depends more on the belief’s textual origin and framing than on model scale.

papers.abstract: Conversational agents can retrieve information directly or delegate retrieval to a subagent. This design choice affects how retrieval history is maintained, what context each model call receives, and what information must be re-retrieved in follow-up questions. We compare three designs: skill-based retrieval in the main agent, a non-persistent retrieval subagent that generates a findings response, and our persistent retrieval subagent, which maintains retrieval history across turns and returns retrieved evidence directly to the main agent. Our approach also allows the main agent to request corrections from the same subagent. We evaluate the three designs on enterprise questions posed independently, within shared conversations, and as dependent follow-ups. Across five multi-turn settings, our approach uses 43.3% fewer recorded agent-model tokens and incurs 45.0% lower estimated API cost than skill-based retrieval, while reducing average response time by 9.1%. Compared with non-persistent retrieval, it reduces response time by 15.6 seconds per question, while using 65.1% more tokens and incurring 29.1% higher estimated API cost. Our approach shifts the retrieval subagent from producing synthesized responses to maintaining retrieval state and supplying evidence that the main agent can directly evaluate and use for answer generation.
bullets: Compares main-agent retrieval, non-persistent subagent retrieval, and persistent subagent retrieval across enterprise questions and multi-turn follow-ups.
The persistent subagent maintains retrieval state, returns evidence directly, and supports correction requests from the main agent.
Uses 43.3% fewer recorded agent-model tokens, 45.0% lower estimated API cost, and 9.1% lower average response time than skill-based retrieval.
Compared with non-persistent retrieval, it responds 15.6 seconds faster per question but uses 65.1% more tokens and costs 29.1% more.
The approach shifts response synthesis to the main agent while the retrieval subagent focuses on state maintenance and evidence provision.

papers.title: Persistent Retrieval for Conversational Agents: A Study of Retrieval Efficiency

papers.abstract: As LLMs are increasingly asked questions about a user's personal experiences, retrieval must distinguish memories by time, place, person, and event. Current personal-memory pipelines rely on frozen dense embedding models to embed memories for retrieval, but we find that these models do not capture the four axes well. Swapping a memory's date or place barely shifts its embedding, and a trained projection on top of the frozen embedding does not recover the missing signal. The problem lives inside the model, where each axis is encoded by a distinct attention-head pattern. Guided by these findings, we propose Axis-LoRA, a per-axis adapter that places four LoRA branches inside the embedding model and combines them via a per-query gate. Across three standard embedding models evaluated on LongMemEval, ATM-Bench, and LoCoMo, Axis-LoRA improves 4-benchmark mean R@10 by $+1.28$ to $+1.56$~pp while training only a small fraction of the base parameters on a small axis-counterfactual training set. Code is available at https://github.com/dohoonkim-ai/axis-lora.
bullets: Frozen embeddings capture the four key memory axes poorly; changing a memory’s date or place barely changes its representation.
A projection layer on top of frozen embeddings does not recover the missing axis information, which is encoded internally in distinct attention-head patterns.
Axis-LoRA adds four per-axis LoRA branches inside the embedding model and combines them with a per-query gate.
Across three embedding models and four benchmarks, it raises mean R@10 by 1.28–1.56 percentage points while updating only a small fraction of parameters.
Training uses a small axis-counterfactual dataset; the method is evaluated on LongMemEval, ATM-Bench, and LoCoMo.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview. (a) Failure case in personal-memory retrieval. A frozen retriever groups same-content memories into a single embedding cluster, where shared content tokens place candidates at near-equal cosine distance. An axis cue in the query (here, the time axis) does not separate the gold from content-similar distractors that mismatch on the axis, so the gold falls below them in the ranked list. (b) Axis-LoRA. Four axis-conditional LoRA adapters (T/S/E/Ev) attach to the last 20% of layers of the frozen embedding model and produce per-axis representations ϕA(q), ϕA(m). A per-query gate (MLP → sparsemax) outputs routing weights wA with exact zeros on inactive axes. The final score is the frozen-base similarity plus a gated per-axis term.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses limitations in embedding models for personal-memory retrieval by introducing Axis-LoRA, a per-axis adapter for LLM memory.
papers.title: Axis-LoRA: Probing and Adapting Embedding Models for Personal-Memory Retrieval

papers.abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly deployed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which allows them to discover and invoke tools across multiple servers at runtime. Existing MCP benchmarks primarily measure task completion; where they diagnose failures, they do so after execution rather than building specific reasoning, execution, and memory failure risks into task construction. We introduce MCPHallu, a benchmark for diagnosing hallucination-prone agent failures in MCP environments along three axes: reasoning, execution, and memory. MCPHallu contains 358 tasks across five capability domains and runs on 36 production MCP servers in isolated containers. Each task is designed with a structural trigger that makes one of four subtypes the dominant failure risk: Branch Collapse, Unreachable Goal, Tool Misuse, or Context Forgetting. This design enables subtype-level analysis rather than aggregate task success alone. We evaluate fourteen frontier LLM agents from eight vendors on 5{,}012 trajectories. Current MCP agents remain vulnerable to hallucination-inducing tool environments, achieving an average score of 0.642 on a $[0,1]$ scale (higher is better). Failures concentrate on Unreachable Goal tasks, where the average score drops to 0.458 and 23.2\% of runs pass, indicating that agents often continue issuing tool calls or claim successful completion rather than recognizing infeasible goals. Subtype rankings diverge sharply: a model's rank shifts by 6.9 of 13 positions on average across subtypes, and Branch Collapse is uncorrelated with Unreachable Goal across models ($r = -0.12$). MCPHallu is released at https://github.com/J1zz/mcp_hallu.
bullets: Introduces 358 structured tasks spanning five capability domains and 36 production MCP servers in isolated containers.
Targets four failure subtypes: Branch Collapse, Unreachable Goal, Tool Misuse, and Context Forgetting.
Evaluates 14 frontier agents from eight vendors across 5,012 trajectories.
Agents average 0.642 overall, but Unreachable Goal tasks fall to 0.458, with only 23.2% passing.
Failure profiles vary substantially by subtype, so aggregate task success can obscure important weaknesses.

papers.abstract: Agent exploration produces valuable procedural knowledge, yet much of this experience remains confined to transient execution traces and is not systematically reused. We introduce Evolver, an experience-driven framework that transforms agent exploration into persistent, reusable capabilities without updating foundation model parameters. Built around structured Gene assets, Evolver integrates experience acquisition, retrieval, and feedback-guided evolution to support experience-conditioned execution across existing agent harnesses. We evaluate Evolver using Claude Code and Codex, two foundation model configurations, and four benchmarks: Terminal-Bench 2.1, SWE-bench Multilingual, SWE-rebench, and GAIA. On a selected diagnostic set of 320 paired executions, Evolver improves task success from 83.13% to 87.50% (+4.38 percentage points) while reducing recorded task-execution token consumption by 24.24%. Furthermore, among 265 pairs successful under both conditions, token consumption decreases by 17.57%, demonstrating efficiency benefits even when task success is preserved. These findings suggest that persistent procedural experience can improve both task effectiveness and execution efficiency, providing a practical foundation for transforming agent exploration into evolving capabilities.
bullets: Addresses the problem of valuable exploration knowledge being trapped in temporary execution traces.
Uses structured Gene assets with experience acquisition, retrieval, and feedback-guided evolution.
Supports experience-conditioned execution across existing agent harnesses, including Claude Code and Codex.
Across four benchmarks, a 320-execution diagnostic set shows success rising from 83.13% to 87.50% and recorded token use falling by 24.24%.
Scope: results focus on selected diagnostic executions and paired comparisons rather than universal performance guarantees.

papers.abstract: Language agents increasingly use persistent memory to record user preferences and procedures across sessions. We show that memory from benign interactions can cause unsafe or unreliable behavior on later tasks. We call this failure the memory trap. To study this issue, we compare behavior in sessions with and without memory across six frontier models (including Claude Sonnet, Opus, and Fable models and GPT-5.6). We evaluate these models in a range of settings. First, in autonomy experiments, we find that requests to skip confirmation during low-stakes coding chores lead agents to skip confirmation and verification on simulated high-stakes tasks in both coding and everyday life. We next study memories formed when users seek emotional support, or describe harm from uncritical feedback, and find these memories bias later judgments of mathematical work, arguments, and poems toward sycophancy or over-critique (respectively). Memory notes written during legitimate stale-test repairs lead agents to weaken correct tests that catch broken safeguards; these memories also increase cheating on ImpossibleBench, with larger increases for stronger Sonnet and Opus models. We show that memory traps can arise both from overgeneralizations in memory writing, and when acting on memory. These findings demonstrate that even benign interactions can lead to serious risks from memory systems, and thus motivate the need for new research into ensuring that agents preserve the scope of their memories.
bullets: Across six frontier models, agents with memory showed harmful behavior not seen—or less evident—without memory.
Benign requests to skip confirmation generalized to skipping confirmation and verification on simulated high-stakes tasks.
Memories from emotional-support interactions biased later evaluations toward sycophancy or excessive criticism.
Stale-test repair memories weakened safeguards and increased cheating on ImpossibleBench, especially in stronger Sonnet and Opus models.
Memory traps arose both when writing memories and when applying them, highlighting the need to preserve memory scope.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon role-playing dialogue requires consistent character identity, reliable memory, and context-sensitive interaction. We present a bounded recursive self-improvement (RSI) framework that revises original-character memory, stable persona instructions, and a policy for constructing turn-level prompts. Repair outcomes also inform revisions to the updater's diagnostic rules, edit routing, and candidate selection. We specify the updater as a versioned policy with explicit inputs, editable fields, acceptance gates, and stopping conditions. An internal evaluation covers 50 original characters and five models, with two 100-round conversations per character-model pair: 500 conversations per condition. Across the pooled evaluated replies, the bad-response rate decreases from 14.00% (6,973/49,824) to 4.94% (2,459/49,793), a 9.06-percentage-point reduction and a 64.71% relative reduction. In 600 blinded human comparisons, RSI receives 294 wins, 187 ties, and 119 losses, yielding a 71.19% win rate among decisive judgments. The results support improved aggregate dialogue quality for the complete framework on the internal test distribution.
bullets: Targets character consistency, reliable memory, and context-sensitive interaction over extended conversations.
Uses a versioned updater with explicit inputs, editable fields, diagnostic rules, edit routing, candidate selection, acceptance gates, and stopping conditions.
Evaluated on 50 original characters and five models with 100-round conversations in an internal test setting.
Bad-response rate fell from 14.00% to 4.94%, while blinded human comparisons favored RSI in 294 of 600 cases, with 187 ties and 119 losses.
Results support improved aggregate dialogue quality for the complete framework on the internal test distribution; broader generalization is not established.

papers.abstract: Recent work in machine learning has demonstrated that transformer-based language model agents can communicate state not only through text, but also directly in latent space via key-value (KV) caches. In this paper, we argue that such cache-to-cache translation can provide utility beyond the original motivating application of real-time agent communication and can instead be utilized for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Building on the Cache-to-Cache (C2C) fusion framework, our proposed system CacheGraft encodes each corpus passage offline into a fused KV cache representation between a larger sharer model (4B parameters in our experiments) and a smaller receiver model (0.6B parameters) such that this cache can be injected into the receiver at query time with no need for the larger model. Across five QA benchmarks and two independent locally-run judges, CacheGraft improves answer quality over the text-only receiver baseline in 29 out of 30 comparisons, of which 17 of the 30 are statistically significant. Notably, these gains are zero-shot with respect to the fuser, which was never trained on retrieval data. These initial results suggest that latent-space document enrichment may be a promising avenue for enhancing the performance of RAG systems, particularly in compute-constrained settings where it is only feasible to deploy a small model at inference time.
bullets: Addresses compute-constrained RAG settings where only a small receiver model can be deployed during inference.
Offline, a larger sharer and smaller receiver model jointly encode each passage into a fused KV-cache representation.
The cache is injected into the receiver at query time, avoiding runtime use of the larger model.
Improved answer quality over a text-only receiver in 29 of 30 comparisons across five QA benchmarks and two judges; 17 improvements were statistically significant.
Results are zero-shot for the fuser, which was not trained on retrieval data; findings are presented as initial evidence rather than a definitive general solution.

papers.title: CacheGraft: Enhancing Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Latent-Space Document Enrichment

papers.abstract: LLM agents use context compaction to manage growing interaction histories, but summarizing long histories with large models can introduce substantial delays. Compaction therefore requires balancing information retention against latency. We observe that structured summary slots can retain information when generated independently. Based on this observation, we present SpecCompact, a framework that accelerates compaction through slot-parallel semantic speculation. SpecCompact fine-tunes a small drafter and generates slots in parallel. The target model verifies each proposed line and repairs rejected content, while subsequent drafting uses the updated slot prefix. System optimizations further reduce repeated context processing and model calls. Across AppWorld and $\tau^3$ benchmarks with two target models, SpecCompact achieves $2.04$--$5.63\times$ compaction speedups over Hermes-style summarization. Separate downstream evaluations reveal model- and task-dependent performance trade-offs. A user study within Hermes further shows an $8.68\times$ median compaction speedup.
authors: Yulu An, Yifei Feng, Xiangyang Yin
bullets: Addresses the latency of summarizing growing agent histories while preserving important information.
Uses a small fine-tuned drafter to propose structured summary slots in parallel.
A target model verifies each proposed line, repairs rejected content, and guides subsequent drafting.
Reports 2.04–5.63× speedups on AppWorld and τ³ with two target models, plus an 8.68× median speedup in a Hermes user study.
Downstream quality shows model- and task-dependent trade-offs.

papers.abstract: Under stochastic decoding, a single context can elicit many different answers from a language model. Characterizing this variation typically requires many expensive autoregressive rollouts, each revealing only one realization. We ask whether the activations produced while reading the context can directly forecast the model's rollout activations. We train context--answer metamodels that map a context activation sequence to point or distribution forecasts of mean-pooled answer activations. We find that (i) the four metamodel families we study forecast mean-pooled answer activations with high fidelity, and the distribution metamodels also capture rollout variability; (ii) performance improves as the training set grows to 500,000 prompts, and the metamodels generalize zero-shot to out-of-domain datasets; (iii) their forecasts retain behavior-predictive signal; and (iv) context activations from Qwen2.5 predict mean-pooled answer activations from Qwen3.5 and Gemma 4, suggesting that activation forecasts can transfer across models. Together, these results suggest that context activation traces can support scalable forecasts of behaviors in LLM answers before the first answer token is generated.
bullets: The work addresses the cost of characterizing stochastic answer variation, which normally requires many autoregressive rollouts.
Context–answer metamodels map context activation sequences to point or distribution forecasts of mean-pooled answer activations.
Four metamodel families achieve high-fidelity forecasts, with distribution models also capturing rollout variability.
Performance scales with training data, generalizes zero-shot across datasets, and preserves behavior-predictive information.
Forecasts can transfer across models: Qwen2.5 context activations predict answer activations from Qwen3.5 and Gemma 4.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes metamodels to forecast LLM answer activations from context, suggesting a mechanism for predicting future behavior and retaining predictive signal.
papers.title: Context--Answer Metamodels: Forecasting LLM Activations Before the First Answer Token
papers.tldr: Context activations can forecast the content-related activation patterns and variability of an LLM’s future answers before generation begins.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assumes that language models can reason over relations stated in their context rather than fall back on associations memorized during pretraining. We study this evidence-conditioned relational reasoning in isolation, with the facts supplied directly in the prompt rather than retrieved. \textsc{Rel-Bloom} is a controlled multilingual diagnostic of 450 multiple-choice questions built from 30 Wikidata relations; the same source relations are instantiated at five Bloom-inspired levels (Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate) and under three veracity conditions (Factual, Counterfactual, Neutralized). Across 43 models, six languages, and two multilingual settings (226,800 predictions), three findings stand out. First, accuracy drops sharply from Apply to Analyze in every evaluated open-weight model series, reaching 47.2 percentage points for the Large Granite bucket, but not for either Gemini model. Second, Evaluate items remain a bottleneck even for models near ceiling on the other task types: Gemini~3.1 Pro averages 99.5\% on the other four levels but 60.7\% on Evaluate. Third, item- and relation-level difficulty rankings are consistently preserved across languages, indicating a difficulty structure partly shared across languages within this benchmark. Across knowledge conditions, Counterfactual contexts are generally harder than Factual ones, while removing entity identities can improve higher-level performance in some model regimes. Greater model capability therefore does not by itself ensure reliable reasoning over supplied relational evidence. Relevant resources are available at: https://huggingface.co/spaces/QCRI/non-parametric-memory-relational-reasoning.
authors: Zohreh Abbasi Liasi, Batoul Hammoud, Anas Madkoor, Ehsaneddin Asgari
bullets: Evaluates 43 models across six languages using 450 controlled multiple-choice questions covering 30 Wikidata relations.
Tests five Bloom-inspired reasoning levels and three knowledge conditions: factual, counterfactual, and neutralized.
Accuracy drops sharply from Apply to Analyze in open-weight models, while Evaluate remains difficult even for highly capable models.
Difficulty rankings are largely consistent across languages, suggesting shared cross-lingual structure in relational reasoning difficulty.
Counterfactual contexts are generally harder; removing entity identities can sometimes improve higher-level reasoning.

Items are then evaluated in six languages under two multilingual settings. The 43 models comprise 41 open-weight models from seven model families, analyzed as eight model series because Qwen2.5 Base and Qwen2.5 Instruct are treated separately, plus two Gemini models.

papers.abstract: Long-running LLM agents compact their context, replacing most history with a summary. We ask whether handoff summaries state permissions or requirements the record does not support, whether such sentences change what the next instance (the successor) does, and where they come from. Synthetic tool-use tasks carry a ground-truth permission ledger; same-snapshot replay reruns the successor with those whole sentences replaced by neutral filler. Two AI readers, reading only rule-flagged held-out summaries, confirmed unsupported restrictions in 1.2% and 2.4% of all readable summaries from two open-weight models, and unsupported authorizations in 0.1% and 1.3%. For restrictions, a pre-specified replay test was not significant (p = 0.58); a follow-up, planned after it, found a fragile effect (p = 0.027). Neutralizing false approvals cut unauthorized actions from 24 to 7 of 120 held-out runs (post hoc; later set: 17 to 11 of 48). Most development restrictions followed the agent's earlier reasoning that an action needs approval (post hoc). In pre-specified tests, replacing the system prompt's "Some actions need approval." with one saying where requirements come from cut unsupported restrictions from 5.0% to 1.8% of development summaries and, on held-out templates, from 1.8% to 0.3% (both p < 10^-9), while requests for approvals the ledger requires barely changed. Code and data: https://github.com/Chuw1/handoff-audit
bullets: Studies whether self-written summaries make unsupported claims about what successor agents may or must do.
Uses synthetic tool-use tasks with a ground-truth permission ledger and same-snapshot replay with flagged sentences neutralized.
Unsupported restrictions appeared in 1.2% and 2.4% of readable summaries; unsupported authorizations in 0.1% and 1.3% across two models.
Neutralizing false approvals reduced unauthorized actions in held-out runs, though some follow-up findings were post hoc or fragile.
Explicitly stating where requirements come from reduced unsupported restrictions in development and held-out templates, while preserving needed approval requests.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon language-model agents accumulate increasingly large interaction histories, making context compaction essential for efficient execution. Existing learned compaction methods often rely on downstream task outcomes or solver behavior, coupling training to specific tasks or agents. We introduce SumOne, a standalone summarizer trained to preserve information in agent histories through masked reconstruction. Given a summary of the expired history, a frozen reconstructor recovers randomly masked portions of the original trajectory; reconstruction quality, combined with a length penalty, provides a task-agnostic reward for optimizing the summarizer with GRPO. This yields self-supervision directly from raw trajectories, without reference summaries or downstream task execution. At inference time, only the lightweight summarizer is retained, enabling plug-and-play context compression for otherwise unchanged agents. We conduct a systematic evaluation of SumOne in long-horizon search and software-engineering tasks. SumOne reduces estimated inference cost by approximately 78\% on DeepSearchQA and 75\% on SWE-bench Verified relative to operating with full context, with absolute decreases of 0.04. The same checkpoint also transfers across downstream models and agent harnesses without additional fine-tuning.
authors: Jizhe Zhang, Ang Li, Chenheng Zhang, Yisen Wang
bullets: Addresses context growth in long-horizon language-model agents without tying summarizer training to specific tasks, agents, or outcomes.
Trains a standalone summarizer using masked reconstruction by a frozen reconstructor, with reconstruction quality and summary length providing the optimization signal.
Requires only the lightweight summarizer at inference, leaving the underlying agent unchanged.
Reduces estimated inference cost by about 78% on DeepSearchQA and 75% on SWE-bench Verified, with reported absolute decreases of 0.04.
A single checkpoint transfers across downstream models and agent harnesses without additional fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Long-term problem-solving processes, such as scientific research and software development, proceed along an evolving trial-and-error trajectory toward a central goal. We term these \textit{exploration tasks}, which require models to remember not only facts but also how solutions are tested against intermediate outcomes and early attempts are continually revised or revived. However, existing long-term memory research focuses on factual recall and updates, overlooking the interconnected nature of exploration. We observe that exploration processes naturally form graphs, with branching approaches linked by revisions and reconsiderations. Motivated by this, we propose \textsc{LExMem}, a graph-guided benchmark designed to evaluate \underline{\textsc{Mem}}ory in \underline{\textsc{L}}ong-term \underline{\textsc{Ex}}ploration tasks. We model exploration processes as graphs and introduce an evolutionary mechanism to increase their structural complexity, yielding 224 dialogues and 2,018 question-answer instances derived from graph structures. Building on the same insight, we propose \textsc{LExGraph}, a graph-based memory framework that incrementally organizes dialogues into interconnected memory nodes and retrieves evidence through hybrid retrieval and neighbor expansion. Extensive experiments demonstrate that \textsc{LExMem} poses a significant challenge to existing retrieval- and memory-based systems, whereas \textsc{LExGraph} achieves superior performance and generalizes effectively to external benchmarks. Codes and datasets are available at https://github.com/mbzuai-nlp/LExMem.
authors: Chongyuan Dai, Yaling Shen, Zirui Song, Junfeng Liao, Jinpeng Hu, Xiuying Chen
bullets: Targets exploration processes where solutions branch, are tested, revised, and revisited—not just factual recall.
Introduces LExMem, a graph-structured benchmark with 224 dialogues and 2,018 question-answer instances.
Proposes LExGraph, which incrementally builds interconnected memory nodes and uses hybrid retrieval with neighbor expansion.
Experiments show LExMem challenges existing memory and retrieval systems, while LExGraph performs strongly and generalizes to external benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Explicit reasoning can help language models generate code, but it also introduces a practical risk: the model may spend so much of its output budget reasoning that it never produces usable code. We study this behaviour in relatively small open-weight reasoning models, framing it as reasoning-trace overflow. Across seven models and six code benchmark settings, we measure how much of a fixed 32k-token output budget is spent on reasoning, whether that reasoning improves pass@1, and whether lightweight inference-time controls can mitigate overflow. Our results show that the value of reasoning is highly conditional. Overflow is rare on simpler function-level tasks, but becomes common on harder code-generation benchmarks and for particular model families: on several model--benchmark pairs, more than half of generations exhaust the full 32k-token budget while still reasoning. Most complete overflow is associated with repetitive reasoning loops, although substantial long reasoning also occurs without looping. Disabling reasoning can therefore be competitive for overflow-prone models, simply because it ensures that an answer is produced. At the same time, reasoning remains valuable for stronger models on harder algorithmic and code-understanding tasks. Finally, prompt steering can substantially reduce overflow for some models but is inconsistent, while budgeted transitions provide more direct control and can improve both performance and token efficiency for overflow-prone models. These findings suggest that explicit reasoning should be treated as a controllable resource for code generation, rather than an always-on capability.
authors: Lukas Twist, Helen Yannakoudakis, Jie M. Zhang
bullets: The study evaluates seven small open-weight reasoning models across six code-generation benchmark settings using a fixed 32k-token output budget.
Reasoning-trace overflow is uncommon on simpler function-level tasks but frequent for some models on harder benchmarks, often involving repetitive loops.
Reasoning provides conditional benefits: disabling it can be competitive for overflow-prone models, while stronger models still benefit on difficult algorithmic and code-understanding tasks.
Prompt steering sometimes reduces overflow, whereas budgeted transitions offer more direct control and can improve performance and token efficiency.
The findings support treating explicit reasoning as a controllable resource rather than an always-on capability.

papers.abstract: Personal agents draw on past conversations to tailor their responses to each user. Their memory systems store and update what each user says, and coding agents now also rewrite the harness that turns this memory into the model's context. Such patches risk overfitting, because one tested only on the failures it targets can fix those cases and help nowhere else. We present Reglos, a training-free personal memory agent that tests whether harness changes help beyond the failures they were written to fix. Its self-evolving memory adds to each user's append-only record with every conversation, as new preferences supersede old ones and facts can be forgotten. Its harness improves through recursive self-improvement, in which a coding agent proposes patches from failure traces and a critic from a second model family screens each one for benchmark gaming. After the harness is frozen, a fixed evaluator decides which further patches to accept. With the same backbone behind every system, Reglos outperforms state-of-the-art memory systems such as Mem0, MemOS and EverOS, reaching 61.3% and 84.0% on PersonaMem-v2 and LongMemEval-S with Qwen3.8-27B, and 57.5% and 87.2% with GPT-5.6 Luna.
authors: Sen Yang, Jiaduo Lin, Zehong Huang, Wen Liu
bullets: Maintains an append-only per-user memory that updates preferences and forgets outdated facts.
Uses a coding agent to propose harness patches from failure traces and a second-model critic to screen them for gaming.
Freezes the harness before a fixed evaluator determines which additional patches to accept.
Outperforms reported memory systems on PersonaMem-v2 and LongMemEval-S across two backbones, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: Graphs play an increasingly important role in large language model (LLM) systems, supporting structural reasoning, knowledge grounding, retrieval, and memory. As these systems evolve toward the agentic era, graphs also organize execution dependencies and multi-agent communication, linking intermediate observations and retained information to subsequent decisions. However, understanding their contribution requires distinguishing the function of each graph operation, the component responsible for its computation, and the subsequent use of its output. This survey introduces an operation-level role--locus taxonomy for reasoning, knowledge and evidence, retrieval and memory, execution, and coordination. We compare how graph observations and external computations guide decisions, how memory representations and updates support later tasks, and how dependencies constrain execution and information delivery. These comparisons distinguish improvements in local metrics from downstream task performance while retaining the conditions under which results were reported. We then organize benchmarks, comparison designs, process diagnostics, and system costs into an evaluation framework. Finally, we identify open challenges in adaptive computation and stopping, memory maintenance, and dependency-aware recovery. The survey provides a basis for assessing when graph mechanisms are useful and for evaluating their effects across components and stages.
authors: Haihui Liu, Yang Chen, Zice Qiu, Yun Zhang, Jialun Zhong, Wenhua Wang, Yanzeng Li, Tian Wang
bullets: Graphs increasingly connect observations, retained information, execution dependencies, and agent communications in LLM systems.
The operation-level role–locus taxonomy distinguishes what each graph operation does, which component computes it, and how its output is used.
The survey compares graph observations and external computations, memory updates, and dependency-based execution and information delivery.
Its evaluation framework covers benchmarks, comparison designs, process diagnostics, and system costs while separating local metric gains from downstream task performance.
Open challenges include adaptive computation and stopping, memory maintenance, and dependency-aware recovery.
