papers.abstract: Reasoning models allocate test-time compute across distinct behaviors such as planning, deriving, and verifying. However, models frequently "overthink," continuing to verify and re-derive long after finding a correct answer. This wastes expensive compute and can even degrade performance. Existing interventions, such as token budgets or steering, primarily regulate reasoning duration rather than targeting specific behaviors. In this work, we demonstrate that Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routers provide a natural, training-free interface for behavioral control. We first split reasoning traces into sentence-level segments and label each with one of six reasoning behaviors (planning, execution, restatement, fact, reflection, and conclusion), so that every token carries the behavior of its segment. Linear probes on router logits predict this label nearly as well as probes on the residual stream, the model's full hidden state and the standard target for probing, while using about half as many features. These signals generalize: experts associated with a reasoning behavior on one dataset predict the same behavior on the others, across six datasets spanning five domains (math, code, science, knowledge, and commonsense). Building on this, we selectively edit expert router scores during inference to curb overthinking. Across four models and four benchmarks, this intervention reduces the number of generated tokens by a median of 30.4% (and up to 63.3%). Crucially, it encourages the model to stop once the problem is solved, rather than skipping essential reasoning steps. Accuracy never drops by more than 0.5 percentage points, and frequently improves. Ultimately, MoE routing offers both an interpretable lens into reasoning states and a lightweight mechanism for optimizing test-time compute.
authors: Shengjie Wang, Mohsen Fayyaz, Nanyun Peng
bullets: Problem: Reasoning models may continue planning, deriving, or verifying after reaching a correct answer, wasting compute and sometimes degrading performance.
Method: Label sentence-level reasoning segments with six behaviors, probe MoE router logits for these behaviors, and selectively edit expert scores during inference.
Routers predict reasoning behavior nearly as well as full residual representations while using about half as many features.
Behavior-associated experts generalize across six datasets and five domains, suggesting routing captures reusable reasoning states.
Across four models and four benchmarks, router editing cuts generated tokens by a median of 30.4%—up to 63.3%—with accuracy decreases no larger than 0.5 percentage points and occasional improvements.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external memory stores to retain information across conversations, typically via dense vector embeddings searched with approximate nearest-neighbor methods. The fruit fly's olfactory circuit computes a locality-sensitive hash of sensory input using a strikingly different mechanism - sparse random projection followed by winner-take-all competition - and prior work (Dasgupta et al., 2017) showed this scheme, dubbed FlyHash, preserves neighbor structure better per bit than conventional random-hyperplane hashing (SimHash) on several benchmarks. We apply FlyHash, to our knowledge for the first time, to LLM agent memory retrieval, and ask three questions a practitioner actually needs answered: does the quality advantage hold under a correctly matched-bit protocol (it does, robustly, across 10 seeds and four datasets spanning two modalities, with one specific, previously undocumented comparison pitfall identified and corrected along the way); does that advantage translate into real memory and latency savings, including against the dense-vector indexing (HNSW) practitioners default to today (no: at equal bits FlyHash's codes are larger and slower to compare than SimHash's, and HNSW dominates both hash methods at ordinary scale; a sparse-set comparison we introduce recovers most but not all of a naive latency gap, leaving hashing's practical case narrower and more specific than the quality result alone implies); and does the advantage survive genuine, non-circular agent-memory relevance labels rather than the nearest-neighbor-by-embedding proxy this literature otherwise relies on (it does). We report all three answers precisely, including the two that narrow rather than flatter the headline result, and release our implementation, a working agent-memory demo, and a full account of the methodological pitfalls we found and corrected.
bullets: Applies FlyHash—sparse random projection with winner-take-all hashing—to LLM agent memory retrieval.
Confirms a robust quality advantage over SimHash across 10 seeds and four datasets spanning two modalities, using matched-bit comparisons.
Identifies and corrects a previously undocumented comparison pitfall in evaluating FlyHash against SimHash.
Finds no general memory or latency advantage: FlyHash codes are larger and slower to compare at equal bits, while HNSW dominates at ordinary scale.
Introduces a sparse-set comparison that narrows, but does not eliminate, the latency gap; the quality benefit also holds with non-circular relevance labels.

papers.abstract: Most memory systems for LLM agents are retrospective, preserving and retrieving past information to inform current decisions. Proactive agents, however, also require prospective memory: retaining future-directed intentions and realizing them when appropriate opportunities arise, even without explicit requests. Crucially, remembering the right intention does not guarantee acting at the right time: a related observation may call for waiting, while a later cue may make the same intention actionable. Inspired by cognitive theories of human prospective memory, we introduce Pro-Memory, a memory framework that separates maintaining future intentions from deciding when and how to realize them. Pro-Memory preserves pending objectives linked to their supporting evidence, assesses new observations against their original goals and activation conditions, and coordinates appropriate contributions with the agent's ongoing actions. It further updates intention states based on actions actually issued or evidence of resolution, while an experience memory distills feedback from completed episodes into guidance for future decisions. Experiments on two benchmarks spanning delayed-intention tasks and open-ended proactive assistance demonstrate consistent improvements in proactive task performance over representative memory approaches across multiple LLM backbones, while limiting unnecessary interventions.
authors: Yuanchen Bei, Zhining Liu, Tianxin Wei, Weizhi Zhang, Zhichen Zeng, Philip S. Yu, Hendrik Hamann, Jingrui He, Hanghang Tong
bullets: Addresses the gap between remembering future goals and deciding when they should become actionable.
Separates intention maintenance from realization, linking pending objectives to supporting evidence and activation conditions.
Updates intention states based on issued actions or resolution evidence, while learning from completed episodes.
Improves proactive performance across delayed-intention and open-ended assistance benchmarks with multiple LLM backbones.
Limits unnecessary interventions by distinguishing cues that require waiting from those that warrant action.

papers.abstract: The memory of production agents is increasingly becoming a bottleneck and is built almost exclusively from text: key points are extracted from out-of-limit context and retrieved into context at query time. Therefore, every new query incurs an additional cost that grows with the accumulated history. Weight memory is a complementary alternative that internalizes knowledge into model parameters and answers with no context at all, and has recently proven effective in self-evolving agents for internalizing skills and behaviors. However, its application in episodic and semantic memory, such as user-specific facts, remains comparatively unexplored, and a gap remains between earlier attempts at weight memory and text-based systems regarding recall performance. We study how to make weight memory competitive as a long-term factual store by applying on-policy self-distillation (OPSD). It trains a context-free student from a teacher, which is the same model conditioned on the user's memory, together with a verify-then-regenerate router that lets weight and text memory each cover the queries they handle best. On the HaluMem benchmark, OPSD matches or surpasses strong text-memory baselines, including full-context prompting and retrieval systems, while reading fewer tokens per query. We further conduct an extensive study that characterizes the behavior of weight memory and analyzes how different training recipes affect its performance. As agent harnesses move toward persistent, multi-session deployments, these results position weight memory as a practical, low-cost component of agent memory and provide insights into feasible training and evaluation protocols for combining it with retrieval.
authors: Zeyu Fang, Jun Yin, Yongsheng Mei, Xu Han, Chaitali Joshi, Zhongkai Sun, Jie Hao, Bin Guo, Chengyuan Ma, Benjamin Z. Yao, Chenlei Guo
bullets: Addresses the cost and scaling limits of text-only memory, where each query requires retrieving accumulated history.
Trains a context-free student from a memory-conditioned teacher using on-policy self-distillation (OPSD).
Uses a verify-then-regenerate router to assign queries to weight memory or text memory based on which handles them best.
On HaluMem, OPSD matches or surpasses strong text-memory baselines while reading fewer tokens per query.
Studies weight-memory behavior and training recipes for combining persistent parameter memory with retrieval.

papers.title: Route to Remember: Adaptive Memory Selection for LLM Agents

papers.abstract: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) demands more than empathic validation, requiring instead a structured formulation of the interplay among situations, automatic thoughts, emotions, and behaviors. Therapists formalize this interplay through a Cognitive Conceptualization Diagram, where maintaining longitudinal coherence necessitates continuous evidential adjudication to separate tentative hypotheses from established findings. Current dialogue systems track conversational history via retrieval or static profiles but lack the representational capacity to encode epistemic status. Consequently, provisional interpretations are often prematurely reified as established facts, inadvertently biasing downstream interventions. Addressing this limitation, CCDWiki is introduced as a plug-and-play advisor conceptualizing longitudinal therapy as evidence-grounded hypothesis adjudication. The approach encodes each clinical hypothesis as a mutable entry bound to corroborating and contradicting evidence. Across sessions, accumulating data strengthens supported entries, preserves provisional ones, and retracts contradicted assumptions. The resulting formulation distills into concise guidance for unmodified therapeutic language models. Experiments demonstrate substantial improvements in both conceptualization and intervention quality without requiring backbone retraining.
authors: Mingwen Zhang, Ruiyang Song, Qinying Wang, Yuchen Wang, Changsheng Ma, Minqiang Yang
bullets: Addresses the problem of therapy systems prematurely treating tentative interpretations as established facts.
Represents each CBT hypothesis as a mutable entry linked to supporting and contradicting evidence.

Distills the evolving formulation into concise guidance for an unchanged therapeutic language model.
Experiments show substantial gains in conceptualization and intervention quality without backbone retraining.

papers.abstract: With the rise of Group Agent such as Claude Tag, agents increasingly serve as digital workers for long-term team collaboration. These agents operate over shared contexts that continuously accumulate through multi-user interactions. However, existing agent memory systems are mainly designed for individual users and struggle to capture group-level knowledge in shared contexts, including group relationships and collaboratively formed knowledge. Manual memory strategies further limit adaptation to diverse and evolving shared contexts. To this end, we propose \textbf{EvoGroup (EvoG)}, a self-evolving harness for group agents that starts from a minimal six-tool cold start and adapts through interaction with shared context. EvoG uses confidence and task outcomes to select informative trajectories, while also eliciting self-reflections on uncertainty in low-confidence cases. The analysis agent then examines selected trajectories through adaptive progressive disclosure, followed by bucketed analysis to synthesize high-level findings that guide the evolve agent in revising the Harness. Empirically, pass@1 on held-out split of EverMemBench improves from 71.07\% to 89.58\%, surpassing both self-evolving memory and human-designed harnesses, including Claude Code (85.83\%). To evaluate generalization, we freeze the evolved harness and evaluate it on the unseen GroupMemBench, where, with GPT-5.5, it demonstrates effective generalization and outperforms both memory baselines and human-designed harnesses.
bullets: Targets the gap between individual-user memory systems and the relationship- and collaboration-aware knowledge needed by group agents.
Starts with six tools and evolves through interaction, using confidence and task outcomes to select informative trajectories.
Uses self-reflection for uncertain cases, adaptive progressive disclosure, and bucketed analysis to guide harness revisions.
Improves EverMemBench held-out pass@1 from 71.07% to 89.58%, exceeding reported self-evolving and human-designed baselines.
A frozen evolved harness also generalizes effectively to the unseen GroupMemBench, outperforming memory and human-designed baselines.

papers.selection_reason: Self-evolving memory harness for group agents operating over shared contexts fits LLM/agent memory mechanisms.
papers.title: EvoGroup: A Self-Evolving Harness for Group Agents in Shared Contexts
papers.tldr: EvoGroup is a self-evolving harness that learns to manage group-level knowledge in shared contexts, substantially improving group-agent memory performance and generalizing to an unseen benchmark.

papers.abstract: LLM-based agents, which increasingly operate persistently across sessions and accumulate memory through interaction, already exhibit the familiar symptoms of unchecked plasticity: semantic drift, degraded retrieval precision, propagation of stored errors, and saturation of memory capacity. Drawing on the selectionist "ringing, resonance and renormalization" (RRR) account of sleep, we propose that each of its three phases maps onto an operation feasible in digital memory architectures. Engineers building stateful agents, meanwhile, are independently rediscovering the problems sleep evolved to solve: what to forget, and when to do the forgetting. From this we derive the falsifiable prediction that selectionist consolidation will outperform instructionist alternatives as memory stores grow large. The core claim concerns the nature of continuous learning itself: plasticity has a price, and for any system that learns continuously under finite capacity while coupled to its environment, that price is sleep.
bullets: Continuous learning under finite memory causes unchecked plasticity and accumulating memory problems.
The selectionist RRR account of sleep—ringing, resonance, and renormalization—can be mapped to operations in digital memory systems.
The framework addresses when and what an agent should forget during persistent operation.
It predicts that selectionist consolidation will outperform instructionist alternatives as memory stores become large.
The claim is theoretical and presents a falsifiable prediction rather than reported experimental results.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes sleep-inspired consolidation for continuous learning and memory management in stateful LLM-based agents.
papers.title: Do agents need to sleep?
papers.tldr: Persistent LLM agents may need sleep-like memory consolidation to prevent drift, retrieval degradation, stored errors, and capacity saturation.

papers.abstract: Large language models often solve independent problems in the same conversation. Can computation from earlier problems help them solve new ones? To answer this question, we first conduct preliminary experiments showing that retained history can raise or lower later-turn accuracy, even within the same domain. To understand these effects, we use controlled replay to isolate internal state changes specific to each problem-history pairing. Across different histories, these changes preserve similar relationships among current problems. To improve reasoning under retained history, we introduce STAIR (Stale-Token Attention for Inter-query Reuse). STAIR captures keys and values from earlier response generation in a fixed bank. It learns to redirect current queries when they read this bank during prompt processing. The base model remains frozen; only 12,288 parameters are trained. Across three Qwen models and four benchmarks, STAIR improves average later-turn accuracy by up to 11.67 percentage points over the unmodified model with history.
bullets: Retained conversation history changes later-turn accuracy even for problems in the same domain.
Controlled replay shows that history induces problem-specific internal state changes with consistent relationships across histories.
STAIR stores earlier-generation keys and values in a fixed bank and redirects current queries to reuse them.
The base model stays frozen; only 12,288 parameters are trained.
Across three Qwen models and four benchmarks, STAIR raises average later-turn accuracy by up to 11.67 percentage points over the unmodified model with history.

papers.abstract: Skill memories encode past experiences as textual prompts to improve reinforcement learning (RL) for self-evolving agents. Complementing RL, On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) provides dense, fine-grained supervision to internalize knowledge from skill-guided trajectories and accelerate policy learning. However, self-generated memories often contain noisy supervision and functionally entangled, redundant, or conflicting knowledge, making direct distillation difficult. Under limited training budgets, these issues can hinder knowledge internalization and even degrade performance. To address this problem, we propose MDSKILL, a multi-view distillation approach for skill memory internalization. MDSKILL organizes skill memories into three complementary functional views (state grounding, action planning, and execution control) and selects high-quality skills using dynamic metrics to construct view-specific and integrated reasoning branches. OPSD then transfers and consolidates complementary experiential knowledge across these branches into a shared policy, enabling efficient skill internalization and continuous agent self-evolution. We evaluate MDSKILL on three agent benchmarks against RL, skill-augmented, and self-distillation baselines that do not rely on stronger external teacher models. Without additional computational overhead, MDSKILL improves upon SOTA performance by up to 7.1% and 8.1% on ALFWorld and WebShop. Extensive ablations and evolution analyses further validate its effectiveness in knowledge internalization and policy improvement. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MDSKILL-CF53.

On-Policy Self-Distillation consolidates knowledge from these branches into a shared policy for continuous self-evolution.
Across three benchmarks, MDSKILL improves performance by up to 7.1% on ALFWorld and 8.1% on WebShop, with ablations supporting its effectiveness.

papers.abstract: Byte level language models avoid tokenizer dependence and provide universal coverage, but processing every byte at full resolution is expensive. We introduce DeepMem, a causal multiscale architecture that separates semantic compression from exact byte preservation. A learned invertible subband transform constructs a hierarchy of shorter sequences, while a lossless carrier and explicit detail sidebands preserve byte identity. Fast weight memory blocks operate along the encoder, with iterative shared state computation at the compressed bottleneck, while an attention based super resolution decoder restores byte resolution representations. DeepMem achieves stronger language modeling performance than a matched byte level Transformer on FineWeb-Edu and PG19, and obtains the best macro average performance across the evaluated FLORES languages. It also improves PIQA accuracy while remaining competitive on code modeling, multiple choice reasoning, and byte level corruption robustness. Bottleneck refinement requires approximately $7{,}600\times$ fewer counted FLOPs than equivalent full resolution reasoning, while maintaining competitive evaluation throughput.
bullets: Byte-level models offer universal coverage but are costly because they process every byte at full resolution.
A learned invertible subband transform builds shorter hierarchical sequences with lossless carriers and detail sidebands for exact byte preservation.
Fast weight memory blocks and iterative bottleneck state computation handle compressed representations, while an attention-based decoder restores byte-resolution representations.
It outperforms a matched byte-level Transformer on FineWeb-Edu and PG19 and achieves the best macro-average performance across evaluated FLORES languages.
Bottleneck refinement uses approximately 7,600× fewer counted FLOPs than equivalent full-resolution reasoning, while throughput remains competitive.

papers.abstract: Speech large language models retain audio history to support multi-turn conversations. Yet remembering an event does not ensure that its information is used only when relevant. We investigate why irrelevant historical audio changes answers even when the queried event remains represented. Controlled experiments on MOSS-Audio and MiMo-Audio show that historical values direct errors toward specific competing answers, beyond a generic effect of context length. Causal interventions distinguish two paths. In open-ended question answering, most history-value errors disappear when subsequent computation cannot directly access the irrelevant source. In multiple-choice answering, many errors persist: early historical influence is carried by question-candidate states even after direct source access is blocked. Low-dimensional interventions further separate source-role information from answer-value information. Their effects peak at different depths, and changing the source-role signal does not eliminate the causal influence of competing values. On naturally occurring errors, strengthening the queried role and counteracting the historical value each improve answers; their joint intervention gives the greatest recovery. These findings support a failure of downstream evidence use beyond source identification alone: source-role information can influence a decision without exclusively controlling which historical values affect it. Reliable conversational memory therefore requires not only retention and retrieval, but also control over how retained information enters answer computation.
authors: HongJin Song, Weiqiao Shan, Runwu Shi, Yifei Wu, Yujin Wang, Jiale Luo, Jiasheng Kuang, Xinyu Yang, Zhaoqi Cui, Chuizheng Kong, Ziyu Wu, Guowu Tan, Qiuyu Fang, Chunxiang Jin
bullets: Irrelevant audio history causes targeted errors toward specific competing answers, not merely generic context-length degradation.
Causal tests show open-ended errors mostly vanish when later computation cannot access the irrelevant source.
In multiple-choice tasks, many errors persist because historical influence travels through question-candidate states.
Source-role and answer-value information peak at different processing depths, and identifying the right source does not eliminate value interference.
Strengthening the queried role and counteracting historical values together yields the strongest recovery on naturally occurring errors.

papers.abstract: Autoresearch has shown that agents can autonomously write code, run experiments, and iteratively improve machine learning solutions. Yet most evaluations start a new agent session from scratch for each new problem, making them costly and leaving unclear whether agents can retain and apply prior insights when adapting to new tasks. We introduce CONTINUAL AUTORESEARCH, an open-ended environment that compares persistent and reset instances of the same agent under matched task streams, data, and time budget. Continual AutoResearch covers nine task families, spanning synthetic tasks, symbolic regression, time-series forecasting, and tabular AutoML. Across five frontier agents, we measure first-solution quality, research efficiency, and final held-out performance. To distinguish insight transfer from session continuity, we run a memory ablation that vary what information agents retain from prior tasks. We show that persistent state improves research efficiency of all five agents, allowing them to find stronger solutions sooner. However, these gains do not consistently translate into better final solutions. Overall, our findings suggest that retaining experience and utilizing it effectively are distinct capabilities.
authors: Jeremy Qin, Ruizhi Deng, Mohamed Osama Ahmed, Frederick Tung, Leo Feng
bullets: Most autoresearch evaluations reset agents between tasks, leaving cross-task learning unclear.
The benchmark compares persistent and reset agents on matched task streams, data, and time budgets across nine task families.
It evaluates five frontier agents using first-solution quality, research efficiency, and final held-out performance.
A memory ablation separates benefits from session continuity from actual transfer of prior insights.
Persistent state improves efficiency for all agents, but effective insight reuse remains a distinct challenge.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving agents write interaction experience into artifacts and reuse them in later tasks. Most work supports such methods with three proxy signals: artifacts accumulate, behavior changes once they are loaded, and metrics rise. We call this signal-based evaluation. What these signals are meant to indicate, however, has not been defined. To fill this gap, we define capability formation from artifacts as five sequentially dependent properties, two of which form a checkpoint for capability formation, and introduce three-scale diagnosis, which judges these properties at the state, game, and lineage levels. In freestyle Gomoku, Reflexion, Voyager, and DGM evolve with the same base model and all show the three signals, yet each exhibits a distinct capability-formation break. Reflexion shows a legalization gain: its pass rate rises only because more of its moves are legal. Voyager shows a compositional override: components that are sound on their own combine to miss all 20 available one-move wins. DGM shows loss-only drift: after passing the checkpoint, later versions only lose passing states. These counterexamples show that signal-based evaluation cannot determine whether a capability has formed.
authors: Ziqian Ban, Haoxiang Yang, Yanfei Zhang, Shixin Liang, Haoran Yu, Xu Lin, Shaobin Zhao, Xuran Li, Zhiyi Cheng

Finds distinct failure modes: legalization gain, compositional override, and loss-only drift.
Concludes that artifact accumulation, behavioral change, and metric improvement are insufficient for capability evaluation.

papers.abstract: The value of memory lies not only in recall but in using it to provide appropriate assistance. Recent benchmarks test memory use in personalisation and agentic tasks, but seldom evaluate assistance without fixed answers or integration across multiple participants. Group chats make both challenges more acute: an assistant must integrate information from multiple members, track revisions and conflicts over time, and produce one response for the group. Yet existing group memory benchmarks rely on synthetic conversations and inherit constrained evaluation from general memory benchmarks, focusing on recall against fixed answers or decisions over a closed set. We introduce GroupAssistBench, the first memory benchmark from real-world group conversations with a deployed group assistant, covering 80,299 messages in 50 groups and costing over $53K. Over the same histories, GroupAssistBench evaluates memory recall (L1) with reference answers and memory use (L2) with service requests without fixed answers across single, distributed, and conflicting memories (M1--M3). Requests are verified to require group history, memories are anchored to their sources, and L2 uses tailored rubrics with penalties derived from real user feedback. Across evaluations of frontier models with full context, retrieval methods, and memory systems, the strongest memory system rivals full context on recall but falls far behind on use, especially for distributed and conflicting memories. Together, two additions that relate retrieved memories and bind remembered facts as response constraints bring consistent gains, showing that group memory systems must improve use, not recall alone.
authors: Zhanghao Hu, Linhai Zhang, Qian Zhao, Qi Zhu, Yuan Hua, Di Liang, Jiasheng Si, Xin Zhao, Yulan He, Zhumin Chen, Lin Gui
bullets: Introduces a real-world benchmark built from 80,299 messages across 50 groups using a deployed group assistant.

Covers single, distributed, and conflicting memories, reflecting revisions and disagreements in group conversations.
Memory systems can approach full-context performance on recall but lag substantially on memory use.
Relating retrieved memories and enforcing remembered facts as response constraints consistently improve assistance.

papers.abstract: Multi-hop retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) supports Web information seeking and fact verification by recovering complementary evidence across related pages within a limited retrieval budget. Scoring evidence independently against the original question can miss supporting units whose relevance emerges through intermediate facts. Iterative retrieval incorporates these facts into subsequent queries, while graph retrieval explicitly models relations among evidence units. Yet fixed-query graph retrievers update entity representations without adapting the query condition to accumulated relational context. We view multi-hop evidence recovery as the coupled evolution of evidence representations and query conditions, with accumulated context informing both what the retriever represents and how it searches for complementary evidence. QueryFlow realizes this perspective by recurrently integrating query-conditioned summaries of graph context into a shared query state, which controls boundary inputs and relation features for subsequent propagation. Across four representative multi-hop question answering (QA) datasets, QueryFlow achieves macro Recall@10 (R@10), Full Recall@10 (FR@10), and LLM-Acc gains of 4.98, 8.40, and 8.0 percentage points over representative baselines, respectively.
authors: Manzong Huang, Chenyang Bu, Yi He, Jiapu Wang, Xindong Wu
bullets: Addresses missed evidence whose relevance emerges only through intermediate facts.
Recurrently summarizes query-conditioned graph context into a shared evolving query state.
Uses the updated query to control boundary inputs and relation features during later graph propagation.
Evaluated on four multi-hop QA datasets, improving macro R@10, FR@10, and LLM-Acc by 4.98, 8.40, and 8.0 percentage points over representative baselines.

papers.abstract: Multi-expert agent marketplaces -- where creators publish domain-specific AI experts for end users to consult -- are an emerging deployment pattern for language technology. A published expert can receive many requests yet little evidence about its creator, who remains active elsewhere: the cold-expert problem. We frame continuous cognitive distillation as converting attributed creator observations into revisable decision rules, communication patterns, and domain procedures. CogniLife proposes a cross-expert attribution design for this problem, with Creator Profiles for transferable creator patterns and Expert Journals for listing-specific knowledge; this design is not yet implemented or evaluated. A deployed platform partially realizes the surrounding lifecycle through creator-authorized authoring, capability-owned proposal filtering, and reversible consolidation of eligible owner-scoped memory. On ProfyBench-v1, an 85-task offline benchmark built from replay seeds and controlled internal tests, the Profy Full configuration as a whole achieves a mean overall score of 4.65/5 from the primary LLM judge, compared with 4.01 for Raw LLM and 4.28 for Expert Prompt, with the largest gains in completeness, specificity, and missing-information tasks. These configuration-level scores do not test cold-expert mitigation, cross-expert transfer, or longitudinal distillation.
authors: Xuwei Tan, Jingchun Huang, Ming Cai, Shuangquan Lyu, Tiange Wang, Yinzhi Wang, Ronghua Shi, Jingwei Song, Yang Jingsong, Yinghui Xia, Hehua Fan, Yifan Zhou, Hanxin Chen, Jiwei Song, Tianyu Shi

Proposes Creator Profiles for transferable creator patterns and Expert Journals for expert-specific knowledge.
Surrounding platform supports creator-authorized authoring, capability-owned proposal filtering, and reversible owner-scoped memory consolidation.
On an 85-task offline benchmark, the full configuration scored 4.65/5 versus 4.01 for Raw LLM and 4.28 for Expert Prompt.
Results do not evaluate cross-expert transfer, longitudinal distillation, or cold-expert mitigation.

papers.abstract: On a public agent leaderboard, a general-purpose agent trails a scaffold built for an airline customer-service benchmark by 13 points on the tasks that touch its database, and a reader could conclude that generality costs accuracy. The gap comes from the grader. The general agent often ends its conversations in a way that never triggers grading, so only about half of its episodes were scored and the rest were stored as failures. Grading the ungraded half under the benchmark's own rule closes the pooled gap, without rerunning any agent. We audit two carefully maintained public leaderboards, HAL and tau2-bench, from their published artifacts alone and find three more instrument errors. A cost column counts nested model calls twice, unevenly across rows. Archived trajectories record grader-written actions as agent actions. Re-grading saved trajectories under a newer evaluator is itself a new measurement: a correct and announced fix reorders a leaderboard, and a mode check that misreads four files collapses their scores by 59 to 82 points while printing no error. Each produced a plausible number, and the HAL maintainers confirmed their three within five weeks. Together the cases show that the infrastructure of agent evaluation, meaning the code that grades, logs, replays and versions an evaluation, is part of the measurement and fails silently, so scores and orderings can move with no visible sign. These failure modes follow from how agent evaluation pipelines are built, and those pipelines change as fast as the agents they measure, so we expect more of them elsewhere. We propose cheap checks that expose the instrument: report the graded fraction, aggregate cost from root spans, tag the provenance of every recorded action, and pin evaluator versions with a published re-grade diff.
bullets: Auditing HAL and tau2-bench found four errors in grading, cost accounting, trajectory logging, and evaluator/version handling.
A general agent’s apparent 13-point deficit disappeared when episodes that had not triggered grading were scored under the benchmark’s own rule.
Double-counted nested model calls, mislabeled grader actions, and a faulty mode check each produced plausible but incorrect measurements.
Regrading archived trajectories under a newer evaluator changed leaderboard rankings, showing that evaluator updates are new measurements.
Recommended safeguards include reporting graded fractions, aggregating cost from root spans, tagging action provenance, and publishing evaluator-version re-grade diffs.

papers.abstract: LLM-powered semantic queries increasingly combine relational processing with multiple LLM-based operators over unstructured data. Efficiently serving such queries is challenging due to runtime dynamism at two coupled levels. Across queries, dynamic arrivals and heterogeneous resource demands continuously change scheduling priorities. Within a query, heterogeneous characteristics across fine-grained input batches cause operator costs and selectivities to vary throughout execution, making a statically optimized plan unreliable. These two forms of dynamism create a circular dependency: inter-query scheduling requires estimates of remaining LLM work, while the remaining work depends on runtime plan choices whose costs become observable only during execution. We present SeqoFlow, a runtime framework that jointly adapts query plans and schedules concurrent semantic queries. SeqoFlow enumerates equivalence-preserving plan alternatives under operator dependencies and decomposes queries into fine-grained units, enabling safe plan adaptation and query preemption at batch boundaries. To support both decisions without exhaustively profiling candidate plans on the target LLM, SeqoFlow uses lightweight speculative estimation to capture runtime costs. These estimates jointly guide plan adaptation and inter-query scheduling, closing the loop between query optimization and LLM inference. Experiments across diverse query structures, data distributions, and arrival rates show that SeqoFlow substantially reduces end-to-end latency compared to existing semantic query systems, adaptive query processing techniques, and conventional scheduling policies.
bullets: Semantic queries face dynamism across queries—changing arrivals and resource demands—and within queries, where batch-level costs and selectivities vary.
These dynamics are coupled: scheduling needs remaining-work estimates, while remaining work depends on runtime plan choices.
SeqoFlow enumerates dependency-preserving plan alternatives and decomposes queries into fine-grained units for safe adaptation and batch-boundary preemption.
Lightweight speculative estimates guide both plan selection and inter-query scheduling without exhaustively profiling every candidate plan.
Experiments across varied query structures, data distributions, and arrival rates show substantially lower end-to-end latency than several existing approaches.

papers.abstract: Foundation models in changing environments can encounter unfamiliar domain knowledge that their original training did not cover. However, new domains rarely provide large amounts of expert-created training data or reliable supervisory signals for further training. We introduce Recursa, a foundation model system that adapts to new domains by learning from its own experience without human experts or a stronger teacher model. Recursa uses a knowledge repository to store what it learns: domain-specific skills and instructions on when to apply them, along with memories of past task experiences and reflections on what to improve. Recursa bootstraps the repository from domain materials and then refines it through recursive self-improvement. It uses parallel learners to execute tasks and synthesize local improvements, then validates and merges the improvements into the knowledge repository. On Harvey LAB's Firm Knowledge benchmark, Recursa raises the all-pass rate on held-out test tasks from 30.0% to 55.0% with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and from 35.0% to 46.0% with Qwen3.8-Flash.

bullets: Addresses domain adaptation when expert-created data and reliable training signals are scarce.
Stores domain skills, usage instructions, task memories, and improvement reflections in a knowledge repository.

Improves held-out all-pass rates on Harvey LAB’s Firm Knowledge benchmark for both evaluated models.

papers.abstract: LLM agents struggle to automate complex enterprise procedures because static, pre-built harness cannot capture proprietary policies, undocumented behaviors, or state-dependent recovery paths that surface only during execution. Procedural memory accrued from agent experience offers a training-free path to closing this gap -- yet unlike episodic records or semantic facts, it must consolidate repeated successes and diagnosed failures into reusable actions and recovery strategies. We introduce WASP-Mem (Wiki-based Agent-Synthesized Procedural Memory), a nimble but effective method that distills execution traces and feedback into persistent, interlinked wiki pages, enabling continual agent learning. On TheAgentCompany benchmark, WASP-Mem raises the checkpoint pass rate by 4.6-6.1% over the strongest baseline we compared across three models while requiring 57-61% less storage. We further present a systematic controlled study spanning consolidation method, feedback type, trace ingestion scope, and refinement rounds. Our results reveal that prescriptive knowledge organization such as human defined schemas and explicit deduplication rules hurts performance rather than closing the procedural-knowledge gap. In contrast, human diagnosis converts failed traces into corrective knowledge and drives sustained improvement: a single round of human diagnosis outperforms four rounds of self-judgment by 7.0-10.9%. These findings point to a simple division of labor: let agents organize procedural memory, and invest human effort where it matters most -- diagnosis.
authors: Peizhi Niu, Ge Shi, Vaibhav Gorde, Sarthak Ghosh, Christos Faloutsos, Min Cheng, Kevin Chen
bullets: Addresses gaps in static agent harnesses, including proprietary policies, undocumented behavior, and state-dependent recovery paths.

Controlled studies find that human-defined schemas and explicit deduplication can hurt performance, whereas human diagnosis substantially improves failed-trace learning.
One round of human diagnosis outperforms four rounds of self-judgment by 7.0–10.9%, suggesting agents should organize memory while humans diagnose failures.

papers.abstract: A stored experience may answer one future question and offer little help with another. We measure this task-conditioned utility rather than assigning each memory a single importance score. A task-blind writer stores a memory without seeing the later task; a frozen reader then answers that task with and without the memory, using identical filler. A cost ledger records the resources used to form, store and expose the memory. On single-call factual-recall tasks built from LongMemEval-V2 web-agent memories, the same memory helps more when it contains information needed for the answer. Its mean paired reward gain on these answer-bearing task pairs exceeds that on matched-control pairs by $+0.33$ (95% interval $+0.21$ to $+0.46$). The tested task-blind summaries and structured records yield smaller gains than Raw, including at fixed total context; a budget sweep is consistent with retention of answer-bearing content contributing to the difference. The bearing--control contrast remains positive in a new session with randomized memory position and under a second reader, although individual memory--task labels change. Generic retrieval performs above chance but misses most screen-defined answer-bearing memories. The factual-recall gains do not extend to the tested software-engineering and scientific-coding benchmarks, where even raw memories have no measurable effect. We provide a public, versioned Conditional Memory Utility Dataset of paired measurements and costs. The practical takeaway is to evaluate memory compression by the task utility it preserves alongside its costs. Task-conditioned measurements make this comparison possible; their stability must also be checked.
authors: Chih-Hsuan Yang, Anjir Ahmed Chowdhury, Feng Yan, Rajeev Thakur
bullets: Measures how much a memory changes a frozen reader’s answer to a task, using identical filler with and without the memory.
On factual-recall tasks, answer-bearing memories produced a larger mean paired reward gain than matched controls: +0.33, with a 95% interval of +0.21 to +0.46.
Tested task-blind summaries and structured records yielded smaller gains than raw memories, including at fixed total context; budget results suggest retaining answer-bearing content matters.
The effect persisted with randomized memory position and a second reader, but generic retrieval missed most screen-defined answer-bearing memories.
The effect did not extend to the tested software-engineering and scientific-coding benchmarks, where raw memories had no measurable impact.

papers.abstract: Next-visit diagnosis prediction forecasts the diagnoses documented at a patient's next encounter, turning retrospective electronic health records into prospective clinical prediction. However, conventional aggregate evaluation obscures its multifaceted nature: distributionally, models must handle variable-size diagnosis sets and long-tailed labels; temporally, they must distinguish persistent, newly recorded, and recurrent diagnoses; and both vary with observed history depth. We introduce an evaluation framework along these dimensions and apply it to rule-based heuristics, LLM-based prompting, retrieval, memory, and multi-agent approaches. This reveals that repeating the last visit outperforms most LLM-based approaches overall despite predicting no new or recurrent diagnoses, and that retrieval and memory exhibit distinct profiles whose relative strengths vary across temporal transitions and backbones. Motivated by this, we propose LONGINUS, a retrieval-memory multi-agent adjudication framework combining evidence retrieved from patient records with structured memory of the patient trajectory. Using cross-view agreement as a reliability heuristic, it preserves shared predictions and adjudicates disagreements without revealing their source. Across MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV with four LLM backbones, LONGINUS achieves the best transition-specific performance among LLM-based methods in nearly all settings while remaining competitive with them on aggregate metrics.
bullets: Aggregate metrics can hide differences in predicting persistent, new, and recurrent diagnoses, especially across varying history depths.
The proposed evaluation framework compares heuristics, prompting, retrieval, memory, and multi-agent methods along distributional and temporal dimensions.
Repeating the last visit outperforms most LLM approaches overall but cannot predict new or recurrent diagnoses.
LONGINUS uses retrieved patient-record evidence, trajectory memory, and cross-view agreement to preserve or adjudicate predictions.
Across MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV with four LLM backbones, it achieves the best transition-specific performance among LLM methods in nearly all settings while remaining competitive on aggregate metrics.

papers.abstract: Knowledge tracing (KT) estimates learners' evolving knowledge states from interaction histories to support adaptive learning. Retrieval-augmented KT improves these estimates using cross-learner behavioral evidence, but existing approaches typically separate evidence retrieval from downstream prediction. This creates a retrieval-inference alignment gap because evidence relevance varies with the learner's evolving state and prediction context. We propose CaRe-KT, a query-adaptive framework that maintains relevance continuity between evidence acquisition and inference without equating retrieval relevance with predictive utility. CaRe-KT introduces an Evidence-Graph Cache (EGC) that combines persistent question-level relational compatibility with interaction-level temporal validity to construct query-specific evidence subgraphs. Historical learning trajectories retrieved through these subgraphs are encoded alongside the target learner's history in a shared representation space using outcome-supervised contrastive learning. An attention mechanism combines acquisition relevance with learned query-evidence compatibility, allowing relevance to inform, rather than determine, each trajectory's predictive influence. Experiments across five benchmarks show that CaRe-KT outperforms strong KT baselines and remains robust under sparse-history and cold-start conditions. These findings support relevance continuity as a design principle for retrieval-augmented knowledge tracing.
authors: Mehrnoush Mohammadi, Kamal Berahmand, Mohammad Morsali, Shazia Sadiq, Wojtek Tomaszewski, Hassan Khosravi
bullets: Addresses the retrieval-inference alignment gap in retrieval-augmented KT, where relevant evidence may not be predictively useful.
Uses an Evidence-Graph Cache to build query-specific evidence subgraphs from persistent question relations and temporally valid interactions.
Encodes retrieved learning trajectories with the target learner’s history using outcome-supervised contrastive learning.
An attention mechanism combines retrieval relevance with learned query-evidence compatibility to determine predictive influence.
Outperforms strong KT baselines across five benchmarks and remains robust with sparse histories and cold-start learners.

Numerical values are illustrative.

(b) CaRe-KT admits a query-adaptive evidence set 1⃝, refines relevance by temporal validity 2⃝, and carries it into inference 3⃝, where it informs but does not dictate influence. papers.abstract: Long-term memory enables large language model (LLM) agents to provide continuous personalized assistance by retaining user information across interactions. Existing systems support this process through fact extraction, organization, updating, and retrieval, but largely maintain memories as independent facts. This fact-centric paradigm may overlook how new facts update, constrain, or conflict with earlier ones, while leaving their applicability, role, and priority for the current request implicit. In this paper, we introduce EvoMemState, a state-centric framework that augments persistent facts with two complementary states: Relational States that capture how facts remain valid and relate to one another as memory evolves, and a Reasoning State that determines how these facts should be applied to the current request. Specifically, EvoMemState consists of three key components: (i) Ontology-Guided Memory State Induction extracts Persistent Facts and constructs Relational States that maintain their validity, scope, and evolving relations. (ii) RL-Based State Evolution internalizes memory-use experience into a policy through reinforcement learning to generate a request-specific Reasoning State. (iii) State-Aware Reasoning then combines the relevant facts with their Relational States and the generated Reasoning State to guide the personal agent. Extensive experiments on long-term dialogue and memory-use benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over existing memory systems in retrieval completeness and memory-grounded response accuracy. Our code and implementation details are available at https://github.com/XMUDeepLIT/EvoMemState.git.
authors: Zhishang Xiang, Yunbo Tang, Zhongqiao Liu, Junkai Chen, Zerui Chen, Qingguo Hu, Yuxuan Zhang, William Grant, Qinggang Zhang, Jinsong Su

Combines relevant facts, relational states, and reasoning states during response generation.
Experiments on long-term dialogue and memory-use benchmarks report improved retrieval completeness and memory-grounded response accuracy over existing systems.

papers.abstract: A memory-augmented agent must decide which memories to keep, merge and retrieve, and its only evidence of their value is its retrieval log: the memories it retrieved in each episode and whether it succeeded. Existing methods assign every memory a value from this log, even when the log cannot separate one memory's contribution from another's. We treat the log as an experiment that nobody designed and ask which memory values it determines. Two counts answer this before any outcome is observed: how often each memory was retrieved, and how often each pair was retrieved together. From these counts, we prove that top-$k$ retrieval leaves every memory value undetermined, however many episodes are logged, and that a question with its own memories, asked once, determines at most one of their values. On fourteen standard memory benchmarks, no memory value is determined in any of 55 configurations. Both causes are choices about retrieval. We introduce LEDGER, which estimates each determined Shapley value in closed form with a confidence interval and reports every other value as undetermined. It merges memories with identical histories without losing a determined value, and it retrieves so that the next log determines more. On pooled HotpotQA, LEDGER raises the fraction of memories determined from 0.001 to 0.797, at a cost of 2.6 accuracy points on HotpotQA and with a gain of 2.7 on LoCoMo.
bullets: Memory value is identifiable only when retrieval histories distinguish a memory’s contribution from others.
Two retrieval statistics—individual counts and pairwise co-retrieval counts—determine identifiability before observing outcomes.

LEDGER estimates determined Shapley values with confidence intervals, merges memories with identical histories, and improves the determined-memory fraction from 0.001 to 0.797 on pooled HotpotQA, with a 2.6-point HotpotQA accuracy cost and a 2.7-point LoCoMo gain.

papers.abstract: Rapid advances in cowork agents are shifting human-AI collaboration toward real-world automation, delivering software, designs, and other artifacts. However, such productivity work demands both high-quality delivery on complex productivity tasks and continued monitoring and decision-making over long horizons, a combination that remains an open challenge. We introduce CoworkOS, a general-purpose harness for long-horizon work that separates task strategy from execution management: the model decides actions, delegation, and acceptance, while the runtime maintains state and feedback. Its three-layer architecture enables direct execution or delegation to Subagents, synchronously or asynchronously, under stable responsibilities. Through a shared application layer, humans and agents inspect and revise the same evolving documents, presentations, CAD models, and Blender scenes, so human-in-the-loop participation can enter both through conversation and through direct modification of the work itself. To sustain continuity across agents and sessions, CoworkOS further introduces hierarchical workspaces and persistent semantic memory, so working files, key decisions, and long-running Job logs remain shareable, reusable, and resumable after interruption. Across 12 benchmarks and 6 categories of real-world applications, CoworkOS proves highly competitive with frontier agent applications such as Codex and DeepSeek Harness. As a sustained-work case study, CoworkOS uses GLM-5.3 as its backbone to conduct RSI-driven automated post-training on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. Over five rounds, the model's average score across eight benchmarks rose from 33.19 to 42.95 (+9.76). Looking ahead, we believe CoworkOS opens a meaningful path toward general cowork-agent intelligence.

papers.abstract: Knowledge is how understanding accumulates across people and generations: durable records that outlive their producers and that others can check, combine, teach, and correct. AI agents are now built and run by many independent users and organizations, and each agent is upgraded, replaced, or retired within months. Yet what an agent learns stays trapped in model parameters, a transient context window, or a system-specific memory store that is appended to and retrieved from rather than processed. We argue that the next generation of AI should be knowledge-centric, built around an explicit, continuously evolving knowledge layer independent of any single agent. In this loop, agents discover knowledge from their environments and trajectories; the layer internalizes it by turning fragmented, heterogeneous records and experience into composable, revisable understanding; and agents across systems and generations use the result and return new outcomes for revision. While discovery and use have advanced rapidly with large language model agents, internalization remains the bottleneck. We argue that internalization should become a persistent object of training and maintenance-centered on condition-preserving conceptualization of events and deductive, inductive, and abductive reasoning across noisy, heterogeneous representations (text, tables, graphs, rules, and programs). To power this layer, we call for knowledge foundation models that provide shared neural capacity for knowledge computation, and outline a research agenda showing how an explicit knowledge layer delivers reuse, cost efficiency, auditability, and continuity across agent generations.
bullets: Current agents keep learning trapped in parameters, context windows, or system-specific memories, limiting reuse and continuity.
The proposed loop separates knowledge discovery, internalization, and use, with internalization identified as the main bottleneck.
Internalization requires condition-preserving conceptualization and deductive, inductive, and abductive reasoning over heterogeneous, noisy representations.
The paper calls for knowledge foundation models to provide shared neural capacity for knowledge computation.
An explicit knowledge layer could improve reuse, cost efficiency, auditability, and continuity across agent generations.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The knowledge-centric loop across agents and generations. Independent agent systems, built on different models and run by different organizations, discover knowledge and contribute it to an explicit knowledge layer. The layer is internalized by transformations and reasoning, and the results are used by other systems and by later generations, which inherit, revalidate, and revise them.

Figure 2: A knowledge foundation model inside the knowledge layer. It combines explicit knowledge, supporting observations and experience, and the implicit capacities of existing models, organizes shared computation across transformation and reasoning layers while delegating exact computation to symbolic components, and produces deductive, inductive, and abductive results whose status is recorded before they are written back. Implicit priors inform inference but do not become knowledge without evidence.

papers.abstract: Long-lived agents rely on persistent memory of users, tasks and decisions, and this memory must stay consistent with a world that keeps changing. When an upstream fact changes, however, memory systems can revise the contradicted memory itself while the beliefs, plans and actions derived from it remain accepted, even though they have lost their support. We therefore formulate dependency-aware state revision, which asks not only what changed but also which dependent states should no longer be trusted. To address it, StateGraph maintains an evolving state dependency graph whose edges are recovered from interaction histories. Its core design is counterfactual verification: each candidate edge is tested by asking whether the dependent state would survive the loss of its premise, which separates support dependence from semantic relatedness, and revision then invalidates a dependent state only when a strict dependency fails and no independent support path survives. To test this design, we introduce StateChangeBench, a controlled benchmark of 50 author-constructed cases annotated with cascade depth, hard negatives and action consequences. On it, StateGraph's Impact-F1 margin over a CUPMem reimplementation is 6.9 percentage points at depth 1 and 26.0 at depth 3+. On public long-term memory benchmarks, its point estimates are comparable to or higher than those of the evaluated baselines on most datasets. These results provide initial evidence that explicit dependency tracking can improve selective memory revision under changing conditions.
bullets: Targets a key consistency problem: revising an upstream fact can leave its dependent memories incorrectly accepted.
Builds an evolving dependency graph from interaction histories.
Uses counterfactual verification to distinguish true support dependence from mere semantic relatedness.
Invalidates a dependent state only when a strict dependency fails and no independent support path remains.

On StateChangeBench, its Impact-F1 margin over a CUPMem reimplementation is 6.9 points at depth 1 and 26.0 points at depth 3+; results on public benchmarks are comparable to or higher than evaluated baselines on most datasets.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The StateGraph pipeline. (A) Direct revision settles what the observation itself contradicts, yielding the seed set It. (B) Dependency reasoning—this paper’s contribution—proposes candidates from six bounded sources, then verifies each counterfactually, so the verified graph is a subgraph of the candidate graph. (C) Conservative revision maps each verified edge to a status instead of invalidating everything reachable. (D) Premise and action gating turns status into behavior. Panels correspond to §4.1–§4.5.

papers.abstract: Enterprise conversational systems require memory to personalize interactions, retain information across sessions, and maintain conversational coherence. At enterprise scale, however, memory must not only retrieve relevant information accurately but also provide it efficiently to the answer-generation model. Existing memory systems face a trade-off between retrieval accuracy and context efficiency. Retrieving more context can improve recall but increases inference cost and latency. We present Scalaris, a scalable enterprise memory architecture that addresses this trade-off through a unified long-term and short-term memory design. We propose that user interactions and assistant responses possess distinct characteristics and roles in a conversation: user interactions capture evolving knowledge about the user and provide value across sessions, whereas assistant responses must be stored efficiently so that only information relevant to the current query is retrieved. We therefore treat them separately and support each with specialized representations and ingestion/retrieval pipelines. Scalaris reaches 92.2 % accuracy on LongMemEval-S and 90.77 % on LoCoMo using Qwen3-32B, state-of-the-art results on both benchmarks, while supplying the answer-generation model with approximately 10 times fewer retrieved context tokens than Hindsight, a leading memory system for conversational AI. When integrated with our proprietary closed-source AI assistants, Scalaris improved overall response quality by 36 %. Together, these results establish Scalaris as a cost-effective framework for building scalable, personalized conversational AI systems.
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between memory retrieval accuracy and inference cost/latency at enterprise scale.
Uses unified long- and short-term memory with specialized representations and ingestion/retrieval pipelines for user interactions versus assistant responses.
Achieves 92.2% on LongMemEval-S and 90.77% on LoCoMo using Qwen3-32B, reported as state-of-the-art on both benchmarks.
Supplies roughly 10× fewer retrieved context tokens than Hindsight and improved response quality by 36% in proprietary assistants.
Scope: evaluated on two memory benchmarks and proprietary closed-source assistants; broader applicability is not established by the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Flow diagram of the ingestion and retrieval pipeline of Scalaris. The ingestion phase organizes user interactions as facts, entities, and summaries in the graph store, assistant responses as atomic units in the vector store, and stores each incoming user query and AI response verbatim in the history store. The retrieval pipeline begins by reformulating the incoming query, which is then used to retrieve information from the graph and vector stores. Summaries are fetched directly from the graph store, and the N most recent exchanges from the history store. All retrieved components are combined during context assembly and passed to the answering system.

Figure 1: Overview of Scalaris’s source-aware memory organization. User interactions are processed to maintain relevant facts, relevant entities, and user and session summaries in a temporal knowledge graph. Assistant responses are decomposed into independently retrievable atomic units and stored in a vector store. In parallel, both user interactions and assistant responses are preserved verbatim in a shared history store.

Figure 2: An illustrative instance of context retrieval in Scalaris. Long-term memory supplies the user’s preference for fuel economy together with prior Honda Civic interactions, while short-term memory supplies the Relevant Assistant Messages, session summary, and recent turns (only the latest exchange is shown, for visual clarity). Together these resolve the referent, let the agent determine that only Corolla information must be retrieved, and enable personalization by focusing on fuel economy and including trade-offs.

Figure 4: Evaluation prompt used by the GPT-4o judge to compare two AI assistant responses. The prompt provides the original user question, recent conversational history, and available memory context, followed by both candidate responses. The judge assesses answer quality, personalization, clarity, actionability, and consistency with the conversation before assigning a score from 0 to 5 to each response and producing a comparative verdict in a strictly specified JSON format.

papers.abstract: Long-term conversational memory faces a timing mismatch: write-time summaries and graphs organize history before a future query is known, while independent retrieval can allocate a limited evidence budget to redundant or fragmented turns. We introduce Chain on Demand (CoD), a query-time evidence organization framework over an unchanged turn-level memory. Given a broad candidate pool, CoD constructs a temporary evidence chain by allocating a fixed anchor budget according to query relevance, lexical diversity relative to selected anchors, and newly covered query terms, followed by deterministic restoration of each selected anchor's same-session neighborhood. The resulting chain is used only for the current query, while the underlying conversational memory remains unchanged. In a paired comparison over all 1,986 LoCoMo questions, CoD achieves 82.2% accuracy on 1,540 non-adversarial questions and 76.3% on all 1,986 questions. On LongMemEval-S, one fixed configuration that indexes both user and assistant turns obtains 86.6% across all 500 questions. These results show that long-term memory can preserve the original conversation while deferring evidence organization until the information need is known.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between write-time memory organization and unknown future queries.
Builds a temporary evidence chain from relevant, lexically diverse anchors that add new query terms.
Restores each selected anchor’s same-session neighborhood to preserve conversational context.
Achieves 82.2% accuracy on 1,540 non-adversarial LoCoMo questions and 76.3% across all 1,986; reaches 86.6% on LongMemEval-S.
Scope: results use fixed configurations and depend on the evaluated conversational-memory benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Cohort memory can support LLM-based recommendation planning through group-level user profiles and advice. As outcome feedback becomes available, this guidance may need to be updated while preserving the underlying observations. We present RecGroupMemory, a workflow that provides this memory to an orchestration LLM and separates memory construction from feedback-based revision. It uses feedback from the previous day to revise decision guidance, while validation checks keep selected source values unchanged. Online comparisons were conducted among Taobao users with low purchasing power selected by the business team. Relative to a no-memory baseline, memory without feedback and memory with feedback showed increases of 1.58% and 1.78%, respectively, in the number of guided transaction users.
bullets: Addresses the need to revise recommendation guidance as outcome feedback arrives without changing underlying cohort data.
Separates memory construction from feedback-based revision for an orchestration LLM.
Uses previous-day feedback to update decision guidance, with validation checks protecting selected source values.
In an online Taobao comparison, guided transaction users increased 1.58% without feedback and 1.78% with feedback versus no memory.
Evaluation focused on Taobao users with low purchasing power selected by the business team.

papers.abstract: Can a language model that reads the full history of an access log say whether a service may act now? On an executable benchmark of grants, withdrawals, reinstatements, expiries, groups and change windows under a known policy, scored on pairs of histories that differ only in the order or one field of the deciding events, open models of 7 to 32 billion parameters fall from 72 to 86 percent after eight or sixteen events to 48 to 55 percent after 256, while reasoning-trained 32B models reading the current state reach 96 and 98 percent. A reasoning model of 120 billion parameters trails the state by four and seven points at 256 and 512 events and by about ten at 1,024, so the length beyond which explicit state outlasts long context grows with the reader. We treat agent memory as recursive filtering. The decision depends on the history only through a state whose size is set by the number of tracked keys. A store holding fewer component records than the state forgets on a time scale set by its capacity, and a reader model predicts its accuracy within 0.02 on average in a registered test. Retaining log lines without regard to time order errs with probability approaching one half, a bound that is attained. A filter in which a model parses each line and an explicit rule applies the updates answers 80 to 89 percent at 256 events and beats relevance retrieval, model-kept ledgers, a reimplementation of StateMem and the Mem0 library. A retriever that selects at query time the lines the queried state depends on matches it at 256 events on the first domain, so what decides is selection by the state's dependencies, which the filter performs when writing, without the query. Applying parsed updates themselves, the models fall to 58 and 59 percent. A frozen replication on a second domain with fresh wording reproduces the horizon.
bullets: Long-context models degrade sharply on access histories: accuracy falls from 72–86% after 8–16 events to 48–55% after 256, while models given current state reach 96–98%.
The effective horizon of long-context reading grows with model size, but even a 120B reasoning model trails explicit state by 4–10 points at 256–1,024 events.
Agent memory is modeled as recursive filtering: only the state relevant to tracked keys needs to be retained, and undersized stores forget on a capacity-dependent timescale.
A parser-plus-rule-update filter achieves 80–89% at 256 events, outperforming relevance retrieval, model-kept ledgers, StateMem, and Mem0.
Selecting history lines by the queried state’s dependencies matches the filter on one domain; a frozen replication on a second domain reproduces the horizon effect.

papers.abstract: AI assistants store values that a language model derived from a person's records under the person's own definitions, such as their important contacts. Keeping such a value correct takes two steps: detection, noticing that an input changed, and repair, producing the correct new value. Benchmarks that score only the final answer cannot tell which step failed, and they state every change as new text. Seeing this limitation, we present MemShift, a benchmark of five shifts: source revision, deletion, redefinition, writer switch, and export. The first three fork a synthetic world into branches that differ only in the shift. Gold values and dependencies are fixed before any text, and a deterministic scorer replaces an LLM judge. For a memory that reports its invalidations, MemShift shows for each changed item whether the memory noticed the change and whether its repair was right. Moreover, we build a reference memory with known detection and repair to validate the measure. By evaluating four open-weight LLMs, we find that detection helps only as much as repair allows: the LLMs re-derive few values computed by the person's definitions correctly, and programs that the LLM writes over typed records close most of the gap to exact recomputation. Code and data are available at https://github.com/zichuanxu/memshift.
bullets: Separates memory-update performance into change detection and value repair, revealing which step fails.
Covers five shifts: source revision, deletion, redefinition, writer switch, and export.
Uses controlled branch construction, fixed gold dependencies, and deterministic scoring instead of LLM judging.
Evaluations of four open-weight LLMs show limited accuracy when re-deriving values from personal definitions.
LLM-generated programs over typed records approach exact recomputation, closing much of the repair gap.

papers.abstract: Software development sessions often involve several unfinished tasks rather than one issue carried through to completion. As coding agents take on repository-level development, they need to recover an earlier task's requirements and partial progress after intervening work. Existing repository-level benchmarks typically score one issue-to-patch episode and do not directly measure whether an agent can resume a task after advancing other unfinished work in the same repository. We introduce \textbf{\ourmethod}, a benchmark for focus-task resumption in sessions that interleave unfinished tasks drawn from the same source repository, with a persistent checkout for each task. Each focus task is evaluated in matched uninterrupted and switched sessions with identical focus requirements and executable verifiers. The switched session interleaves ordered stages from other unfinished tasks in the same repository, while only the final focus patch is scored. \ourmethod~contains 200 focus tasks from 19 Python repositories, reconstructed from issue, pull-request, and review histories and rendered as 400 matched session specifications. Across 7 coding agents, interleaved unfinished work produces an average focus-task resolution gap of 11.5 percentage points, ranging from 6.0 to 15.0 percentage points. Trajectory analysis identifies cross-task requirement confusion and loss of task state as recurrent resumption behaviors. We introduce a plug-in context-management module that selects task-relevant history and maintains concise task-state summaries. On OpenCode, the module improves focus-task completion under same-repository task switching by 5.5 to 15.5 percentage points across the evaluated models. Code is available at github.com/Miraclecsc/Switch-SWE.
bullets: Introduces a benchmark for evaluating focus-task resumption in interleaved coding sessions, unlike standard single-issue evaluations.
Matches uninterrupted and switched sessions using persistent task checkouts and executable verifiers; only the final focus-task patch is scored.

Common failures include confusing requirements across tasks and losing track of partial task state.
A context-management module that selects relevant history and summarizes task state improves completion by 5.5–15.5 points on OpenCode.

papers.abstract: Memory systems for LLM agents are evaluated mostly on social dialogue, where facts accumulate and rarely change, so remembering reduces largely to finding the turn in which something was said. Financial dialogue breaks this assumption: figures are revised, stances shift without being restated, rules stated once govern later questions, and a single company is discussed under several analytical lenses. Memory systems that retrieve the passages most similar to a question, or the most recent ones, therefore return superseded values, miss rules that share no wording with the question, and cannot recover a stance spread across sessions. We present TrackMem, a per-speaker graph memory that tracks the history of figures, separates perspectives by entity and lens, and preserves each speaker's actions in chronological order. To evaluate it, we introduce FinLoCoMo, a benchmark of 15 long-horizon investment conversations with 765 questions in two splits: one following the LoCoMo categories and one targeting four failure modes. With two readers, TrackMem outperforms existing memory systems on both splits. On the failure-mode split it reaches 73.9% macro accuracy against 69.4% for the strongest baseline, with the largest gains on questions about revised figures (86.5% against 73.4%).
bullets: Financial conversations challenge standard retrieval because values change, stances evolve implicitly, rules may be stated only once, and entities are discussed through multiple lenses.
TrackMem uses a per-speaker graph memory to preserve figure histories, distinguish entity–perspective combinations, and order actions chronologically.

With two readers, TrackMem outperforms existing memory systems on both splits, achieving 73.9% macro accuracy versus 69.4% for the strongest baseline on failure-mode questions.
Its largest improvement concerns revised figures: 86.5% accuracy versus 73.4% for the strongest baseline.

papers.abstract: Understanding mobility dynamics and the effects of urban transportation management policies requires examining how individual travel decisions, traffic conditions, and policy interventions influence one another over time. We present AgenticMobility, an open-source experimental platform for studying how mobility AI agents and other AI agents interact, adapt through repeated experience, and collectively shape mobility outcomes. Persistent agents retain identities and relevant states across rounds, with explicit interfaces defining information access, admissible actions, and decision schedules; linked records trace decisions, execution, and feedback. In the current implementation, large language model (LLM) agents act as travelers choosing routes and departure times and as a manager periodically adjusting link charges within MATSim. A preliminary demonstration spans 100 simulated days in each of five configurations, with one run per configuration and a shared simulation seed. In the joint traveler--manager run, all 1,179,300 finalized target decisions satisfied action constraints; execution checks verified implementation of accepted choices and preservation of personal memories across days. Trajectories show stable route choices alongside departure-time adjustments and differences between controlled-trip and population-wide outcomes. The platform supports experiments on individual adaptation, collective outcomes, and management interventions by varying information access, retained experience, and management feedback. Source code is available at https://github.com/Agentic-City-Research/Agentic-Mobility
