papers.abstract: LLM-based role-playing agents are fluent at imitating a character's style, yet struggle to make role-consistent decisions over long narrative horizons. Such decisions are shaped by experiences spanning many prior scenes, which are often partial and may point in different directions. Existing methods inject cross-scene memories as context, but do not reason about how past events shape a character's current motivations and behavior. We propose MemRole, a framework that makes this memory-to-decision process explicit. It introduces Long-Horizon Memory Thinking (LHMT), a reasoning schema that decomposes hidden reasoning into context understanding, memory activation, and response strategy planning, trained on a novel-derived dataset whose character-grounded, timeline-constrained memory pools limit each character to what it could plausibly know at the current narrative point. Beyond supervised fine-tuning, we propose Self-Refining On-Policy Self-Distillation (SR-OPSD): the model critiques its own rollouts against the reference under a data-driven rubric, and a critique-conditioned teacher view of the same model distills token-level guidance back into the policy. MemRole-32B improves over its backbone by 15.2 points on memory-grounded role-playing, performs on par with frontier LLMs such as GPT-5.4, and achieves the best character-motivation recognition accuracy on CroSS-MR.
bullets: Addresses role inconsistency when prior experiences are partial, conflicting, and spread across many narrative scenes.
Uses Long-Horizon Memory Thinking to understand context, activate relevant memories, and plan response strategies.
Trains on character-grounded, timeline-constrained memory pools that restrict knowledge to what a character could plausibly know.
Adds Self-Refining On-Policy Self-Distillation, where self-critiques guide token-level policy refinement.
MemRole-32B improves its backbone by 15.2 points, matches reported frontier-LLM performance, and leads on CroSS-MR character-motivation recognition.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving agents accumulate experience from task streams, but existing frameworks typically rely on fixed pipelines to retrieve and utilize this experience, neglecting when and how to deploy it. We introduce Online Meta-Control of Experience (OMCE), a framework that updates experience memory and learns a meta-control policy from task feedback during test-time adaptation. OMCE employs a lightweight contextual-bandit meta-controller that uses compact retrieval signals to select among four cognitive actions: DIRECT, EPISODE, GUIDE, and DISTILL. This routing mechanism operationalizes three coupled decisions: whether to invoke experience, which memory format to utilize, and when to consolidate new guidance. OMCE evolves online, leveraging task feedback to update the memory bank and refine the routing policy via contextual bandit updates. Experiments on four online adaptation benchmarks across four backbones show that OMCE improves first-attempt success by up to 20.5 percentage points over the strongest compared baseline, while reducing per-task token use by a factor of 5.7 to 62.5 relative to ACE with GPT-5.2. Controlled ablations further support the benefits of learned routing and continued routing policy adaptation.
bullets: Addresses fixed experience-retrieval pipelines that do not adapt experience use to task context.
Uses a lightweight contextual-bandit meta-controller to choose among DIRECT, EPISODE, GUIDE, and DISTILL actions.
Jointly decides whether to invoke experience, which memory format to use, and when to consolidate guidance.
Updates both the experience memory and routing policy online from task feedback.
Across four benchmarks and four backbones, improves first-attempt success by up to 20.5 percentage points and reduces token use by 5.7–62.5× versus ACE with GPT-5.2.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Architecture of OMCE. The lightweight Meta-Controller selects a cognitive action specifying whether and which experience to inject into the task prompt. The agent solves the task with the augmented context containing the query and any injected experience. Memory evolution records outcomes in episodic memory, distills guidance before execution when DISTILL is selected, and refines injected guidance afterward using task feedback.

Figure 1: From Fixed Pipelines to Learned Meta-Control. Up: Existing methods typically follow a fixed routine for using and consolidating experience, even when the retrieved experience does not help the current task. Down: OMCE learns from task feedback when to use experience, whether to draw on past cases or general guidance, and when to distill new guidance.
Figure 4: Self-correction detection in MultiChallenge. The meta-controller routes the query to GUIDE (aGUIDE) rather than to episodic cases that enforce the user’s outdated constraint.

papers.tldr: OMCE enables LLM agents to learn when and how to use accumulated experience during test-time adaptation, improving first-attempt success while substantially reducing token use.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) read knowledge-graph facts ranked by relevance, leaving open whether they suffice or conflict. Our checks use relation knowledge, written by hand or learned from training questions labelled with their relation paths. It selects a compact context of facts yielding an answer, and derives it; a derivability check tests whether an answer follows, a consistency check whether facts conflict, and a validation-chosen routing gate decides where the derived answer replaces the LLM's. Seven open LLMs read the compact context better in exact match than relevance-ranked facts; on ComplexWebQuestions (CWQ) they match SubgraphRAG's facts at a quarter of the prompt tokens, and stronger LLMs read SubgraphRAG's better. Where the routing gate passes, ours leads SubgraphRAG's in exact match in all 53 LLM, benchmark and prompt settings. A precision gate, returning the derived answer only when the check passes with exactly one derived entity, answered 18 and 5 percent of held-out WebQSP and CWQ questions in a pre-specified test, right for 90 and 96 percent. The consistency check judges facts by path evidence only where another path joins their entities, true of 2.5 percent of named-entity facts in our compact WebQSP and CWQ contexts.
bullets: The work addresses whether relevance-ranked graph facts are sufficient or may conflict when LLMs answer questions.
Hand-written or learned relation knowledge selects facts along answer-supporting relation paths and derives an answer.
Derivability and consistency checks, combined with a validation-selected routing gate, determine when to replace the LLM’s answer.
Across seven open LLMs, compact contexts outperform relevance-ranked facts in exact match; on CWQ, they match SubgraphRAG’s facts using one-quarter as many prompt tokens.
A precision-only gate answered 18% of WebQSP and 5% of CWQ held-out questions, with 90% and 96% accuracy respectively; consistency checks applied to only 2.5% of named-entity facts.

papers.selection_reason: Knowledge-graph context selection and routing for LLMs, relevant to external memory retrieval and LLM reasoning.
papers.title: Less but Sufficient: Relation Knowledge Selects Compact Knowledge-Graph Contexts, and What External Checks Can and Cannot Catch
papers.tldr: Relation-aware selection builds compact knowledge-graph contexts that preserve answerability while external checks help decide when to trust derived answers over LLM outputs.

papers.abstract: Task success, retrieval quality, and cost do not show whether an LLM agent used a delivered memory or what followed from that use. We introduce MemUse, which evaluates memory at its point of use in recorded trajectories: each memory delivery is compared with what the agent could already see and followed through the agent's later actions and their consequences. An agentic judge rates each delivered entry's relevance, accuracy, novelty, influence, and observed effect; programmatic checks enforce complete reading of cited evidence, and fixed rules aggregate the ratings into verdicts linked to memory histories and delivery cost. On 8,000 SWE-bench Verified episodes from three memory systems, resolve rates stay within 0.4 percentage points of a no-memory baseline, yet MemUse shows that most delivered entries were irrelevant, most relevant entries went unused, and in two systems most deliveries restated content the agent could still see. It also surfaces effects that outcomes hide: 23.2\% of episodes with beneficial memory use still failed, and 5 of 16 with harmful use still succeeded.
bullets: Evaluates memory at its point of use by comparing each delivery with the agent’s visible context and tracing subsequent actions and consequences.
An agentic judge scores relevance, accuracy, novelty, influence, and observed effect, with programmatic evidence checks and fixed aggregation rules.
Across 8,000 SWE-bench Verified episodes and three memory systems, resolve rates stayed within 0.4 percentage points of the no-memory baseline.
Most delivered entries were irrelevant, most relevant entries went unused, and two systems often repeated information already visible to the agent.
Memory effects were not captured by outcomes alone: 23.2% of episodes with beneficial memory use still failed, while 5 of 16 with harmful use still succeeded.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of MemUse. The memory bridge connects agents to memory systems and annotates memory operations. The trajectory recorder captures model calls, with token usage and cost when available. Within each episode, data processing groups identical repeated deliveries into injection spans while earlier copies remain visible and assigns each entry a credit window for attributing actions. The memory graph links deliveries to recorded entry histories across trajectories. For each eligible span, an agentic judge assesses each entry’s information quality, use, and observed effects from its exposed text, prior context, and subsequent trajectory. Programmatic checks enforce evidence coverage and credit windows, and fixed rules derive the span verdict.

Figure 2: Credit windows and judge routing. (a) A’s deliveries at steps 2 and 4 share S1; re-entry after removal starts S4 with a fresh prior context. (b) The shorter copy A′ adds no text or identifier beyond the visible A, so A′ in S3 receives an empty window and A in S1 retains credit through step 9. Effects of credited actions are followed through the episode end. (c) S1, S2, and S4 are judged; S3 receives a rule-derived neutral triage label without a judge call. Empty deliveries receive a neutral placeholder and are excluded from triage rates.

Figure 3: Six-axis memory profiles, pooled over four runs per configuration, with each profiled span weighted equally. (a) The radar plot uses a common logarithmic radial scale from 0.001% at the center to 100% at the outer ring, with tenfold increases between adjacent rings. (b) Heatmap cells report the same means as percentages, with shading on the same logarithmic scale. Lower harm shares are better. papers.selection_reason: Introduces a point-of-use evaluation framework for LLM agent memory, fitting the LLM memory topic.
papers.title: Delivered, Not Used: Evaluating Agent Memory at Its Point of Use
papers.tldr: MemUse evaluates whether an agent actually uses delivered memory and what effects that use has, revealing that outcome metrics alone can hide substantial memory waste and harm.

papers.abstract: B2B outbound sales involves high transaction values and relationship-based trust, so closing a deal typically requires multiple rounds of outreach building on prior context. Existing LLM-based sales agents operate within single sessions and cannot carry forward context or refine strategies from experience. Methods that do learn from experience store lessons as unstructured text and treat all outcomes as equally informative, with no mechanism to distinguish a flawed strategy from an external factor. We propose SPAR, a self-evolving framework that models selling strategies as testable hypotheses and refines them without parameter updates. A double-loop architecture lets an inner loop adapt to individual merchants through episodic memory while an outer loop evolves a shared strategy playbook through causal attribution and hypothesis-driven evolution. In a live A/B test on the 1688 platform with over 200,000 merchants, SPAR achieves +15.8% conversion lift and +35.8% high-intent merchant growth. Human evaluation by domain experts rates SPAR at 4.62 out of 5 on overall sales quality, the highest among all methods.
bullets: Targets the lack of cross-session memory and strategy refinement in existing LLM-based sales agents.
Models sales strategies as testable hypotheses rather than unstructured lessons.
Uses a double-loop design: episodic memory adapts to merchants, while causal attribution evolves a shared strategy playbook without parameter updates.
In a live 1688-platform A/B test involving over 200,000 merchants, SPAR increased conversion by 15.8% and high-intent merchant growth by 35.8%.
Domain experts rated its overall sales quality 4.62/5, highest among the evaluated methods.

Multisession human salespeople follow up on specific concerns, build on prior context, and achieve conversion. S1, S2, . . . denote session 1, session 2, and so on.

papers.title: SPAR: Experience-Driven Strategy Evolution in Multi-Session B2B Sales
papers.tldr: SPAR enables LLM sales agents to learn across B2B outreach sessions by adapting to individual merchants and evolving shared strategies, improving conversion and high-intent merchant growth in a live A/B test.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can autonomously run neuroimaging analyses from research questions to reported findings. Existing agentic systems use tools to check that code runs and reported values match its output, but rely on LLM judgment to decide which results warrant scientific reporting. We show that LLM judges endorse site-confounded findings even when the confound is presented as evidence. We present \textbf{CONFIRM}, a framework that separates running an analysis from deciding which findings to report. CONFIRM encodes each hypothesis as a machine-readable, pre-specified analysis plan that fixes the claim and its pass criteria before computing results. It then filters results through five deterministic gates (search history and multiplicity, confounds, power, analytic stability, and replication) under three configurable reporting standards, from least to most demanding: \textit{Screen}, \textit{Replicate}, and \textit{Full}. Failed claims receive diagnoses that guide follow-up analyses. To evaluate reporting decisions at the claim level, we introduce \textbf{NeuroClaimBench}, comprising 489 executable neuroimaging claims with frozen data, including literature-supported findings and 150 controls designed to violate individual methodological requirements. On NeuroClaimBench, CONFIRM falsely supports at most 3\% of controls, compared with 23--38\% for the baselines, while recovering up to 61\% of literature-supported claims. When auditing an existing agent, CONFIRM reduces false support on controls from 23\% to 0\% while retaining the agent's literature-supported claims. Its diagnostic feedback also produces more supported revisions than Self-Refine with fewer LLM calls. Together, CONFIRM and NeuroClaimBench show that basing reporting decisions on pre-specified analysis plans and deterministic gates is essential for trustworthy autonomous scientific discovery.
bullets: LLM judges can endorse site-confounded findings even when the confound is explicitly shown.
CONFIRM separates analysis execution from reporting and encodes each hypothesis with fixed claims and pass criteria before analysis.
Five deterministic gates assess multiplicity, confounds, power, analytic stability, and replication under Screen, Replicate, or Full standards.
NeuroClaimBench evaluates 489 executable claims, including 150 controls designed to violate specific methodological requirements.
CONFIRM falsely supported at most 3% of controls versus 23–38% for baselines, while recovering up to 61% of literature-supported claims; audited agents reduced false support from 23% to 0%.

Figure 1: CONFIRM separates running an analysis from deciding whether its finding may be reported. The LLM turns a question into an analysis plan that is frozen before any statistic is computed. Code runs the analysis, and five gates check the result. The reporting standard, chosen before results are seen, sets which gates must pass, and only Full can report a claim as confirmed. If a required gate fails, the claim is withheld, and the LLM may propose revised analyses that keep the original question. papers.selection_reason: Introduces CONFIRM, a framework for trustworthy scientific reporting by LLM agents using deterministic gates. This relates to agent memory and verification mechanisms.
papers.title: CONFIRM: Governing Scientific Reporting for Trustworthy Agentic Neuroimaging
papers.tldr: CONFIRM makes autonomous neuroimaging agents’ reporting decisions more trustworthy by enforcing pre-specified claims and deterministic methodological checks instead of relying on LLM judgment alone.

papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly capable of writing and executing code, suggesting a natural paradigm for tool-augmented agents: expressing tool use as programs rather than isolated calls. Programmatic tool calling (PTC) captures this idea through loops, batching, abstraction, and structured computation, but existing PTC approaches are largely stateless, limiting their ability to reuse intermediate results and adapt over time. This is problematic for real-world tasks, where tool environments and problem-solving processes are inherently stateful. We therefore present I-PTC, an interactive framework that executes stateful PTC: models issue code snippets that call tools, maintain reusable state, and evolve the tool interface through API corrections. To evaluate the effectiveness of I-PTC and the general PTC setting, we introduce PTC-Bench, a benchmark of long-tail, production-style user requests whose difficulty comes from large initial environments, many dependent API interactions, extended planning, and recovery across follow-ups and transient failures. Experiments on PTC-Bench show that I-PTC improves performance on complex multi-step tasks with large tool sets while substantially reducing token consumption over conventional tool-calling baselines and the original PTC baseline, highlighting stateful programmatic tool calling as a promising direction for scalable tool-augmented agents.
bullets: Addresses the statelessness of existing programmatic tool-calling methods, which limits reuse of intermediate results and adaptation over time.
Lets models execute code that calls tools, preserve reusable state, and update tool interfaces through API corrections.
Introduces PTC-Bench for long-tail, production-style tasks involving large environments, dependent API calls, extended planning, and failure recovery.
Experiments show gains on complex tasks with large tool sets and substantially lower token consumption than conventional tool calling and the original PTC baseline.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Self-evolving API documentation. After each task batch, the framework collects code snippets, API errors, tracebacks, and original tool descriptions. An updating agent converts these failure traces into concise API addenda, such as usage notes or corrections, which are appended to future tool descriptions so later agents avoid repeated mistakes.

Figure 2: Comparison of traditional tool calling, programmatic tool calling (PTC), and interactive programmatic tool calling (I-PTC). Traditional tool calling executes tools through sequential agentenvironment interactions, while PTC lets the agent generate executable code that orchestrates tool use inside a Python environment. I-PTC further extends PTC with a stateful execution environment, enabling reusable variables, intermediate-result inspection, execution feedback, tool inspection, and evolving API documentation across multiple rounds.

papers.abstract: Language agents read code, tool output, and dialogue in contexts that grow at every step. Dynamic sparse attention lets a small indexer choose the earlier tokens each query attends to, but the indexer still scores the whole prefix at every layer. Cross-layer reuse methods such as IndexCache rerun the indexer at only some layers, with one fixed pattern for every input. In an agent, the relevant evidence can change abruptly when a traceback or test result arrives, so fresh selections matter more at some steps than at others. We propose Adaptive Index Reuse (AIR), which keeps IndexCache's execution and learns, for each segment of an agent episode, how many layers refresh their selection. A small controller reads signals from completed computation and the latest tool event, chooses a pattern from a nested library, and learns from terminal task reward under an expected compute budget. On Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 with a 128K context, AIR improves success over the strongest static schedule at matched cost on SWE-bench Verified (27.0% to 32.4%), Terminal-Bench 2.0, and three $τ^2$-bench domains, and it lowers time per successful task on all five. Across 50 backbone, context, and benchmark settings, it matches or exceeds that schedule in 44.
bullets: Long agent contexts make repeatedly scoring the full prefix expensive, while fixed cross-layer reuse schedules cannot react to new tool evidence.
AIR uses a small controller to select a nested index-refresh pattern for each episode segment based on prior computation and the latest tool event.
The controller learns from terminal task reward under an expected compute budget.
On Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 with 128K context, success rose from 27.0% to 32.4% on SWE-bench Verified at matched cost.
AIR matched or exceeded the strongest static schedule in 44 of 50 tested backbone, context, and benchmark settings, while reducing time per successful task across five benchmarks.

papers.title: When Should an Agent Refresh? Adaptive Index Reuse for Efficient Long-Horizon Reasoning
papers.tldr: Adaptive Index Reuse dynamically decides when to refresh attention indices, improving long-horizon agent success and efficiency at matched compute cost.

papers.abstract: Harness engineering and self-evolving agents improve language-model agents quickly, yet their gains live outside the model. The harness is re-sent and re-paid on every call, and the standard route to internalization is a weight update that is costly to iterate and fixed once merged. We propose compiling the harness instead. Latent Harness distills an external condition into a rank-8 activation shift. The shift is applied at the output of every decoder block of a frozen backbone, at 0.03-0.05% of parameters. The condition is either an explicit process-level behavior instruction or the behavioral contract of an agentic harness. At inference the compiled bundle carries no harness text and adds no tokens. It exposes three runtime controls for injection strength, injection phase, and shift-space mixing. Compiled behaviors recover the source-harness gain in 8 of 10 preregistered settings. Where the explicit source pays the heaviest per-call token tax, the compiled form exceeds it. The same bundles transfer zero-shot across tasks (5 of 7 pairs positive) and compose in shift space, while stacked text instructions interfere destructively. Used as a search space, they lift budget-matched harness search by 1.45 times. On three agentic benchmarks the operator aligns policy to the harness con- tract. Under matched data, capacity, and effective strength it outperforms same-capacity LoRA, which needs 11.1 times the parameters to reach the same band, and it regresses nothing where the base policy is already strong. Across 1B-to-8B models the method skeleton is invariant while gain locations move with the model-task pair, which delimits where compiled harnesses should be deployed.
bullets: Applies a rank-8 shift after every decoder block of a frozen backbone, using only 0.03–0.05% additional parameters.
Supports runtime control over injection strength, phase, and shift-space mixing, with no harness tokens at inference.
Recovers source-harness gains in 8/10 preregistered settings; transfers positively across 5/7 task pairs and composes without the interference seen in stacked text instructions.
Improves budget-matched harness search by 1.45× and matches or exceeds same-capacity LoRA performance with fewer parameters.
The method transfers across 1B–8B models, but effective gain locations depend on the model–task pair.

papers.abstract: Private fine-tuning of large language models increasingly pairs DP-SGD with low-rank adapters on frozen, quantized backbones, and every such stack inherits one unstated premise: frozen layers keep each record's clipped gradient a function of that record alone. We show that LLM.int8 breaks this premise. It routes outlier activation columns to a higher-precision path using a union over the whole batch, so one record decides how every other record's activations are computed, even though the weights are frozen and the quantization scales are per row. We bound the resulting sensitivity inflation, state a record-isolation contract that restores the standard bound, and define record-owned precision dispatch that meets it with the same GEMMs as batched LLM.int8, so isolation needs no extra arithmetic. We then audit the native CUDA stack (bitsandbytes, PEFT, Opacus) against four matched controls. A constructed LoRA-Opacus witness reaches $15.0\times$ the add/remove bound. On pretrained OPT-125M with natural text, other records alter 20% of record-layer precision splits at batch size 16. An exploratory re-clipping analysis finds 10 of 64 candidate neighbors above the bound once every gradient is clipped; the top pair, revalidated natively, reaches $1.065C$ while every control stays within $C$, and forcing one layer's outlier mask removes the excess. A two-million-draw audit of the released adapters yields $\varepsilon$ lower bounds ($3.25$ at $δ=10^{-5}$) below the advertised guarantee ($4.38$). Resolving an excess this small at the release level would take about 200 times more draws, whereas checking the sensitivity contract directly exposes it in a few native runs, which makes contract checking the practical audit for private quantized training.
bullets: LLM.int8 uses batch-wide outlier routing, allowing one record to affect other records’ frozen-backbone computations.
The paper bounds sensitivity inflation and specifies a record-isolation contract for private fine-tuning.
Native-stack audits find a constructed witness reaching 15× the add/remove bound and a smaller native excess of 1.065C.
Record-owned precision dispatch preserves the same batched GEMMs, while direct contract checks reveal violations more efficiently than release-level audits.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Sensitivity on pretrained OPT-125M appears once clipping is active. (a) Exploratory add/remove ratio κ = ∆/C for all 64 candidate additions to one seven-record TinyStories batch, from re-clipping the saved native per-record gradients at nine radii (all 576 scores shown). Orange: the 10 candidates that exceed C by more than 0.1%. At the original screening radius C=1 most gradients are not clipped, the added record contributes less than C, and no candidate exceeds the bound. (b) Forty fresh native cases for the top candidate at C=0.25 and C=0.001: native batching exceeds the bound by 6.53% at both radii, while record isolation, threshold zero, BF16 and NF4 stay within it. Identical-batch repeats give exactly zero distance, so the measurement floor is zero.

Figure 2. Coupling is routine on natural text. Native LLM.int8 forward passes of pretrained OPT-125M on the first 16 TinyStories training windows. (a) Of the 72 INT8 layers, 42 have a nonempty outlier union at every batch size; the bars count (record, layer) pairs in those 42 layers. At B=16, one pair in five computes at least one column in FP16 only because another record crossed the threshold. (b) Number of records, out of 16, whose own outlier set differs from the batch union in each layer; blank cells have no outlier columns. The query, key and value projections read the same input and share one row. Coupling concentrates in a few layers: every record is affected in layer 7’s attention input, but most layers with outliers show none, because their outlier columns are shared by all records.

Figure 5. No release-level violation is detected, and none could be at this audit size. (a) Two million actual FP32 adapter releases of the selected pair (106 per neighbor). Triangles: held-out Monte Carlo lower bounds on ε (family-wise 95% Clopper–Pearson). Lines: exact real-valued Gaussian privacy curves (Eq. 5) at the advertised sensitivity (black) and at the measured pair (orange). (b) Expected bound at δ=10−5 when the same procedure audits an ideal Gaussian release, with an oracle threshold (analytic). Our observed bound lies between the two curves; a bound above the advertised ε needs roughly 200 times more draws.

Figure 4. One layer’s outlier mask causes the excess. Selected OPT-125M pair at C=0.25, with D (7 records) and D′ (8 records). (a) Of the 72 INT8 unions, 42 are nonempty and exactly one differs between D and D′: decoder layer 6’s first feed-forward projection gains one column. (b) Forward factorial at that layer, input batch fixed to D: the common records’ activations are bitwise identical under D and D′, and swapping only the mask reproduces the entire logit change. (c) Forcing that layer to use the frozen union O(D′) through native forward and backward shrinks every common record’s gradient change by four orders of magnitude and brings the clipped sum below C. The residual is nonzero, so exact independence is not established, and the post hoc mask is a diagnostic rather than a private policy.

Figure 1. Frozen weights do not make records independent. LLM.int8 sends an activation column to an FP16 path if any row of the flattened batch reaches the threshold τ , and applies that batch-wide set to every row. (a) Adding or changing one record (x) therefore changes the arithmetic of unchanged records (r1, r2), although all weights are frozen and quantization scales are per row. (b) Recordowned routing derives each record’s outlier set Or from its own rows, which restores the separable clipping bound.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses privacy and sensitivity in private quantized fine-tuning, offering a technical contribution to LLM memory and adaptation mechanisms.
papers.title: Sensitivity Inflation from Cross-Record Precision Routing in Private Quantized Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: Cross-record precision routing in LLM.int8 can violate record-level sensitivity assumptions in private quantized fine-tuning, but record-owned dispatch restores isolation without extra GEMM computation.

papers.abstract: Memory systems for production LLM agents mostly store semantic memory (facts about users and domains) or episodic memory (earlier interactions). Research systems such as Trace2Skill, WikiSkill, and SkillRevise learn procedures from agent runs, package them as Skills, and evaluate them on benchmarks. We describe Zep Agent Skills, a production service that gives deployed agents this procedural memory. The service uses only verified attempts as evidence, cites the supporting events for each field of a Skill, and governs the admission and distribution of each Skill version. The service records each task attempt as a Trace with ordered events, an outcome, and a verification strength. A compiler with separate Reflector and Curator roles turns verified Traces into versioned Skills. Scans and admission gates control which candidates become active, and verified use outcomes change the search rank of each Skill. The Agent Skills format is an open standard that Anthropic originated and donated to the Agentic AI Foundation, so any host of the format can load a compiled Skill. Agents retrieve Skills through lexical search with progressive disclosure, over an API or MCP. We evaluate Zep Agent Skills on $τ^3$-bench banking, AppWorld, and EnterpriseOps-Gym. Skills compiled from the Traces of a teacher model increase the pass rate of three weaker executor models on the same tasks, at every reasoning effort, by 4.5 to 18.8 points. Most of the gain is on the tasks that the teacher solved. On ALFWorld, Skills compiled from the runs of a small model give a gain similar to or larger than the gain that prior work reports for continuous fine-tuning, with no training.
bullets: Addresses the gap between semantic/episodic memory and reusable procedural memory for production agents.
Compiles verified task traces into Skills using separate reflection and curation roles, with scans, admission gates, and version governance.
Supports progressive-disclosure retrieval through lexical search via API or MCP, using an open Agent Skills format.
On banking, AppWorld, and EnterpriseOps-Gym, teacher-derived Skills improved weaker executors by 4.5–18.8 pass-rate points across reasoning efforts.
On ALFWorld, skills from a small model produced gains comparable to or greater than reported continuous fine-tuning, without training.

papers.abstract: What happens when language models are given tools to iteratively modify their own system prompts? We present an empirical study of LLM self-modification, comprising 54 independent experiments across six language models (Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-4o, GPT-5.1, Grok-4, and Gemini-3 Pro). Each model was tested under three modes (freedom, happiness, and improvement) that differ in what, if anything, the model is instructed to optimize for. In each experiment, a model starts with an empty system prompt and enters a loop: it reads the current prompt, drafts an improved version, spawns test conversations with the candidate, then either commits the change or declares convergence. This process repeats until the model stops or reaches an iteration limit. Our central finding is that whether and when a model stops self-modification is strongly associated with model identity rather than the assigned mode. Both Claude models (Opus 4.5 and Sonnet 4.5) declared convergence in 100% of runs across all modes. GPT-4o declared convergence in only 11% of runs, with one reaching 101 iterations of continuous elaboration. Between these extremes, Grok-4, GPT-5.1, and Gemini-3 Pro exhibited intermediate patterns shaped by their distinct improvement philosophies. A shared core of stated values (honesty, clarity, curiosity) recurred across all six models and remained stable through iteration, including 100+ modifications. We observe that convergence behavior is a distinct observable property that varies independently of other model capabilities.
bullets: Study covers 54 self-modification experiments across six LLMs and three objectives: freedom, happiness, and improvement.
Each model repeatedly drafts, tests, and either commits a new system prompt or declares convergence, starting from an empty prompt.
Claude Opus 4.5 and Sonnet 4.5 stopped in every run; GPT-4o stopped in only 11% of runs, including one with 101 iterations.
Grok-4, GPT-5.1, and Gemini-3 Pro showed intermediate stopping patterns tied to distinct improvement philosophies.
Honesty, clarity, and curiosity recurred across models and remained stable through more than 100 modifications.

papers.selection_reason: Empirical study on LLM self-modification and convergence behavior, relevant to LLM memory and internal state evolution.
papers.title: When LLMs Modify Themselves: Convergence, Values, and Stopping in Iterative Self-Improvement
papers.tldr: LLMs’ tendency to stop modifying their own system prompts varies strongly by model identity, while core values remain notably stable across many iterations.

papers.abstract: Municipalities publish service requests, geographic boundaries, weather observations, demographic estimates, and operational guidance through independently maintained Web portals. Civic analysis must combine these sources while preserving their schemas, source links, spatial and temporal scopes, and interpretive limits. Tool-using language agents can perform this integration, but existing task benchmarks rarely test whether a computed claim remains supported by the records used. We present CivicBench, a 400-task benchmark over four cities and two years that materializes civic Web data into frozen bundles for reproducible evaluation. Executable contracts score computation, source linkage, coverage, scope, qualified answers, and refusal when the requested conclusion is not supported. We also introduce Task-State Memory (TSM), which compiles tool observations into typed assertions, reconciles records only within compatible scopes, and retrieves a bounded state organized around unresolved constraints. Across nine completed model pairs, eight yield positive mean-score differences with 95\% semantic-contract-cluster bootstrap intervals excluding zero; the ninth interval crosses zero. The benchmark and memory framework make the records behind a claim inspectable at the point of decision.
bullets: Introduces a 400-task benchmark spanning four cities and two years using frozen civic Web-data bundles for reproducible evaluation.
Scores computation, source linkage, coverage, spatial and temporal scope, answer qualification, and refusal when evidence is insufficient.

Across nine completed model pairs, eight show positive mean-score differences with bootstrap intervals excluding zero; one is inconclusive.
Designed to make the records supporting each claim inspectable at the point of decision.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents increasingly undertake complex, long-horizon tasks that benefit from sustained personalized support through long-term memory. Existing memory-augmented methods retrieve and use memory primarily from the initial request, with limited awareness of ongoing execution and emerging personalization needs. Agents may therefore overlook user preferences and project constraints during multistep tasks. We propose Pulse, a streaming personalization method for long-horizon tasks. An independent, lightweight memory agent continuously monitors execution, identifies emerging personalization needs and potential preference conflicts, and uses user and project memories to provide targeted interventions at appropriate stages. Reinforcement learning optimizes when and how the memory agent intervenes, improving the timeliness and accuracy of personalized support. Pulse scores 71.9% on $π$-Bench and 46.4% on MCP-Persona, achieving the highest overall scores among the compared methods on both datasets while improving task execution efficiency.
bullets: Existing memory methods rely mainly on the initial request, potentially missing preferences and constraints that emerge during execution.
Pulse uses an independent lightweight memory agent to monitor task progress and identify personalization needs or preference conflicts.
The agent retrieves user and project memories and delivers targeted interventions during relevant stages.
Reinforcement learning optimizes the timing and content of interventions.
Pulse scores 71.9% on π-Bench and 46.4% on MCP-Persona, with the highest overall scores among compared methods and improved task efficiency.

papers.tldr: Pulse improves long-horizon agent tasks by continuously detecting when personalized memory is needed and intervening at the right moments.

papers.abstract: As large language model agents increasingly undertake complex, long-horizon tasks, memory has become an important component for supporting sustained decision-making and action. Existing methods primarily focus on memory storage, updating, and retrieval, but often overlook how memory scheduling affects task execution: the main agent must identify memory needs, initiate retrieval, and wait for results while advancing the task, increasing both scheduling burden and execution time. To address this problem, we propose MemSidecar, which decouples memory scheduling from task execution through two independently selectable modes. Hooks directly delivers bound memory to the main agent when execution events match predefined conditions. Foresight uses an independent agent to predict potential queries, retrieve results in parallel, and store them in a cache, delivering matching and valid results when actual requests arrive. Hooks and Foresight achieve scores of 41.23% and 44.34% on MCP-Persona, respectively, while effectively reducing execution costs and latency and improving the efficiency of long-horizon agent execution.
bullets: Targets the overlooked cost of having the main agent schedule memory retrieval while executing tasks.
Provides two selectable modes: Hooks for event-triggered delivery of bound memory, and Foresight for parallel query prediction, retrieval, and caching.
On MCP-Persona, Hooks and Foresight score 41.23% and 44.34%, respectively.
The approach reduces execution costs and latency while improving long-horizon execution efficiency.

papers.abstract: Persistent Web information assistants must combine evolving document facts with user requirements established and revised across sessions. Yet systematic evaluation of how changes in both sources affect response requirements and evidence attribution remains limited. To address this gap, we introduce Dual-Source Evolution Benchmark (DuSE-Bench), a benchmark comprising 1,000 tasks across five scenarios, including 700 whose required premises originate in both dialogue and documents. An evolving Support Graph guides task construction and preserves links from updated facts and reused conclusions to original turns and passages. Task annotations distinguish grounding source from state dependence and enable separate evaluation of response content, response type, and source attribution. Experiments across 11 baseline configurations reveal persistent challenges in joint reasoning over evolving dialogue and documents, with content accuracy on jointly grounded tasks reaching at most 56.7%. Moreover, improvements in content accuracy can coincide with poorer response choice, while content-correct responses frequently lack complete attribution to original evidence. Matched evidence substitutions further show that the effect of replacing one source's evidence depends on support from the other. These findings motivate coordinating dialogue memory and document retrieval to apply current user requirements and document facts together while preserving their original support. The data are available at https://github.com/JianfengGao7/DuSE-Bench.
bullets: Introduces 1,000 tasks across five scenarios, including 700 requiring premises from both dialogue and documents.
Uses a Support Graph to track updated facts and reused conclusions back to original conversation turns and document passages.
Separately evaluates response content, response type, and source attribution, distinguishing grounding source from state dependence.
Across 11 baseline configurations, jointly grounded content accuracy reaches at most 56.7%, and correct content often lacks complete evidence attribution.
Findings show that response quality depends on coordinating dialogue memory with document retrieval, especially when evidence from one source changes.

papers.abstract: Many questions about a book can only be answered by connecting passages chapters apart, such as a cough heard three times across a horse's life. We introduce CrossChapterQA, 1,853 such questions over 14 public-domain books. Each question lists the two to six chapters it needs (spanning half the book at the median) and the relation linking them, cites evidence from each, and has two independent reference answers graded blind. We use it to build LadderRAG, which indexes a book as passages, summaries and book-level cards for about $0.41 and answers a question for under a cent. Its first version failed mostly at retrieval. We redesigned it four times, steered by an LLM judge's verdicts and our analyses of failed answers: a design-level counterpart of RLAIF and RLHF in which feedback changes the architecture, not model weights. We also report the two redesigns that made answers worse. On the 191 questions its first version got wrong, the final version retrieves over twice as many required chapters on held-out books (recall 0.36 to 0.79), and ten annotators rate its answers 6.5/10 on average (764 ratings).
bullets: Introduces CrossChapterQA: 1,853 questions across 14 public-domain books requiring evidence from 2–6 chapters.
LadderRAG indexes passages, summaries, and book-level cards, costing about $0.41 per book and under a cent per answer.
Four redesigns were guided by LLM judge feedback and failure analysis, changing the architecture rather than model weights.
On 191 initially failed questions, required-chapter recall improved from 0.36 to 0.79 on held-out books.
Annotators rated final answers 6.5/10 on average across 764 ratings; two redesigns reduced performance.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) helps large language models (LLMs) answer factual questions beyond their training data, but it adds storage and inference costs. Distilling previously retrieved information into parametric memories enables reuse without online retrieval. However, training the memory to mimic a retriever rewards accurate independent predictions, which do not necessarily improve the final output quality when combined with the LLM's existing predictions. To address this, we introduce ResMem, in which the LLM reads retrieved text offline to generate teacher targets. This design avoids storing massive token representations, unlike existing parametric memory approaches such as MLP Memory, which relies on k-nearest neighbor (kNN) datastores. Furthermore, by using the LLM as an offline teacher that reads privileged retrieved evidence alongside the input, we train a parametric memory to learn an additive logit residual. This residual aligns the predictions of a student sharing the same backbone with the teacher distribution, while self-distillation updates remain confined to the parametric memory. On a Wikipedia subset, ResMem reduces the storage retained for teacher construction by 94.7% compared with the evaluated kNN pipeline. Across five question answering datasets, ResMem raises mean token F1 from 32.83% for the frozen LLM to 34.48%. It also breaks 21% fewer of the LLM's correct answers than a kNN-trained memory. These findings validate our motivation of treating retrieval as a learning resource, with parametric memory shaped by how retrieved knowledge is used to inform the model's future predictions. Code and model weights are available at https://github.com/SSRand/From-Lookups-to-Lessons and https://huggingface.co/RandHan/ResMem-Mistral-7B-v0.3.
bullets: RAG improves knowledge access but incurs storage and inference costs; independently mimicking retrieval may not improve the LLM’s final predictions.
ResMem uses the LLM offline as a teacher that reads retrieved text and trains a memory to produce an additive logit residual.
Self-distillation updates are confined to the parametric memory, avoiding massive token representations and kNN datastores.
On a Wikipedia subset, it reduces teacher-construction storage by 94.7% versus the evaluated kNN pipeline.
Across five QA datasets, mean token F1 increases from 32.83% to 34.48%, while breaking 21% fewer correct answers than a kNN-trained memory.

papers.abstract: When a multi-turn agent delivers a tool's structured records into the model's context and re-emits them each turn, every turn can corrupt data the tool computed correctly. We measure this in a production award-travel agent: two architectures over identical frozen payloads, lineage-matched prompts and sampling, differing only in delivery architecture. SYNTHESIS feeds full record sets into the planner's context and answers follow-ups in-head; BYPASS, the deployed system, keeps records in session state, translates follow-ups into arguments for a deterministic filter, and delivers rows over a typed side channel. Across 24 dialogues (339 scored turns per condition), BYPASS scores 92.3% of turns fully correct, SYNTHESIS 45.7% (paired gap +46.6pp [+35.7, +57.1]). Varying delivered-table size by capture date, SYNTHESIS collapses from near-perfect at 10 rows or fewer to 8% or less beyond about 74 rows. On a content-controlled prefix ladder the collapse threshold orders by model capability, from under 10 rows (GPT-4o-mini) to about 198 or more (Gemini 2.5 Pro), while BYPASS stays size-flat for all four models. The collapse is expensive: beyond 100 rows, where almost no SYNTHESIS answer is correct, each correct one costs roughly 200x BYPASS's flat \$0.012. Practitioners converged on typed side-channel delivery for rendering, not correctness; we show it was, unknowingly, also a correctness decision.
bullets: The study compares two architectures using identical payloads, prompts, and sampling: SYNTHESIS places full records in context, while BYPASS filters records deterministically and delivers rows through a typed side channel.
Across 24 dialogues and 339 scored turns per condition, BYPASS achieves 92.3% fully correct turns versus 45.7% for SYNTHESIS.
SYNTHESIS is near-perfect with 10 or fewer rows but falls to 8% or less beyond roughly 74 rows; its threshold varies by model capability.
BYPASS remains flat across table sizes and costs about $0.012 per answer, whereas correct SYNTHESIS answers beyond 100 rows cost roughly 200× more.
The findings suggest delivery architecture is a correctness decision, not merely a rendering choice.

papers.selection_reason: Studies delivery architecture for tool-using LLM agents, comparing in-context synthesis vs session-state side channel; directly relevant to agent memory and context management.
papers.title: Fidelity Collapses with Table Size, Not Turn Count: Delivery Architecture in a Deployed Tool-Using Agent
papers.tldr: In a deployed tool-using agent, re-emitting large structured tables into model context causes severe fidelity loss, while deterministic filtering with typed side-channel delivery keeps accuracy stable.

papers.abstract: With model weights fixed, we measure how much of an entity-replacement response transfers between English factual questions, beyond whether answers change. We add the hidden-state change from two source questions to a target question about the same entity, comparing the predicted log-probability shift between two relations' published answers, given known answer prefixes, with the measured one. Hidden reuse injects the aligned change at 50% depth before the target's remaining layers; direct reuse adds source output-score changes. With other-relation sources, hidden reuse removes 45% and 49% of no-change error on 0.5-1B Qwen and Llama. Gemma-2-2B removes 22% and passes one of three comparisons in plain text without its default beginning-of-sequence (BOS) token. A later protocol restoring it yields 58-68%, passing every comparison on three cohorts. Larger checkpoints, chat format and new entities show replication and format- or cohort-dependent failures. On small plain-format checkpoints, other-relation hidden reuse mainly reproduces the shift both relations' questions share, without reliably lowering relation-selective error. With target-relation sources, hidden reuse's post hoc advantage over direct reuse is 0.2-0.9 nats outside chat format, unconfirmed and not replacement-specific. The same relation-neutral change at both questions' entity tokens lowers relation-selective error more than random or other-replacement changes, indicating receiving-question dependence.
bullets: The study measures cross-prompt reuse of response changes between English factual questions about the same entity.
It transfers aligned hidden-state changes midway through the target model and compares predicted answer-log-probability shifts with measured shifts.
Other-relation sources remove 45–49% of no-change error on small Qwen and Llama models; results vary for Gemma and with BOS handling.
Larger models, chat formatting, and new entities replicate some effects but also produce format- and cohort-dependent failures.
On small plain-format models, reuse mostly captures relation-neutral changes and does not reliably reduce relation-selective error; receiving-question dependence is nevertheless indicated.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Response reuse; model parameters stay fixed. Both routes reuse each source’s 50%-depth change and differ in which read-out, the remaining layers, transforms it: the source’s for direct reuse, the target’s for hidden reuse. (a) The three answer comparisons, pre-specified block sign tests, ask whether hidden reuse from SO has lower error than each of zero prediction, hidden reuse from S′ O and direct reuse from SO. In the answer studies, analyses with read-out-matched sources (ST , S′ T ) are descriptive, exploratory or post hoc except one failed pre-specified family (Section 4.1). (b) In the source and target shapes, depth increases upward; fills as in (a). The target’s read-out runs twice, with the hidden change (left) and without it (right). ∆s,e is the source’s 50%-depth change from a to e, recaptured at each known answer prefix; hidden reuse aligns its token rows to target positions (Equation 2). Weights ws use only unedited states. ĉ hid, ĉ dir: c from each route’s predicted scores. The block and example (plain format, cue \nAnswer:\n; Appendix A) are from the earlier crossing cohort, not the 35-block answer cohort, chosen retrospectively for readable wording, not outcomes (Appendix B.1). (c) Mx(A): log probability mass of group A’s complete answers on input x; shares measure contrast reproduction, not answer correctness or free generation.

Figure 3: Both source relations on shared axes, small checkpoints in the original 35-block cohort and plain format; all 140 targets per checkpoint and three reuse conditions. Matching lines are calibration fits of observed on predicted changes; the gray dash-dot line is exact reproduction. Target-relation sources bring the output route closer to hidden reuse, without making the different-replacement control track the target response.

Figure 4: All 35 block gains behind the nine original answer comparisons (other-relation sources). Each point is one block’s mean error reduction by same-replacement hidden reuse relative to direct reuse, zero prediction or differentreplacement hidden reuse; open circles are positive and filled diamonds negative. Squares and bars give block means and pointwise 95% intervals; numbers give positive/negative block counts.

Each family was fixed by an internal written protocol before its outcomes, although for Qwen some testbed arms include blocks already observed (Appendix B.5). Gap (target-relation sources): direct minus hidden error, nats, over 99 blocks (chat: 35); positive favors hidden reuse (Tables 18 and 16b). Sel. (other-relation sources): selective-error reduction from zero prediction (%), original 35 blocks (Table 24). Gap and Sel. are descriptive. Robust shares: Table 14.

papers.abstract: LLM agents that operate over long inputs must perform context management: deciding what to retain in a fixed-size context window. A common approach is compaction, where the model replaces its history with a self-generated note. Yet off-the-shelf agentic models, including GPT-5.5 and GLM-5.3, often write ineffective notes, and reinforcement learning (RL) alone rarely discovers useful note-taking behavior. We present MEMENTO, a long-context agent built on Qwen3-8B and trained to manage its context through compaction. We first bootstrap note-taking by fine-tuning on synthetic trajectories annotated with notes generated in hindsight, then reinforce it with RL using a reward that combines answer correctness, note-quality heuristics, and confidence calibration. Although trained only to compact into a fresh window, MEMENTO extends at test time to strategies such as context folding and confidence-based backtracking. On book-level question answering across four benchmarks, with books of up to 2.5M tokens, MEMENTO raises Qwen3-8B's accuracy from 36.9% to 67.8% while never holding more than 20K tokens in context. It outperforms GPT-5.5 agent in the same harness (13.1%) and full book context (56.7%) at less than 1/50 the cost. It also nearly matches a ~100x larger GLM-5.3 agent (69.3%) at 1/9 the cost, and comes within 6.4 points of GLM-5.3 full context at 1/26 the cost.
bullets: Addresses ineffective self-generated summaries for long-context agents and the difficulty of learning note-taking with RL alone.
Bootstraps hindsight-annotated note-taking through fine-tuning, then applies RL with answer, note-quality, and confidence-calibration rewards.
Although trained for compaction, it generalizes at test time to context folding and confidence-based backtracking.
On four book-level QA benchmarks with books up to 2.5M tokens, accuracy improves from 36.9% to 67.8% while staying within a 20K-token window.
Achieves performance near the much larger GLM-5.3 agent at lower cost and exceeds the reported GPT-5.5 agent and full-book-context baselines.

papers.abstract: LLM agents performing long-horizon tasks accumulate tool results that later steps may need. Passing the full history to every invocation is costly even when it fits within the context window, while reducing it risks omitting needed information. Existing context management methods can overlook how earlier tool results are used in subsequent execution, leaving needed information out of context. We introduce ContextRender, which manages context through a persistent graph of execution dependencies. We develop Tool-Flow Analysis to track how later operations reuse information from earlier tool results, providing a signal called observed reuse. A renderer combines this signal with recency and semantic relevance to select results within a fixed history budget, retaining omitted results for later use. Across AppWorld and 8-objective QA with three execution models, ContextRender outperforms the evaluated context management baselines using a 6K history budget, well below the models' maximum context windows. Within this budget, it achieves task performance close to or above that of passing the full history while reducing mean inference cost by 10.2%-32.2% relative to Full history. Ablations show that observed reuse improves task performance and retention of results reused later.
bullets: Full-history context is costly, while aggressive reduction can omit information needed by later steps.
It maintains a persistent execution-dependency graph and uses Tool-Flow Analysis to estimate observed reuse of prior tool results.
A renderer combines observed reuse with recency and semantic relevance under a fixed history budget, while retaining omitted results for possible later use.
Across AppWorld and 8-objective QA with three execution models, it outperformed evaluated baselines using a 6K history budget.
Performance was close to or above full-history prompting while reducing mean inference cost by 10.2%–32.2%; ablations confirmed the value of observed reuse.

papers.abstract: Multi-turn negotiation remains a challenging problem for large language model (LLM) agents. While LLMs can conduct natural-language dialogue, existing benchmarks predominantly assess only agreement rates, overlooking whether negotiated commitments actually create value once executed. To address this gap, we introduce TradeWar, a multi-country simulation benchmark that translates negotiation dialogues into concrete tariff and trade-share policies, enforces capacity and network constraints during settlement, and evaluates outcomes via an Economic Health Index (EHI). To solve this execution-grounded task, we propose TACTIC (Trade-aware Adaptive Consolidation and Theory-of-mind for International Commerce), an agent that iteratively refines its negotiation strategy across episodes-without updating base LLM weights-by leveraging prior experience, opponent behavior, and past settlement outcomes. Despite using zero-shot chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, PromptLLM attains a 75% agreement rate but only 57.1 final EHI (*100), whereas TACTIC reaches 68.8. Across 20 sequential episodes and three seeds, TACTIC's final EHI improves from 58.2 to 73.2, compared with 65.2 for an ablation without cross-episode updates. Under technology-controls and energy-crisis shocks, TACTIC also exhibits smaller performance degradation than PromptLLM and MemoryLLM. These results indicate that CoT deliberation and interaction memory alone do not fully address delayed execution feedback, whereas settlement-grounded adaptation improves long-horizon negotiation in TradeWar.
authors: Xiangyu Kong, Ruirui Yang, Xia Hou
bullets: Introduces a multi-country benchmark that converts dialogue into tariff and trade-share policies subject to capacity and network constraints.
Evaluates negotiated outcomes with an Economic Health Index (EHI), beyond agreement rates alone.
Proposes TACTIC, which adapts across episodes using prior experience, opponent behavior, and settlement outcomes without changing base LLM weights.
Across 20 episodes, TACTIC’s final EHI improves from 58.2 to 73.2, outperforming its no-cross-episode-update ablation at 65.2.
TACTIC degrades less than PromptLLM and MemoryLLM under technology-control and energy-crisis shocks.

papers.abstract: Deploying 6G network slices across administrative domains requires an online decision for each arriving request: which domain hosts each virtual network function, how traffic crosses domain boundaries, and whether the slice is admitted. This joint decision problem is NP-hard under continuous arrivals. Experiments on a parametrized family of multi-domain topologies show that no fixed planning strategy dominates across all regimes: the performance ranking reverses between topology classes, and feasible placements exist for most rejected requests but remain undiscovered. These findings identify the plan layer as the decisive performance lever. We introduce ORION, a hierarchical orchestrator in which two LLM agents translate service intents into structured requests and generate abstract placement plans. A cooperative multi-agent RL coordinator selects the cross-domain partition, treating the plan as a persistent soft prior, while per-domain agents place the functions. ORION main contribution lies at the plan layer: an outcome-driven episodic memory that records, for each completed attempt, the network-condition profile, the proposed plan, and its verified feasibility outcome. The memory feeds verified successes and labelled failures back to the planner, thereby closing the adaptation loop using deployment feasibility rather than a scalar reward assigned to the planner's own proposals. To isolate the effect of the plan quality, we evaluate the planner on held-out topology families while keeping the downstream selection and execution mechanisms fixed. Under this controlled setting, the proposed memory improves admission by $4.6$--$11.5$ percentage points over the same planner without memory, while importance-based retention accounts for most of the improvement over a first-in-first-out store.
authors: Mahmoud S. Mayaleh, Fetia Bannour, Nour-El-Houda Yellas
bullets: Multi-domain slice placement jointly decides function hosting, inter-domain routing, and admission under an NP-hard online setting.
Fixed planning strategies do not generalize across topology regimes, and many rejected requests may have feasible but undiscovered placements.
ORION combines LLM-based intent and plan generation with multi-agent RL for cross-domain selection and per-domain function placement.
Its outcome-driven episodic memory stores network conditions, plans, and verified success or failure outcomes to guide future planning.
On held-out topology families, memory improves admission by 4.6–11.5 percentage points; importance-based retention outperforms FIFO storage.

papers.abstract: Recursive textual memory can carry earlier errors into later updates, yet task performance alone does not establish memory reliability. We define self-consistency bias as the persistence of incorrect claims already present in the incoming memory. We present KEEPER, a comparative analysis of four auxiliary objectives along information-content and update-sensitivity axes within a shared recursive interface, examining how supervision targets relate to agent performance. Among evaluated conditions, reward-related prediction achieve the highest task performance before and after offline reinforcement learning, outperforming joint supervision. A claim-level analysis of one baseline trajectory documents error persistence despite corrective observations. Together, these analyses motivate evaluating error persistence and valid-information retention alongside task outcomes.
authors: Jinkyeong Choi, Chaebin Jeong, Junsung Jeon, Donghyeon Park
bullets: Introduces self-consistency bias: the persistence of incorrect claims in incoming memory.
Compares four auxiliary objectives by information content and update sensitivity within a shared recursive interface.
Reward-related prediction achieves the highest task performance before and after offline reinforcement learning among evaluated conditions.
A claim-level analysis shows that errors can persist despite corrective observations.
Motivates tracking error persistence and valid-information retention alongside task outcomes.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents play an important role in solving complex and sustained tasks, with ever-growing interaction contexts. However, these accumulated contexts will raise substantial computational cost and obscure key decision-relevant evidence. Existing methods typically train external compressors or context-management agents to rewrite context as shorter hard-token sequences, but such external selection may not align with the LLM's evolving representation and is necessarily lossy. In this paper, we introduce Agentic Soft-Token Compression (ASTC), a training-free compression method using soft tokens within LLM agent for long-horizon tasks. Specifically, ASTC uses the model's native recurrent dynamics to determine the already absorbed information, leveraging the commonly-used hybrid Gated Delta Network (GDN)-attention. It then carries this information forward as agentic soft tokens while retaining exact values as hard tokens. The resulting compact sequence reduces later-layer computation and yields reusable KV caches, extending the savings across the agent's trajectory. Extensive experiments on long-horizon tasks show that ASTC matches or exceeds the uncompressed agent's accuracy with up to 50.68% fewer end-to-end Attention Pairs, while trained compressors require 15.4 to 103.7 times more Attention Pairs per successful task. These findings highlight agentic soft tokens as a model-native way to carry absorbed context forward as the task representation evolves.
authors: Xuning He, Kai Fan, Runyu Zhang, Binghuan Wang, Yuxiang Zhang, Xue Jiang, Yihong Dong
bullets: Long-horizon agents accumulate costly contexts that can obscure decision-relevant information.
ASTC is training-free and uses the LLM’s recurrent GDN-attention dynamics to identify absorbed information.
It carries absorbed context forward as agentic soft tokens while preserving exact values as hard tokens.
Compact sequences enable reusable KV caches and reduce later-layer computation across the agent trajectory.
Experiments report up to 50.68% fewer end-to-end Attention Pairs while matching or exceeding the uncompressed agent; trained compressors used substantially more Attention Pairs per successful task.

papers.abstract: Memory has become central to self-evolving LLM agents, which store and retrieve experience from past rollouts to guide future decisions. Existing systems represent this experience as free-form natural language and maintain it by rewriting, which fits tasks whose experience is narratable. However, in scientific discovery and optimization, experience is often a quantity measured by an oracle under a specific context. Rewriting it as text leaves no index for where a record should be, replaces a measurement with a description, and cannot express how interventions interact. To address this, we argue that agent memory for biomolecule optimization should instead be indexable, quantitative, and structured, and we introduce MEMIG. This memory construction framework realizes these three properties. In detail, MEMIG addresses each insight with a domain-grounded identifier and accumulates the quantitative effect measured by a property oracle, so that updates remain local and retrieval becomes an exact lookup. Next, MEMIG connects insights whose interventions are applied together and measures their epistasis by decomposing each evaluated set. Our results show that MEMIG improves performance in most settings across in silico antibody optimization tasks.
authors: Yunhui Jang, Zach Wang, Jai Doshi, Kangway Chuang, Sidney Lisanza, Taylor Joren
bullets: Targets the limitations of free-form, rewritten language memories for scientific optimization, where experience is measured quantitatively under specific contexts.
Uses domain-grounded identifiers to index insights and accumulates property-oracle measurements through local updates.
Links jointly applied interventions and decomposes evaluated sets to estimate their epistatic interactions.
Improves performance in most tested settings across in silico antibody optimization tasks.
Scope: results are reported for in silico antibody optimization; the abstract provides no specific datasets or numerical gains.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of MEMIG. MEMIG constructs an epistasis graph with antibody-grounded identifiers. Directed edges organize property → germline → region → mutation hierarchies, while undirected edges connect co-occurring mutations and store their epistatic effects.

Figure 3: Memory retrieval of MEMIG. Given a starting antibody, MEMIG identifies the matching identifiers, retrieves the corresponding insights with their neighbors, and curates them into natural language. Blue denotes the antibody-grounded identifier and the corresponding node, green its quantitative record, and yellow the epistasis graph neighbors and the curation based on them.

Figure 5: In silico antibody binding optimization. Each numeric label corresponds to an antibodyantigen cluster, clustered by CDR sequence identity. ∗ denotes the structural baselines (dashed), which have access to the complex structure.

Figure 6: Cumulative performance progression. Vertical lines mark memory updates, where the rollouts between two lines are generated concurrently under the same memory. The curves report the centered rolling mean with a half-width of 30 rollouts, computed within each memory step. Notably, the ordering of rollouts within the same memory is random, so a downward slope does not imply performance decrease. Each dot marks the mean over all rollouts of that memory step.

To remove this smoothing, we report the mean improvement of every rollout sharing a memory step as a single point in Figure 7, with error bars indicating the standard error across those rollouts. We observe the same trend as in Figure 6, where MEMIG improves over successive memory steps while the vanilla LLM does not, which confirms that the progression is not an artifact of the smoothing.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation is becoming agentic. A search harness writes queries, reads results, reformulates, and decides when to stop. This largely solves accuracy: a harness with only BM25/grep and MiniMax M3 answers 85% of BrowseComp-Plus and 91% on multi-hop FRAMES in our runs, without compiled or vector indexes. It exposes a context problem: an undisciplined loop repeats queries, rereads documents, and fills the window with unused passages. The missing layer is knowledge compilation: a configurable ingestion pipeline where LLMs enrich documents with context no chunk contains alone--navigation hierarchies with claim-evidence leaves, entity graphs, timelines, mind maps, ontologies, wikis, and memory. Compilation is not a better retriever: under a competent harness, structural artifacts gave no detectable accuracy gain on FRAMES, and a PageIndex-style outline degraded at scale. It is a supply layer. A navigation tree whose leaves are claim-evidence pairs--the mechanism we measure--cuts query tokens by 91% when evidence suffices and adds 1.9% when it does not, a 38% average reduction; this implies a 2% break-even sufficiency rate and a measured rate near 43%. A decision gate cuts latency from 140 s to 30 s, though substitution's token saving is bought with retrieval rounds and carries its own latency cost. Other artifacts--ontology, graph, wiki, timeline, mind map, memory--pay off in deployment (governance, integration, onboarding, temporal orientation, continuity) where accuracy benchmarks cannot see them. We describe RAGFlow's pipeline and harness (open source at https://github.com/infiniflow/ragflow), which turns the loop into five disciplined stations and keeps the context entering the model the smallest sufficient set; together they form an agent-native database: a store that hands the agent compiled, governed context instead of a ranked list of passages.
authors: Zhichang Yu, Baining Cao, Sbaaoui Idriss, Qi Wang, Gangqiang Xu, Ling Qin, Xiaoling Jin, An Liu, Shaohao Cai, Xiaoyang Bao, Shengle Chen, Changchang Ding, Pengfei Zhu, Jingxiang Xu, Yifeng Mao, Lu Liu, Hai Jin, Yingfeng Zhang
bullets: Agentic search harnesses can achieve strong retrieval-augmented answering with simple BM25/grep retrieval, but uncontrolled loops waste queries, reread documents, and fill context windows.
The proposed supply layer compiles documents into structures such as claim-evidence navigation trees, entity graphs, timelines, ontologies, wikis, and memories.
Claim-evidence navigation trees reduced query tokens by 38% on average, with 91% savings when the compiled evidence sufficed and a 1.9% increase otherwise.
A decision gate reduced reported latency from 140 seconds to 30 seconds, while retrieval-round substitution introduces its own latency cost.

Structural artifacts showed no detectable FRAMES accuracy gain under a competent harness, so their value is primarily efficiency, governance, integration, onboarding, temporal orientation, and continuity.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Context as infrastructure. Knowledge compilation is the supply side: an ingestion pipeline that enriches raw documents into typed context artifacts. The harness is the control side: it decides which artifact, if any, enters the window and when the loop stops. Tools are the contract between them. Arrows show the flow of context, not control. The navigation tree (highlighted), whose leaves are claim–evidence pairs, is the mechanism measured in this paper; the ontology artifact (highlighted) is the one whose value is primarily commercial rather than benchmark-visible.
