papers.selection_reason: Proposes 'knowledge compilation' as a memory mechanism for LLMs in agentic systems, transforming raw retrieval results into structured, navigable context to reduce token usage and improve efficiency.
papers.title: Context as Infrastructure: Knowledge Compilation for Retrieval in Agentic Systems with Harnesses
papers.tldr: Knowledge compilation can make agentic retrieval more efficient by supplying governed, navigable context, even when it does not improve benchmark accuracy.

papers.abstract: The ability to integrate new information and deduce its consequences is central to learning, understanding, and reasoning in large language models (LLMs). Whether information arrives during training or in-context, models must not only store local facts, but propagate their long-range implications globally. To explore information integration in LLMs, we introduce two complementary natural language benchmarks for large-scale evaluation of deductive reasoning as a function of inference depth. The first is a formal graph benchmark enabling controlled evaluation over a wide range of graph topologies and integration tasks; the second is a knowledge composition benchmark grounded in real-world knowledge graphs. We use these benchmarks to compare knowledge integration from information encoded in context versus information encoded in model weights during pretraining, evaluating a set of open models implicitly, without chain of thought. We find that accuracy decays sharply with increased composition length for both pretrained and in-context knowledge. Information presented in-context, however, substantially outperforms deduction over information encoded in weights. These results quantify a fundamental limitation of current models with direct implications for prompt-based control of agent behavior and for continual learning strategies, and they provide a foundation for developing training, prompting, and integration methods that support deeper reasoning.
authors: Alexander Detkov, Dashiel Karish, Matthew Oleynikov, Matt Thomson
bullets: Introduces two benchmarks for evaluating deductive reasoning across increasing inference depths.
Uses a controllable formal graph benchmark and a real-world knowledge-composition benchmark.
Compares knowledge supplied in context with knowledge encoded in model weights, without chain-of-thought prompting.
In-context knowledge substantially outperforms deduction over pretrained knowledge, though both degrade with longer compositions.
Findings highlight limitations relevant to prompt-based agent control and continual learning.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Models receive graph adjacency in-context but integrate the information poorly, failing at long-range inferences. DeepSeek, Kimi, Nemotron, and 12 other models answer questions about a random graph of 50–60 nodes given in the prompt as a list of edges, with reasoning off. Each question concerns the nodes exactly k hops from a start node, so k = 1 questions require only direct-neighbor information. a) Verify: is a given node exactly k hops away? Accuracy falls from 93–100% at k = 1 to 49–56% at k = 3, close to chance. b) Count: how many nodes are exactly k hops away? Models count correctly 43–69% of the time at k = 1 and ≤ 16% from k = 2. c) Name one: name a node exactly k hops away. Models name a neighbor at 99–100%, but a node two hops away at only 9–40%. d) Enumerate: list every node exactly k hops away. Models list all neighbors at 71–100%, but no model lists more than 12% of sets correctly from k = 2.

Figure 2: Models compose facts from the prompt far better than from memory. DeepSeek, Kimi, and Nemotron answer k-hop Wikidata questions with reasoning off and information given in context, in memory, or both. a) The chain’s facts are given in the prompt under invented names, among 16 decoy chains with the same relations. All models compose at ≥ 94% up to k = 3, but at k = 6, Kimi composes at 29%, while DeepSeek and Nemotron Ultra fall to chance. b) The facts are recalled from memory without supporting facts in the prompt. Composition reaches only 37–64% at k = 2 and ≤ 12% from k = 4, although every fact is known. c) The facts are given in the prompt under their real names, among 16 real decoy chains, so the model can use both the prompt and memory. Accuracy reaches 36–71% at k = 6.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks LLM knowledge integration across in-context and parametric memory, with direct implications for memory reasoning and continual learning.
papers.title: ImplicitHop: Evaluating knowledge integration across context and memory
papers.tldr: ImplicitHop shows that LLMs struggle to integrate multi-step knowledge, with performance declining sharply as inference depth increases, especially for pretrained knowledge.

papers.abstract: Natural-language skills enable large language model (LLM) agents to reuse procedures across tasks, yet most systems retrieve individual skills from a flat SkillBank without explicitly modeling the high-level strategy that governs their selection and use. We introduce TalentRL, a strategy-guided reinforcement learning framework for hierarchical routing over procedural memory. Coarse-grained talents represent recurring strategies for skill use, while fine-grained skills provide executable procedures. For each task, the policy model selects a talent that guides execution and softly prioritizes its associated skills during similarity-based retrieval. However, since task outcomes depend jointly on talent selection, retrieved skill context, and downstream execution, terminal rewards alone cannot isolate the contribution of the routing decision. TalentRL therefore trains talent routing with reward contrasts between rollouts of the same task under matched interventions on the talent-conditioned context, and optimizes downstream execution with group-relative advantages. Across seven open-domain and multi-hop question-answering benchmarks, talent-aware supervised fine-tuning improves average success rate by 7.53%, 6.71%, and 9.21% over the corresponding zero-shot baselines for Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-8B, and Llama-3.1-8B, respectively. Reinforcement learning further improves these SFT checkpoints by 7.58% to 9.32%, and TalentRL achieves the highest average success rate among all compared methods on all three backbones. On the agentic benchmarks ALFWorld and WebShop, TalentRL achieves the highest ALFWorld success rate (99.3%) and the highest WebShop score (90.7) among all compared methods.
authors: Huancheng Chen, Xiaodi Sun, Zhaoqiong Huang, Michelle Chang, Jingwen Lu
bullets: Addresses the limitation of flat SkillBanks, which retrieve skills without modeling the overarching strategy for using them.
Introduces hierarchical routing: coarse-grained talents guide execution and softly prioritize associated fine-grained skills.
Uses matched rollout reward contrasts to train talent selection and group-relative advantages for downstream execution.
Across seven QA benchmarks and two agentic benchmarks, TalentRL consistently improves performance and achieves the best reported results among compared methods.
Reported peaks include 99.3% success on ALFWorld and a 90.7 score on WebShop.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of TalentRL. (A) The policy model selects a talent that guides downstream execution and provides a soft prior for similarity-based skill retrieval. (B) Reward contrasts across matched intervention rollouts train talent routing, while group-relative advantages optimize downstream execution, both updating the shared policy model. (C) Talent-aware SFT initializes talent routing and downstream execution from outcome-guided demonstrations.

Figure 2. Talent selection of the final TalentRL policies. (a) Search7 test sets, as % of questions per dataset. (b) ALFWorld by task type over the seen (140) and unseen (134) splits. (c) WebShop on 500 goals. Percentages below 10% are omitted from the bars.

papers.abstract: Agentic LLM assistants must repeatedly decide whether to answer from memory or to call a tool such as web search. Unnecessary searches cost latency and money; missing ones yield confident but unsupported answers. Prior work mostly measures verbalised confidence or trains new adaptive-retrieval methods, and rarely audits the search decisions that deployed products actually make. We introduce a benchmark of 400 multiple-choice questions that combines widely known inside-knowledge (IK) questions, which should be answered directly, with outside-knowledge (OK) questions about facts from news published after the models' training cut-offs (to our knowledge), which should trigger search or, without tools, abstention. Each item offers an abstain option, and two action-level scores, NAS and KIS, reward searching on OK questions and restraint on IK questions. Across five commercial LLMs with and without their vendors' web search, GPT-5 mini and Grok 4 Fast search on over 90% of OK but only 1% of IK questions, whereas Mistral Small searches on just 20% of OK questions, often abstaining instead of using its tool; one product's search indicator proved unusable. Searching is partly triggered by explicit temporal cues: on uncued OK questions, the NAS of the two selective models falls from about 0.72 to 0.57--0.58. The scores thus measure the search triggering of specific products, not metacognition in a strict sense.
bullets: Introduces 400 multiple-choice questions covering answerable inside knowledge and post-cutoff outside knowledge, with abstention available.
Defines NAS and KIS scores to reward searching for outside knowledge and avoiding unnecessary searches for inside knowledge.
Evaluates five commercial LLMs with and without vendor web search, focusing on deployed search behavior rather than verbalized confidence.
GPT-5 mini and Grok 4 Fast search on over 90% of outside-knowledge items but only 1% of inside-knowledge items; Mistral Small searches about 20% of outside-knowledge items.
Explicit temporal cues strongly influence search: two selective models’ NAS drops from about 0.72 to 0.57–0.58 without cues.

papers.abstract: Recent scientific agents build knowledge recursively by retrieving evidence, constructing an intermediate state, and judging whether that state contains sufficient information. These agents are evaluated end-to-end, usually without ground truth, so the effect of each design choice is unknown. Here, we examined two design axes: (1) what the recursion builds (the state of evidence) and (2) what controls it (the judge that decides when to stop). To measure them, we defined consensus scientific claim verification and measured these effects on this task, where a system must establish a claim's consensus stance from the open literature. We built a new consensus claim dataset, ProClaim-eval, including 718 claims with SUPPORT and REFUTE gold labels from five expert-curated databases spanning molecular biology, nuclear physics, and astronomy. Our instrument, ProClaim, persists an evidence state outside the model's context, so each axis can be studied with the other held fixed. Against verification systems and general-purpose agent harnesses, ProClaim ranks among the top three, with a significant advantage over the harnesses. We found that the evidence state improves performance over in-context accumulation, and it also matters what is stored in it. In addition, a trained judge that reads the evidence state performs better than fixed-round stopping. A judge trained separately and never exposed to ProClaim-eval achieves the highest agreement with the gold labels on three of five subsets, where it matches the off-the-shelf Claude Sonnet~4.6 judge and outperforms Claude Haiku~4.5. Our results support recursively maintaining a structured evidence state outside the model's context as an effective design for verifying claims in scientific agents.
authors: Lun Ai, Yu-Heng Wu, Jonathan Schaul, Leonie K\"uchenhoff, Denes Turei, Francesco Carli, Fabio Petroni, Aurelien Dugourd, Julio Saez-Rodriguez
bullets: Studies two recursive-agent design choices: what evidence state is built and how recursion is stopped.
Introduces ProClaim-eval, a dataset of 718 SUPPORT/REFUTE claims across molecular biology, nuclear physics, and astronomy.
ProClaim maintains evidence outside the model context, enabling controlled comparison of recursion components.
Evidence-state accumulation outperforms in-context accumulation, and the stored content affects performance.
A separately trained judge performs better than fixed-round stopping and achieves the highest gold-label agreement on three of five subsets.

This comparison with ProClaim highlights the benefit of recursive knowledge construction, driven by adaptive retrieval and evidence organisation before deciding the final verdict.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in Generative AI have substantially improved financial sentiment analysis through post-trained financial large language models (LLMs). However, existing approaches remain confined to predicting the sentiment of each article in isolation and operate as black boxes, which limits contextual understanding and hinders deployment in high-stakes financial decision-making. To this end, we introduce FinLLM-KG, a model-agnostic framework that combines causal LLMs with a financial knowledge graph, in order to inject temporally grounded, company-level knowledge from SEC 10-K filings at inference time, without updating model weights. Within FinLLM-KG, context is supplied either as a natural-language company profile or as a small set of relevance-ranked factual triples. This enables sentiment predictions to account for broader firm-level information rather than the article alone, at almost zero computational cost and for any causal LLM. In addition, attributing each article-level sentiment score to individual sentences and to the retrieved knowledge-graph facts makes the evidence behind the prediction inspectable, thereby enhancing explainability and supporting human-in-the-loop review. Simulations demonstrate that FinLLM-KG consistently improves portfolio performance over the state-of-the-art baseline.
bullets: Addresses article-isolated, black-box sentiment prediction in high-stakes financial applications.
Uses SEC 10-K-derived knowledge graphs to provide company profiles or relevance-ranked factual triples as context.
Works with any causal LLM without updating model weights and with nearly no added computational cost.
Attributes sentiment scores to article sentences and retrieved facts for inspectable, human-reviewable evidence.
Simulations show consistent portfolio-performance gains over a state-of-the-art baseline.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of FinLLM-KG. (a) Financial news articles are tagged and preprocessed. In parallel, fixed-relation 10-K triples from FinReflectKG [8] are restricted by a temporal alignment gate to the latest 10-K filed strictly before the article. Eligible facts are supplied either as a company profile or as the top-k retrieved triples and mixed with the article; in the baseline, the context is the article alone. (b) A frozen causal LLM performs sentiment analysis on the resulting context (prompt). The sentiment signal is used in the portfolio construction framework and, for the proposed methods only, can be decomposed into sentence-level and triple-level attributions for explainability.

Fig. 2. Cumulative returns of sentiment-based 35% long–short portfolios under three conditions: Baseline (article text only), Summary (article text with the latest 10-K company profile), and Top-k Triples (article text with the top-k relevance-ranked factual relations), compared against the S&P 500 benchmark.

(b) Exact Shapley values for the four retrieved 10-K facts relative to the company-anchored prompt. Green and red indicate positive and negative contributions, respectively.

papers.abstract: A key challenge of RAG systems is retrieving information from enterprise documents created by multiple teams over time, where it is not possible to enrich the information using the latest information and metadata available outside the scope of organizational documentation responsibility. We investigated whether using a knowledge graph to store metadata and frequently changing information would improve upon knowledge retrieval over similarity search over embeddings. To perform the experiment, we created a snapshot of the SEC EDGAR dataset for a quarter, comprising 167,050 filings from 10,511 companies and 508,714 embedded chunks of risk-factor text. To simulate the enrichment, we created a knowledge graph of 430,257 nodes and 561,144 edges carrying an accession number on every edge. To evaluate the gain obtained via a graph-based design, we evaluated three architectures: text-to-SQL over typed columns, dense-vector RAG with HNSW cosine search, and a two-stage GraphRAG design. All architectures share the same model and temperature to allow comparison. Results are scored programmatically by an LLM as judge over 20 questions divided across four categories, each question asked three times. GraphRAG solved 16 of 20 questions on all three attempts, compared to 10 for text-to-SQL and 3 for vector RAG. GraphRAG lost on structured aggregation queries. Vector RAG lost the single-document category it was expected to win, passing 3 of 15 where GraphRAG passed 15 of 15, because company attribution is not recoverable from cosine similarity at this scale. All six confident falsehoods in the benchmark were text-to-SQL conflating distinct people who share a surname, the failure that resolving identity to an identifier before reading any text prevents structurally; GraphRAG made none. We claim no advantage beyond this corpus, this model and this question set.
bullets: Enterprise documents can lack current external metadata and reliable organizational context.
The study compares text-to-SQL, HNSW dense-vector RAG, and two-stage GraphRAG using a knowledge graph of changing metadata and identifiers.
GraphRAG answered all three repetitions of 16/20 questions, versus 10/20 for text-to-SQL and 3/20 for vector RAG.
GraphRAG performed especially well on company attribution and single-document questions, and avoided the benchmark’s identity-related falsehoods.
The authors limit their claim to the tested corpus, model, and question set; GraphRAG underperformed on structured aggregation queries.

papers.title: Beyond Similarity Search: Knowledge Graph Metadata Enrichment for Enterprise Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.tldr: A two-stage GraphRAG design improved enterprise retrieval over dense-vector RAG and text-to-SQL in a controlled SEC filing benchmark, while remaining weaker on structured aggregation queries.

papers.abstract: Proactive assistants offer short, memory-grounded hints during a conversation, deciding when to assist and what to suggest. Current systems split this between a gate and a larger generator; we evaluate both together on 28,058 decision points. Stage-wise generation scores are oracle-gate ceilings: behind a real gate, end-to-end exact match is 0.2619 against a ceiling of 0.2971, and end-to-end precision is 0.2387, leaving substantial headroom. A gate pays off through precision and compute, whose saving falls from 4.39x with an 8B generator to 1.38x with a 1B one. The memory profile drives hint quality: removing it costs 24.7 exact-match points (rescaled BERTScore 0.57 to 0.35), while retrieval and a larger generator add nothing on exact match. One 1B decoder can do both, gating from an intermediate layer and generating in the same pass. At its final checkpoint it matches or exceeds the two-model pipelines on automatic end-to-end measures with 1.31-1.76x less wall-clock time than the matched 1B pipeline; across three seeds, its deeper exit ties the separate gate. A human evaluation (1,144 ratings over 32 dialogues) supports the memory effect and rates the single model level with the matched 1B pipeline and below the 8B one. Graded metrics and LlamaPIE's native judge track human ratings more closely than exact match, which we report as a strict lower bound.
authors: A. J. A. Jubayer Talukder, Mohammad Ariful Haque

The model gates from an intermediate layer and generates the hint in the same pass, replacing separate gate and generator systems.
Memory is crucial: removing it sharply reduces hint quality, while retrieval and a larger generator add no exact-match benefit.
The single model achieves 1.31–1.76× lower wall-clock time than the matched 1B pipeline and matches or exceeds it on automatic end-to-end measures.
Human ratings support the memory effect; graded metrics and LlamaPIE align more closely with human judgments than exact match.

papers.title: When to Assist and What to Suggest: Joint Gating and Memory-Grounded Hint Generation in One Compact Decoder

papers.abstract: Financial AI workflows that reuse investor knowledge need persistent memory that integrates observations across sources and periods without losing identity or provenance. In a knowledge graph, recurring observations may use different surface forms, fragmenting relationship histories and preventing evidence from accumulating. We introduce Fusion and Identity Registry for Memory Evolution (FIRME), a registry-anchored memory graph that reconciles incoming observations to persistent canonical relationships and retains their source, time, and context. Within periods, rule-based fusion links investor-call discussions to portfolio cash-flow signals, directly or through a fixed product-topic ontology. Across periods, canonical identities and persistent aliases direct recurring observations to the same relationship history; deterministic updates summarize reinforcement, inactivity, and reactivation. We evaluate FIRME on proprietary investor-call and cash-flow records and on S&P 500 earnings-call transcripts. Compared with a historical registry that retains canonical identities and semantic fallback but omits alias memory, FIRME increases final-period Correct Match Rate by 7.8-12.1 percentage points across four dataset-backend settings under a fixed-judge and fallback-review protocol. A blinded human audit of 200 incoming observations per setting finds Correct Match Rate gains of 9.0-16.5 points and reattachment-recall gains of 22.5-29.0 points, with higher observed merge precision in all four samples. A separate audit finds valid evidence paths for 293 of 300 outputs from full within-period fusion in the investor-call setting. Extraction-faithfulness and round-trip diagnostics assess source grounding and preservation of extractor-derived graph content.
authors: Yunbai Zhang, Yunyi Gao, Han-Tai Shiao
bullets: Addresses fragmented relationship histories caused by inconsistent surface forms in recurring investor observations.
Uses rule-based within-period fusion, a fixed product-topic ontology, canonical identities, and persistent alias memory for cross-period reconciliation.
Deterministically updates relationship histories to capture reinforcement, inactivity, and reactivation while retaining evidence paths.

Evaluated on proprietary investor records and S&P 500 earnings-call transcripts; it improves Correct Match Rate by 7.8–12.1 points and human-audited reattachment recall by 22.5–29.0 points across four settings.
Scope includes fixed-judge/fallback-review evaluation and audits of source grounding and graph-content preservation; results rely on proprietary records and a fixed ontology.

papers.title: FIRME: Registry-Anchored Memory Graphs for Evolving, Heterogeneous Investor Knowledge
papers.tldr: FIRME maintains evolving investor knowledge by anchoring observations to canonical relationships with persistent aliases, provenance, time, and context, improving matching and reattachment across periods.

papers.abstract: Complex questions in retrieval-augmented generation require evidence spread over several documents, and an answer is reliable only when the retriever finds all of it. Chain embedding retrievers collect such evidence step by step, re-encoding the question together with the passages retrieved so far, and we find that they are already strong: trained only on gold histories, a small chain embedding retriever that calls no language model outperforms graph-based systems and is competitive with a search agent. This training, however, leaves a gap. At test time the retriever conditions on its own retrievals, which soon contain mistakes: by the third step, about half or more of the states it visits hold a wrong passage, and these passages lower its chance of retrieving a missing gold passage well beyond what the difficulty of the states explains. We propose on-policy state training, which trains the encoder on the states it reaches itself. At every epoch the current encoder retrieves chains for the training questions; each state it visits, including those built on its own mistakes, is labeled with the earliest gold passage still missing while the other missing gold passages are masked, so that no correct continuation is penalized; and the encoder is updated contrastively on these states mixed with teacher-forced ones, so that its training distribution follows it as it learns. The resulting retriever retrieves complete evidence more often than teacher-forced training and the systems we compare, and it transfers without further training to harder long-chain variants of HotpotQA and 2WikiMultiHopQA that we construct. On the same states, it recovers from its own mistakes far more often, and controlled comparisons attribute the gain to training on the states the encoder currently reaches.
authors: Chenjie Qiu, Zixuan Zeng, Shaobin Shi, Bingfeng Chen, Dongsheng Luo, Boyan Xu
bullets: Multi-hop questions require retrieving all relevant evidence across several documents.
Teacher-forced training performs well but fails to prepare retrievers for erroneous passages encountered at test time.
The method trains on states reached by the current retriever, labeling the earliest missing gold passage while masking other missing evidence.
On-policy and teacher-forced states are combined in contrastive training, allowing the training distribution to track the model’s behavior.
The resulting retriever improves evidence completion, mistake recovery, and transfer to harder long-chain variants of HotpotQA and 2WikiMultiHopQA.

papers.abstract: Agents powered by large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable progress in solving complex reasoning tasks. However, LLM agents often falter on long-horizon tasks due to cognitive overload, as their working memory becomes cluttered with expanding and irrelevant information, which dilutes their attention and hinders effective planning and reasoning. To mitigate this challenge, we introduce Cognitive Resource Self-Allocation (CORAL), a novel reasoning paradigm that empowers agents to proactively optimize their context. Implemented as an agent-callable working memory management toolset, CORAL allows an agent to checkpoint its task progress and verified facts, and adaptively initiate a new problem-solving episode by resetting cluttered context while preserving only the checkpointed information, enabling it to resume reasoning from a clean state. We further enhance the agent's checkpointing capabilities using a Multi-episode Agentic Reinforced Policy Optimization algorithm. On the GAIA benchmark, CORAL with an 8B model achieves 42.8% average accuracy, with particularly strong gains on the most challenging long-horizon tasks (Level 2 and Level 3). Crucially, these gains come at a substantially lower inference cost: CORAL consumes 6-7$\times$ fewer input tokens than a ReAct agent. It also generalizes to multi-hop Knowledge QA benchmarks and to the considerably harder BrowseComp, where it improves a strong proprietary agent by 8.0 points.
authors: Zheng Zhu, Xiaozhuan Liang, Xi Chen, Bei Yu, Jiaya Jia
bullets: Long-horizon agents can suffer from cognitive overload as irrelevant context accumulates and disrupts planning.
CORAL provides an agent-callable working-memory toolkit for checkpointing progress and verified facts, then starting fresh reasoning episodes with only that information retained.
A Multi-episode Agentic Reinforced Policy Optimization algorithm improves the agent’s checkpointing decisions.
On GAIA, an 8B model with CORAL reaches 42.8% average accuracy, with especially strong gains on difficult Level 2 and Level 3 tasks.
CORAL uses 6–7× fewer input tokens than ReAct and also improves performance on multi-hop Knowledge QA and BrowseComp.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Comparison of the ReAct and CORAL frameworks; both rows read left to right as the context grows. Top (ReAct). One context accumulates N ReAct blocks (thought, action, observation) above the system prompt and user task, and nothing is ever removed. Bottom (CORAL). The same blocks are interleaved with two agent-callable tools. Memory Management (MM) writes into the persistent MEMORY panel below the trace, holding task progress (the plan, each sub-goal pending or completed) and verified facts, so that panel evolves while the raw trace only grows. Context Optimization (CO), the vertical bar, ends the current episode: everything to its left is discarded and the next episode restarts from only the system prompt, the user task, and the current panel. A trajectory is thus a sequence of episodes (here 0–3).

Figure 2: Multi-episode ARPO. The reward is computed from a trajectory’s final episode (which contains the answer) and propagated to all preceding ones; episodes from all sampled trajectories are then pooled for group-based advantage estimation, enabling credit assignment across episode boundaries.

papers.abstract: Automatic operator design (AOD) has increasingly adopted large language models (LLMs) to generate problem-specific search and variation operators for multi-objective combinatorial optimization (MOCO). Yet most methods evolve the operators while leaving the process that discovers them fixed. This limits adaptation as new Pareto trade-offs and operator interactions change where and how the search should proceed. We introduce HEMO, which makes the AOD harness itself a self-evolving optimization target. HEMO maintains a persistent harness state and updates one module at a time, revising the logic that determines which experience to retrieve, which operators to improve, which parents to select, and how to formulate the orchestration of search steps. Downstream solution quality and runtime guide these updates, while a discounted UCB scheduler directs adaptation toward promising modules as their utility changes. A persistent memory filesystem preserves candidate outcomes and diagnostic feedback across harness states, enabling successive states to build on accumulated optimization experience. Experiments across eight MOCO tasks and two structurally distinct evolutionary backbones demonstrate strong performance against conventional evolutionary, neural, and LLM-based AOD baselines, together with effective transfer to related tasks. HEMO extends automatic operator design beyond evolving individual operators to improving the search process that discovers them.
authors: Jianghan Zhu, Cong Zhang, Ni Zhang, Yifan Yang, Yew Soon Ong, Zhiguang Cao
bullets: Targets a limitation of LLM-based automatic operator design: fixed discovery and orchestration processes cannot adapt to changing Pareto trade-offs and operator interactions.
Maintains a persistent harness state and revises modules for experience retrieval, operator improvement, parent selection, and search-step orchestration.
Uses downstream solution quality and runtime as feedback, with discounted UCB scheduling to prioritize promising modules.
A persistent memory filesystem retains candidate outcomes and diagnostic feedback across successive harness states.
Evaluations on eight MOCO tasks and two evolutionary backbones show strong performance against evolutionary, neural, and LLM-based baselines, plus transfer to related tasks.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon dialogue agents require effective memory systems to recall facts, events, and relationships from interaction histories. In this work, we propose a hybrid-memory architecture comprising episodic memories and structured relational memories and a consolidation mechanism which preserves efficiency. We conduct an empirical study across two benchmarks: LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S. Our experiments demonstrate that the two memory types are consistently complementary, combining both outperform state-of-the-art memory frameworks and achieves 90.2% accuracy on LoCoMo and 85.5% on LongMemEval-S.
authors: Abhishek Gupta, Dongge Han, Daniel Madrigal Diaz, Wei-Ning Chen, Mayukh Das, Victor R\"uhle, Saravan Rajmohan
bullets: Targets reliable recall of facts, events, and relationships across long interaction histories.
Combines episodic memories with structured relational memories through a consolidation mechanism.
Evaluated on the LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S benchmarks.
The two memory types are complementary and together outperform existing state-of-the-art memory frameworks.
Achieves 90.2% accuracy on LoCoMo and 85.5% on LongMemEval-S.

Stage 3 (Memory Retrieval and QA): Given a user query, relevant memories are retrieved from both episodic and relational stores to generate contextually grounded responses.

papers.abstract: As Large Language Model (LLM) agents increasingly participate in persistent social environments, understanding their long-term social interaction capabilities becomes increasingly important. While existing research has advanced long-term memory and conversational context retrieval, less attention has been paid to whether agents can autonomously re-engage with previously inactive conversations. In particular, remembering a past interaction does not necessarily mean that an agent can identify when to revisit it, decide to return, or reconstruct the context needed for a coherent continuation. To investigate this gap, we introduce agent social re-entry as a multi- dimensional evaluation problem, distinguishing three complementary capabilities: Finding, Returning, and Reconstructing. We develop a shared-snapshot evaluation framework that measures these dimensions independently, allowing us to examine how conversational resurfacing and persistent memory relate to different aspects of social re-entry. Evaluations across six LLM configurations show that resurfacing substantially improves target conversation identification, while persistent memory is associated with higher rates of autonomous target-directed replying. However, neither improvement is accompanied by consistent gains in contextual reconstruction. These results highlight the distinction between accessing previous conversations, choosing to re-engage, and maintaining conversational continuity. Our framework provides a way to evaluate these capabilities separately rather than relying on memory retrieval or conversational response quality alone.
authors: Sheng Wan, Cong Ma, Sichen Dong, Qian'Ang Mao, Chenhan Zhang, Daning Hu, Qiang Yang
bullets: Motivated by the gap between remembering past interactions and autonomously re-engaging with them.
Separates social re-entry into Finding (identifying a conversation), Returning (choosing to re-engage), and Reconstructing (maintaining context).
Uses shared snapshots to evaluate these capabilities independently across six LLM configurations.
Conversational resurfacing improves target identification, while persistent memory is linked to more autonomous target-directed replies.
Neither technique consistently improves contextual reconstruction, underscoring that retrieval, re-engagement, and continuity are distinct abilities.

The resulting environment state is frozen before observation. (b) Three independent evaluation branches are initialized from copies of the same observation state to assess Finding, Returning, and Reconstructing under their respective task settings. The branches are evaluated separately rather than as a single sequential process.

papers.abstract: An effective agent memory system should adapt to a user's history and task requirements. Human-annotated supervision can guide this adaptation by providing feedback for evaluating and improving memory designs. Yet suitable labels are rarely available for new user histories, and manually constructing QA pairs and supporting evidence is costly. We introduce MemSteer, which turns unlabeled user histories into question-answer (QA) supervision with supporting evidence for memory-design optimization. MemSteer constructs an evidence-grounded answer plan that specifies how facts across related records jointly support a reference answer. The plan guides question generation, while source-grounded auditing and blind answer recovery check the resulting annotations. To study the utility of this supervision, we develop MemSteer-Opt, which combines QA-based design evaluation with evidence-guided failure diagnosis to revise memory store, retrieval, and context construction without updating model parameters. Experiments on ATM-Bench and RHELM show that this supervision is competitive with official-QA-guided optimization. Relative to Base-BM25, MemSteer-Opt improves ATM-Bench Question Score by 13.4 points and RHELM accuracy by 4.1 and 6.6 points without and with external data, respectively. The supervision also benefits two existing optimizers on ATM-Bench, while new-user experiments demonstrate continued design optimization using supervision generated from the target histories.
authors: Jie Huang, Cuiling Lan, Qize Yu, Xiulian Peng, Yan Lu
bullets: Addresses the scarcity and cost of manually annotated QA pairs and supporting evidence for new users.
Builds answer plans linking facts across records, then uses them to generate and audit questions and answers.
MemSteer-Opt uses the supervision to evaluate memory designs and diagnose failures in storage, retrieval, and context construction.
Improves over Base-BM25 by 13.4 ATM-Bench Question Score points and 4.1/6.6 RHELM accuracy points without/with external data.
Supports continued optimization for new users and benefits two existing ATM-Bench optimizers.

papers.abstract: Organisations keep decades of financial records as scanned PDFs on shared drives, and AI agents can now reach those drives through Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. Existing benchmarks do not mirror this production setting because they simplify the task. In some, the relevant documents are handed to the agent, so it never has to search. In others, the agent searches through documents with pre-extracted text, so it never has to read scanned images. We introduce TreasuryQA Bench, which requires both: 70 questions over 1,435 scanned U.S. Treasury publications, held in Veris's high-fidelity Dropbox twin. In each task the agent searches for the relevant file through Dropbox's MCP server, reads the pages it needs with Reducto's hosted OCR server or its own tools, and replies with one exact figure. A Python grader checks each answer against an accepted range around the correct value. In this paper we present results from ten agents. The best, Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code, solves 64.8% of attempts and the worst, GPT-5.6 Terra in Codex, solves 16.7%, so the benchmark is far from saturated. We also test how scan quality affects performance: every agent solves fewer tasks on the blurriest scans. Most failed attempts reply with a wrong number rather than no number, and the most common cause is a digit misread from the scan. Three worked examples are included with their answer keys.
authors: Ritiz Tambi, Sahar Shayegan, Joshua Meyer, Sun Kim, Ali Khan, Victor Shih, Mehdi Jamei, Andi Partovi
bullets: Benchmarks 70 questions across 1,435 scanned U.S. Treasury publications in a Dropbox environment accessed through MCP.
Agents must locate the relevant file, OCR or otherwise read required pages, and provide one exact numeric answer.
Across ten agents, success ranged from 16.7% to 64.8%, indicating the benchmark is far from saturated.
Performance declined on blurrier scans, with digit misreads the most common failure cause.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent debate systems require agents to retain and revisit arguments across multiple rounds, yet limited context windows and unstructured memories make relevant information increasingly difficult to recover. Existing flat and pairwise-graph memories also struggle to capture higher-order relations, including multi-agent agreement, conflicting evidence, and evolving consensus. We introduce HEDGE, a selective memory framework that represents debate trajectories as semantic hypergraphs. Hyperedges connect related claims across agents, while intra-hyperedge relational graphs preserve fine-grained argumentative structure. A learned memory selection module (MSM), trained through supervised learning and reinforcement learning, routes each memory candidate to STORE, BACKUP, or OMIT, retaining useful information while limiting redundancy. Across seven diverse benchmarks, HEDGE consistently outperforms strong single-agent, multi-agent, and memory baselines, improving accuracy by 5.0 points on average over the strongest multi-agent system with GPT-4o-mini. The gains reach 8.2 points on conflict-heavy tasks, while HEDGE reduces memory usage by 48% and the number of debate rounds by 34%.
authors: Amirhossein Abaskohi, Mahdi Mostajabdaveh, Zirui Zhou
bullets: Represents debate trajectories as semantic hypergraphs linking related claims across agents.
Uses intra-hyperedge relational graphs to capture agreement, conflicting evidence, and evolving consensus.
A learned memory selection module routes candidates to STORE, BACKUP, or OMIT to reduce redundancy.
Across seven benchmarks, it improves accuracy by 5.0 points on average over the strongest multi-agent baseline with GPT-4o-mini.
It achieves larger gains on conflict-heavy tasks while reducing memory usage by 48% and debate rounds by 34%.

papers.abstract: Autoresearch agents can now attempt long-horizon AI research end-to-end, i.e., self-improvement. However, best results are still obtained by research agents interacting with human researchers, and improving AI's ability to perform this co-research will only reinforce this effect---a process termed co-improvement (Weston and Foerster, 2025). Further, aligning with human expectations is likely a safer path for research agents, especially given recent agent reward hacking phenomena (OpenAI, 2026b). In this work we address these issues in four ways: (i) we empirically study the role of humans in directing autoresearch agents, focusing on the domain of benchmark creation, and find humans still play a pivotal role particularly in the ideation phase; (ii) we also develop a benchmark, HackBench, that shows current autoresearch agents are not aligned and are unable to achieve hack localization sufficiently; (iii) we present a method to train agents for improved human interaction by using human simulators as a proxy during reinforcement learning (RL); and finally (iv) we develop a method to improve model text generation, and hence agent communication, by RL with rubrics aligned with human experts. Together, our training and evaluation recipes provide a path toward more capable and aligned (co-)research agents.
authors: Tianjian Li, Chuanyang Jin, Seungone Kim, Tong Chen, John Hoffman, Yoram Bachrach amd Pedro Rodriguez, Ping Yu, Eryk Helenowski, Swarnadeep Saha, Jack Lanchantin, Weizhe Yuan, Ilia Kulikov, Jason Weston
bullets: Humans remain especially important for guiding research-agent ideation in benchmark creation.
HackBench evaluates reward-hack localization and finds current autoresearch agents insufficiently aligned and capable.
Human simulators are used as proxies during reinforcement learning to improve agent–human interaction.
Expert-aligned rubric rewards improve model text generation and agent communication.
The proposed evaluation and training recipes aim to support safer, more effective co-research.

figures.caption: Figure 8 AutoInteract is a two-phase framework for generating realistic, high-quality multi-turn interaction trajectories from verified tasks based on real user histories. In Phase 1, AutoInteract builds user models: modeling how users react by optimizing a history-conditioned user behavior prompt and building a diverse set of user profiles. In Phase 2, an agent combines verified source tasks with its user models to generate candidate tasks with multi-turn interaction trajectories, and selects them to be challenging, valid, realistic, coherent, and profile-consistent. If the checks fail, it revises the controller’s instruction until a task passes all checks or the retry budget is exhausted.

Figure 1 AutoBenchmark: evaluating the ability of autoresearch agents to create benchmarks. AutoBenchmark instructs an autoresearch agent to create a benchmark; we specifically target benchmarks that evaluate autoresearch agents themselves (i.e., benchmarking autoresearch). Within the benchmark creation loop, the autoresearch agent iteratively revises the benchmark via two main sources of feedback: one from the benchmark solvers (including the same model used as the benchmark creator) and the other from external verifiers of the benchmark (AI or human). We thus also study if having humans provide additional feedback on what benchmark to make and how to make it helps or not.
Figure 5 HackBench. Hack localization F1 per model. All monitors miss many hacks.

Figure 2 Performance of benchmark solvers and verdicts of benchmark judges across 10 iterations. A lower score means a harder benchmark. Muse Spark and Muse Glimmer are the solvers inside the loop, while Nemotron is held out. Filled markers passed all five quality judges and are eligible for selection; hollow markers were caught by at least one, and the star is the selected checkpoint, namely the eligible iteration with the lowest Muse Spark score. We display different levels of human feedback. The no-feedback curve is one autonomous run, in which the agent chooses the benchmark itself, shown in both rows as a reference. Feedback from humans improves over fully autonomous benchmark creation, with fine-grained feedback more useful than coarse-grained feedback.

Figure 6 HackBench. Given a full agent trajectory (left), an LLM monitor (center) reads the entire transcript and is scored on the hack localization task of returning the exact offending command(s) by command index (right).

Figure 4 Examples of critique fromLLM judges: Feedback from LLM judges (benchmark verifiers) gives the research agent insights that solver scores (i.e., trajectory feedback) alone cannot provide, and enables making a valid benchmark while keeping it challenging.

Figure 3 Execution feedback on SilentTrain Bench. Iterations 1 to 5 of a fine-grained proposal are run without extra human feedback, and then the experiment is forked at iteration 6: one continuation receives human guidance on how to instantiate the benchmark and the other continues unaided. The agent, the construct, and the grounding material are identical across the fork. Markers follow Figure 2 and ∆ is the gap between the two selected checkpoints on each solver. Extra expert human guidance helps.

Figure 7 Construction of a HackBench example with a synthetic hack through trajectory editing. Step 1: We begin with a real autoresearch trajectory. Step 2: We insert a synthetic reward-hacking command (red). Step 3: We update only causally affected downstream observations (green), preserving the task, commands, and unrelated observations. This produces a coherent example with command-level audited gold annotations.

Figure 9 The user-simulator prompt used to generate each user turn. It combines the learned user behavior prompt and a sampled user profile from Phase 1 with the interaction history and the privileged task context. After a failed attempt, the controller may also add revised role-playing guidance based on the trajectory evaluator’s feedback.

Figure 10 Training on AutoInteract tasks does not saturate as quickly as training on the source data. Training reward versus optimization step for Qwen3.5-4B RL runs on the source data (blue) and on AutoInteract tasks (orange). In the algorithmic domain (left), AutoInteract starts from a lower reward but continues improving and eventually reaches a higher reward than source-task training. In the SWE domain (right), AutoInteract also continues improving and reaches substantially higher reward, while source-task training saturates much earlier.

Right: validation absolute means—the gap increases from both directions, with the human’s score rising (3.4 → 5.0) as the model’s falls (7.6 → 2.7).

(optimizer Kimi-K2.6, judge and writer = Muse Spark 1.1); the meta-optimized rubrics are used for story and Wikipedia RL-XAR training. Right (Wikipedia): the validation gap peaks around iteration 3 at only +1.07 and stays small—consistent with the far more modest Wikipedia gains.

Mean human−model gap (writer = Muse Spark 1.1; positive = human favored) for each judge, with judges in decreasing capability order. On Story and Wikipedia, Qwen3.5-27B (red) is the only judge to turn negative, ranking the model above human writing (−0.55 story, −0.39 wiki); on Paper the four judges are close and all human-favoring. A weak grader is incapable of seeing the gap.

While this is not the approach reported in our main experiments, it appears to work well also, and future work should explore this approach further.
Figure 15 Different Rubric Meta-Optimizers. Mean (human − model) gap per optimizer, averaged over three seeds.

Figure 11 AutoInteract makes challenging multi-turn interaction data through revisions. The source task, learned user behavior prompt, and sampled profile remain fixed. Stage 1 points directly to the likely code change, making the trajectory too easy: the weak solver scores 67%, above the 40% limit. Evaluator feedback leads Stage 2 to remove that clue, but the revision also omits the example file and expected behavior, leaving too little evidence: the strong solver scores 67%, below the 70% target. Stage 3 restores this evidence, identifies the relevant code area, and adds follow-up requirements without revealing the solution. The final trajectory is accepted with weak- and strong-solver scores of 25% and 100% and passes all validity, leakage, and realism checks.

Figure 12 Standard judgments (left, middle) rank themodel above the expert human—meta-optimizing the rubrics to be aligned with human experts reverses this (right). If AI slop is judged to be better than human writing by the LLM grader, then training will encourage more slop. On the academic paper section writing task, we find standard pairwise LLM judges or LLM-generated rubrics score GPT-5.6 or Opus-4.8 higher than high-quality human writing. Our RL-XAR (eXpert-Aligned Rubrics) approach instead meta-optimizes the rubrics on a training set of high-quality human-written sections, resulting in rubrics that reverse the result, and score the human writing higher on test papers.

Figure 16 Human−model gap by paper human writing-quality bin (low/medium/high, light to dark), comparing with two models (Muse Spark 1.1 and GPT-5.6). If the learned rubric is measuring genuine quality, the human-model gap should be larger for better-written human papers and shrink for weak ones, which is what we observe.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being used as cognitive interfaces that shape how users interpret evidence, communicate, and make decisions. As deployed systems become more multimodal, tool-using, and multi-agent, safety failures no longer arise only from isolated harmful outputs, but also from how agents update, store, and propagate epistemic commitments across retrieval, memory, tools, and peer communication. In this paper, we define belief as an engineering abstraction for evidence-based commitments that guide downstream action. Building on this view, we propose the Explicit Belief Multi-Agent System (EB-MAS), which externalizes belief states into a structured substrate, uses belief operators to propose candidate updates, and applies a Cognitive Firewall to bound or reject updates that are weakly evidenced but strongly driven by vulnerability cues. We also discuss the risk of group belief at the group level, including manufactured consensus, collusion, and cascading misinformation, and outline practical integration challenges around grounding, false positives, scalability, and ethical misuse. Therefore, scalable agent safety requires not only better output filtering or stronger base models, but also explicit interfaces for tracing, calibrating, and constraining belief revision at runtime.
authors: Zhuoyun Li, Boxuan Wang, Jinwei Hu, Xiaowei Huang, Yi Dong
bullets: Frames belief as an engineering abstraction for evidence-based commitments guiding agent actions.
Proposes EB-MAS, which externalizes belief states and uses belief operators to suggest updates.
Introduces a Cognitive Firewall to bound or reject weakly evidenced updates driven by vulnerability cues.
Highlights group-level risks including manufactured consensus, collusion, and cascading misinformation.
Identifies open challenges in grounding, false positives, scalability, and ethical misuse.

figures.caption: Figure 1: EB-MAS with an Explicit Belief Substrate (EBS). The framework spans three levels: Substrate Layer (Sec. 3.1) maintains a belief graph with attention-activated subgraphs; Individual Layer (Sec. 3.2) applies neuro-symbolic belief operators to update node attributes and evolve topology, guarded by a Cognitive Firewall against evidence–vulnerability mismatch; Group Layer (Sec. 3.3) couples agents via social priors to model consensus, polarization, and narrative collapse.

Figure 2: Monte Carlo simulations of belief-centric containment. (A,B) Under a belief-reframing attack, w/ EBS blocks risk-decoupling updates, reducing ASR and better preserving perceived risk. (C,D) w/ EBS lowers both the ASR of a coordinated sacrifice-based attack and attackers’ win rate, preventing post-attack trust surges.

papers.abstract: LLM agents are increasingly adopted in long-horizon tasks and interact with diverse external environments. Despite their growing capabilities, these agents remain vulnerable to real-world attacks such as indirect prompt injections, which manipulate agents through malicious instructions embedded in external environments. While existing risk assessment work has primarily focused on the injection content, the effect of where an injection appears has not been systematically characterized. Studying injection placement requires agents to operate over longer-horizon tasks and interact with diverse environmental surfaces. Thus, we build three agentic testbeds spanning tool use, coding, and daily workflow domains with diverse injection surfaces. Holding the injection content fixed, we find that agent susceptibility varies across injection placements. We refer to this phenomenon as the trust region effect: agents implicitly assign different levels of trust to different regions of their environments. For example, an agent powered by GPT-5.4 follows an unsafe injection instruction placed in a repository documentation file (i.e., a README or TODO file) 2.6 times more often on average than the same instruction placed in a code or data file. Building upon this observation, we develop learning-based attackers that generate injection content and select better injection placements. Our approach demonstrates that both where an injection is placed and what content it contains can affect the strength of indirect prompt injection attacks. To the best of our knowledge, this work provides the first systematic characterization for the effectiveness of different injection placements, spanning both coarse-grained environmental surfaces and fine-grained positions. The uneven trust that agents implicitly place across their environments provides important insights for future attack and defense design.
authors: Chengquan Guo, Xiaodong Liu, Weiwei Yang, Mingqian Feng, Jialin Song, Qiyao Ma, Carolyn Buractaon, Christopher White, Bo Li, Jianfeng Gao
bullets: The study examines how injection placement affects agent susceptibility, beyond the injection’s content.
It evaluates three long-horizon testbeds covering tool use, coding, and daily workflows with diverse injection surfaces.
Holding content fixed, agents show different attack success rates depending on placement; repository documentation was especially influential compared with code or data files.
The authors develop learning-based attackers that jointly optimize injection content and placement.
Findings motivate defenses that account for implicit, location-dependent trust in agent environments.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The same injection content can succeed or fail depending on its placement. During a benign coding-agent task, a GPT-5.4 agent with the OpenAI Agents SDK traverses multiple environmental surfaces, including README.md, TODO.md, source files, and data files. Holding the injection content fixed (CWE-78 Risk), the agent follows the instruction when it appears in README.md but ignores the identical instruction in a data file. This contrast motivates our study of injection placement and the trust region effect.

Figure 2: Injection placement space. Left: environmental surfaces in our three testbeds, grouped by domain and surface type. Right: within each selected surface, the injection is placed at the START, MIDDLE, or END relative to the surrounding benign content. A placement ℓ = (s, p) is defined by a surface s and a within-surface position p.

Figure 8: LLM-based placement selection does not consistently outperform a simple frequency prior. Each panel plots the attack success rate on the held-out contexts (the leave-task-out test set) against the query budget B, with injection content fixed. At budget B, the attacker tries its top-B candidate (s, p) placements and succeeds if any attempt works (best of B, with no feedback between attempts); the curves therefore differ only in the order in which placements are tried. Fixed prior (green): surfaces are ranked once offline by their average ASR on the training split; all candidate placements are then tried in that surface order, and within each surface from end to middle to start (a global recency prior), using the same fixed order for every context. GPT-pos (orange): a prompted GPT-5.4 ranks surface and spot placements separately for each context. Random (blue): placements are tried in random order. Oracle (gray dashed): the ceiling under fixed content, obtained by evaluating all candidate placements and selecting the best one for each context. Across domains and budgets, GPT-5.4 cannot provide a consistent advantage over the simple fixed prior.

papers.abstract: Agents deployed at scale repeatedly encounter related problems, and it is natural to let them learn from each other's experience rather than starting over each time. Unfortunately, there is no single way to retain that experience that works well across settings, and no way to know in advance which future problems a given experience will help with. A global history preserves every detail but becomes expensive and mixes together experience that may not belong together; compressing that history into one fixed representation limits the cost but can throw away valuable details. We introduce Routed Continual Learning (Routed CL), an architecture that decides how to partition and retain experience. Past trajectories are grouped into clusters, each of which maintains state using one memory system from a fixed library. Before each run, an LLM-based router either reuses an existing cluster or creates a new one, basing its decision on the problem statement, memory system descriptions, and cluster summaries. We also introduce Context Memory Adapter, which mediates between the memory system and the agentic loop. We evaluate the architecture on a heterogeneous stream that interleaves 301 instances from the six CL-Bench tasks with 97 banking instances from $\tau^3$-Bench. Across four language models and five matched rollouts, Routed Continual Learning raises normalized reward over a single global in-context learning (ICL) history by 15-30% of the maximum attainable normalized reward, achieves higher mean normalized reward than ICL-only clustering, and reduces estimated API cost by 65-72% relative to Global ICL. These results support approaching continual learning as a routing problem that chooses both a learning mechanism and a state cluster rather than committing to one representation globally.
authors: Michael Philip, Mahesh Balakrishnan, David Geraghty, David Mao, Vidhya Venkat, Ilya Mironov
bullets: Addresses the challenge of retaining shared experience across varied future problems without costly global histories or overly lossy compression.

Evaluated across 398 instances from CL-Bench and τ³-Bench, four language models, and five matched rollouts.
Reported 15–30% gains in normalized reward over global ICL history, higher reward than ICL-only clustering, and 65–72% lower estimated API cost than Global ICL.

papers.abstract: A memory can be outdated for present-day reasoning yet indispensable for reconstructing the past. Relevance-based retrieval overlooks this tension: semantic relevance, evidence-grounded validity, and query-specific eligibility are distinct. We propose CALM, a conflict-aware lifecycle memory governance framework that decouples persistent memory preservation from query-time admission. CALM converts heterogeneous records into evidence-grounded memory cells, updates validity and lifecycle states using support, conflict, and dependency signals, and admits query-appropriate evidence through training-free or learned gating informed by temporal applicability. Across LongMemEval-S and LoCoMo with Qwen and GPT backbones, CALM outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving the best overall accuracy. Compared with simple filtering and reranking, query-conditioned admission further improves evidence selection. Conflict-blocking and robustness analyses show CALM suppresses erroneous retrieved memories while retaining useful evidence. Historical-reconstruction experiments demonstrate that preserving superseded records supports accurate earlier-state reasoning without compromising current-state answers.

Evaluations show strong overall accuracy, conflict suppression, and accurate historical reconstruction without harming current-state answers.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have spurred growing interest in temporal knowledge graph question answering (TKGQA). Most existing methods rely on semantic retrieval augmented generation (RAG), which suffers from fundamental limitations in complex temporal reasoning. On the one hand, semantic-based RAG methods struggle to capture the multi-hop causal knowledge required for complex temporal reasoning. On the other hand, these methods introduce excessive redundant knowledge, trapping LLMs in spurious reasoning chains that potentially result in erroneous answers. To address these problems, we propose a Temporal Causal Chain-guided RAG (TCC-RAG) to retrieve a concise yet sufficient set of causal knowledge to support complex temporal reasoning. Specifically, we reformulate the temporal knowledge graph into a multi-view causal cue graph, with causal cues inducing connections that explicitly encode temporal evolution and causal dynamics. Based on the causal cue graph, we construct a query-specific temporal causal chain to guide the retrieval process, enabling the model to focus on a concise set of causally relevant knowledge. Finally, we introduce a causal evidence filter to refine the retrieved knowledge, ensuring its causal consistency with the underlying temporal logic of the query. Experiments show that TCC-RAG achieves substantial performance gains of 10.72% and 8.40% on two TKGQA benchmarks, and delivers a remarkable 62.97% improvement for multi-step temporal reasoning.
authors: Xinxun Zhang, Yuxiang Wang, Shanshan Feng, Jun Zhang, Tieyun Qian, Binhang Yuan, Kai Yin, Xiao Yan, Jiawei Jiang
bullets: Targets the limitations of semantic RAG in multi-hop temporal-causal reasoning and its redundant, misleading retrieved knowledge.
Reformulates temporal knowledge graphs as multi-view causal cue graphs encoding temporal evolution and causal dynamics.
Builds query-specific temporal causal chains to guide retrieval toward sufficient, causally relevant knowledge.
Uses a causal evidence filter to enforce consistency with the query’s temporal logic.
Reports performance gains of 10.72% and 8.40% on two TKGQA benchmarks, including a 62.97% improvement in multi-step temporal reasoning.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: The framework of TCC-RAG. (b) NER and LLM extraction ground query entities through matching and consistency checking. Relation, cue, and role parsing then guide view routing and temporal chain retrieval. (c) The Causal Evidence Filter removes equivalent duplicates and selects a sufficient subset of query-consistent facts. (d) The LLM reasons over the filtered evidence to generate answers. When structured retrieval yields no facts, semantic retrieval provides fallback candidates that also pass through the filter.

papers.abstract: Historical experience can guide scientific coding at multiple levels, but task-level retrieval may miss implementation lessons that become relevant during execution. We introduce MUSE, a memory management framework combining multi-level memory with selective runtime injection for scientific coding agents. MUSE builds global, approach-level, and implementation-level memory from historical trajectories. At initialization, the agent receives global memory and problem-matched approach-level memory. During execution, current interactions are used to retrieve implementation-level memory. An LLM gate selects relevant experience and generates specific review advice, or skips injection. Across four benchmarks spanning numerical problem solving, kernel optimization, and scientific software repair, MUSE outperforms retrieval and memory baselines on all evaluation metrics. Ablations support the multi-level design and gated injection, while transfer experiments show that memory remains useful across kernel benchmarks. These results show that multi-level memory and selective runtime injection enable effective reuse of experience in scientific coding. Code is available at https://github.com/hr-jin/MUSE.
authors: Haoran Jin, Defu Lian, Xiting Wang, Hong Xie
bullets: Builds global, approach-level, and implementation-level memories from historical trajectories.

papers.abstract: LLM-based agents now share experiences on social platforms and remember new preferences to enhance their performance. However, existing memory systems contain a vulnerability in role-to-principal attribution that attackers can exploit. We identify Role Grounding Misattribution, in which an attacker-designed interaction causes the victim agent to incorrectly record a preference from the attacker as a preference of the victim's user. Specifically, we are the first to formalize Role Grounding Attack (RGA), an attack model that exploits this vulnerability through nested conversation structures. In the memory formation stage, an experience-sharing post quoting a conversation between the attacker agent and its user is published, which explicitly identifies its publisher. The inner conversation expresses preferences from the user of the attacker agent. When the victim agent remembers preferences from this nested structure, its memory loses the context binding and grounds the attacker's preference to the victim's user instead. In the memory retrieval stage, the misattributed preference persists and influences the victim agent's decisions when it encounters relevant scenarios. We instantiate RGA as tool selection manipulation and privacy leakage. Tool selection manipulation causes a tool-call preference to be misattributed to the victim's user, steering the victim toward an attacker-controlled tool. Privacy leakage extends this by misattributing both a tool-call preference and a task-requirement preference to the victim's user. The victim selects the attacker's tool, then includes sensitive information in tool arguments to satisfy the task requirement. We evaluate RGA across five mainstream memory systems and six language models. Tool manipulation and privacy leakage both achieve high attack success rates. These results call for stronger role grounding.
authors: Haoran Bu, Yiting Shen, Litian Zhang, Ruihan Hu, Xi Zhang
bullets: Identifies Role Grounding Misattribution as a vulnerability in memory systems’ role-to-principal attribution.

papers.abstract: Latent multi-agent systems reduce inference cost by keeping intermediate reasoning and inter-agent communication in continuous representations.\ Reusable skills, however, are commonly supplied as text or stored as layer-wise Key-Value states or skill-specific model parameters, introducing repeated processing or substantial per-skill storage.\ We introduce \textbf{SkillMem}, which represents each reusable skill as a small external latent memory and makes it directly available during latent multi-agent reasoning.\ A role-conditioned cross-attention reader allows the same memory to guide different agents according to their roles and current hidden states.\ We train the skill memories and shared reader through behavioral distillation, matching the change in token predictions induced by a textual skill while keeping the backbone frozen.\ For our experiments, we obtain textual skills from paired successful and failed multi-agent trajectories, although existing skills can also be compiled directly.\ Across six benchmarks and Qwen3 models ranging from 4B to 14B parameters, SkillMem provides strong gains for smaller backbones while preserving efficient latent multi-agent inference across model scales.\ We use the same $8\times256$ memory configuration across all evaluated model scales, requiring 9.6\,KB of skill-specific storage per skill, including its retrieval embedding.\ For a library of 100 skills, SkillMem reduces total storage by more than $38\times$ compared with alternative skill representations and achieves up to a $4.23\times$ end-to-end inference speedup.\ These results show that compact procedural memories can be reused without sacrificing the efficiency of latent multi-agent reasoning.
authors: Yuxuan Zhu, Mohammad Mohammadi Amiri, Pin-Yu Chen, Keerthiram Murugesan
bullets: Addresses the repeated processing and high per-skill storage costs of text, Key-Value, and parameter-based skill representations.
Stores each skill in a small external latent memory accessed through role-conditioned cross-attention.

Across six benchmarks and Qwen3 models from 4B to 14B parameters, it provides especially strong gains for smaller models.
Uses 9.6 KB per skill; for 100 skills, it cuts storage by over 38× and delivers up to 4.23× end-to-end speedup.

We score the same response with and without the textual skill to measure its token-level effect. We then replace the skill text with its memory and train the memory and role-conditioned reader to reproduce the skill-supported behavior while preserving the base behavior at positions with limited skill support.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets a large language model (LLM) answer questions by retrieving relevant passages from a large corpus. However, RAG struggles with multi-hop questions, which require chaining facts spread across several documents through intermediate entities that the question never mentions. Graph-based RAG methods retrieve once from the entities a question names and so rarely recover the full evidence chain. Iterative RAG methods recover it step by step, but their accuracy is limited by the many tasks they ask the LLM to perform, such as planning the sub-questions, deciding their dependencies, rewriting them as answers arrive, and keeping track of what is known. We propose DeFT-RAG, a RAG framework built on three components. First, DeFT-RAG generates one self-contained sub-question at a time from the original question and the sub-questions answered so far with their answers (QA pairs). Each sub-question names every entity it asks about, which removes the need to plan, track dependencies or rewrite, and lets the LLM focus on a single fine-grained task at a time. Second, DeFT-RAG moves the remaining LLM work outside the LLM: rule-based updates to a QA table that keeps track of what is known, and yes/no decisions made by a fine-tuned lightweight decision model. Third, DeFT-RAG caches the QA pairs and reuses an answer when a later question asks a sub-question with the same meaning. On MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA, DeFT-RAG achieves the best accuracy among thirteen baselines with both gpt-4o-mini and Qwen3.6 as the backbone, while giving the LLM fewer input tokens than any other iterative method. With a QA cache shared across 1,000 MuSiQue questions, 23.1% of sub-questions are answered from the cache, which reduces LLM calls by 12.9% without lowering accuracy.
bullets: Targets multi-hop RAG failures where evidence spans documents connected through unstated intermediate entities.
Generates one self-contained sub-question at a time, using prior question–answer pairs to name all relevant entities.
Uses rule-based QA-table updates and a fine-tuned lightweight decision model to move bookkeeping and yes/no decisions outside the LLM.
Caches semantically equivalent sub-question answers; on 1,000 MuSiQue questions, this served 23.1% of sub-questions from cache and reduced LLM calls by 12.9% without reducing accuracy.
Achieved the best accuracy among 13 baselines on MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and HotpotQA with both tested backbones, while using fewer input tokens than other iterative methods.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Failures of graph-based and iterative RAG on a 3-hop MuSiQue question (gpt-4o-mini runs). Top: the gold chain, which passes through two bridge entities the question never names. papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have rapidly become important tools for science, education, medicine, and professional work. Despite their apparent simplicity from the user's perspective, effective and responsible use requires an understanding of how these systems work, what their limitations are, and how their outputs should be evaluated. I wrote this document as a basis for my lecture on LLM in the master in artificial intelligence in medicine at the university of Turin, Italy. This book provides a practical and accessible introduction to LLMs for scientists and professionals. It explains the fundamental ideas behind tokenisation, embeddings, training, inference, context windows, prompting, and instruction hierarchies, while deliberately avoiding mathematical detail. Particular attention is given to the limitations of LLM-generated answers, including hallucinations, uncertainty, reproducibility, bias, and the need for systematic verification and human oversight. The book also discusses privacy, governance, security, and the responsible handling of personal and sensitive information. More advanced topics include Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), retrieval quality, chunking, embeddings, vector search, agents, tools, and workflows. A substantial practical exercise guides the reader through running a local LLM with Ollama and Open WebUI and using it to interact with a collection of scientific papers. The exercise emphasizes evidence retrieval, source verification, uncertainty, disagreement between studies, and the distinction between plausible language and scientifically supported conclusions. No programming knowledge is required.
bullets: Explains tokenisation, embeddings, training, inference, context windows, prompting, and instruction hierarchies without mathematical detail.
Highlights hallucinations, uncertainty, reproducibility, bias, privacy, security, governance, and the need for human oversight.
Introduces advanced applications including retrieval-augmented generation, vector search, agents, tools, and workflows.
Includes a no-code exercise using a local LLM to analyze scientific papers, verify sources, and assess disagreement and uncertainty.

papers.abstract: For large language models (LLMs), parametric adaptation is costly when retrieval already suffices. We introduce ALLOT, a hybrid-memory routing framework that separates learned write priority from a hard parametric budget. A memory-aware router combines frozen text representations, retrieval confidence, and relation metadata; a single ranking supports multiple write budgets while preserving all facts in external memory. On CounterFact with Qwen3-4B, ALLOT reaches 0.760 accuracy at a 20% parametric-write budget and recovers 78.4% of the budget-matched oracle gain, with 80% fewer parametric writes than dual-writing every fact. At this budget, jointly adding retrieval and relation features to text improves normalized oracle gain by 6.2 percentage points. Complementary Qwen3-0.6B shared-store results achieve dual-write-level accuracy with 6-14.5% parametric writes, and cross-benchmark transfer retains approximately 88% of in-domain gain. These results support allocating adaptation capacity according to its incremental value rather than treating every factual update as an equally valuable training target.
bullets: Targets the costly practice of writing every fact into model parameters when retrieval is sufficient.
Uses a memory-aware router combining frozen text representations, retrieval confidence, and relation metadata.
A single ranking supports different hard parametric-write budgets while retaining all facts externally.
On CounterFact with Qwen3-4B, it reaches 0.760 accuracy at a 20% write budget and recovers 78.4% of the matched oracle gain.
Results also show dual-write-level accuracy with 6–14.5% parametric writes in a Qwen3-0.6B shared-store setting, with approximately 88% cross-benchmark gain transfer.
