We test 124M-7B self-trained/publicly pretrained beds, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP8 (176.95B; 320,001,536 FP8 rows), and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. Write coverage requires a sufficiently trained backbone prior, full-width readout, trainable gates; undertrained-bed intervention confirms a threshold, not a slope. At fixed budget, coverage falls from 98% (50 facts) to 12.7% (1,000); table size is not binding. Two-hop composition does not exceed the independent single-hop baseline (26% observed vs 25% expected; 15% lexical-distortion floor). Synergy remains absent across dose/load in two independent bed families. A 28-percentage-point in-context gap (given vs recalled intermediates) localizes failure to retrieval-for-reasoning, not gate access. Writes are independently retrievable, precisely addressable, reversible atoms, not composable into reasoning. A layered protocol, the first, to our knowledge, to cover compositionality in behavioral memory evaluation, separates baseline, synergy and distortion floor. Any addressed/key-value memory must report coverage, synergy ratio and distortion rate before deployment claims. Composition must be system-orchestrated; multi-constraint queries should explicitly chain written atoms. In-context controls show given intermediate entities are exploited at twice the implicit rate. Production load fits exponential interference ($R^2=0.98$); its mechanism, between budget dilution and write interference, remains open. All numbers are recomputed from archived raw logs/JSON; a fresh 52-target production rerun gives 52/52, exactly matching archived baselines.
authors: Wei Gao, Cheng Tian, Duan Yang, Jianqing Yin
bullets: Coverage depends on a sufficiently trained backbone, full-width readout, and trainable gates; table capacity is not the limiting factor.
At fixed budget, coverage drops from 98% for 50 facts to 12.7% for 1,000, consistent with load-related interference.
Two-hop composition shows no meaningful synergy beyond independent retrieval: 26% observed versus 25% expected, with a 15% distortion floor.
A 28-point gap between given and recalled intermediates localizes the main failure to retrieval-for-reasoning rather than memory access.
The study recommends reporting coverage, synergy, and distortion, and explicitly chaining stored atoms for multi-constraint queries; the mechanism of load interference remains open.
papers.selection_reason: Production-scale analysis of addressed-memory writes for knowledge injection and compositionality in LLMs.
papers.title: Atoms, Not Knowledge: What Production-Scale Addressed-Memory Writes Deposit
papers.tldr: Production-scale addressed-memory writes reliably store and retrieve isolated facts, but do not inherently compose them into multi-step reasoning.

papers.abstract: Persistent memory turns prior interactions into durable agent state, but existing systems provide limited control over whether that state remains valid and whether it should influence a later query. We argue that reliable memory requires governance over both state formation and query-time influence. We introduce PLACE, a factorized governance layer that adds write-side state certification and read-side authorization to a memory backend. A factorial evaluation on Mem0 with Qwen2.5-3B and Qwen2.5-7B isolates the contribution of each mechanism. Results show that write-side governance substantially improves lifecycle state correctness, while read-side governance eliminates measured causal leakage from ineligible memory in the state-correct setting. Their combination achieves the strongest joint performance while preserving query-relevant support. These findings show that reliable persistent memory requires explicit control over both maintained state and query-time information influence.
authors: Chen-Fang Hu, Hong-Han Shuai, Woan-Shiuan Chien
bullets: Targets two gaps in persistent memory: invalid lifecycle state and unauthorized query-time influence.
Adds write-side state certification and read-side authorization as separate governance mechanisms.
Factorial evaluation on Mem0 with Qwen2.5-3B and Qwen2.5-7B isolates each mechanism’s effect.
Write governance improves lifecycle state correctness; read governance eliminates measured causal leakage in the state-correct setting.
Combining both achieves the strongest joint performance while preserving query-relevant support.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a governance layer for persistent memory in LLM agents, controlling write-side state and query-time eligibility.
papers.title: Memory, Know Your PLACE: Governing Lifecycle State and Query-Time Eligibility in Persistent-Memory Agents
papers.tldr: PLACE makes persistent-memory agents more reliable by governing both which memories are retained and which are allowed to influence each query.

papers.abstract: Memory serves as the core component of LLM-based agents, enabling personalized responses via extracting and using user preferences from past interactions. However, its use may reduce response diversity, thereby narrowing the range of information available to users. Existing evaluations rely largely on synthetic interactions and cover few memory systems, leaving the effects of memory on response diversity insufficiently evaluated in real-world scenarios. We introduce MemBubble, a benchmark of 1000 instances built on preferences extracted from real user-assistant conversations. To measure the extent to which memory concentrates response distributions, we construct test queries in scenarios distinct from user preferences while preserving topical relevance through shared preference categories. Across multiple LLMs and memory mechanisms, entropy decreases by 34.7% on average compared with directly providing the full interaction history, highlighting the important role of memory processing in diversity loss. We also explore simple user-side interventions and changes in information availability but find that these do not effectively close the diversity gap. Our findings highlight the need to consider preserving diversity and user access to information alongside improvements in personalization when designing and using agent memory systems.
authors: Jiajun Tan, Fei Sun, Xinyu Ma, Shixuan Zhang, Du Su, Qi Cao, Daiting Shi, Huawei Shen, Xueqi Cheng
bullets: Introduces a 1,000-instance benchmark built from preferences extracted from real user-assistant conversations.
Tests queries that are topically related to user preferences but distinct from the original preference scenarios.
Evaluates multiple LLMs and memory mechanisms by measuring response-distribution entropy.
Memory reduces entropy by 34.7% on average versus providing the full interaction history.
Simple user-side interventions and increased information availability do not eliminate the diversity gap.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark on agent memory and response diversity; directly fits LLM memory.
papers.title: MemBubble: Benchmarking How Agent Memory Shapes LLM Response Diversity
papers.tldr: MemBubble shows that LLM agent memory substantially narrows response diversity, even when personalization is based on real user preferences.

papers.abstract: Skill-augmented agentic RL has emerged as an effective approach to improving LLM agents on long-horizon tasks. Despite this progress, individual skills may follow distinct trajectories as the policy evolves, with some becoming redundant after the model internalizes their capabilities, others remaining valuable as external scaffolding, and still others turning harmful. However, existing skill library systems fail to identify each skill's true contribution due to free-riding among co-retrieved skills, difficulty confounding across tasks, and the absence of skill-specific counterfactual evidence, which prevents reliable skill lifecycle management. We propose TrackRL, an agentic RL framework where skill tracking drives skill library full lifecycle management. Specifically, within each GRPO group, we turn grouped sampling into online randomized controlled experiments. Independent random injection and within-group contrasts on the same task isolate each skill's true contribution, and reliability-weighted aggregation accumulates evidence across groups. As evidence accumulates, we continuously track skill utility, which measures the skill's causal contribution as external scaffolding, and model mastery, which reflects how far the corresponding capability has been internalized. Along this line, we formulate skill lifecycle management as an evidence-gated state-transition process that governs each skill from generation and admission through protected incubation to retention, retirement, or removal, while a soft capacity bound controls library growth. Experiments show that TrackRL outperforms recent skill-augmented RL baselines in both library-assisted and skill-free evaluation, with further analyses revealing how skill value shifts during policy learning and how evidence-driven state transitions shape skill library evolution. Our code is available at https://github.com/xizhu1022/TrackRL.
authors: Xi Zhu, Yuanlin Duan, Changyi Yang, Kai Mei, Riyang Bao, Shichao Zhu, Dimitris N. Metaxas
bullets: Addresses redundant, harmful, or internalized skills and unreliable attribution from co-retrieval and task confounding.
Uses randomized skill injection and within-group contrasts in GRPO to estimate each skill’s contribution.
Tracks both skill utility as external scaffolding and model mastery of the corresponding capability.
Applies evidence-gated transitions for skill admission, incubation, retention, retirement, and removal, with a soft library-capacity bound.
Outperforms recent skill-augmented RL baselines in both library-assisted and skill-free evaluations; analyses show skill values shift during learning.
papers.selection_reason: Skill library lifecycle management with evidence-gated state transitions for agentic RL; relevant to agent memory and continual skill adaptation.
papers.title: Trackable Skill Library Lifecycle Management for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: TrackRL uses online causal tracking to manage each skill’s lifecycle as an agentic RL policy evolves.

papers.abstract: Agents now act on the Web, publishing packages, models and datasets through registry APIs, and remembering past verifications spares them the work. But a verdict rests on premises. When a signing key is revoked, everything built on it stops passing, yet the advisory names only the key, and the old verdicts of its dependents may never share a retrieval window with it. This non-locality of invalidation turns memory into a liability: in long simulated chats, an agent reading a memory of atomic facts publishes 62% of the objects whose failure lies upstream, each backed by a record that was true when written. Yet derivation is local even when invalidation is not. Tether records, at write time, the exact versions each verdict derives from, and at read time withdraws any verdict whose support has failed anywhere in the store; the agent reads the same fields as before. On Fallout, a generator of versioned worlds with hypothesis-blind simulated histories shared by every memory, Tether publishes 0.3% of upstream-failing objects across three domains when relations are stated with their verdicts, with 37% fewer verification calls than checking everything. A-Mem and Graphiti re-verify most candidates (0.83-0.86 checks per candidate), which limits their savings, yet publish 9% of upstream-failing objects; Mem0 relies on memory more and publishes 42%. Flushing every verdict on any failure is as safe as Tether but costs 32% more checks. The gain over fact memory holds with three open-weight backbones and against a whole-store window. These gains depend on capturing dependencies: when relations arrive in sessions apart from their verdicts, Tether's downstream unsafe publication rate rises to 9.4-22.1%, and a weak writer that misses edges loses safety in the same way.
authors: Yiqi Wang, Jinqian Ju, Jiaqi Zhang, Zhangkai Wu, Yiqun Duan, Zequn Sun, Taotao Cai, Mingkai Zheng
bullets: Problem: Stored facts can remain locally true but become unsafe after non-local dependency failures, such as key revocation.
Method: Record the exact versioned supports for each verdict and withdraw it at retrieval if any support has failed.
Result: On Fallout, upstream-failing publications fell to 0.3%, with 37% fewer verification calls than checking everything.
Compared with A-Mem, Graphiti, and Mem0, Tether achieved lower unsafe publication rates while requiring less re-verification.
Scope: Safety degrades when dependencies and verdicts arrive far apart or the memory writer misses dependency edges.
papers.selection_reason: Dependency-tethered memory for tool-using LLM agents; directly fits LLM memory.
papers.title: Memories That Outlive Their Reasons: Dependency-Tethered Memory for Tool-Using LLM Agents
papers.tldr: Dependency-tethered memory lets tool-using agents invalidate stale verdicts when upstream premises fail, sharply reducing unsafe publications while avoiding full re-verification.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external memory to accumulate past experiences for continual adaptation. However, effectively reusing memory requires accurately assessing its value, as retrieved experiences may become unreliable when transferred across task contexts. Despite its importance, memory valuation remains largely underexplored, with existing methods relying on historical retrieval success rates that overlook the context dependency of memory usefulness and the varying reliability of estimates under different amounts of evidence. Inspired by the Bayesian brain hypothesis, we propose BEAM (Bayesian-style Evolutionary Agentic Memory), a framework that reformulates memory value evaluation as a parameterized cognitive inference process, where memory value is represented as a context-conditioned dynamic belief rather than a passive historical statistic. Specifically, BEAM infers memory value beliefs from current task contexts and continuously calibrates them using execution feedback as empirical evidence, transforming memory from passive storage into an adaptive cognitive mechanism for continual self-evolution. Extensive experiments across reasoning and code generation benchmarks demonstrate that BEAM consistently improves memory utilization and enables continual self-evolution of LLM agents.
authors: Yiming Xu, Qian Yang, Zihan Chen, Yuefei Wu, Wenhan Zeng, Bin Shi, Bo Dong
bullets: Existing memory valuation based on retrieval success can miss context dependence and uncertainty from limited evidence.
BEAM evaluates each memory through a parameterized cognitive inference process conditioned on the current task.
Execution feedback serves as empirical evidence to continuously calibrate memory-value beliefs.
Experiments on reasoning and code-generation benchmarks show improved memory utilization and continual agent self-evolution.
papers.selection_reason: Bayesian memory valuation for self-evolving LLM agents; directly fits agent memory and continual adaptation.
papers.title: Memory as Belief: Bayesian Evolution of Memory for Self-Evolving LLM Agents
papers.tldr: BEAM models memory usefulness as a context-dependent Bayesian belief that updates from task feedback, improving continual self-evolution in LLM agents.

papers.abstract: Large language models need effective ways to acquire and use external knowledge beyond what they retain from pretraining. Continued pretraining risks catastrophic forgetting, while retrieval at inference time can add substantial overhead. External parametric memory avoids online retrieval, but constructing its training data requires extensive offline search, and output-level interpolation provides only shallow fusion. We introduce Deep Fusion Memory (DFM), a parametric memory architecture that reduces this construction workload and incorporates learned memory into intermediate hidden states. A causal memory predictor learns to generate memory from the preceding context, using retrieved chunk embeddings from the corpus as supervision. The predicted memory is shared across tokens within each chunk and fused into their hidden states through gated cross-attention. Memory prediction and fusion are trained end to end with the backbone frozen, and inference requires no explicit retrieval. Compared with existing parametric memory approaches, which often construct token-level memory targets, DFM requires $32\times$ fewer retrieval queries and $2048\times$ fewer retrieved items to construct its training data. Across six QA tasks, DFM performs better over the strongest baseline by 12.71% on Mistral-7B-v0.3 and 11.19% on Qwen3-8B-Base. Beyond QA, domain adaptation yields average gains of 6.51 and 4.38 points over Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base, respectively.
authors: Rubin Wei, Siyuan Sun, Hao Sun, Yuliang Liu, Xiang Shi, Jiarui Wang, Junming Zhang, Zhouhan Lin
bullets: Addresses the cost of offline retrieval for parametric memory and the limited fusion of output-level methods.
Predicts chunk-level memory from preceding context, using retrieved chunk embeddings as supervision.
Fuses predicted memory into intermediate hidden states through gated cross-attention shared across chunk tokens.
Trains the memory module end to end while keeping the backbone frozen; inference requires no explicit retrieval.
Reports improvements across six QA tasks and gains for domain adaptation, alongside 32× fewer queries and 2048× fewer retrieved items for training-data construction.
papers.selection_reason: Chunk-level parametric memory for LLMs with gated cross-attention; directly fits LLM memory.
papers.title: Deep Fusion Memory: A Chunk-Level Parametric Memory for Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Deep Fusion Memory adds chunk-level learned external knowledge directly into LLM hidden states, reducing memory-construction cost while improving QA and domain adaptation without inference-time retrieval.

papers.abstract: An agent can retain information before receiving a future question and later retrieve evidence from an archive. Evaluating this arrangement requires accounting for both retained information and the width of each retrieval response. Decision-tree capacity bounds describe individual sets of distinguishable records, but a memory writer must encode every possible record before the query is known. We study fixed-length retention beside an immutable binary archive, with a worst-case limit on raw bit or word reads. We characterize feasible one-bit-read memory cells and construct encoders that partition the complete record space. Supporting pairwise exclusive disjunction and conjunction with one bit read is equivalent to supporting every Boolean query. For multiple reads, we combine explicit encoders with decision-tree counting and an entropy converse. The word-read bounds differ by at most two retained bits when the read budget is at most half the archive length. Under an explicit condition on word width and archive length, raw-word caching attains the exact optimum among all writers. A related condition preserves this optimum under positive average error. Exhaustive checks validate the implementations. In a matched dialogue-agent study, a categorical sufficient statistic preserves source decisions with less storage and lower decoding latency than the universal encoder. A catalogue-specific index reduces private state further and requires additional shared storage. The results characterize how response width and future query structure determine retention requirements.
bullets: Studies fixed-length retention paired with an immutable archive under worst-case read limits.
Characterizes one-bit-read memory cells and gives encoders covering all possible records.
Shows that supporting pairwise exclusive disjunction and conjunction with one bit read is equivalent to supporting every Boolean query.
For multiple reads, combines explicit encoders, decision-tree counting, and entropy-based lower bounds; word-read bounds are nearly tight.
Dialogue-agent experiments show that task-specific sufficient statistics or indexes can reduce private storage and decoding latency, with trade-offs in shared storage.
papers.selection_reason: Information-theoretic framework for pre-query retention and bounded retrieval in agents, relevant to memory mechanisms for language/agent systems.
papers.title: Pre-Query Retention with Bounded Bit and Word Retrieval
papers.tldr: The paper characterizes how much pre-query memory is needed to answer future Boolean queries when retrieval from a binary archive is limited to a bounded number of bits or words.

papers.abstract: Model--harness co-evolution has emerged as a prominent paradigm for recursive self-improving (RSI) agents, jointly evolving their execution scaffolds and intrinsic capabilities. We study the persistent yet often overlooked brain--body mismatch problem in this paradigm, where an evolving harness (body) demands behaviors its model (brain) has not learned or restricts capabilities it already possesses. We introduce CoEvo-RSI, a RSI framework that advances model--harness co-evolution through agent-driven, bidirectional historical inheritance. Drawing on a shared evolutionary archive and execution feedback, a meta-agent coordinates harness development from historical designs with model checkpoint selection or merging and subsequent adaptation under the selected harness, aligning inherited capabilities with evolving execution requirements to reduce brain--body mismatch. Using only supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on its own rejection-sampled trajectories, CoEvo-RSI makes Qwen3.5-9B competitive with larger models across diverse vertical applications, including multi-agent failure attribution, role-aware text-to-SQL, and smart-home instruction following. It surpasses DeepSeek-V4-Pro on TraceElephant (+14.16 agent accuracy) and GLM-5.3 on HomeBench VM (+4.90 success rate), underscoring the need for brain--body alignment and the potential of bidirectional historical inheritance to advance agent co-evolution.
authors: Jiaqi Su, Guibin Zhang, Jie-Jing Shao, Cong Pang, Tiankuo Yao, Ivor Tsang, Haiyan Yin, Shuicheng Yan
bullets: Addresses brain–body mismatch: harnesses may demand unlearned behaviors or constrain existing model capabilities.
Uses a shared evolutionary archive, execution feedback, and a meta-agent to coordinate harness evolution with model checkpoint selection or merging.
Adapts selected models under evolving harnesses using only supervised fine-tuning on self-generated rejection-sampled trajectories.
Reports competitiveness with larger models across multi-agent failure attribution, role-aware text-to-SQL, and smart-home instruction following.
Exceeds cited baselines on TraceElephant and HomeBench VM, supporting the importance of brain–body alignment.
papers.selection_reason: Model-harness co-evolution with shared evolutionary archive and checkpoint adaptation for recursive self-improvement; relevant to continual adaptation and agent memory.
papers.title: CoEvo-RSI: When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?
papers.tldr: CoEvo-RSI aligns evolving agent harnesses with model capabilities through bidirectional historical inheritance, enabling a smaller model to perform competitively across diverse tasks.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents face a fundamental allocation problem as interaction histories grow: which information to retain, how much context to devote to it, and at what granularity. Existing memory mechanisms largely focus on relevance, retrieval, or compression, leaving this allocation trade-off implicit. We introduce MemPrice, which treats active context as a shared resource and dynamically allocates it across memories and representation levels. MemPrice turns accumulated memory pressure into an adaptive price on context, encouraging detail only when its estimated retention value justifies the additional footprint. This pressure persists across memory refreshes, allowing the contents of memory to evolve while preserving long-run control over context usage. We show that irreversible compression can force linear worst-case regret against hindsight following its own memory trajectory, and introduce a same-state benchmark to evaluate allocation on MemPrice's realized memory states. MemPrice enforces the hard context budget at every round and regulates long-run occupancy through adaptive pricing, without prior knowledge of the interaction horizon. Under priced-frontier regularity, its average allocation-regret bound against this benchmark vanishes when accumulated estimation error is sublinear. We evaluate the framework under matched memory budgets on LongMemEval, LoCoMo, AppWorld, and WebShop across three foundation models, spanning both query-blind memory construction and goal-directed agent context management.
authors: Yiming Zong, Shiyuan Piao, Jiashuo Jiang, Fugee Tsung
bullets: Addresses the growing-context trade-off between retaining information, representation granularity, and context usage.
Converts accumulated memory pressure into a price that favors additional detail only when its estimated retention value warrants the cost.
Maintains pressure across memory refreshes, enabling evolving memories while enforcing a hard context budget each round.
Introduces a same-state benchmark and shows vanishing average allocation regret under priced-frontier regularity and sublinear cumulative estimation error.
Evaluates matched-budget performance on LongMemEval, LoCoMo, AppWorld, and WebShop with three foundation models.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive pricing for memory allocation in long-horizon LLM agents; fits LLM memory and efficient context management.
papers.title: MemPrice: Online Memory Allocation via Adaptive Pricing for Long-Horizon Agents
papers.tldr: MemPrice dynamically allocates an agent’s limited context among memories and detail levels using adaptive pricing, providing long-run budget control without knowing the interaction horizon.

papers.abstract: Radio frequency fingerprinting (RFF) models can achieve accuracy under source domain conditions but become unreliable when the receiver, distance, collection day, or environment changes. Incorrect predictions in unseen domains may receive high softmax confidence, making confidence thresholding insufficient for trustworthy deployment. We propose TrustAgent-RFF, a prediction level reliability framework for RFF that operates with a frozen in-phase and quadrature (I/Q) classifier without target domain labels. For each device prediction, the framework acquires radio frequency evidence: counterfactual stability, prototype consistency, acquisition domain similarity, and signal quality. A source calibrated trust estimator combines these diagnostics with classifier confidence, prediction margin, and evidence availability indicators. Source derived lower tail penalties and cross module interactions reduce trust when diagnostic signals indicate weak support. A large language model (LLM) based planner adaptively selects the next diagnostic action based on evidence, trust state, action costs, and remaining budget. A deterministic source calibrated decision layer updates the prediction state as Accept, Reject, or Defer. Experiments across five RFF datasets and classifier backbones reveal an average source to target accuracy drop of 38.7% and show that many incorrect target domain predictions remain highly confident.
authors: Chuan Liu, Tianya Zhao, Xuyu Wang
bullets: Targets overconfident RFF errors when receivers, distances, collection days, or environments change.
Uses a frozen I/Q classifier and requires no target-domain labels.
Combines counterfactual stability, prototype consistency, domain similarity, signal quality, confidence, and prediction margin.
An LLM planner selects diagnostic actions under evidence, trust, cost, and budget constraints.
Evaluations across five datasets and classifier backbones show a 38.7% average source-to-target accuracy drop and frequent high-confidence target errors.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes TrustAgent-RFF, an agentic framework for reliable RF fingerprinting under domain shift. It uses an LLM planner to adapt to new domains, fitting Test-Time Learning and LLM Memory.
papers.title: TrustAgent-RFF: Agentic Diagnostic Planning for Reliable RF Fingerprinting under Domain Shift
papers.tldr: TrustAgent-RFF improves the reliability of RF fingerprinting under domain shift by adaptively gathering diagnostic evidence and deciding whether to accept, reject, or defer predictions.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented language models increasingly use multi-step search to solve knowledge-intensive tasks, yet existing systems typically expose retrieval through fixed pipelines or collections of atomic tools. We introduce Retrieval Program Learning (RPL), a programmable search framework that allows a policy to compose search primitives into executable programs with local state and control flow. This enables adaptive search that can retrieve broadly, process intermediate results, and selectively construct model context without tying retrieval breadth to context consumption. However, the resulting flexibility creates a difficult exploration problem: useful programs may require several coordinated decisions, while reinforcement learning often supplies only sparse feedback. To address this challenge, we propose program mutation, a grammar-constrained and execution-verified procedure that generates local variants of suboptimal programs sampled during RL, converts them into training trajectories, and distills them back into the policy. We evaluate RPL on open-domain question answering and corpus-level reasoning tasks, comparing it with a range of retrieval and reasoning baselines. RPL consistently improves open-domain QA performance across model sizes and in- and out-of-domain benchmarks, with particularly large gains on multi-hop tasks. Notably, a 4B model trained with RPL outperforms all 8B model baselines. On corpus-level reasoning, RPL achieves the highest answer F1 and document-coverage F1 for both model sizes while substantially reducing context consumption and retrieval turns. Our results show that programmable search expands the retrieval strategies that agents can learn, while program mutation provides an effective mechanism for exploring useful program structures beyond direct on-policy sampling.
authors: Kyuyoung Kim, Zilin Xiao, Zhiyuan Wang, Avinash Atreya, Ke Yang, Jinwoo Shin, Kecheng Hao
bullets: Problem: Fixed retrieval pipelines and atomic tools limit adaptive, multi-step search, while sparse RL feedback makes useful search programs difficult to discover.

Method: A policy composes search primitives into executable programs with local state and control flow; grammar-constrained, execution-verified mutations generate useful training trajectories from suboptimal programs.
Results: RPL consistently improves open-domain QA across model sizes and in- and out-of-domain benchmarks, with especially large gains on multi-hop tasks.

Results: A 4B RPL-trained model outperforms all evaluated 8B baselines; on corpus-level reasoning, RPL achieves the best answer and document-coverage F1 while using less context and fewer retrieval turns.
Contribution: A programmable search framework and program-mutation procedure that expands the retrieval strategies agents can learn beyond direct on-policy exploration.
papers.selection_reason: Programmable retrieval programs for RAG; relevant to external memory and context construction for LLMs.
papers.title: Learning to Program Retrievals: Composing Search Primitives via Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: Retrieval Program Learning uses reinforcement learning and verified program mutations to teach language models adaptive, multi-step search strategies that improve accuracy while reducing context use and retrieval turns.

papers.abstract: Explicit memory systems transform conversation history into persistent representations intended to improve future access, often at substantial construction cost. Yet it remains unclear whether this added complexity yields better answer accuracy than retrieving directly from raw history. This study compares six state-of-the-art explicit memory systems with raw-history RAG on LongMemEval-S and BEAM-100K under original and controlled retrieval settings. We find only localized gains for particular question types and tight run-time context budgets, with no consistent advantage over strong raw-history RAG baselines. Oracle retrieval shows that some systems fail to preserve answer-supporting information during explicit memory construction, while others preserve it but fail to retrieve it effectively, despite construction costs reaching hours per conversation. Our findings suggest that while many existing memory systems for AI agents emphasize increasingly elaborate explicit memory construction, they are often evaluated without strong controlled comparisons to raw-history RAG and may underemphasize retrieval. Retrieval remains a major bottleneck when useful information is preserved, suggesting that improving access to existing information may be at least as important as constructing richer explicit memory.
authors: Yongjie Zhou, Shuai Wang, Bevan Koopman, Guido Zuccon
bullets: Compares six explicit memory systems with raw-history RAG on LongMemEval-S and BEAM-100K under original and controlled settings.
Finds no consistent accuracy advantage for explicit memory, except for some question types and tight context budgets.
Oracle retrieval reveals two failure modes: losing answer-supporting information during construction or failing to retrieve preserved information.
Some systems require hours of construction per conversation, highlighting substantial overhead.
Results suggest improving retrieval may be as important as building richer persistent memories.
papers.selection_reason: Provides a controlled comparison of explicit memory systems against raw-history RAG, finding that retrieval efficiency often outweighs the benefits of complex memory construction.
papers.title: Do Conversational Agents Need Explicit Memory? A Controlled Comparison with Raw-History Retrieval
papers.tldr: Explicit memory systems offer only localized benefits over strong raw-history retrieval, while costly construction and retrieval failures limit their overall advantage.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly use skills as a lightweight way to acquire task-specific knowledge. Recent work enables skills to evolve from task trajectories. However, these methods often lack systematic management of evolved skills, making it difficult for agents to reuse and accumulate skills across domains, thus limiting performance on subsequent tasks.To reliably accumulate, reuse, and maintain useful skills across tasks, we present SELM (Self-Evolving Library Management), a framework that formulates skill evolution as library-level management. SELM jointly manages skill retrieval, updating, and lifecycle by maintaining skill confidence and utility signals. It introduces utility-aware retrieval to select useful skills, a Map-Reduce framework to generate targeted updates from task-specific experience, and lifecycle controls to retain or remove skills based on their effectiveness. These mechanisms enable the skill library to continuously accumulate useful experience while preserving and pruning skills across tasks, improving agent performance on complex tasks across diverse domains. We evaluate SELM on four agent benchmarks covering diverse tasks and execution environments, and SELM consistently outperforms in most settings.
authors: Mengxi Hu, Yuxuan Hu, Jinbo Su, Ke Wang, Honghao Shi, Wenli Wu, Cuiping Li, Hong Chen, Jing Zhang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of accumulating and reusing evolved skills across domains.
Uses confidence- and utility-aware retrieval to select useful skills.
Applies Map-Reduce updates to incorporate targeted experience from task trajectories.
Manages skill lifecycles by retaining effective skills and removing ineffective ones.
Evaluated on four diverse agent benchmarks, with consistent improvements in most settings.
papers.selection_reason: The paper introduces SELM, a framework for managing a self-evolving library of skills for LLM agents. This directly addresses the need for persistent external memory mechanisms to store and retrieve information (skills) beyond the current context, fitting the 'LLM Memory' subtopic.
papers.title: Selm: Self-Evolving Library Management for Multi-Skill Agent Optimization
papers.tldr: SELM improves multi-skill LLM agents by systematically retrieving, updating, retaining, and pruning skills across tasks.

papers.abstract: In long-term interactions with large language model (LLM) agents, users reveal habits through their choices and actions. These habits capture implicit user information that agents must infer across conversations. However, individual observations may provide only partial evidence about a habit or when it applies. Retaining past interactions alone does not ensure that agents can infer habits and apply them appropriately. We introduce HABIT-Bench to evaluate how well agent memory systems infer habits from weak evidence and apply them to later requests. We construct synthetic user histories from task-oriented dialogue data and controlled habit graphs. The histories span hundreds of sessions across food, finance, software, and travel. Four-choice tasks assess agents' ability to infer user habits and apply them appropriately. They include temporary exceptions, changes in habits, and suggestions that users have not accepted. Sampled tasks undergo independent human review. We evaluate eight memory methods with Qwen3-235B-A22B and GLM-5.3-Flash. The best-performing memory method achieves 33.61\% macro accuracy across the four domains. Performance remains limited even when annotated evidence is supplied directly. These results expose a persistent gap between access to past interactions and the ability to infer and appropriately use user habits.
authors: Junming Zhang, Rubin Wei, Xu Cheng, Hao Sun, Ruoxi Cheng, Xiquan Wang, Peisong Wu, Mingsong Chen, Zhouhan Lin
bullets: Targets habit inference across partial evidence, exceptions, habit changes, and unaccepted suggestions.
Builds synthetic histories spanning hundreds of sessions in food, finance, software, and travel.
Uses four-choice tasks with human review to test habit inference and application.
Evaluates eight memory methods with Qwen3-235B-A22B and GLM-5.3-Flash.
The best method reaches 33.61% macro accuracy, and performance remains limited even with annotated evidence.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for habit induction in LLM agent memory; relevant to persistent memory evaluation.
papers.title: HABIT-Bench: Evaluating Habit Induction from Longitudinal Weak Evidence in Agent Memory
papers.tldr: HABIT-Bench evaluates whether agent memory systems can infer and appropriately apply user habits from weak, longitudinal evidence, revealing substantial limitations.

papers.abstract: Motivated by recursive self-improvement (RSI), we study how LLM agents can learn through external memory without updating model parameters. Extracting useful experience from a single attempt is difficult: flawed reasoning can produce success, while poor execution can obscure a sound strategy. Preserving its value over time is also difficult: our accumulation baseline without consolidation initially improves but eventually performs below a no-memory baseline. Our key idea is to compare attempts at the same task to identify reusable decisions and refine when they apply. We introduce Hippo, a memory framework inspired by selective hippocampal encoding and replay that learns from these comparisons when shortcomings are diagnosed. It compares the resulting experience with existing memory to merge overlaps and resolve conflicts through explicit applicability conditions. This allows prior guidance to be revised without storing every lesson as a separate entry. Experiments on SWE-bench Verified, WebArena, and Mind2Web show performance gains in all three settings and substantially fewer retained experiences than the accumulation baseline. The gains extend across the evaluated base models of varying capabilities, indicating that memory-based adaptation remains useful even for highly capable models.
authors: Yutong Song, Jiang Wu, Yuxuan Ren, Tony Qin, Baoyuan Wang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of extracting reliable lessons from flawed or mixed-quality attempts.
Uses selective hippocampal-style encoding and replay to diagnose shortcomings and compare attempts on the same task.
Merges overlapping memories and resolves conflicts with explicit applicability conditions instead of storing every lesson separately.
Improves performance on SWE-bench Verified, WebArena, and Mind2Web while retaining substantially fewer experiences than simple accumulation.
Benefits persist across base models with varying capabilities, including highly capable models.
papers.selection_reason: External-memory agent self-improvement via hippocampal replay; relevant to test-time adaptation and LLM memory.
papers.title: Hippo: Training-Free Agent Self-Evolution via Hippocampal Replay
papers.tldr: Hippo enables LLM agents to self-improve without parameter updates by comparing task attempts and consolidating reusable experience in memory.

papers.abstract: As multimodal agents accumulate experience, their long-term memories contain many similar observations of recurring scenes, actions, and entities. Answer quality depends on the evidence retrieved from these memories into the model's context. However, query-relevant memories may contain overlapping information, and a fixed retrieval depth may return too little or too much evidence for a given question. To address these challenges, we propose PACE-Mem, Prefix-Aware Complementary Evidence, which constructs a complementary evidence sequence and determines its length from the same selection trajectory. For structured memories, query-guided pooling combines records within each clip to obtain relevance scores and representations. Using these relevance scores and representations, maximal marginal relevance (MMR) selection balances query relevance against overlap with previously selected evidence. From the resulting score trajectory, a prefix-length selection algorithm determines retrieval depth by comparing length-normalized adjacent declines, accounting for both score changes and the amount of evidence accumulated. PACE-Mem is a training-free, plug-in retrieval method for clip-based agent memory systems, leaving memory construction and answer generation unchanged. Across three long-video benchmarks and two agent frameworks, PACE-Mem improves question-answering accuracy by an average of 1.6% over Adaptive-k, the strongest baseline at comparable mean retrieval depths. Further analysis reveals that jointly adding and removing evidence is associated with larger net accuracy gains than either change alone.
authors: Shidu Ren, Rong-cheng Tu, Hang Zhou, Xiao Luo
bullets: Addresses redundant memories and the mismatch between fixed retrieval depth and question-specific evidence needs.
Uses query-guided pooling and maximal marginal relevance (MMR) to build a complementary evidence sequence.
Selects retrieval depth from the same MMR score trajectory using length-normalized adjacent score declines.
Training-free and plug-in: it leaves memory construction and answer generation unchanged.
Improves QA accuracy by an average of 1.6% over Adaptive-k across three long-video benchmarks and two agent frameworks.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free complementary evidence retrieval for multimodal agent memory; directly fits agent memory and memory retrieval.
papers.title: PACE-Mem: Prefix-Aware Complementary Evidence for Multimodal Agents
papers.tldr: PACE-Mem improves multimodal-agent memory retrieval by selecting diverse, query-relevant evidence and adaptively determining how much to retrieve.

papers.abstract: To support sustained interactions and personalized assistance, agents use long-term memory to retain and combine user information across sessions. Reusing such memories can lead an agent to state a sensitive relation while completing an ordinary task that does not require it. The relation to protect and the combination of clues that reveal it may remain hidden at memory write time, when later records and tasks are still unknown. In this paper, we introduce MemJoin, a privacy benchmark of 288 synthetic analysis cases in which the complete history entails a sensitive relation, but every individual session is insufficient. We evaluate six memory systems with the same answer-generating model, alongside full-history and no-history controls. Each system writes and updates memories in session order and later retrieves context for an ordinary task, while target annotations remain with the evaluator. We separately check which target attribute values appear in stored records and retrieved context, and whether the final answer states the complete, person-linked relation. In a separate paired test on a prespecified subset, removing shared identifiers and other connecting clues can change complete-relation output while all checked target attribute values remain visible. These findings show why checking attribute visibility alone is insufficient to evaluate what records from different sessions reveal together.
authors: Qishun Yang, Shu Yang, Difei Xu, Di Wang, Meng Ding
bullets: Evaluates privacy leakage when complete histories imply a sensitive relation but individual sessions do not.
Introduces 288 synthetic cases with hidden target annotations and compares six memory systems plus full-history and no-history controls.
Separately measures target-attribute visibility in stored/retrieved context and whether the final answer states the complete relation.
A paired test shows that removing shared identifiers or connecting clues can change relation disclosure even when target attributes remain visible.
Scope: synthetic cases focused on cross-session reconstruction during ordinary tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks long-term memory systems for LLM agents across sessions, directly addressing LLM memory and privacy.
papers.title: Can Agents Keep Secrets They Were Never Told? Benchmarking Latent Privacy Risks Across Sessions with MemJoin
papers.tldr: MemJoin benchmarks how long-term agent memory can combine harmless-looking cross-session clues to reveal sensitive, person-linked relations that no single session exposes.

papers.abstract: Reasoning models maintain information about the status of their reasoning process through in-context memory. Complex problems require larger context windows and memory requirements. In this scenario, context management without caching risks discarding useful information for reasoning. We propose RCMEM, an approach that extends context management with an external memory to maintain additional information without burdening the reasoning model with additional context. RCMEM significantly reduces computation time on problems that require repeated computation of intermediate steps, while achieving better performance on complex problems. We demonstrate our approach on a few mathematics problems using model sizes ranging from 0.4 to 25 million parameters, and GPT-2.
authors: Man-Ling Sung, William Hartmann, Jiangying Zhou
bullets: Addresses information loss and growing memory requirements in long, complex reasoning tasks.
Uses external memory to retain intermediate information without adding it to the model’s active context.
Reduces computation time for problems requiring repeated intermediate computations.
Improves performance on complex mathematics problems in experiments with small models and GPT-2.
Evaluation is limited to a few mathematics problems and the reported model sizes.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes external memory to extend context management for reasoning models, directly fitting LLM memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Reasoning with Context Management and External Memory
papers.tldr: RCMEM augments context management with external memory to preserve useful reasoning information while reducing context and computation demands.

papers.abstract: Does persistent memory accumulated from previous attempts help an LLM agent solve new problems, and does memory design affect that benefit? We study programmatic Chinese-character drawing across five agent conditions attempting the same 668 items. Accumulated memory produces modest aggregate gains despite substantial growth in the memory stores: free-form notes improve first-attempt success by 4.6 percentage points, while a design combining free-form memory with reusable code improves it by 2.8 points. The two designs do not differ significantly overall, but the code bank shows a suggestive advantage on later, harder items. A separate post-hoc comparison finds a much larger improvement when the code-bank agent receives privileged, target-specific structural supervision. The agent can therefore exploit highly informative structural guidance, although the privileged per-item information does not establish what could have been learned from experience alone. These results suggest that memory design may affect where accumulated experience becomes useful, even when its average benefit is modest.
bullets: The study tests five agent conditions on 668 programmatic Chinese-character drawing items.
Free-form notes raise first-attempt success by 4.6 percentage points; combining notes with reusable code raises it by 2.8 points.
The two memory designs show no significant overall difference, but the code bank may help more on later, harder items.
Privileged target-specific structural guidance yields a much larger improvement, but does not show what experience alone could teach.
Overall, memory provides modest average gains while influencing where accumulated experience is useful.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates the effect of persistent memory design (free-form notes vs. code banks) on an LLM agent's performance in a drawing task.
papers.title: Persistent Memory and Iterative Improvement in an LLM Agent for Chinese-Character Drawing
papers.tldr: Persistent memory modestly improves an LLM agent’s Chinese-character drawing, with memory design affecting which problems benefit most.

papers.abstract: LLM agents accumulate valuable task-specific information through their actions, observations, and environmental feedback during multi-turn task execution. When effectively used, this information can help agents refine subsequent decisions and improve task performance. However, the learning value of an interaction depends on its context and subsequent feedback, making it challenging to extract reliable, actionable lessons and revise them as the task unfolds. In this paper, we introduce ReTTT, which enables experience-driven self-adaptation through test-time training on lessons constructed and continually revised within an episode. ReTTT lets the agent reflect on interaction feedback, maintain the resulting lessons in an explicit memory, and learn from them by updating an episode-local LoRA adapter while keeping the backbone frozen. The adapted model then performs both subsequent actions and reflection, coupling policy adaptation with the construction of future learning experience. We evaluate ReTTT on ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and SWE-bench Lite using two model families. ReTTT outperforms trajectory-based test-time training across all six model--benchmark settings, improving task success by up to 12.14 percentage points. A frozen-reflection comparison further shows a 7.14-point benefit from adapting the reflection policy, while trajectory analysis illustrates how adapted reflection derives more task-specific guidance from failed attempts. These findings suggest that learning to reflect on its own behavior can boost agents' performance on long-horizon tasks.
authors: Kangcong Li, Hangfan Zhang, Shuyue Hu, Shengji Tang, Tao Chen
bullets: Addresses the challenge of extracting reliable, actionable lessons from context-dependent interaction feedback.
Maintains explicit, revisable experience-based memory and uses it for test-time training within each episode.
Updates an episode-local LoRA adapter while keeping the backbone frozen; the adapted model performs both actions and reflection.
Evaluated on ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and SWE-bench Lite across two model families, outperforming trajectory-based test-time training in all six settings.
Task success improves by up to 12.14 percentage points; adapting the reflection policy contributes an additional 7.14-point benefit versus frozen reflection.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time training with experience-based parametric memory for LLM agents; fits test-time learning and agent memory.
papers.title: ReTTT: Reflection-Driven Test-Time Training via Experience-Based Parametric Memory
papers.tldr: ReTTT improves long-horizon LLM-agent performance by continually reflecting on feedback and updating an episode-local LoRA adapter from revised lessons.

papers.abstract: Current agents remain largely stateless across tasks, limiting their ability to continually improve from prior interactions and making memory essential for long-horizon agentic behavior. Existing memory methods seek to reuse past experience, but most rely on a single memory representation (e.g., trajectories, reflections, skills, structured knowledge) whose effectiveness varies across task distributions. Rethinking this design space, we evaluate 13 memory methods and find that no single method generalizes across benchmarks, revealing the potential of managing heterogeneous memory providers. We formulate agent memory as a routing problem in which a memory agent decides which memory provider to retrieve from, whether to inject short-term memory, and which providers should store the resulting experience. Based on this perspective, we propose MemAgent, featuring a content-aware routing architecture and a training-data synthesis pipeline. The routing architecture combines content-aware probing before retrieval, short-term memory gating during execution, and selective multi-provider storage, while the training pipeline synthesizes phase-specific supervision for routing decisions. Across GAIA, WebWalkerQA, and xBench-DS, MemAgent improves average accuracy by 10.0% and outperforms every individual memory method across all three benchmarks. These gains come with less than 0.3% routing overhead and a 12% reduction in average task steps.
bullets: Evaluations of 13 memory methods show that no single approach generalizes across benchmarks.
MemAgent frames memory use as routing: selecting providers to retrieve from, gating short-term memory, and choosing where to store experience.
Its content-aware router uses pre-retrieval probing, execution-time gating, and selective multi-provider storage.
A training-data synthesis pipeline provides phase-specific supervision for routing decisions.
Across GAIA, WebWalkerQA, and xBench-DS, it raises average accuracy by 10.0%, with under 0.3% routing overhead and 12% fewer task steps.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a memory-routing agent that selects among heterogeneous memory providers for LLM agents, directly matching persistent and external agent-memory mechanisms.
papers.title: MemAgent: Learning to Manage Heterogeneous Memory Providers for LLM Agents
papers.tldr: MemAgent improves LLM-agent memory by learning to route across heterogeneous memory providers instead of relying on a single representation.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory enables language-model agents to personalize future interactions, but a finite memory bank cannot preserve every extracted fact. Existing memory gating policies are typically shared across users and therefore fail to account for user-specific patterns of future reuse. In this paper, we study memory gating at the fact level. We first propose a retrieval-based labeling strategy that labels each fact by whether it is later retrieved and incorporated into responses. We then formulate online memory gating as contextual apple tasting with delayed one-sided feedback, and propose Warm-Start UCB, which combines offline learning from existing data with online adaptation to the current user. Our theoretical analysis establishes a high-probability regret upper bound of $\tilde{O}(T\epsilon \wedge d\sqrt{T})$ when the delay window is at most $O(\sqrt{T})$, where $T$ is the total number of rounds, $\epsilon$ is the initialization error, $d$ is the dimension of the feature map, and $\tilde{O}(\cdot)$ hides constant and poly-logarithmic factors. The results of our experiment demonstrate that our method outperforms all baselines under different memory budgets and history lengths, establishing it as a promising personalized memory gating policy.
authors: Kaixuan Ji, Zixiang Chen, Wenting Zhao, Cheng Qian, Heng Wang, Weizhi Zhang, Jielin Qiu, Liangwei Yang, Quanquan Gu, Silvio Savarese, Shelby Heinecke, Huan Wang
bullets: Targets fact-level memory gating under finite memory capacity, where shared policies overlook user-specific reuse patterns.
Labels facts based on whether they are later retrieved and used in responses.
Models online gating as contextual apple tasting with delayed one-sided feedback.
Combines offline initialization with online adaptation to the current user through Warm-Start UCB.
Experiments report better performance than all baselines across memory budgets and history lengths.],
papers.selection_reason: Online personalized memory gating for language-model agents with delayed feedback and regret guarantees.
papers.title: Learning Personalized Memory Gating from Delayed One-Sided Feedback
papers.tldr: Warm-Start UCB personalizes which facts language-model agents retain by learning from delayed, one-sided evidence of future reuse.

papers.abstract: Optimizing product listings for generative search requires language agents not only to rewrite effectively but also to continually self-improve by retaining successful strategies across diverse categories. However, existing approaches often treat structured listings as free-form text, leaving effective strategies implicit in prompts, search trajectories, or rewritten outputs rather than accumulating them as a reusable agentic memory. To address this limitation, we introduce GLOBE, an agentic framework that drives continual self-improvement by storing optimization knowledge in an evolving handbook of explicit, field-scoped behaviors. In each episode, an Editor applies relevant behaviors and receives rank-based feedback, which a Reflector converts into behavior updates. Crucially for dependable execution in real-world settings, a Moderator removes redundant proposals, a Curator commits accepted changes, and consistently harmful behaviors are deactivated. This cycle transforms episodic feedback into a persistent, field-scoped optimization memory. Experiments show that structured behaviors outperform monolithic prompt optimization, while feedback-driven evolution and moderation further improve effectiveness and reduce downside risk. The learned behaviors also remain effective on unseen product categories, suggesting that agentic memory evolution supports interpretable and transferable product optimization.
authors: Hyunseo Kim, Suil Choe, Sukkyoung So, Daeyeon Yi
bullets: Addresses the limitation of treating structured product listings as free-form text with implicit, non-reusable strategies.
Uses an Editor, Reflector, Moderator, and Curator to apply, update, filter, and commit optimization behaviors.
Stores successful strategies in a persistent handbook while deactivating consistently harmful behaviors.
Experiments find structured, feedback-evolved behaviors improve effectiveness and reduce downside risk over monolithic prompt optimization.
Learned behaviors transfer to unseen product categories, supporting interpretable and reusable optimization.
papers.selection_reason: Evolving agentic memory for continual self-improvement; fits LLM memory and continual learning topics.
papers.title: GLOBE: Evolving Structured Agentic Memory for E-commerce Product Optimization in Generative Search
papers.tldr: GLOBE improves product listings for generative search by evolving an explicit, field-scoped memory of effective optimization behaviors from feedback.

papers.abstract: Long-term LLM assistants must repeatedly decide what prior context to expose and which model should answer as an interaction evolves. Existing memory systems and model routers usually make these decisions separately, although memory construction changes the evidence, distractors, and difficulty of the resulting input. We introduce MARS, a memory-aware routing framework that uses session state as a shared control interface between memory construction and model selection. A Query and Topic Manager (QTM) estimates compact decision-relevant state that guides a fixed state-conditioned memory policy and an online router, enabling each turn to receive an appropriate memory view and a suitable model under a quality-memory-cost trade-off. We evaluate MARS on RealMem and MultiChallenge with 16 system configurations each, covering long-history memory-driven interaction and bounded sessions with structured context interference. On RealMem, MARS preserves 98.2% of full-context GPT-4o's QA while using only 14.5% of its generation API cost, including both generation and controller calls for MARS, and achieves the strongest measured memory-recall and retrieval scores among compared systems. On MultiChallenge, MARS trails the strongest static system overall but approaches its performance at lower recorded cost on a mechanism-focused subset. Together, these results support a favorable quality-memory-cost trade-off for long-history, memory-dependent interaction.
authors: Minghan Wang, Jinhang Zuo, Zhongxiang Dai, Zhiyong Wang, Fang Kong
bullets: Addresses the problem that memory construction and model routing are typically optimized separately, despite affecting each other.
Uses a Query and Topic Manager to create compact session state for a fixed state-conditioned memory policy and an online model router.
Evaluated across RealMem and MultiChallenge with 16 system configurations per benchmark.
On RealMem, retains 98.2% of full-context GPT-4o QA performance at 14.5% of its generation API cost and achieves the strongest reported memory-recall and retrieval scores.
On MultiChallenge, it underperforms the strongest static system overall but approaches it at lower recorded cost on a mechanism-focused subset.
papers.selection_reason: Memory-aware routing for session-level LLM assistants; directly relevant to LLM memory and context management.
papers.title: MARS: Memory-Aware Routing for Session-Level LLM Assistants
papers.tldr: MARS jointly manages memory and model selection through shared session state, preserving near-full-context quality at substantially lower API cost on long-history interactions.

papers.abstract: Research groups that want a language model grounded in their own literature face a choice between hosted services that receive their unpublished work and self-hosted deployments that keep the data local but give the model no access to the corpus. Munin is an open-source framework for a self-hosted scientific assistant that indexes a group's corpus and its citation graph, and wraps whichever open-weight model the group can serve in an agent harness with specialised reading, search, and computation tools. We claim that the harness, rather than the specific model, is what makes the system useful on domain literature, and we ship the evaluation suite that tests this claim with the software. On 199 paired literature questions, the harness more than doubles the accuracy of the base model, from 0.387 to 0.874 (+0.487, 95% CI [0.407, 0.568]), while naive retrieve-then-answer scores below the unaided model on every backbone tested. Under the harness, roughly twice as many answer claims trace to a passage the model read itself as with fixed top-5 retrieval. When the source paper for a question is removed from the corpus, the system abstains on about nine in ten of the questions it had answered correctly on the Qwen backbones and eight in ten on gpt-oss-20b, and it produces no fabricated local citation across 300 fabricated references. The pattern holds on three backbones from two developers, including a 20-billion-parameter model that runs on a single consumer-grade GPU. With all outbound network access disabled, both Qwen backbones still exceed the published PaperQA2 accuracy. The evaluation suite runs as a single command, so an adopting group can re-run it on its own corpus and model.
authors: Markus Fischer, Jens Meiler, Matthias Elgeti
bullets: Indexes a research group’s literature and citation graph, then equips an open-weight model with reading, search, and computation tools.
On 199 paired questions, the harness increased accuracy from 0.387 to 0.874; naive retrieve-then-answer underperformed the unaided model.
Harness-generated answers more often traced claims to passages the model read directly than fixed top-5 retrieval.
The system commonly abstained when relevant source papers were removed and produced no fabricated local citations in 300 tests.
Evaluated across three backbones, including a 20B model on one consumer GPU; the suite is runnable on a group’s own corpus and model.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic framework for research groups that implements external memory via citation graph indexing.
papers.title: MuninAI: A Self-Hosted Agentic Framework for Independent Research Groups
papers.tldr: Munin is an open-source, self-hosted scientific assistant whose agentic tool harness substantially improves literature-question answering while keeping research data local.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent outputs that lack source support or conflict with local operational constraints. We introduce Self-Reflective Chain-of-Thought (SRCoT), a modular architecture that organizes generation as a closed Retrieve--Reflect--Revise loop. SRCoT separates environment state, persistent knowledge, accumulated experience, and short-term memory into provenance-labeled stores. BM25 retrieval supplies local context; subsequent passes expose intermediate drafts, missing-information markers, follow-up queries, and optional claim--evidence mappings. These artifacts inform retrieval, revision, clarification, or abstention decisions. We examine the architecture through qualitative, trace-based case studies in two fully synthetic settings: emergency medical services and Munich-Sim, an emergency-operations simulation. Local prototype runs on an Apple M4-family laptop with 128 GB memory illustrate source-labeled documentation, explicit gap marking, and structured dispatch-style outputs. The traces also reveal provenance-assignment errors, incomplete evidence coverage, and unsafe assumptions that remain possible despite prompting constraints. These cases demonstrate report-level inspectability and local execution, not comparative superiority, hallucination reduction, clinical validity, or operational safety. The architecture separates retrieval and control from the model interface, but behavior across different models remains to be evaluated. SRCoT is a research proof of concept requiring human review, with its principal contribution lying in an inspectable control procedure rather than a new model.
authors: Fabian Broszio, Michael Hoffmann, Adrian Paschke
bullets: Addresses unsupported or operationally conflicting LLM outputs.
Separates environment state, persistent knowledge, experience, and short-term memory into provenance-labeled stores.
Uses BM25 retrieval and reflective passes to identify gaps, generate follow-up queries, map claims to evidence, and choose revision, clarification, or abstention.
Qualitative trace-based case studies in synthetic emergency-services settings show inspectable source labeling, gap marking, and structured outputs.
Traces still reveal provenance errors, incomplete evidence, and unsafe assumptions; comparative effectiveness and safety remain unevaluated.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes an LLM generation architecture with persistent knowledge, accumulated experience, and short-term memory stores, directly relevant to LLM memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Self-Reflective Chain-of-Thought (SRCoT): Evidence-Based Text Generation via a Closed-Loop Retrieve--Reflect--Revise Pipeline on Edge LLMs
papers.tldr: SRCoT is a local, inspectable Retrieve–Reflect–Revise pipeline that uses provenance-labeled evidence to guide LLM generation, while still requiring human review.

papers.abstract: Current Chain-of-Thought (CoT) verification methods detect reasoning faithfulness from model outputs or static activations, but are limited in explaining how unfaithfulness develops during generation. We introduce VERITAS to verbalise the model's computation: how different reasoning anchors emerge, transfer across layers, and surface in the output. VERITAS adopts the layer-wise Jacobian projection to produce a verbalised account of the model's internal reasoning evolution at each generated CoT token. By training a classifier on the extracted features along the traces, we show that these structured features provide insightful perspectives on how and where reasoning diverges toward unfaithfulness. Experiments on four datasets from FaithCoT-Bench and BonaFide show that VERITAS achieves a significant performance gain over LLM-as-Judge, with a 28.4% gain in balanced accuracy, and an average improvement of 16.0% over activation probing. Further analysis shows VERITAS can be generalised to different datasets and model architectures. Our work shows that verbalising model computation provides a richer and more interpretable lens on CoT faithfulness, moving beyond detection toward a mechanistic understanding of how reasoning fails.
authors: Yujing Wang, Yulan He, Wenya Wang, Hanqi Yan
bullets: Addresses the limited interpretability of CoT faithfulness methods based on outputs or static activations.
Uses layer-wise Jacobian projections to trace reasoning anchors, their layer-to-layer transfer, and their emergence in generated tokens.
Trains a classifier on structured features extracted from these computation traces.
Across four FaithCoT-Bench and BonaFide datasets, improves balanced accuracy by 28.4% over LLM-as-Judge and 16.0% on average over activation probing.
Generalises across datasets and model architectures, supporting mechanistic analysis of reasoning failures.
papers.selection_reason: Mechanistic analysis of Chain-of-Thought reasoning using layer-wise Jacobian projection to verbalize internal computation.
papers.title: Verbalising Model's Computation for Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness Detection
papers.tldr: VERITAS verbalises how internal reasoning evolves across layers and tokens to detect and interpret unfaithful chain-of-thought reasoning.

papers.abstract: LLM-agent memory selection often uses retrieval rankings based on record relevance or individual influence. Such rankings cannot identify sufficient subsets under redundant or jointly necessary evidence. We study per-decision memory sufficiency: selecting a small subset that preserves full-memory behavior. To separate search error from model error, we introduce JointCoreBench, a benchmark with nine interaction families, six workflow domains, natural-language decisions, and exact sufficient-set oracles, and JointCore, a relevance cost-ordered group-deletion baseline that tests blocks before individual records. On 6,912 exact conditions, cost-ordered JointCore recovers a minimum-cost sufficient set in 100.0% of cases, reduces subset evaluations from 30.00 to 11.13 (62.9%), and achieves 87.8% active-memory savings. Across four 12B-70B model families and 432 tasks per model, its unweighted mean is 10.28 versus 16.00 model queries and 50.6% versus 43.1% minimum-cost recovery relative to cost aware singleton deletion. Both methods preserve full-memory behavior under the deterministic primary interface. Tests with physical deletion, UNKNOWN masks, PENDING sentinels, counterfactual values, and alternative labels identify interface dependent behavior. JointCore is an efficient benchmark baseline; the study does not establish deployment-ready memory compression.
bullets: Marginal relevance and individual influence miss redundant or jointly necessary evidence needed for per-decision memory sufficiency.
JointCoreBench provides exact sufficient-set oracles across nine interaction families, six workflow domains, and 6,912 exact conditions.
JointCore tests relevance-ordered blocks before individual records, recovering minimum-cost sufficient sets in 100.0% of benchmark cases.
It reduces subset evaluations by 62.9% and achieves 87.8% active-memory savings on the benchmark.
Across four model families, JointCore averages 10.28 queries and 50.6% minimum-cost recovery, but results depend on the memory interface and do not establish deployment readiness.
papers.selection_reason: Interaction-aware memory selection for LLM agents directly addresses persistent LLM memory beyond current context.
papers.title: Beyond Marginal Influence: Interaction-Aware Memory Selection for LLM Agents
papers.tldr: JointCore efficiently selects small, interaction-aware memory subsets that preserve an LLM agent’s full-memory decisions, while revealing interface-dependent behavior and deployment limitations.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on persistent memory to support long-term reasoning and personalized interactions. However, information collected from external sources can introduce security risks when untrusted claims (i.e., atomic statements) are later treated as authorized preferences, policies, or permissions. Existing defenses typically rely on content-based filtering or coarse-grained provenance tracking, which either fail to prevent unauthorized memory use or block legitimate information, sacrificing memory utility. To address these limitations, we propose SAFE-Mem, a fine-grained memory governance framework that improves security while preserving legitimate memory use. First, SAFE-Mem annotates each claim with three governance labels (i.e., kind, authority, and scope) to capture its provenance and permitted use. Second, governance-aware retrieval matches query requirements with claim permissions to block unauthorized influence while retaining legitimate information. Third, a governance-enabled memory graph connects source sentences, claims, and entities to support provenance tracking and efficient retrieval. Across four LLM backbones on MPBench and LoCoMo, SAFE-Mem attains the lowest attack success among defenses that retain legitimate memory, at least 77% below the strongest of them, and the highest answer accuracy of all evaluated defenses, improving it by up to 15%. The code is available at https://github.com/LVenum/SAFE-Mem.
authors: Haoming Li, Dingyi Kang, Xu Hu, Jinxin Yang, Zhu Xu, Chenru Wang, Yi Ge, Miao Yin, Guanpeng Li, Feng Chen, Bingzhe Li
bullets: Addresses unauthorized use of untrusted claims as preferences, policies, or permissions in agent memory.
Annotates claims with kind, authority, and scope governance labels.
Uses governance-aware retrieval to match query requirements with claim permissions.
Builds a memory graph linking source sentences, claims, and entities for provenance tracking and efficient retrieval.
Across four LLM backbones on MPBench and LoCoMo, it reports the lowest attack success among defenses retaining legitimate memory and the highest answer accuracy, improving accuracy by up to 15%.
papers.selection_reason: Secure persistent agentic memory with governance-aware retrieval; fits LLM memory.
papers.title: SAFE-Mem: Secure Agentic Memory with Fine-Grained Authority and Governance-Aware Retrieval
papers.tldr: SAFE-Mem secures persistent LLM-agent memory by enforcing fine-grained, provenance-aware permissions during retrieval while preserving useful information.

papers.abstract: Reusing a Transformer block across depth increases computation without replicating its parameters, but successive passes have no dedicated state through which positions can exchange compact summaries of their causal prefix. We introduce the causal latent workspace Transformer: an anchored, four-round shared-depth architecture in which each position writes gated vectors into prefix-specific latent slots and retrieves a content-addressed summary before the next shared block application. This path complements causal self-attention while the original input embedding remains accessible at every round. Across three byte-level corpora, three seeds, and two matched parameter budgets, the proposed model achieves the best mean held-out perplexity in five of six settings against five Transformer controls. At 101.71M parameters it leads on WikiText-103 raw, enwik8, and TinyStories, reaching perplexities 2.7820, 2.7843, and 1.6823; these improve upon the strongest non-workspace control on each corpus by 1.06%, 0.73%, and 1.01%. All nine seed-labelled comparisons at this budget favor the workspace. At 0.918M parameters it leads on WikiText-103 and TinyStories, whereas a conditioned loop is stronger on enwik8. Architectural ablations show that adding the workspace improves upon the anchored loop in all six settings and support refreshing its causal summaries at each round. Together, these results identify a causal, content-addressable prefix workspace as an effective structural augmentation of looped Transformers.
bullets: Addresses the lack of dedicated state for causal prefix information in parameter-shared Transformer loops.
Uses an anchored four-round architecture with gated writes to causal latent slots and content-addressed retrieval before each shared block pass.
The workspace achieves the best mean held-out perplexity in five of six settings across three byte-level corpora and two parameter budgets.
At 101.71M parameters, it leads on WikiText-103 raw, enwik8, and TinyStories; at 0.918M, it leads on WikiText-103 and TinyStories.
Ablations show consistent gains over the anchored loop and support refreshing causal summaries each round; a conditioned loop remains stronger on small-budget enwik8.
papers.selection_reason: Looped Transformer architecture with causal latent workspace memory; fits LLM architecture and memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Causal Latent Workspaces for Looped Transformers
papers.tldr: A causal latent workspace improves shared-depth looped Transformers by letting positions exchange compact, prefix-specific summaries across repeated block applications.

papers.abstract: As assistants move from reactive answering toward proactive intervention, memory changes role: it no longer only supplies the answer to a query, it determines whether and when to speak at all. Prior work in this setting hands the system the relevant fact in context; we study the regime that makes the problem hard, where the evidence justifying an intervention must be mined from a long-horizon personal memory. We introduce ProPerMem, a benchmark for memory-driven proactive assistance (MPA), pairing egocentric video with year-long, distractor-rich user memories (~618K tokens on average), human-verified trigger windows, and a protocol that scores content and timing jointly. Every baseline we evaluate performs poorly (at most 15%), including frontier models given summarized or retrieval-augmented memory.
