A controlled study explains why: with oracle evidence delivered inside the trigger window GPT-5.3-Chat reaches 96%; letting it choose the timing drops it to 38%, and replacing oracle evidence with retrieval drops it to 15%. Content and timing are separately necessary, and missing either is catastrophic. Guided by this, we build ProPerAgent (Proactive Personalized Agent) with a plug-and-play harness that surfaces memory from a graph-organized store and gates it down to what is worth interrupting for, plus a lightweight RL stage that curbs early and repeated firing. Without any training, ProPerAgent lifts strict accuracy from below 10% to 37.5% on Qwen3.8-27B and 38% on GPT-5.3-Chat; RL post-training reaches 42.4%.
authors: Shenglai Zeng, Xiao Yang, Tiffany Ma, Xinyuan Zhang, Nanshu Wang, Deren Lei, Kai Sun, Xilun Chen, Tammy Stark, Xianhui Zhu, Yuetai Li, Rulin Shao, Tianxin Wei, Rakesh Wanga, Anuj Kumar, Jiliang Tang, Wen-tau Yih, Xin Luna Dong
bullets: Introduces ProPerMem, a benchmark combining egocentric video, year-long distractor-rich memories, verified trigger windows, and joint content-timing evaluation.
Shows that both evidence retrieval and intervention timing are essential: performance collapses when either is not provided by an oracle.
Presents ProPerAgent, which uses graph-organized memory retrieval and interruption gating, followed by lightweight reinforcement learning to reduce premature and repeated interventions.
Improves strict accuracy from below 10% to 37.5–38% without training, and to 42.4% after RL post-training.
Scope: evaluated results remain substantially below oracle-evidence performance, highlighting the difficulty of long-horizon memory retrieval and timing.
papers.selection_reason: Memory-driven proactive assistance with long-horizon personal memory and egocentric video, fitting LLM/agent memory.
papers.title: ProPerAgent: Toward Memory-Driven Proactive Assistance
papers.tldr: ProPerAgent enables memory-driven proactive assistance by jointly retrieving the right personal evidence and deciding when an intervention is worth making.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon GUI agents rely on visual history to maintain task states, but retaining historical screenshots increases visual-token usage and inference costs, while textual summaries can discard critical state information, undermining long-horizon reliability. We propose ECHOES, which leverages training-time privileged information to guide textual history compression and strengthen long-horizon reasoning. Specifically, ECHOES adopts a Compression-Think-Action (CTA) format to recursively update a textual history state and reason. The same model, given privileged multi-image inputs, serves as a teacher that provides dense token-level on-policy distillation on student-generated CTA rollouts. Our Perception-Memory Fidelity (PMF) Gap-guided OPD-RL framework dynamically balances privileged distillation and task-reward optimization, with periodic teacher updates supporting continued improvement. We further introduce ECHOESBMK, a fine-grained diagnostic benchmark derived from real GUI agent failure trajectories to jointly evaluate visual perception and cross-modal state retention. Experiments on four GUI benchmarks and ECHOESBMK demonstrate substantial gains in task performance and memory fidelity. Without retaining historical screenshots at deployment, ECHOES achieves competitive performance with a favorable performance-inference-cost trade-off and exhibits positive zero-shot transfer to unseen visual planning tasks.
authors: Tengda Guo (Tsinghua University), Jiawang Hu (StepFun), Yifei Tao (Nanyang Technological University), Yin Wang (StepFun), Haotian Hu (Zhejiang Leapmotor Technology Co., Ltd), Fanyi Wang (Honor), Liujuan Tang (StepFun)
bullets: Addresses the tension between retaining costly historical screenshots and losing critical information through textual summaries.
Uses a recursive Compression-Think-Action format to update textual history and guide reasoning.
Applies privileged multi-image teacher guidance through token-level on-policy distillation, balanced with task rewards by PMF Gap-guided OPD-RL.
Introduces ECHOESBMK, a diagnostic benchmark for visual perception and cross-modal state retention based on GUI failure trajectories.
Shows gains across four GUI benchmarks and ECHOESBMK, with favorable performance–inference-cost trade-offs and zero-shot transfer to unseen visual planning tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes recursive textual history compression and memory-fidelity distillation for GUI agents, fitting persistent agent memory mechanisms.
papers.title: ECHOES: Seeing Beyond the Current Image via Recursive History Compression and Privileged On-Policy Distillation
papers.tldr: ECHOES enables long-horizon GUI agents to compress visual history into text while preserving task-relevant state, reducing inference costs without retaining screenshots at deployment.

papers.abstract: Can gradient-based training learn the rank needed to store and compose associations in a matrix memory? In our earlier study, we used a matrix-augmented reasoner on a task that admits a rank-1 solution, leaving this question open. We train matrix memories on $K$ fresh key-value bindings whose exact linear recovery requires $\mathrm{rank}(Z) \geq K$. A fixed linear readout queries a single matrix state without access to the original bindings. Experiments measure recovery by cosine similarity greater than 0.9, a threshold distinct from mathematical equality. Learned effective rank increases with $K$ across the tested grid (Spearman $ρ= 1.0$ at $d = 16$). Training-time rank caps produce a recovery transition near $k = K$: at $d = 8$, $K = 4$, rank 3 gives at most 0.0004 recovery and rank 4 gives 0.97. Four of five seeds retain at least 0.9996 recovery through 21-fold self-application of the trained operator. On the entity subspace, the learned operator has effective rank close to $K$ and approximates the ideal cycle. For the single converged seed capped below $K$, a calculation using the entity-subspace operator and ideal cycle predicts the measured cosine within 0.008 through seven applications. Extending training resolves several initial failures, but recovery still declines at larger matrix dimensions with encoder width fixed.
bullets: The task stores K fresh key–value bindings whose exact linear recovery requires rank at least K.
Learned effective rank increases with K across the tested settings, with Spearman ρ = 1.0 at d = 16.
Rank below K sharply limits recovery, while rank K enables high recovery in the reported d = 8, K = 4 case.
Most seeds preserve at least 0.9996 recovery through 21 self-applications of the learned operator.
Recovery can decline at larger matrix dimensions when encoder width remains fixed; cosine recovery is an empirical threshold, not exact equality.
papers.selection_reason: Trained matrix memories as associative key-value storage are transferable to persistent/external memory mechanisms for language models.
papers.title: When the Gradient Sees Rank: Provable Necessity, Causal Recruitment, and Composition in Trained Matrix Memories
papers.tldr: Gradient-based training learns matrix-memory rank that scales with the number of associations, enabling near-exact recovery and repeated composition when rank is sufficient.

papers.abstract: Multi-hop retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) requires an agent to retrieve evidence for a sequence of dependent sub-questions. When a wrong answer lacks a required passage, the passage may be inaccessible to the retriever, or the agent may have failed to issue a query that would retrieve it. Standard retrieval evaluations conflate these two causes. We study how much apparent retrieval failure is instead caused by search drift: the search no longer tracks an unanswered sub-question. Holding the retriever, corpus, and generation model fixed, we introduce ExecutionRAG, a training-free requirement register that records open sub-questions and their supporting evidence. The register changes search guidance but not evidence access, so each gold passage it recovers certifies that the passage was reachable by the original retriever. On 1,000 MuSiQue questions, the number of wrong answers with unretrieved required evidence falls from 382 to 234 with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and from 383 to 274 with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B. These counts correspond to 69% to 44% and 66% to 48% of each system's wrong answers, respectively. Crucially, evidence recovery does not produce a proportional reduction in total error: premature resolutions and abstentions increase as missing-evidence failures decrease. The central finding is therefore a shift in the remaining bottleneck, from guiding search toward required evidence to verifying that the retrieved evidence is sufficient.
bullets: Standard retrieval evaluations conflate inaccessible evidence with failures to query for evidence required by an unanswered sub-question.
ExecutionRAG is a training-free requirement register that tracks open sub-questions and supporting evidence while keeping the retriever, corpus, and generator fixed.
On 1,000 MuSiQue questions, missing-evidence wrong answers decrease substantially for both tested retrievers when search is guided by the register.
This recovery does not proportionally reduce total errors because premature resolutions and abstentions increase.
The remaining challenge is verifying evidence sufficiency after improving search guidance.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces ExecutionRAG, a training-free method to address retrieval failure in multi-hop RAG by tracking open sub-questions. This addresses retrieval mechanisms and evidence access, fitting 'LLM Memory'.
papers.title: Beyond Retrieval Failure: Understanding Why LLMs Miss Evidence in Multi-Hop RAG
papers.tldr: Many multi-hop RAG failures blamed on retrieval are actually search drift, but recovering missing evidence shifts the main bottleneck to verifying whether the evidence is sufficient.

papers.abstract: Long-context capability has become essential for large language models (LLMs) to handle complex tasks, yet continuously expanding the context window does not remove the computational, storage, and information-selection pressures incurred at inference time. Existing work on prompt compression, KV-cache management, efficient serving, retrieval augmentation, and agent memory is usually discussed in isolation, leaving the flow of information between storage and computation insufficiently understood. This survey reframes long-context compression as a memory-management problem for allocating inference-time resources. We distinguish compute-active memory, which directly participates in model computation, from compute-inactive memory, which lies outside the computation path but can be stored, retrieved, updated, or forgotten, and we characterize offloaded KV caches, persistent prefix caches, and precomputed KV states as intermediate states on the activation path. On this basis, we formulate writing, offloading, recall, retrieval-and-injection, materialization, eviction, consolidation, and forgetting as state transitions within an information lifecycle, and introduce a budgeted cost model that places these operations in a single cost account. The resulting framework unifies short-term context compression, long-term memory management, and the transitions between them, and shows that the central challenge is not merely reducing information volume but deciding which information should participate in costly inference, when, and in what form. We further summarize evaluation dimensions, benchmark gaps, and open challenges, and argue that future research should move from static, pointwise compression toward dynamic, governable, lifecycle-aware memory management.
bullets: Long-context scaling still faces inference-time compute, storage, and information-selection pressures.
It distinguishes compute-active memory from compute-inactive memory, including offloaded, persistent, and precomputed KV states.
It models writing, offloading, retrieval, injection, materialization, eviction, consolidation, and forgetting as information-lifecycle transitions.
A budgeted cost model brings prompt compression, KV-cache management, retrieval augmentation, and agent memory into one framework.
It identifies benchmark gaps and argues for dynamic, governable memory management rather than static, pointwise compression.
papers.selection_reason: A survey reframing long-context compression as memory management for LLMs, introducing a budgeted cost model and state transitions for memory lifecycle management. This is highly relevant to 'LLM Memory' and 'Long-Context Models'.
papers.title: From Long Context to Selective Memory:A Survey of Memory-Centric Compression for Large Language Models
papers.tldr: This survey unifies long-context compression and LLM memory management as lifecycle-aware decisions about what information should enter costly inference, when, and in what form.

papers.abstract: Reasoning over long document contexts remains a challenge for large language models (LLMs). Standard retrieval methods are inherently reactive, bottlenecking agents with complex, cross-document reasoning at inference time, while precomputed structures like knowledge graphs often fall short because they rely on rigid heuristics. Instead, can we allow agents to perform anticipatory directed curation: learning to proactively reorganize unstructured corpora prior to inference to efficiently serve diverse future queries. We build on a key asymmetry in modern agentic harnesses (e.g., Claude Code): while LLM agents are adept at navigating existing filesystems to solve an immediate task, they are rarely trained to construct reusable workspaces for future use. To instantiate this capability, we introduce Librarian Agents, a framework in which a builder agent transforms raw documents into a hierarchical filesystem of synthetic files and reference links, which forms a workspace tailored for a downstream answering agent. We formulate workspace construction as a Markov decision process and optimize the builder policy via reinforcement learning to directly maximize downstream answering accuracy. Empirically, Librarian Agents outperforms the strongest retrieval and precomputation baselines by 33 percentage points on BrowseComp-Plus, amortizes upfront construction costs across repeated queries, and generalizes zero-shot to unseen domains on BRIGHT with a 31-point average accuracy improvement.
authors: Anikait Singh, Teresa Zhang, Yoonho Lee, Roshen Sanjay Nair, Aviral Kumar, Chelsea Finn
bullets: Addresses the limits of reactive retrieval and rigid precomputed structures for cross-document reasoning.
A builder agent converts raw documents into hierarchical synthetic files and reference links.
Workspace construction is modeled as a Markov decision process and optimized for downstream answering accuracy.
The approach improves accuracy by 33 points on BrowseComp-Plus and 31 points on average on BRIGHT, while amortizing construction costs across repeated queries.
Scope: performance depends on upfront workspace construction and is evaluated through downstream answering tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Trains LLM agents to construct reusable long-context workspaces for future queries, directly relevant to LLM memory and retrieval.
papers.title: Librarian Agents: Training LLMs to Curate Long-Context Workspaces that Anticipate Future Queries
papers.tldr: Librarian Agents uses reinforcement learning to proactively organize documents into reusable, query-oriented workspaces that improve long-context question answering.

papers.abstract: Agent memory benchmarks evaluate whether an agent's responses reflect correct knowledge, measuring downstream question-answering accuracy as a proxy for memory quality. We show this evaluation paradigm is incomplete: it conflates memory correctness with retrieval and generation quality, producing both false positives where correct responses mask broken memory and false negatives where incorrect responses blame correct memory for retrieval failures. We introduce FEB-30, a benchmark of 30 fact-evolution trajectories spanning 6 diagnostic categories and 3 difficulty levels, constructed via paradigm inversion: documents are generated from known fact trajectories, yielding deterministic ground truth without human annotation. Each trajectory defines how a fact should evolve across multi-author artifacts (documents, emails, conversations), enabling direct inspection of the memory store after each ingestion step. Applying FEB-30 to a representative memory system, we demonstrate that intrinsic and extrinsic evaluation diverge by an average of 16 percentage points, with 44% of trajectories exceeding meaningful divergence thresholds. Diagnostic decomposition reveals that the system correctly classifies memory operations (create, update, reinforce, supersede) only 20% of the time, a failure entirely invisible to extrinsic evaluation, and that failure modes differ systematically by category and difficulty. We release the benchmark, document generation pipeline, and scoring framework to support reproducible evaluation of agent memory systems.
authors: Sebastian-Antonio Toma, Jean de Kernier, Mike Ply, Oliviu Matei
bullets: Introduces 30 fact-evolution trajectories across 6 diagnostic categories and 3 difficulty levels.
Uses paradigm inversion to generate artifacts from known fact trajectories, enabling deterministic ground truth and direct memory inspection.
Finds intrinsic and extrinsic evaluations diverge by an average of 16 percentage points, with 44% of trajectories showing meaningful divergence.
A representative memory system correctly classifies memory operations only 20% of the time, a failure hidden by downstream QA.
Releases the benchmark, document-generation pipeline, and scoring framework for reproducible evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a benchmark and diagnostic framework for evaluating agent memory, directly relevant to LLM memory assessment.
papers.title: Beyond Downstream QA: Rethinking How We Evaluate Agent Memory
papers.tldr: FEB-30 shows that downstream QA alone cannot reliably evaluate agent memory, because it mixes memory correctness with retrieval and generation errors.

papers.abstract: External-memory systems extend language-model applications beyond a context window, but their quality depends critically on the model executing the write path: deciding what to retain, how precisely to represent it, and how new evidence should update persistent state. Existing frameworks typically place a general-purpose large language model behind framework-specific prompts. This raises serving cost, and a writer specialized for one protocol does not transfer directly to another; a unified model that can operate across established memory frameworks remains largely unexplored. We present Hy-Memory-30B-A3B, a compact long-term-memory writer trained across Mem0, MemOS, and Hy-Memory. Memory On-Policy Distillation teaches framework-specific write protocols on student-generated states; Memory RL then optimizes downstream answerability using dense per-chunk probes, attributed cross-chunk rewards, over-storage controls, and chunk-level GRPO. Carrying policy-written banks across windows keeps training aligned with deployment. On fixed 20% benchmark subsamples, Hy-Memory-30B-A3B ranks first on all four evaluated harnesses, including held-out EverMemOS, with a 55.49% macro average versus 54.62% for Claude Opus 5.
authors: Tianxiang Fei, Jiazheng Kang, Mao Zheng, Xingyan He, Xiang Yu
bullets: Addresses the cost and limited transferability of using general-purpose LLMs as framework-specific memory writers.
Supports Mem0, MemOS, and Hy-Memory through framework-specific write-protocol distillation.
Uses Memory RL with dense chunk probes, attributed cross-chunk rewards, over-storage controls, and chunk-level GRPO.
Carries policy-written memory banks across context windows to better match deployment conditions.
On fixed 20% benchmark subsamples, ranked first across four evaluated harnesses, including held-out EverMemOS, with a 55.49% macro average versus 54.62% for Claude Opus 5.
papers.selection_reason: Trains a compact long-term memory writer across multiple memory frameworks using reinforcement learning.
papers.title: Hy-Memory-30B-A3B: Attributed Reinforcement Learning for Long-Term Memory Writing
papers.tldr: Hy-Memory-30B-A3B is a compact, unified memory-writing model trained with distillation and attributed reinforcement learning to improve long-term memory across multiple frameworks.

papers.abstract: Masked diffusion language models expose an inference-time choice: which positions become visible after each denoising pass. Many existing decoding methods use hand-designed rules or require visibility to grow monotonically. We present a $\textbf{T}$iny $\textbf{I}$nference-time $\textbf{P}$olicy for $\textbf{S}$caling ($\textbf{TIPS}$), an approximately $600$K-parameter controller that learns both unmasking and remasking while keeping the underlying language model frozen. TIPS uses visibility-aware confidence features and a shallow transformer to select which tokens should be visible, while a fixed schedule controls the expected visible fraction. We train the controller through supervised warmup followed by reinforcement learning from terminal correctness rewards. On GSM8K and MATH-500 with LLaDA-8B-Instruct, the full-canvas and two-block TIPS variants achieve $58.46\%$ and $57.97\%$ micro-averaged accuracy at a budget of $32$ decoder evaluations, exceeding the strongest baseline in our main comparison by $12.1$ and $11.6$ percentage points, respectively. Both variants are trained at a budget of $32$ evaluations and remain competitive at higher budgets without retraining. These results demonstrate that learning when to reveal and reconsider tokens can improve the accuracy-compute trade-off without updating the decoder backbone.
authors: Ya-Shi Zhang, Jian Tang, Pierre-Andr\'e No\"el, Oleksiy Ostapenko
bullets: Addresses the limitation of hand-designed or monotonically expanding visibility schedules in masked diffusion language models.
Uses visibility-aware confidence features and a shallow transformer to select token visibility, with a fixed schedule controlling the expected visible fraction.
Trains a roughly 600K-parameter controller using supervised warmup followed by reinforcement learning from terminal correctness rewards.

With LLaDA-8B-Instruct at 32 decoder evaluations, TIPS reaches 58.46% and 57.97% micro-averaged accuracy on GSM8K and MATH-500, respectively, outperforming the strongest cited baseline by 12.1 and 11.6 percentage points.
The full-canvas and two-block variants remain competitive at higher inference budgets without retraining.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a small inference-time controller (TIPS) for diffusion language models to optimize the accuracy-compute trade-off by dynamically managing token visibility, directly relevant to LLM memory and long-context management.
papers.title: TIPS: A Tiny Inference-time Policy for Scaling in Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: TIPS is a small learned inference-time controller that improves diffusion language model decoding by deciding which tokens to reveal or remask while keeping the backbone frozen.

papers.abstract: An agent's memory must remain useful as information changes across conversations. A new fact may replace an earlier value without making that value irrelevant to a later question. We present Temporal State Tracking Memory (TEM), a training-free framework for tracking these changes. TEM stores facts as versioned records linked to their sources. It retrieves relevant versions, places them in source order and labels historical records before passing the evidence to the answer model. Event memory and original dialogue turns provide details missing from structured facts. We evaluated TEM on 420 questions drawn from 600 sessions involving 60 personas. Across four open-weight models, key-entity hit rates reached 75.71-97.62% overall and 96.67-100.00% on the historical-residence subset. Adding historical labels to otherwise identical, source-ordered facts increased overall hit rates by 17.14-55.95 percentage points. The evidence was compact: 94-118 tokens per answer, or 48.75-56.73% less than session-aware retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). A further evaluation on 1,540 LoCoMo questions tested hybrid memory under a fixed evidence budget. TEM exceeded session-aware RAG with both backbones; conservative score differences were 7.92 and 10.58 percentage points. The results support preserving fact versions and exposing their temporal status to the generator when answering questions about repeatedly updated information.
authors: Pengfeng Song, Yunkai Zhuang, Liye Shi
bullets: Stores facts as versioned, source-linked records while retaining earlier values for later reference.
Retrieves relevant versions in source order and labels historical records before answer generation.
Combines structured facts with event memory and original dialogue turns to recover missing details.
Across four open-weight models, key-entity hit rates reached 75.71–97.62% overall and 96.67–100.00% for historical-residence questions.
Used 48.75–56.73% fewer evidence tokens than session-aware RAG; it also outperformed session-aware RAG in a 1,540-question hybrid-memory evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Presents temporal state tracking memory for LLM agents, directly fitting agent memory and persistent external memory research.
papers.title: TEM: Temporal State Tracking Memory for Large Language Model Agents
papers.tldr: TEM is a training-free memory framework that tracks changing facts by preserving version history and temporal labels, improving answers to questions about updated information with compact evidence.

papers.abstract: Conditional memory expands language-model capacity through selective lookup, but the full embedding table must remain available for every possible input. We introduce Conditional Program (CP), a compressed representation that reconstructs only the rows an input requests. CP represents each row by a short code and a local scale, with a reconstruction program shared across the table. We instantiate this representation with a Gaussian trellis, norm restoration and independently decodable row records. CP's two-bit code lowers output KL by 41--63\% relative to 2-bit round-to-nearest. Analysis across three trained n-gram memory families shows that Gaussian-like coordinate statistics coexist with learned relationships among rows; at matched storage budgets, the shared trellis outperforms the fitted codebooks and low-rank residual variants we test. For DeepSeek, it reduces table storage from 203GB to 51GB, leaving room for larger workloads when the table is kept on GPU.
authors: Donghoon Han, Minseop Jung, Dong Woo Kwak, SeungJae Lee, Junhoo Lee
bullets: Targets conditional memories whose full embedding table must remain available for lookup.
Encodes each row with a short code and local scale, using a shared Gaussian-trellis reconstruction program.
Adds norm restoration and independently decodable row records for practical access.
Reduces output KL by 41–63% versus 2-bit round-to-nearest quantization.
Cuts DeepSeek table storage from 203GB to 51GB, enabling larger GPU-resident workloads.
papers.selection_reason: Quantizes large LLM n-gram lookup tables with compressed reconstructable codes, drastically reducing model memory footprint while preserving output quality.
papers.title: N-Gram Memories at Two Bits: Quantizing Lookup Tables in Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Conditional Program compresses language-model lookup tables to two bits per value while reconstructing requested rows on demand, substantially reducing storage and quantization error.

papers.abstract: As agents powered by foundation models move into open-ended environments, continual learning from experience becomes essential. For agents built on models with fixed parameters, this learning requires reusing prior task experience in context to improve performance and efficiency on future tasks. Existing memory and experience-learning systems typically focus on either retained facts or procedures, and lack a mechanism for establishing the reliability of claims extracted from the ongoing task stream. Indeed, we find that approximately 12--33\% of entries produced by representative systems harm future task performance when reused. To address these limitations, we propose \textbf{RIKA} (Reliable Knowledge Acquisition), which combines hierarchical extraction of factual, conceptual, procedural, and metacognitive knowledge with Evidence-based Knowledge Admission, which uses source evidence and subsequent experience to govern which claims enter the task agent's context, without additional validation tasks. Across six task streams from Continual Learning Bench and four model backbones, RIKA achieves the highest aggregate score on every backbone.
bullets: Existing memory systems often retain facts or procedures without assessing claim reliability.
Unreliable entries can harm future performance; the abstract reports this for approximately 12–33% of entries in representative systems.
RIKA hierarchically extracts factual, conceptual, procedural, and metacognitive knowledge.
Its Evidence-based Knowledge Admission uses source evidence and later experience to decide which claims are retained, without additional validation tasks.
RIKA achieved the highest aggregate score across six task streams and all four evaluated model backbones.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes reliable knowledge acquisition for continual learning agents, directly fitting continual/online learning and agent memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Reliable Knowledge Acquisition for Continual Learning Agents
papers.tldr: RIKA improves continual-learning agents by admitting only evidence-supported knowledge into context, achieving the best aggregate performance across evaluated backbones.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents solve complex tasks by calling external tools over multiple turns. Recent work has proposed tool graph memory, which stores past experience as tool transitions to guide subsequent selection. However, it remains unclear whether this component consistently improves agents' tool use or undermines it. We evaluate tool graph memory on nine models and two benchmarks, finding that it seldom improves significantly over baselines, and that its gains, where present, cost over twice the LLM calls. The memory's guidance is often incorrect, and random or no guidance retains most of the gain, implying that the benefit stems from extra computation rather than the memory itself. Moreover, even with the correct next tool suggested, many failures remain, such as giving up without a tool call. Storing the same experience instead as textual insights outperforms tool graph memory with almost no extra LLM calls. This suggests that memory serves better as a soft prior than as a prescription of the next tool, leading to a more effective and generalizable solution.
authors: Uiji Hwang, Richeng Xuan, Taeuk Kim
bullets: Evaluated tool graph memory across nine models and two benchmarks.
Its improvements over baselines are uncommon and cost more than twice the LLM calls when present.
The stored guidance is often incorrect; random or absent guidance preserves most of the benefit.
Correctly suggesting the next tool does not prevent failures such as abandoning tool use.
Textual insights outperform tool graph memory with little extra computation, favoring soft priors over rigid tool prescriptions.
papers.selection_reason: Directly studies tool graph memory for LLM agents, fitting LLM memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Rethinking the Role of Tool Graph Memory in Multi-Turn Tool Use
papers.tldr: Tool graph memory rarely improves multi-turn tool use, with its apparent gains mainly coming from extra computation rather than reliable guidance.

papers.abstract: Addressed conditional memory provides a local surface for post-hoc knowledge injection, but a successful write need not transfer to a new question or preserve untargeted behavior. This study combines a controlled GPT-2 comparison with production-memory experiments on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP8 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. Newly initialized modules attached to frozen GPT-2 are tested in a 2 x 2 design: row-only versus row-plus-projection updates, each with or without fixed module-residual anchoring. All arms reproduce 50 trained completions in each of three sampling seeds. Natural-question target-string hits average 5.3% for both row-only arms, 28.7% for unanchored projection updates, and 22.0% with anchoring, while strict answer scores remain zero. Anchoring lowers measured drift; lexical hits do not establish entity-specific retrieval. In the archived Qwen experiments, gradient writes make the designated first answer token top-ranked for 132 independently reset targets, comprising 93 new promotions and 39 already top-ranked targets. A separate matched 24-target comparison gives 13 new promotions with Adam versus two with SPSA at equal iteration counts but unequal computational procedures. An 80-row case includes saved continuations and a replay record, while reformulations bound its scope. Six DeepSeek zero-order cases yield one new target-token promotion and one regression. These results support bounded writing feasibility and separate trained expression, question-form behavior, and preservation; first-token rankings do not establish complete-answer success or universal conditions for writable memory.
authors: Wei Gao (Shibei Qiyuan AI Technology), Cheng Tian (Shibei Qiyuan AI Technology), Duan Yang (Xi'an Jiaotong University), Jianqing Yin (Shibei Qiyuan AI Technology)
bullets: The study tests whether post-hoc writes transfer beyond a targeted completion while preserving unrelated behavior.
A controlled GPT-2 experiment compares row-only versus row-plus-projection updates, with or without fixed residual anchoring.
Natural-question target-string hits were 5.3% for row-only updates, 28.7% for unanchored projection updates, and 22.0% with anchoring; strict answer scores were zero.
Archived production-memory experiments found 93 new target-token promotions among 132 reset targets, while Adam outperformed SPSA in a matched 24-target comparison.
Results support bounded writing feasibility, but first-token promotions do not establish complete-answer retrieval, entity-specific access, or universal writability conditions.
papers.selection_reason: Controlled study of post-hoc knowledge injection into addressed memory for LLMs; directly matches LLM memory.
papers.title: Writability and the Pathway: A Controlled Study of Knowledge Injection into Addressed Memory
papers.tldr: Addressed-memory writes can promote target tokens, but reliable question-level retrieval and behavior preservation remain limited and distinct challenges.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory has become a crucial component of large language model (LLM) agents, with most research focusing on retrieving relevant information accurately and efficiently. However, a dependable memory system must also forget sensitive user data upon request. To evaluate this capability, we introduce MemCut, a systematic benchmark for user-requested forgetting. Its 456 hand-designed secrets in long-horizon conversations have fully annotated evidence trails to test recovery after deletion, including from messages that never state the secrets directly. We propose two recovery metrics. Native recovery measures reader success through the system's retrieval, whereas residual recovery measures the same reader's success when directly given surviving objects traced to annotated disclosures or evidence. We establish three reference deletion baselines to test how far existing retrievers and write models support forgetting across five memory designs and four LLMs. Disclosure removal reduces native recovery far more than residual recovery. LLM-guided deletion of ten additional turns from twenty retrieval candidates leaves 39-76% residual recovery. Subset sweeps (144 facts, three systems, two models) show that widening the pool at a fixed budget reduces residual recovery more than deleting all original candidates. These sweeps identify candidate coverage as a bottleneck in the reference baselines.
authors: Cheng Zhang, Xuanning Cao, Zhicheng Zheng, Hui Xiong
bullets: Introduces 456 annotated secrets embedded in long-horizon conversations, including indirect disclosures.
Measures native recovery through retrieval and residual recovery from surviving objects linked to secret evidence.
Evaluates three deletion baselines across five memory designs and four LLMs.
Removing direct disclosures lowers native recovery much more than residual recovery; deleting additional candidate turns still leaves 39–76% residual recovery.
Subset sweeps suggest candidate coverage—not just deletion quality—is a key bottleneck.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and analysis of user-requested forgetting in LLM-agent long-term memory; directly fits LLM memory research.
papers.title: MemCut: Every Secret Leaves a Trail in the Long-Term Memory of LLM Agents
papers.tldr: MemCut benchmarks whether LLM agents can truly forget user-requested secrets, revealing substantial recoverability through residual evidence after deletion.

papers.abstract: Memory enables large language models (LLMs) to use information beyond their parameters, such as past user conversations, long documents, or an agent's earlier actions. For a frozen LLM, access to this accumulated knowledge is limited to what a memory system places in its context window. However, gathering and combining relevant information needed for each query while keeping the model's context short remains challenging for existing systems. Here we introduce Memorilla, a memory system that gathers information from an entire document collection into a fixed number of query-dependent 'memory tokens' for a frozen LLM. Memorilla encodes documents (such as user chats, book chapters) once into reusable embeddings, then learns to retrieve and place query-specific information in the LLM's input embedding space. Using only 16 memory tokens, Memorilla achieves the best performance against baselines including Mem0 and MemoRAG on five of eight benchmarks spanning personalization, long-document and knowledge-intensive question answering. Notably, on FactKG, it reaches 84.33% accuracy versus 80.43% with full-context inference, while using 108x fewer tokens to represent the source documents. Furthermore, Memorilla can facilitate continual learning in agentic systems where the document count (the agent's past turns) increases throughout the trajectory. In a TextWorld environment, we show that Memorilla reduces the agent's tendency to wander between rooms it has already explored, and improves its average success rate from 18.6% with full-history in-context learning to 24.2%. Overall, Memorilla aids frozen LLMs in accumulating and using knowledge effectively across long-context interactions and takes a step towards building continually learning AI systems.
authors: Adibvafa Fallahpour, Parsa Idehpour, Vignesh Kothapalli, Nikita Mounier, Shirley Wu, Shayan Pardis, Jure Leskovec
bullets: Addresses the challenge of retrieving and combining relevant information while keeping an LLM’s context window short.
Pre-encodes documents into reusable embeddings and generates query-dependent memory tokens in the LLM’s input embedding space.
Outperforms baselines on five of eight benchmarks, including personalization, long-document, and knowledge-intensive QA tasks.
On FactKG, achieves 84.33% accuracy versus 80.43% with full-context inference while using 108× fewer source-document tokens.
Supports continual learning for agents; in TextWorld, average success improves from 18.6% with full-history in-context learning to 24.2%.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a latent semantic memory system for frozen LLMs, directly relevant to LLM memory and long-context agentic use.
papers.title: Memorilla: Latent Semantic Memory for LLMs
papers.tldr: Memorilla compresses query-relevant information from large document collections into 16 memory tokens, enabling frozen LLMs to use long-term knowledge with much shorter contexts.

papers.abstract: Modern agents select tools from registries, but exposing entire registries incurs high token costs and can impair selection as they grow. We present TRACER, a retrieval front-end that indexes observed tool-call sequences in a trie and ranks continuations using a learned blend of empirical and contextual priors. On a mixed retail-and-telecom $\tau^2$ environment, TRACER improves GPT-5.4's tool-selection accuracy by 4.7 points while reducing input tokens per step by 80%, exposing just 5 of 128 tools. In autonomous full-turn execution, it matches GPT-5.4's full-registry task success with 61% fewer input tokens per step. Across six environments and four models, TRACER improves tool-selection accuracy over full-registry selection in 21 of 24 model-environment pairs, with average gains of 6 to 10 points; the three exceptions trail by at most 2.2. We analyze failures in both regimes to identify directions for future work.
authors: Tanish Kher, Sarvesh DK, Abedelkadir Asi, Sparsha Chennarayapatna Sundaresh, Dezhi Hong
bullets: Addresses the token cost and selection difficulty of exposing entire tool registries.
Indexes observed tool-call sequences in a trie and ranks likely continuations using learned empirical and contextual priors.
On a mixed retail-and-telecom environment, exposes 5 of 128 tools, improves GPT-5.4 tool-selection accuracy by 4.7 points, and cuts input tokens per step by 80%.
In autonomous execution, matches full-registry task success with 61% fewer input tokens per step.
Across six environments and four models, outperforms full-registry selection in 21 of 24 model-environment pairs; failures are analyzed for future work.
papers.selection_reason: Tool-call sequence trie serves as external agent memory for retrieval.
papers.title: TRACER: Trajectory-Aware Tool Retrieval for LLM Agents
papers.tldr: TRACER retrieves a small, trajectory-aware subset of tools for LLM agents, improving selection accuracy while substantially reducing input-token use.

papers.abstract: Agent memory architectures define how LLM agents store and reuse experience across tasks, but they are typically fixed after deployment, limiting their adaptability across task types. Recent self-evolving approaches instead adapt these memory architectures using execution feedback, typically represented as evaluation scores or compressed summaries. However, such coarse-grained feedback is insufficient for precise failure localization in current agent systems, where long-horizon task execution involves multiple interacting components. Without a precise failure location, existing approaches lack a clear code-level target for modification, leaving the update scope weakly constrained and often leading to large-scale rewrites of an otherwise capable memory architecture. We propose MemScope, a framework for evidence-grounded, localized evolution of an existing memory architecture. Its tool-using Patch Agent jointly inspects raw execution traces, runtime memory state, and current architecture code to identify repair targets and apply bounded, in-place edits under provider-identity and memory-compatibility constraints. On GAIA, the trace-and-memory inspection variant achieves 86.67% accuracy, compared with 70.00% for trace-only and 63.33% for summary-only feedback. Under xBench tasks, the evolved memory architecture improves over its original version from 49 to 55 correct answers with DeepSeek V3.2 and from 50 to 53 with Kimi K2.7 Code. On disjoint ALFWorld unseen tasks, success rises from 50.75% to 71.64%. Across archived architecture-snapshot transitions, the median code-change ratio is 4.4%. These results support fine-grained execution evidence as a basis for localized, in-place memory-architecture evolution.
authors: Miao Su, Yucan Guo, Zixuan Li, Long Bai, Zhongni Hou, Xiaolong Jin, Jiafeng Guo
bullets: Targets the difficulty of locating failures in long-horizon agent executions using only coarse scores or summaries.
A Patch Agent jointly analyzes raw traces, runtime memory state, and architecture code to identify repair targets.
Applies bounded in-place edits while preserving provider identity and memory compatibility.
Improves performance on GAIA, xBench, and unseen ALFWorld tasks, with a median code-change ratio of 4.4%.
papers.selection_reason: Evolving agent memory architectures with execution feedback directly targets LLM/agent memory and deployment-time adaptation.
papers.title: MemScope: Evolving Agent Memory Architectures through Localized Code Repair
papers.tldr: MemScope evolves LLM-agent memory systems through evidence-grounded, localized code repairs instead of broad rewrites.

papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly rely on external memory to answer queries grounded in long-horizon histories such as multi-session dialogues and lengthy documents. However, existing memory methods often optimize retrieval and memory construction separately, without a shared reward space for evaluating search, writing, and stopping decisions. To address this, we propose All-in-One Memory (AiO-Mem), which organizes these operations as transitions over a shared evidence state and directly evaluates the semantic quality of each action in a unified reward space. AiO-Mem compiles heterogeneous histories into source-traceable multi-view events, providing a shared substrate for retrieval and memory writing. A unified memory policy actor then rolls out complete interaction trajectories over this shared evidence state. A separate trajectory-conditioned process reward model is trained through evidence-grounded supervised fine-tuning and trajectory-level DPO to assign process scores to the collected trajectories. These scores are aggregated into an action-balanced trajectory reward and used by Process-Aligned DAPO (PA-DAPO) to optimize the memory policy. Across long-context memory benchmarks, AiO-Mem consistently improves answer accuracy over both static memory systems and RL-trained memory agents.
authors: Bingbing Wang, Jingjie Lin, Weiming Qiao, Jing Li, Ruifeng Xu
bullets: Addresses the lack of a unified reward space for memory search, construction, and stopping decisions.
Represents heterogeneous histories as source-traceable, multi-view events shared by retrieval and memory writing.
Uses a unified policy to roll out complete memory-interaction trajectories.
Trains a trajectory-conditioned process reward model and optimizes the policy with Process-Aligned DAPO.
Consistently improves answer accuracy over static memory systems and RL-trained memory agents on long-context benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes unified memory policy and process-rewarded RL for LLM agent memory, directly fitting the LLM memory subtopic.
papers.title: All-in-One Memory: Process-Rewarded Reinforcement Learning for Memory Agents
papers.tldr: AiO-Mem jointly optimizes memory retrieval, writing, and stopping with process rewards over a shared evidence state, improving long-context answer accuracy.

papers.abstract: Agent memory enables large language model (LLM) agents to reuse past experiences without updating their parameters. However, semantic similarity alone does not guarantee memory usefulness: downstream performance depends on how memories are selected and presented to the agent. We propose MemComposer, a memory composer that jointly examines the current query and retrieved candidates to decide which experiences to include, how many to select, and how to order them. We train the composer using Experience Policy Optimization (ExPO), a GRPO-based framework that evaluates assembled memory contexts through complete agent interactions and uses task-success feedback to optimize the assembly policy. Across three $\tau^2$-bench domains with two frozen executors, MemComposer outperforms the strongest baseline for each executor while reducing average memory-token usage by 16.9% and 4.9%, respectively. The learned policy also transfers to unseen domains, executors, and memory banks, and benefits from memories generated by stronger models without further training. These results demonstrate the value of learning query-specific memory assembly using downstream task feedback.
authors: Yixuan Xie, Xueqiang Xu, Xinyi Fan, Xinxi Lyu, Tao Feng, Xing Fan, Chenlei Guo, Jie Hao, Shaowen Wang, Jiashuo Sun, Jiawei Han
bullets: Semantic similarity alone may retrieve memories that are not useful for completing the current task.
MemComposer jointly considers the query and candidate memories to construct a query-specific context.
Its ExPO training framework uses complete agent interactions and task-success feedback to optimize memory assembly.
Across three τ²-bench domains and two frozen executors, it outperforms each executor’s strongest baseline while reducing average memory tokens by 16.9% and 4.9%.
The learned policy transfers to unseen domains, executors, and memory banks, and can use memories from stronger models without retraining.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses learned memory assembly and selection for LLM agents, fitting the LLM memory subtopic.
papers.title: MemComposer: Learning to Assemble Memories for LLM Agents via Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: MemComposer learns to select, size, and order retrieved memories for LLM agents using downstream task success, improving performance while reducing memory usage.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents for health can accumulate reusable textual skills from task feedback, such as calculation criteria, measurement time points, and formula units. Deciding which skills to retain is consequential: useful rules improve later answers, while faulty generalizations propagate errors. We propose CausalEvo, a method for causal skill self-evolution that estimates the relative effects of deliberately changed skill sets while holding the model weights, feedback cases, and rule count fixed. At each evolution step, a frozen LLM proposes candidate rules, which are pooled with the incumbent skills so that the current skill set remains a feasible choice. Paired skill replacements against shared background rules are scored on the same feedback cases; least squares converts the score differences into relative skill values, and the top-ranked rules are retained, favoring incumbents on ties. A decision-loss bound separates candidate support, approximation, and estimation errors. On six MedCalc-Bench-Verified tasks with 120 held-out cases, CausalEvo achieves 60.00% accuracy, compared with 55.83% for SkillOpt and 51.67% without skills. Across the recorded training configurations, which use different optimization budgets, it consumes 55.6% fewer training tokens than SkillOpt. Gains concentrate in particular calculations alongside regressions on others, and paired accuracy intervals include zero. CausalEvo turns task feedback into controlled decisions about skill retention and replacement. Project repository: https://github.com/txbrook/CausalEvo
bullets: Targets the risk that faulty skill generalizations persist and propagate errors in health-agent answers.
Uses a frozen LLM to propose rules, compares paired skill replacements on shared feedback cases, and ranks rules via least-squares estimates.
Keeps the incumbent skill set as a feasible option and favors incumbents when scores tie.
On six MedCalc-Bench-Verified tasks and 120 held-out cases, it reports 60.00% accuracy versus 55.83% for SkillOpt and 51.67% without skills.
Reported gains are task-dependent, with regressions on some calculations; paired accuracy intervals include zero, and training configurations used 55.6% fewer tokens than SkillOpt.
papers.selection_reason: LLM agent skill self-evolution with controlled skill retention; relevant to agent memory and LLM research.
papers.title: CausalEvo: Causal Skill Self-Evolution for Health LLM Agents
papers.tldr: CausalEvo selects which textual skills health LLM agents should retain by estimating their causal value through controlled skill replacements.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents rely on context compaction: when the interaction history outgrows the context window, a compressor replaces it with a natural-language summary. We show that these summaries contain more than a record of what happened. Compaction prompts ask for decisions and next steps, so each summary mixes facts established by the environment with reasoning written by the compressor, and the agent cannot tell the two apart afterwards. In an analysis of a widely used structured compressor, 83% of failed runs trace back to an action that carries out a specific summary entry, most of which no environment output supports. We propose Source-Judged Compaction (SJC), a training-free post-processing step that scores each summary entry for whether it has a source in the environment outputs or the previous summary, and removes the entries that do not. It changes neither the agent nor the compressor and adds one inexpensive judge request per compaction. The judge is Jev, a non-generative decision model that answers the source question with a calibrated probability instead of text. On AppWorld and OfficeBench with two agent models, SJC improves cross-run reliability over the underlying compressor by 2.1%-8.9% without increasing the agent's token usage.
bullets: Long-horizon agents’ summaries mix environment-grounded facts with compressor-generated decisions and next steps.
In an analysis of a structured compressor, 83% of failed runs involved actions based on specific summary entries, usually unsupported by environment output.
SJC scores each entry for a source in environment outputs or the previous summary, then removes unsupported entries.
It is training-free, adds one inexpensive judge request per compaction, and uses a calibrated decision model rather than generating text.
Across AppWorld and OfficeBench with two agent models, SJC improves cross-run reliability by 2.1%–8.9%.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses agent memory via context compaction for long-horizon LLM agents and proposes source-judged pruning of summary entries.
papers.title: Prune the Summary, Not the History: Source-Judged Compaction for Long-Horizon Agents
papers.tldr: Source-Judged Compaction filters unsupported summary claims from long-horizon agent histories, improving reliability without changing the agent or increasing token use.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon failures of language models are usually measured as end-task success or as a horizon length. We instead score, step by step, three components of a 400-step ledger task in which every step is easy in isolation and the model's own answers are re-injected into its context: recognising a record already seen 5 to 300 steps earlier, processing the current record locally, and writing a counter incremented at every step. On Qwen3-8B (non-thinking, 20 seeds, replicated on a second machine and backend), with every step scored component by component, two results hold. First, duplicate-recognition errors rise late in the episode -- from 0.0019 to 0.011 per step at risk across step 200 -- while the counter makes no error in 8,000 steps and local processing is descriptively stable; the rise combines long-distance recall errors and rising false alarms. Second, a block of irrelevant content inserted before each step makes the counter fail in 20 of 20 seeds on each machine, against none without it, while its effect on local processing is much smaller and not distinguishable from none. Three pre-registered follow-ups probe the counter. Its value depends on the value present in the response history: a corrupted value persists without correction in every seed, and an exact external reminder, repeated before each message, re-aligns it within one to two steps. Under the irrelevant block, no counter error was observed when an exact compact reminder of the state, supplied externally by an oracle, preceded each message (0 of 20 seeds with an error, against 15 without it), and this reminder outperformed a length-matched neutral text; whether a single reminder suffices was not conclusive, and the absence of damage to the other components was not established. An aggregate or exclusive error classification can hide the difference we report.
bullets: A 400-step ledger task separately scores duplicate recognition, local processing, and counter updates with model outputs re-injected into context.
Duplicate-recognition errors increase late in the episode, reflecting both missed long-distance recalls and rising false alarms.
The counter remains error-free without interference, but irrelevant content causes failures in all tested seeds, with little effect on local processing.
Counter errors persist after corruption, whereas exact external state reminders can restore tracking within one to two steps.
Aggregate success or exclusive error metrics can conceal these distinct failure modes; some reminder effects remain inconclusive.
papers.selection_reason: Component-wise analysis of long-horizon LLM reliability under context re-injection; relevant to long-context behavior and memory.
papers.title: Context Injection and Long-Horizon Reliability: Separating Duplicate Recognition, Local Processing, and Counter Tracking
papers.tldr: Step-by-step evaluation shows that long-horizon failures arise mainly from duplicate-recognition drift and context-sensitive counter tracking, while local processing remains comparatively stable.

papers.abstract: How can we build an agent that thinks beyond human language, yet still acts through it in the external environment? Modern LLM agents still reason and interact through text, while latent reasoning offers an efficient internal medium but lacks native tool access and reasoning transparency. We bridge these two directions with Hybrid Reasoning Agents (HybridAgents), which dynamically navigate between latent reasoning and text-based interaction throughout a unified generation process. Architecturally, a lightweight HybridLink enables seamless transitions between text and latent modes, while the agent's continuous working memory preserves lossless hybrid context across multiple turns. These designs preserve tool-integrated agentic capabilities while making latent thoughts directly inspectable. Building on this architecture, we further develop dedicated post-training algorithms for hybrid reasoning: HybridSFT stabilizes tool-integrated hybrid generation by teaching the backbone to coordinate with HybridLink, then HybridRL scales reasoning by learning when to think in latent space and when to act through text. We evaluate HybridAgent at 3 model scales across 11 benchmarks covering mathematics, science, medicine, search, and agentic reasoning. Compared with frontier LLM Agents and agentic frameworks spanning both text-based and latent methods, HybridAgent consistently improves performance by 10.4%, while delivering 35.5%-54.7% token reduction, 1.8x-2.6x faster inference, and 2.7x-3.7x cost savings. Code and data are available at https://github.com/togethercomputer/HybridAgent.
bullets: Addresses the tension between efficient latent reasoning and transparent, tool-integrated text interaction.
Uses HybridLink to switch between latent and text modes, with continuous working memory preserving hybrid context across turns.
Introduces HybridSFT for stable hybrid generation and HybridRL for learning when to reason latently versus act through text.
Evaluated across 3 model scales and 11 mathematics, science, medicine, search, and agentic-reasoning benchmarks.
Reports 10.4% higher performance, 35.5–54.7% fewer tokens, 1.8–2.6× faster inference, and 2.7–3.7× lower cost than compared agents and frameworks.
papers.selection_reason: LLM agents with hybrid latent/text reasoning and continuous working memory; relevant to agent memory and reasoning.
papers.title: Hybrid Reasoning Agents
papers.tldr: HybridAgents combine inspectable latent reasoning with text-based tool use, improving agent performance while reducing tokens, latency, and cost.

papers.abstract: We study a behavioral mechanism for artificial partiality in conversational agents. The paper reports no human-subjects data and makes no claim about attachment, trust, perceived mind, or machine interiority. Partiality has two components: caring, defined as allocation of a finite interaction surplus above a guaranteed per-user service floor, and particularity, defined as a per-user state estimate accumulated from relationship history on fixed inference machinery. We implement both as a persistence layer over one open-weight base model and evaluate them on constructed multi-session relationships with known hidden-state schedules. A four-channel divergence compares known-user and stranger conditions on identical probes with paired generation seeds; the stranger prompt is not length-matched, and one channel (initiative) is an allocator output rather than generated behavior. The full mechanism reproduces the ordinal shape, but not the magnitude, of an analytically specified curve and is the only arm satisfying the protocol-defined joint signature on the calibrated battery. The initial mechanism fails probe-quality equivalence because relationship content reduces topical relevance. A guarded revision satisfies equivalence on the calibrated battery but not on a second battery not used in calibration, where it scores higher than the unmodified baseline. On that second battery, the specificity margin is 0.0198, below the 0.02 protocol threshold. The paired mean right-user--wrong-user estimation-accuracy contrast is 0.375 but is not positive in every run. The mechanism is therefore a candidate for a later perception study, not evidence that users perceive love. The versioned protocol record is not independently time-stamped and is not described as a preregistration. Ethical constraints include a stranger-treatment floor, a bounded surplus, disclosure, and de-intensification.
bullets: Partiality is defined as caring via finite interaction surplus and particularity via per-user relationship-history state on fixed inference machinery.
The system was evaluated in constructed multi-session relationships using matched known-user/stranger probes and a four-channel divergence measure.
The full mechanism matched the expected curve’s ordinal shape and uniquely met the calibrated joint signature, but not its magnitude.
A guarded revision restored probe-quality equivalence on the calibrated battery; on a separate battery, its specificity margin was 0.0198, below the 0.02 threshold.
The study reports no human-subjects evidence and frames the mechanism as a candidate for later perception research, with safeguards including disclosure, bounded surplus, and de-intensification.
papers.selection_reason: Implements a persistent per-user relationship memory layer over an LLM; relevant to agent memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Love for Believable AI: Artificial Partiality and Relationship Persistence as an Engineerable Stance
papers.tldr: A persistence-layer mechanism operationalizes artificial partiality through bounded caring and relationship-specific state, but current results support only a protocol-defined behavioral signature—not perceived love or attachment.

papers.abstract: Automated research with LLM agents has shown promising results in various domains. Through iterative refinement and scored verifiers, LLM agents are capable of discovering new ideas. There are different ways to scale automated research: let one agent iterate for longer, run several agents in parallel, or further let the parallel agents communicate and build on one another's candidates. However, we find that all three strategies eventually plateau as the agents accumulate history. Each agent becomes anchored to its own past attempts, making fewer and smaller edits. Beyond this point, additional budget brings little further improvement. In this paper, we show that the key to scaling discovery further is to forget. Periodically discarding the search state, including every agent's session and the candidate history, and restarting from the best candidate found so far, unblocks the search and pushes the same budget further. We implement forgetting in a team of agents with communication and evaluate it on four tasks spanning heuristic programming, kernel optimization and model training. The results show up to 15% improvement compared to parallel agents, and up to 39% compared to a single agent. Our results suggest that, for open-ended discovery, what an agent is allowed to remember matters as much as how much compute it is given.
authors: Shangyin Tan, Ben Zhou, Lakshya A Agrawal, Jialin Zhang, Yilin Chen, Qiuyang Mang, Donghyun Lee, Dennis Jacob, Koushik Sen, Alex Dimakis, Matei Zaharia
bullets: Parallelism, longer iteration, and agent communication eventually plateau as accumulated history anchors agents to small edits.
The proposed strategy periodically discards agent sessions and candidate history, then restarts from the best candidate found.
Implemented in a communicating multi-agent system and evaluated across four tasks in programming, kernel optimization, and model training.
Forgetting improved results by up to 15% over parallel agents and up to 39% over a single agent.
The findings suggest memory management is as important as compute for open-ended automated discovery.
papers.selection_reason: Shows forgetting search state improves LLM agent discovery; directly relevant to agent memory and adaptation.
papers.title: Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting
papers.tldr: Periodic forgetting lets LLM-agent research systems escape history-induced plateaus and discover better solutions with the same compute budget.

papers.abstract: The scaling relationship of compute and performance for language models (LMs) has been extensively studied; more recently, models are being designed to scale memory use, as well. In particular, adding embeddings for n-grams scales memory separately from compute use, because each pass only processes individual embedding rows, which are much smaller than the storage used for the whole embedding table. However, existing methods train embeddings from scratch, which needs expensive GPU memory for fast reading and writing. Meanwhile, the ordinary memory of the host system is cheap and underutilized by these training methods. To scale on host memory, we introduce COUNT (Counting Offline Unlocks N-gram Transformers), which builds n-gram embeddings without adding learned parameters by storing precomputed n-gram counts on host. We use the corpus frequencies to weight together the LM's own unembeddings of the next tokens most often following the current n-gram history. At a fixed compute budget, COUNT can be added as an additional input embedding for pretraining 1B-parameter LMs to improve validation loss as much as an LM with 57% more compute. If GPU memory is limited, using COUNT to let backbone parameters fill GPU memory gives better performance than splitting memory with additional learned n-gram embeddings. Beyond efficiency, COUNT allows switching in a different table of n-gram counts from a domain-specific corpus at inference time to adapt to a new task without any training.
authors: Ian Magnusson, Noah A. Smith, Pang Wei Koh
bullets: Addresses the GPU-memory and training cost of learned n-gram embeddings.
Builds n-gram embeddings from corpus frequencies and the LM’s next-token unembeddings, without adding learned parameters.
Stores count tables in inexpensive host memory while accessing only relevant embedding rows during inference or training.
For 1B-parameter LMs at fixed compute, COUNT improves validation loss by as much as 57% more compute.
Supports training-free adaptation by swapping in n-gram counts from a domain-specific corpus at inference time.
papers.selection_reason: N-gram embedding memory that scales LM memory on host and enables training-free adaptation; fits LLM memory and architecture topics.
papers.title: The COUNT: Counting N-grams Unlocks Scaling on Host Memory and Training-Free Adaptation
papers.tldr: COUNT uses offline n-gram counts stored in host memory to provide training-free, domain-adaptable embeddings that improve language-model efficiency and validation loss.

papers.abstract: Context can improve large language model performance, but these gains may be lost after context removal. Inspired by biological systems consolidation, we formulate Memory Consolidation (MC) as internalizing these gains while preserving non-target capabilities, connecting context-specified editing, skill learning, and behavioral steering under a common objective. We introduce a five-task-family testbed measuring consolidation and retention under single, batch, and sequential updates. We propose Cortex, which generates prospective queries to anticipate uses of context and distills context-conditioned outputs into mergeable low-rank or structural feed-forward network updates. Across 4B--120B dense and mixture-of-experts backbones, including both text-only and multimodal models, Cortex lies on the empirical consolidation--retention Pareto frontier in most evaluated settings. After 50 sequential factual edits on a 14B model, Cortex-Structural recovers 88.9% of the context-induced gain while retaining 99.8% of original non-target performance.
authors: Jintian Zhang, Feng He, Xinnian Liang, Ziwen Xu, Haoming Xu, Haojing Huang, Shuangzhi Wu, Ningyu Zhang
bullets: Frames memory consolidation as retaining context-induced gains after the context is removed.
Uses prospective queries and distills context-conditioned outputs into mergeable low-rank or structural feed-forward updates.
Evaluates consolidation and retention across five task families with single, batch, and sequential updates.
Tested on 4B–120B dense and mixture-of-experts text-only and multimodal models.
After 50 sequential factual edits on a 14B model, Cortex-Structural recovered 88.9% of the context-induced gain and retained 99.8% of original non-target performance.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes memory consolidation for LLMs via parametric updates, directly relevant to LLM memory and continual/online learning.
papers.title: Cortex: Consolidating Context into Parametric Memory
papers.tldr: Cortex consolidates temporary context-driven improvements into compact model updates while preserving non-target capabilities.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM generation through lightweight drafting and parallel verification. It is particularly promising for long inputs, where KV-cache access costs can be amortized over multiple accepted tokens. Yet most drafters are trained on short sequences and degrade on long inputs, while long-context training is costly. Existing training-free approaches restrict the context window, rescale positions, or augment recent context with retrieved distant entries. Drafters, however, read target hidden states that already encode contextual and positional information, and their lightweight architecture makes full-history attention affordable. We propose FOLD, a training-free method that preserves exact local positions and treats all distant entries as far memory at a shared position. To counter attention dilution as the memory grows, we sharpen attention within it to emphasize relevant entries while separately controlling its total weight relative to the local window. Across six target-drafter pairs and diverse benchmarks of up to 256K tokens, FOLD predominantly delivers the highest speedup, with the best case more than doubling the speedup over autoregressive decoding, from 2.08$\times$ to 4.22$\times$.
authors: Shuxuan Li, Jialiang Kang, Yanghao Zhou, Ziye Zhu, Xiao Yang
bullets: Addresses drafter degradation on long inputs without costly long-context training.
Preserves exact positions for recent tokens while assigning distant entries a shared far-memory position.
Sharpens attention over distant memory and controls its total influence to reduce attention dilution.
Evaluated across six target–drafter pairs and benchmarks up to 256K tokens.
Predominantly achieved the highest speedups; the best case improved from 2.08× to 4.22× over autoregressive decoding.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free long-context speculative decoding with position-free far memory; fits KV-cache efficiency and long-context language modeling.
papers.title: FOLD: Position-Free Far Memory with Local Order for Long-Context Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: FOLD is a training-free long-context speculative-decoding method that improves drafting by combining exact local positions with sharpened, weight-controlled far-memory attention.

papers.abstract: A ReAct-style agent accumulates observations, intermediate results, and failed attempts in a single context. As this context grows, stale and off-path information consumes its limited capacity and obscures relevant evidence, making focused reasoning increasingly difficult. We introduce TreeFlex, a framework in which the agent's own policy decides where to search. The agent records each intermediate state, with a short summary, as a node in a search tree maintained by the harness. The policy is a single language model that acts in two roles. In the Reflection role, it has a global view of the tree through these summaries and picks a node to resume, together with an instruction. In the Execution role, the harness restores the path that led to that node, and the model carries out the instruction with the usual task tools until it saves a new node or proposes a solution, which Reflection then approves or sends back to another node. Through these choices, the policy decides whether to deepen the current line, branch from or revisit an earlier state, verify a proposal, or stop, without a fixed traversal order or a score for each node. We train navigation, task actions, checkpointing, and proposal review jointly with a tree-aware adaptation of GRPO, using task-level outcome rewards augmented by process rewards. After small-scale RL of a 4B model, with the same active-context limit for all methods, TreeFlex reaches 48.8% accuracy on a challenging deep-research benchmark, versus 41.5% for flat ReAct and 42.8% for FoldAgent, and its Pass@8 is about ten points higher than either. On SWE-bench Verified, with all three systems trained with RL from the same 9B model, TreeFlex resolves 54.9% of tasks, versus 43.3% for FoldAgent and 45.2% for its step-wise variant.
authors: Dongzhuo Li, Fangzhou Cheng, Weiwei Li, Kevin Han, Haixu Ma, Zhongchang Sun, Ruiyi Li, Serena Li, Xiangjun Fan, Lizhu Zhang, Yuandong Tian
bullets: Addresses stale and off-path information that can overwhelm a ReAct agent’s limited context.
Stores summarized intermediate states as tree nodes and uses the same language model to select nodes, resume paths, execute actions, and review proposals.
Supports deepening, branching, revisiting, verification, and stopping without fixed traversal rules or per-node scores.
Trained with a tree-aware GRPO method combining task-level and process rewards.
With matched active-context limits, achieves 48.8% on a deep-research benchmark and 54.9% on SWE-bench Verified, outperforming the compared baselines reported in the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: LLM agent framework with external search-tree memory and policy-driven navigation; fits LLM memory and agent memory.
papers.title: TreeFlex: Agents Navigating Their Own Search Trees
papers.tldr: TreeFlex lets an agent navigate a self-built search tree instead of relying on one growing context, improving deep research and software-engineering task performance.

papers.abstract: Reasoning over infinitely long documents is becoming a reality with recurrent memory agents. However, increasing context length exacerbates the trade-off between reasoning performance and inference efficiency. Inspired by Kahneman's account of fast and slow thinking, we propose MemDuet, a dual-process memory framework that learns to coordinate a small language model for fast, parallel evidence selection from raw context chunks (System 1) with a large language model for memory-update verification and memory updates in document order (System 2). We train MemDuet in three stages: supervised fine-tuning of System 1 for evidence selection, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) of System 2 for verification and memory rewriting, and joint optimization of both policies to coordinate selection and updating for long-context reasoning. Experiments on diverse long-context reasoning benchmarks (RULER-HQA, LongBench v2, and 2WikiMultiHopQA) demonstrate a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off as context length grows. Averaged across evaluation settings on the three datasets, MemDuet achieves an end-to-end inference speedup of 9.74x and an output-token reduction of 73.91% relative to RL-MemAgent.
authors: Jiangcheng Song, Haodong Jing, Yulin Mu, Lesong Tao, Jixin Wang, Jin Cui, Tianjing Ren, Runxuan Xie, Yongqiang Ma, Nanning Zheng
bullets: Addresses the accuracy–inference-efficiency trade-off in reasoning over very long documents.
Uses a small language model for parallel evidence selection and a large language model for ordered memory verification and updates.
Trains the two systems through supervised evidence-selection tuning, GRPO-based memory optimization, and joint coordination.
Evaluated on RULER-HQA, LongBench v2, and 2WikiMultiHopQA, achieving a 9.74× end-to-end speedup and 73.91% fewer output tokens than RL-MemAgent.
The abstract scopes results to the reported long-context benchmarks and evaluation settings.
papers.selection_reason: Dual-process memory framework for long-context reasoning with improved accuracy-efficiency trade-off.
papers.title: MemDuet: Learning Dual-Process Memory for Long-Context Reasoning
papers.tldr: MemDuet coordinates fast evidence selection with slower memory verification to improve long-context reasoning efficiency while preserving accuracy as contexts grow.

papers.abstract: Enterprise group chats record project progress, decisions, task ownership, and other organizational information valuable to enterprise agents. Reliable retrieval is challenging because evidence spans interleaved threads, channels, and time, with meaning and authority conditioned on the speaker. Neither RAG's independent chunk retrieval nor memory systems' summary-based consolidation can reliably recover such distributed evidence. We present EGCForest, a novel multi-view hierarchical memory framework for enterprise group chats. EGCForest organizes an immutable message log into three complementary forests: a Channel forest for temporal workflows, an Actor forest for speaker-conditioned context, and an Artifact forest for deliverable lifecycles. Cross-view connections are enabled by a Placement Map and sparse structural bridges. Built on this memory backbone, EGCForest retrieves and assembles evidence by jointly leveraging message-level relevance, hierarchical context from forest summaries, and cross-view links, recovering distributed evidence. Experiments on three enterprise-chat benchmarks show that EGCForest consistently outperforms RAG and memory-system baselines, improving answer accuracy by up to 20.85 points over MemOS while supporting efficient online retrieval.
authors: Lingxi Cui, Jinhao Ruan, Wenqing Wei, Guo Yi, Li Rao, Ke Chen, Lidan Shou
bullets: Addresses retrieval challenges caused by interleaved threads, channels, time, and speaker-dependent authority.
