Lastly, observation staleness, surfaced explicitly in the prompt, together with task-and event-triggered re-prompting, keeps the team vigilant. In a simulated urban search-and-rescue mission with spreading fire and moving evacuees, our framework rescues 98% of civilians versus 89% for the strongest baseline while using six times fewer tokens. Additional ablations isolate the contribution of each mechanism.
authors: Maria G. Mendoza, Victoria M. Tuck, Zachary Ravichandran, Shankar Sastry, George J. Pappas
bullets: Targets failures in persistent missions: unbounded prompts, degraded reasoning as complexity grows, and reduced monitoring after initial coverage.
Replaces interaction history with a Markovian state summary rebuilt from the semantic map at each invocation.
Partially delegates robot subsets to autonomous multi-agent protocols, reserving LLM reasoning for parameter-sensitive, ordered subtasks.
Uses explicit observation staleness and task/event-triggered re-prompting to maintain vigilance as conditions change.
In simulated urban search and rescue, rescued 98% of civilians versus 89% for the strongest baseline with six times fewer tokens; ablations assess each mechanism.
papers.selection_reason: LLM orchestration of persistent robot teams with state summarization and delegation; fits embodied AI and LLM memory.
papers.title: Persistent LLM Orchestration of Heterogeneous Robot Teams via Partial Delegation to Multi-Agent Protocols
papers.tldr: A persistent LLM orchestrator enables heterogeneous robot teams to handle changing, non-terminating missions more effectively while using far fewer tokens.

papers.abstract: Deep research requires connecting multiple steps of search, reasoning, and computation, with intermediate findings guiding what to investigate next. As investigations grow, agents must maintain research state across model calls and check findings before errors propagate into subsequent work. We introduce PANINI-DR, a multi-agent harness that separates coordination of the overall investigation from the research and verification of individual subquestions. A shared workspace, built on the Generative Semantic Workspace representation, records subquestions, their dependencies, findings, and supporting evidence. Researchers investigate individual subquestions, while a separate verification agent checks proposed answers against those subquestions and their evidence. Verification feedback guides further investigation, and recorded findings inform subsequent assignments. We evaluate PANINI-DR on BrowseComp-Plus, FRAMES, and MoNaCo against seven state-of-the-art deep-research harnesses, all using a shared language-model backbone and frozen corpora. PANINI-DR achieves the strongest average performance across the three benchmarks. On BrowseComp-Plus, it achieves 73.3% accuracy, outperforming the next-best harness by 16.0 points. Its advantage is strongest on hard questions, where it answers nearly twice as many as the next-best harness. Ablations further show that structured planning and persistent state improve performance, as does checking each finding against its cited evidence before it is reused. Because a model can answer correctly from memory alone, we also analyze the evidence retained by each harness. PANINI-DR achieves the highest answer recoverability from saved evidence on all three benchmarks, while complementary claim-support audits show stronger evidence-backed answers. Accounting for this evidence changes how harnesses compare and further strengthens PANINI-DR's advantage.
authors: M. Yigit Turali, Shreyas Rajesh, M. Efe Lorasdagi, Chenda Duan, Kartik Sharma, Vwani Roychowdhury
bullets: Separates overall investigation coordination from research and verification of individual subquestions.
Uses a Generative Semantic Workspace to track subquestions, dependencies, findings, and supporting evidence across model calls.
Verification feedback guides follow-up research and prevents unsupported findings from propagating.
Evaluated on BrowseComp-Plus, FRAMES, and MoNaCo against seven harnesses with a shared model and frozen corpora.
Achieves the strongest average performance; on BrowseComp-Plus, reaches 73.3% accuracy and improves evidence recoverability and support.
papers.selection_reason: Persistent shared workspace and evidence tracking for research agents constitute agent memory beyond current context.
papers.title: PANINI-DR: Controlled Deep Research through Generative Semantic Workspaces
papers.tldr: PANINI-DR improves deep research by coordinating subquestion-solving with persistent shared state and explicit evidence verification.

papers.abstract: Test-time memorization of sequential information is a foundational capability for any intelligent system that needs to rapidly store and retrieve data, as demonstrated by the attention mechanism in large language models. However, Transformers and linear attention variants are trained via backpropagation through time (BPTT), which has drawbacks such as its enormous memory requirements. Predictive coding (PC), an algorithm that optimizes a prediction-error energy function with local updates, offers a compelling solution but still lacks test-time memory for sequential data. We develop a solution to this problem by treating the per-step memory update $\Delta S_t$ as a latent variable, as opposed to a slow weight to be learned. By taking the log probability of a standard PC-based probabilistic model, we derive a PC-native solution for verbatim sequence memory, and relate our update rule to common choices in the linear attention literature (e.g., DeltaNet). We present an extensive set of empirical tests to probe our system's properties, including its scaling capacity, memory footprint, and ability to infer a context from evidence (e.g., bank (river) vs. bank (money)). We show how DeltaNet-PC can be used for storing single sequences of data, multiple sequences of data, and key-value associative memory pairs with perfect recall accuracy.
bullets: Addresses the lack of test-time sequential memory in predictive coding while avoiding BPTT’s large memory demands.
Treats each per-step memory update as a latent variable rather than a slowly learned weight.
Derives a predictive-coding-native update rule from a probabilistic model and connects it to DeltaNet-style linear attention updates.
Evaluates scaling, memory footprint, contextual inference, single- and multi-sequence storage, and key-value associative memory.
Reports perfect recall for the tested sequence and associative-memory tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time memory update for linear attention/LLM-style sequence models, derived from predictive coding without BPTT.
papers.title: DeltaNet-PC: Test-Time Memory Without Backpropagation Through Time
papers.tldr: DeltaNet-PC enables predictive-coding models to memorize and retrieve sequential information at test time without backpropagation through time.

papers.abstract: Can an autonomous AI agent reverse engineer a binary as well as a skilled human analyst? Do they adopt the same strategy, and can agents scale to real-world programs? We compare human and LLM-based software reverse engineering (SRE): nine models tackle two compact static-analysis challenges previously solved by human analysts, scored with a common understanding rubric, and we record their complete interactions with IDA Pro. This lets us compare not only what humans and agents recover, but also how they investigate a binary. The best agents (GPT-5.5 Pro, Claude Opus 4.8, and Kimi K3) achieve statistically human-competitive understanding on both tasks, while weaker models remain far behind. Ablations show that the gap depends on code representation and workflow demands, not on model capability alone: open-weight models improve substantially with richer code representations, whereas frontier models show no significant change. Similar success rates hide different workflows. Humans repeatedly revisit functions and follow local program structure; strong agents jump across the binary, retrieve information broadly, and rarely return to inspected code, a behavior we call greedy fetching. This strategy is not fixed: given semantically richer code, agents fetch less without losing understanding. Because greedy fetching aggregates large amounts of code in the agent's context, we measure context-window saturation across 4,000 real-world binaries: large windows accommodate many programs, but larger applications and lower-level representations quickly exhaust them. Autonomous reverse engineering is becoming competitive, with a large speed advantage, but scaling it will require better navigation, selective retrieval, and persistent analysis state, not merely larger context windows.
authors: Samuele Doria, Stefano De Rosa, Ruoyu Wang, Zion Leonahenahe Basque, Eleonora Losiouk, Simone Aonzo
bullets: Nine LLM agents were compared with human analysts on two static-analysis challenges using a shared rubric and recorded IDA Pro interactions.
GPT-5.5 Pro, Claude Opus 4.8, and Kimi K3 achieved statistically human-competitive understanding; weaker models lagged substantially.
Performance depended on code representation and workflow demands: richer representations helped open-weight models but not frontier models.
Humans revisited functions and followed local structure, while strong agents broadly fetched information and rarely returned to prior code—a behavior termed “greedy fetching.”
Across 4,000 real-world binaries, context saturation increased with application size and lower-level representations, highlighting the need for selective retrieval and persistent analysis state.
papers.selection_reason: Examines LLM-agent context-window saturation, greedy fetching, and need for persistent analysis state; informative for LLM memory design.
papers.title: Humans vs. Machines: A Comparison With AI Agents in Software Reverse Engineering
papers.tldr: Top AI agents can match skilled humans on compact binary reverse-engineering tasks, but their broad, context-heavy workflows limit scalability to larger programs.

papers.abstract: Activation steering has recently been used as a memory for skills: past experiences of an agent are stored as steering vectors and retrieved later. Facts and preferences about the user are assumed to need text instead. We test that assumption with a training-free activation memory beside a frozen LLM. The change an experience causes in late-layer states is stored as a shift, filed under a whitened key for the conversation's gist, and added back in a later session only when the gist matches. We argue that such a shift is a fixed average of an effect that attention, in context, recomputes for every question, so only question-independent content can survive. In a pre-registered study on Qwen3.5-2B and 9B, with judges from four model families, the memory is selective (about 98% of unrelated replies are unchanged), but facts are stored as the word to say, in the last layers only, and are almost never used (at most 15% clean use, against 96-98% in context). Leanings transfer only in a narrow strength window. Most strikingly, the reference subtracted when writing a preference decides whether its concept or its direction survives: unless the opposite is subtracted, a stored dislike is recalled as a like.
bullets: A frozen LLM stores experience effects as late-layer activation shifts keyed by a whitened conversation gist.
The method assumes stored shifts approximate effects that attention would otherwise recompute for each question.
Memory is selective: about 98% of unrelated replies remain unchanged.
Facts are rarely used correctly—up to 15% clean recall versus 96–98% when provided in context—and preferences transfer only within a narrow strength range.
The subtraction reference determines preference behavior; without subtracting the opposite, dislikes can be recalled as likes.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates activation steering as persistent memory for LLMs; fits LLM memory subtopic.
papers.title: What Survives When Activation Steering Is Used as Memory
papers.tldr: Training-free activation memories are highly selective but preserve only limited, question-independent information, often distorting facts and reversing preferences.

papers.abstract: Personalized assistants accumulate long conversation histories, and passing the whole history to an LLM with every request is costly. We show that it is also unnecessary. On PersonaMem-v2 (180 questions), with GPT-5.6-terra and Claude Opus 5.5 as judges, a relevance-filtered context, built by sentence-level retrieval that ranks the history by similarity to the current request and stops at a fixed budget, matches full-history accuracy with only 5% of the text, cutting the judge's input about 20-fold. An LLM summary of the same length performs on par, but it needs an LLM to read the entire history, whereas retrieval needs only a small embedding model. While both sentence-level retrieval and LLM summary perform strongly, retrieval does so while placing the relevant evidence in the context for only 61% of the questions, and an oracle given only that evidence beats the full history by 15.6 points, making better context selection a promising path to surpassing the full history.
bullets: Full conversation histories are costly and often unnecessary for personalized assistants.
Retrieval ranks history sentences by similarity to the current request and selects a fixed-size relevant context.
On PersonaMem-v2, retrieval matched full-history accuracy with GPT-5.6-terra and Claude Opus 5.5 judges.
Retrieval performed comparably to an equal-length LLM summary without requiring an LLM to process the entire history.
Relevant evidence was included for only 61% of questions; an oracle using that evidence exceeded full history by 15.6 points, highlighting context selection as a key opportunity.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a relevance-filtered context method to reduce the memory footprint of personalized LLMs by matching full history with only 5% of text, relevant to LLM memory optimization.
papers.title: Do Personalized LLMs Need the Whole Conversation? Matching the Full History with Only 5% of Its Text via Relevance-Filtered Context
papers.tldr: Sentence-level retrieval can preserve full-history personalization accuracy using just 5% of conversation text, reducing judge input costs about 20-fold.

papers.abstract: A language model that keeps learning online must not slowly erode its own base capabilities. We ask which part of a modern LLM should absorb continual updates, by measuring how each choice changes the model's internal representations. On a 48-layer mixture-of-experts model with a native pretrained N-gram memory, we train a seven-task chain under three update mechanisms with identical data and budgets: updating only the N-gram memory table, continually training one shared LoRA adapter, and training a fresh LoRA per task that is merged into the backbone. We capture fixed-context representations at every layer and task boundary. Updating only the N-gram memory changes the base model's representations of general math and code inputs by 26%/15% (relative RMS), against 64%/35% for merged and 97%/39% for shared LoRA. This drift does not grow with the number of tasks: it reaches 25% after the first task and stays there for all seven, while both LoRA variants keep accumulating. Its generic behaviour is essentially unchanged (no code problem lost, math NLL -0.01), and every change is confined to inspectable, reversible table rows. The cost appears elsewhere: N-gram memory acquires new tasks more weakly and its stored tasks interfere with one another, losing as much old-task NLL as shared LoRA. We show that this forgetting is governed by drift on the learned tasks' own inputs, measured from the checkpoint at which each was learned, not by generic drift (Spearman rho=0.85; rho=0.71 on Llama-3-8B), and we derive the exact relations behind it: with a frozen head, every pairwise logit margin changes by the projection of drift onto a head-difference direction. These results support a design principle for long-running online learning: write new knowledge only into the memory table and keep the backbone fixed; the remaining problem, interference between stored tasks, then lies inside the memory.
bullets: The study compares N-gram memory updates, one continually trained shared LoRA, and per-task LoRAs merged into the backbone under matched conditions.
N-gram updates cause substantially less representation drift on general math and code inputs than either LoRA strategy, with drift plateauing after the first task rather than accumulating.
Generic behavior remains essentially unchanged under memory-only updates, and changes are localized to inspectable, reversible table rows.
Memory-only learning acquires new tasks more weakly and suffers task interference, causing old-task forgetting comparable to shared LoRA.
Forgetting tracks representation drift on learned-task inputs—not generic inputs—and follows an exact frozen-head logit-margin relation.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes representation drift in continual LLM updates and compares LoRA with N-gram memory; directly relevant to continual learning and LLM memory.
papers.title: Representation Drift in Continual Learning: LoRA versus N-gram Memory
papers.tldr: Updating only an LLM’s N-gram memory preserves backbone representations far better than LoRA-based continual learning, but shifts forgetting and interference into the memory itself.

papers.abstract: Experience-based learning enables large language model (LLM) agents to improve over time by reusing knowledge from past executions. However, existing methods typically rely on final task outcomes as feedback for experience learning, overlooking the execution process and limiting their ability to evaluate and optimize experience based on trajectory quality. To address this limitation, we propose TQG-Exp, a trajectory-quality-guided experience-based learning framework that introduces process feedback. Specifically, we introduce Trajectory Quality Loss (TQL), which jointly considers task completion and process quality to provide a learning signal beyond final task outcomes. Based on this signal, we employ paired rollouts with and without retrieved experience to guide experience optimization. Representative trajectories are selected based on their outcomes and trajectory quality to extract task-level and task-type-level experiences. Meanwhile, differences in trajectory quality between the paired groups are used to estimate the contribution of retrieved experience and update its utility. The learned utility is then combined with semantic relevance to guide subsequent experience retrieval. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld with two backbone LLMs show that TQG-Exp outperforms existing experience-based methods, improving Avg.@3 over the strongest baseline by 4.50 and 8.55 percentage points on DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen3.5-Flash, respectively.
authors: Bingjie Zhang, Yibo Yang, Qiantong Liu, Benshuo Fu, Yi Chang, Dandan Guo
bullets: Existing experience-based learning often uses only task success, overlooking the quality of the execution process.
Trajectory Quality Loss (TQL) combines task completion with process quality to provide process-aware feedback.
Paired rollouts with and without retrieved experience estimate how much each experience improves trajectory quality.
Experiences are selected by outcome and quality, while learned utility is combined with semantic relevance for retrieval.
Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld, TQG-Exp improves Avg.@3 over the strongest baseline by 4.50 and 8.55 percentage points with two backbone LLMs.
papers.selection_reason: Experience-based learning with trajectory-quality feedback for LLM agents; fits agent memory and retrieval.
papers.title: Beyond Outcome Feedback: Trajectory-Quality-Guided Experience-based Learning
papers.tldr: TQG-Exp improves LLM agent experience reuse by evaluating and optimizing execution trajectories, not just final outcomes.

papers.abstract: Biomedical Named Entity Linking (BioNEL) is the task of mapping mentions extracted from biomedical texts to canonical entities or concepts in the standardized knowledge base. Although existing methods have achieved remarkable performance in mapping accuracy, most rely on training with domain-specific datasets, which fundamentally limits their cross-domain adaptability. To address this limitation, we propose BioNEL-RAG, a novel training-free framework that combines retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with large language models (LLMs). Within this framework, the RAG module focuses on retrieving candidate entities, while the large language model module plays the role of selecting the most appropriate candidate for entity normalization, which is based on the analysis of the mention's context, with the aid of its remarkable text comprehension capabilities. Experimental results demonstrate that BioNEL-RAG achieves performance comparable to existing methods without requiring training on subdomain datasets, whereas these methods necessitate fine-tuning on specific subdomains such as genes, diseases, or chemical compounds.
authors: Ziyi Chen, Hui Liu, Ziyang Ling, Ronald X. Xu, Mingzhai Sun
bullets: Addresses the limited cross-domain adaptability of methods trained on subdomain-specific datasets.
Uses RAG to retrieve candidate biomedical entities from a standardized knowledge base.
Uses an LLM to select the best candidate based on the mention’s context.
Achieves performance comparable to existing methods without fine-tuning on gene, disease, or chemical subdomains.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a training-free RAG framework for Bio-NEL, utilizing retrieval to augment LLM context, which is relevant to LLM memory and context management.
papers.title: Training-Free BioNEL-RAG: Advancing Biomedical Entity Linking through Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Large Language Model
papers.tldr: BioNEL-RAG enables biomedical entity linking without domain-specific training by combining candidate retrieval with LLM-based context-aware selection.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory benchmarks for language agents primarily evaluate whether information from earlier interactions can be retrieved and used when relevant. Persistent memory systems face an additional problem before future use is known: deciding whether a memory should remain exact, be compressed, consolidated, or deleted. Existing benchmarks capture long-range retrieval, temporal reasoning, evidence reuse, and incremental interaction, but do not directly evaluate these earlier representation decisions. We formalize memory lifecycle evaluation and introduce VitaBench, a benchmark that makes lifecycle decisions measurable through repeated memory reviews and full-horizon counterfactual evaluation. VitaBench contains a controlled Diagnostic tier that isolates future-use patterns and a Naturalistic tier that composes them into generated customer-service-style interaction streams. We characterize lifecycle decision structure with three diagnostics: lifecycle headroom, measuring the advantage of adaptive choices over the best fixed strategy; horizon reversal, measuring when short-horizon decisions change under delayed consequences; and optimal-action diversity, measuring whether different memory states favor different lifecycle operations. Across both tiers, VitaBench exhibits substantial lifecycle structure: lifecycle headroom is 1.364 in Diagnostic and 1.405 in Naturalistic, and 60.2% and 56.5% of states, respectively, change their preferred action between short and full horizons. A learned delayed lifecycle policy further improves over the best fixed strategy on VitaBench-Naturalistic, reaching 101.5 versus 83.4 joint utility. These results show that retrieving past information and deciding how it should persist are distinct evaluation problems, and that lifecycle management requires evaluation of the delayed consequences of representation decisions.
bullets: Introduces memory lifecycle evaluation through repeated reviews and full-horizon counterfactuals.
Includes a controlled Diagnostic tier and a naturalistic customer-service-style interaction tier.
Measures adaptive-choice potential, horizon reversals, and diversity of optimal lifecycle actions.
Finds substantial delayed-decision structure across both tiers, with many states changing preferred actions over longer horizons.
A learned delayed lifecycle policy improves joint utility over the best fixed strategy on the Naturalistic tier.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces VitaBench, a benchmark for evaluating memory lifecycle decisions (compression, consolidation, deletion) in language agents, addressing the gap between retrieval and persistence management.
papers.title: VitaBench: Memory Lifecycles Beyond Retrieval
papers.tldr: VitaBench evaluates whether language-agent memories should be preserved, compressed, consolidated, or deleted based on their delayed future value—not just retrieved.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) support social simulation, but faithfully reproducing real users requires grounding both structured platform decisions and language in sparse, noisy behavioral evidence. We introduce PsyMemBehav, which maps psychology-informed profiles and retrieved memories to target-first platform behavior through two-level identity-to-action reasoning. To support this approach with comprehensive behavioral traces, we construct a dataset PsyMemBehav-bench from 5.57M observed behaviors of 5,862 real users (approximately 950 per user) across Reddit, Bluesky, and Twitter. Each recorded engagement is modeled as target selection followed by Comment, Like, or Repost and optional response generation. PsyMemBehav combines 41-dimensional user descriptors, top-5 BM25 memories, reverse-CoT supervision, and rubric-guided DPO over complete reasoning-action trajectories. Experiments show that PsyMemBehav 27B ranks first in 11 of 12 reported individual-level metrics, improving average response quality over GPT-5.4 from 54.28 to 59.68 (9.95% relative), and obtains the lowest group-level MAE (0.081) and MSE (0.009) among simulated systems. These results support evidence-grounded user modeling for observed-thread continuation; the benchmark remains conditional on recorded engagement and does not model no-action decisions.
authors: Wenji Zhang, Xilong Cheng, Yunxiao Qin, Mai Tu, Tongye Zhu, Yuhao Zhou, JingBo Ji, Yuting Tan, Duoyin Li, Hongjiang Xiao, Yuan Zhang
bullets: Introduces PsyMemBehav-bench with 5.57M behaviors from 5,862 users across Reddit, Bluesky, and Twitter.
Models engagement in two stages: target selection, followed by Comment, Like, or Repost and optional response generation.
Combines 41-dimensional user descriptors, top-5 BM25 memories, reverse-CoT supervision, and rubric-guided DPO.
PsyMemBehav 27B ranks first on 11 of 12 individual-level metrics and reports improved response quality and group-level error metrics.
Scope is limited to observed engagements and does not simulate no-action decisions.
papers.selection_reason: Memory-grounded LLM user simulation with retrieval and DPO; relevant to LLM memory and agent memory.
papers.title: PsyMemBehav: Psychology-Informed and Memory-Grounded Two-Level Identity-to-Action Reasoning for Social-Media Behavior Simulation
papers.tldr: PsyMemBehav simulates social-media users by combining psychology-informed profiles, retrieved memories, and two-level reasoning to predict targets, actions, and responses from behavioral traces.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory enables LLM agents to learn from past interactions but exposes memory formation to adversarial influence. Existing studies primarily organize memory poisoning by attack channels, corruption patterns, or lifecycle stages, leaving formation interfaces insufficiently characterized. We formulate Memory Formation Poisoning as adversarial manipulation of the interfaces through which persistent agent memory is produced and committed, and introduce MemForm, a controlled diagnostic benchmark covering five interfaces: Content, Evidence, Scope, Selection, and Path Poisoning. We introduce Selection and Path Poisoning as controlled intervention categories that isolate retention and consolidation order effects, respectively. Each category pairs clean and poisoned conditions with interface-specific controls. Evaluations across six LLMs and two response formats reveal broad susceptibility at all five interfaces under the evaluated memory protocols and implementations. Crucially, authentic experiences with successful outcomes do not guarantee reliable behavior after memory formation: changes to contextual support, retention, or consolidation order can induce undesirable downstream behavior. In particular, consolidation order can alter behavior even with identical retained experiences, depending on the memory formation procedure. Additional analyses show that interface applicability depends on memory architecture and that Path Poisoning susceptibility depends on the updater. The evaluated defenses provide incomplete mitigation that varies by interface. These findings motivate protecting both what is committed to persistent memory and how memory is formed from experiences. Code and data are available at https://github.com/opanhw/memform-code.
authors: Haowen Pan, Pengyang Shao, Yunshan Ma, Yanzheng Jin, Naixin Zhai, Xiang Wang, Xun Yang
bullets: Introduces Memory Formation Poisoning as adversarial manipulation of how persistent agent memory is produced and committed.
Benchmarks five interfaces: Content, Evidence, Scope, Selection, and Path Poisoning.
Evaluations across six LLMs and two response formats find susceptibility at all five interfaces under the tested protocols.
Shows that successful authentic experiences do not ensure reliable behavior when contextual support, retention, or consolidation order changes.
Finds that vulnerability depends on memory architecture and updater, while evaluated defenses provide incomplete, interface-dependent mitigation.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for memory formation poisoning in LLM agents; directly addresses persistent memory formation and interfaces.
papers.title: MemForm: Benchmarking Memory Formation Poisoning in LLM Agents
papers.tldr: MemForm shows that LLM agents can be broadly manipulated through multiple interfaces involved in forming persistent memory, including retention and consolidation order.

papers.abstract: Enterprise workflow automation typically requires retrieving a complete and accurate set of relevant information from large operational document corpora (SOPs, policy documents) given a specific scenario or request. In customer support (CS), for example, human specialists must determine the correct sequence of resolution steps for each case, a task that demands precise grounding in policy documentation. Meeting this bar in production typically requires complex document chunking, indexing, and retrieval pipelines, often layered with learned re-rankers, query rewriters, and bespoke agentic RAG infrastructure. We report a deployment case study of a simpler alternative: a portable skill consisting of a natural-language instruction, lightweight tools (a retrieval API, format-checking scripts), and a corpus enriched with an LLM-generated navigation layer, which is a structured "Wikipedia-style" index over the underlying documents. This agentic RAG approach is straightforward to implement (1-2 engineer days), portable across capable agentic harnesses (e.g., Claude Code), and performs strongly on the challenging task of CS resolution workflow generation, achieving 99.2% procedural equivalence to human-approved ground truth and 83.3% evidence sufficiency. It is also roughly an order of magnitude slower per case than our deployed production assistant (~90 s vs. ~8-9 s), so we claim no latency advantage. Our claim is scoped to that setting: a mature, well-curated corpus, a latency-tolerant workflow, and human review of every case. There, the skill did the work of a complex RAG stack, and maintenance became a matter of editing text and data rather than retraining models.
authors: Istok Bako, Bonan Min, Tiffany Shao, Claire Cheng, Yashar Mehdad
bullets: Targets accurate, complete retrieval of policy-grounded resolution steps from enterprise support documents.
Uses natural-language instructions, lightweight retrieval and validation tools, and an LLM-generated Wikipedia-style navigation layer.
Implemented in 1–2 engineer days and portable across capable agentic harnesses.
Achieved 99.2% procedural equivalence and 83.3% evidence sufficiency in the reported case study.
Scope is limited to mature corpora, latency-tolerant workflows, and human review; inference took roughly 90 seconds versus 8–9 seconds in production.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a portable skill-based RAG approach for customer support using an LLM-generated navigation layer to structure document retrieval, demonstrating a simple yet effective method for external memory and information retrieval.
papers.title: Frustratingly Easy Agentic RAG via Portable Skills: A Case Study in Customer Support
papers.tldr: A simple, portable agentic RAG skill with a navigable document index can generate customer-support resolution workflows nearly as well as human-approved procedures, but is much slower than a production assistant.

papers.abstract: Scientific research increasingly depends on curating experimental data from literature. Scientific data curation requires verifying exact experimental conditions (e.g., specific assays, clinical outcomes, and data availability) across long, heterogeneous files, which is a highly time-consuming process. Existing benchmarks evaluate only broad relevance on short queries, failing to capture this complexity. We introduce SciCurateBench, a benchmark of 200 expert-annotated papers from major life-science journals that challenges systems to verify conjunctive biological experimental criteria from raw, unprocessed scientific literature. We show that plain LLMs and popular reasoning, tool-using, and feedback-based agents all struggle with this task. To study what makes the task tractable, we further propose LangPoli, an integrative system in which a policy agent generates natural language action guidelines that actor agents convert into executable tools. LangPoli showed strong performance on both Paper Classification (83.16% F1 vs. 58.22% for its base LLM) and Structured Information Retrieval, and also improves re-ranking on the public benchmarks of LitSearch, BEIR, and TREC. We further explore curriculum transfer, a method that distills generalizable strategies from solved tasks to accelerate the solving of related problems. We hope this work facilitates research in truly practical scientific AI assistance. The anonymized pre-release can be found from https://anonymous.4open. science/r/scicuratebench-D885/.
authors: Minuk Ma, Kaiyun Guo, Jiarui Ding
bullets: Presents 200 expert-annotated papers from major life-science journals for evaluating experimental-data curation.
Targets verification of specific assays, clinical outcomes, and data availability across long, heterogeneous documents.
Finds that plain LLMs and existing reasoning, tool-using, and feedback-based agents struggle with the task.
LangPoli achieves 83.16% F1 on Paper Classification, compared with 58.22% for its base LLM, and improves performance on LitSearch, BEIR, and TREC re-ranking.
Explores curriculum transfer to reuse strategies from solved tasks for related curation problems.
papers.selection_reason: Focuses on LLM agents (LangPoli) for scientific data curation, addressing agent design and test-time learning strategies.
papers.title: SciCurateBench: Curating Experimental Data from Heterogeneous Scientific Literature with Verbal-Action Agents
papers.tldr: SciCurateBench evaluates whether AI systems can verify detailed, conjunctive experimental criteria in messy scientific literature, and introduces LangPoli, which uses natural-language action policies to improve curation and retrieval.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are highly vulnerable to memory-poisoning attacks. Existing defenses primarily rely on external modules for either static memory isolation or continuous online auditing, resulting in low memory efficiency and high computational overhead. To address these limitations, inspired by neuroscientific mechanisms that weak reactivation can destabilize memories and induce decay in the absence of reinforcement, we propose an agent-intrinsic training-free memory repair framework, DREAM (Dynamic Reactivation for Engram Attenuation in Memory), that enables selective functional forgetting of poisoned memories. Specifically, DREAM implements a three-stage pipeline: perturbation-induced implicit reactivation to reveal the structural fragility of malicious memories, adaptive anomaly diagnosis based on multi-dimensional activation patterns to detect topological anomalies, and a dynamic memory repair module that selectively suppresses harmful memories while reinforcing benign ones. Extensive experiments across diverse attackers and real-world tasks demonstrate that DREAM reduces attack success rates by over 95\% against backdoor poisoning while preserving strong benign utility. DREAM also achieves competitive robustness against injection attacks. In terms of runtime and token consumption, DREAM achieves up to a 2.13$\times$ speedup and a 37.7\% reduction in token consumption compared with A-MemGuard. Furthermore, DREAM also achieves a task success rate of 92.96\% on poisoned multi-agent systems.
bullets: Addresses memory-poisoning attacks without external auditing or isolation modules.
Uses perturbation-induced reactivation, activation-pattern anomaly diagnosis, and dynamic memory repair.
Suppresses detected malicious memories while reinforcing benign memories through a training-free, agent-intrinsic process.
Reports over 95% reduction in backdoor attack success, competitive injection-attack robustness, and 92.96% task success in poisoned multi-agent systems.
Compared with A-MemGuard, achieves up to 2.13× speedup and 37.7% lower token consumption.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a training-free memory repair mechanism for selectively forgetting poisoned memories in LLM agents.
papers.title: Forgetting is Not Always Bad: A Neuro-Inspired Memory Repair Mechanism for Poisoned LLM Agents
papers.tldr: DREAM repairs poisoned LLM-agent memories by selectively forgetting harmful memories while preserving benign ones, reducing attack success and overhead.

papers.abstract: Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) reporting is critical for corporate accountability, with Large Language Models (LLMs) and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) offering strong potential to automate KPI extraction. However, open-source LLM performance in domain-specific ESG tasks remains insufficiently understood. This paper evaluates open-source LLMs in ESG contexts using a structured framework and evaluation resource based on 498 real-world ESG reports from EU-listed companies (2010-2024). We evaluate seven open-source models (2B to 30B parameters) -- glm-4.7-flash, nemotron-3-nano:4b, qwen3:4b-instruct, gemma3:4b, gemma4:e4b, gemma4:e2b, and ministral-3:8b -- using 100 persona-based synthetic QA pairs covering ESG information needs. System performance is assessed via RAGAS metrics, including contextual recall, precision, relevance, faithfulness, answer relevancy, and factual correctness. Results show notable performance variations across architectures. Retrieval performance is strong across models (context recall around 0.58-0.61, context precision around 0.78-0.81, context relevance 0.965-0.985). Generation diverges most on faithfulness (0.607-0.822) and least on answer relevancy (0.760-0.881): glm-4.7-flash leads in faithfulness (0.822), qwen3 in factual correctness (0.449), and ministral-3 in answer relevancy (0.881). Low overall factual correctness (0.387-0.449) highlights the need for domain-specific fine-tuning. This work provides data-driven guidance for deploying open-source models in ESG reporting.
bullets: Evaluates open-source LLMs for ESG KPI extraction using 498 EU-listed-company reports from 2010–2024 and 100 persona-based QA pairs.
Assesses RAG with RAGAS metrics covering retrieval quality, faithfulness, answer relevancy, and factual correctness.
Retrieval performance is consistently strong across models, while generation varies substantially by architecture.
glm-4.7-flash leads in faithfulness, qwen3 in factual correctness, and ministral-3 in answer relevancy.
Low factual-correctness scores indicate that domain-specific fine-tuning is still needed for dependable ESG reporting automation.
papers.selection_reason: Empirical evaluation of retrieval-augmented generation directly concerns external-memory retrieval and generation behavior in language models.
papers.title: Empirical Evaluation of Open-Source Large Language Models for Retrieval-Augmented Generation in ESG Domain
papers.tldr: A systematic evaluation of seven open-source LLMs finds that RAG retrieves ESG information reliably, but generation quality—especially factual correctness—remains limited and model-dependent.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle to answer questions over long interaction histories, where relevant evidence may be scattered across distant sessions. Existing memory systems typically construct and maintain sophisticated memory representations offline, before user queries are observed, incurring substantial overhead and limiting their ability to adapt memory construction to query-specific information needs. In this paper, we propose T$^2$Mem, a Test-Time Memory construction framework that defers memory construction to inference and progressively builds memory along the reasoning process. Specifically, T$^2$Mem extracts lightweight episode-level metadata offline to capture key events and temporal associations as retrieval cues, while retaining links to the original interactions to facilitate the reconstruction of dependencies across episodes. At test time, the LLM adaptively retrieves and organizes metadata and raw interactions, progressively constructing query-specific memory as reasoning unfolds. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval show the effectiveness of T$^2$Mem by consistently outperforming strong baselines across different backbone LLMs while substantially reducing the overhead of memory construction. Further analysis demonstrates that deferring memory construction to inference enables the memory construction process to dynamically adapt to the information needs of individual queries. All code is available at https://github.com/OpenBMB/T2Mem.
authors: Zijun Wang, Yifan Ji, Haidong Xin, Zhenghao Liu, Yukun Yan, Zulong Chen, Yu Gu, Ge Yu, Maosong Sun
bullets: Addresses the challenge of retrieving relevant evidence spread across distant sessions.
Stores lightweight episode-level metadata and links to original interactions as retrieval cues.
At test time, progressively retrieves and organizes metadata and raw interactions during reasoning.
Evaluations on LoCoMo and LongMemEval show consistent gains over strong baselines across backbone LLMs.
Deferring construction enables memory organization to adapt dynamically to each query’s information needs.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes test-time memory construction that adaptively builds query-specific memory during inference, directly relevant to LLM memory and test-time learning.
papers.title: Test-Time Memory Construction
papers.tldr: T²Mem builds query-specific memory at inference time, helping LLMs answer questions over long, scattered interaction histories with lower construction overhead.

papers.abstract: Memory-augmented assistants retrieve evidence from stored conversations and documents to answer queries. Most embedding-based retrievers compare single-vector representations of queries and memories, even when relevance depends on a small part of the content. Such local evidence can be matched to queries using the contextual token representations already computed by the same embedding models. Our method uses sparse token matching to improve retrieval without additional training. Each query token retrieves a small set of matching tokens across candidate memories. The matching scores are aggregated for each memory and combined with whole-memory similarity to rank memories. An optional low-rank query adapter can be trained with supervision while keeping the encoder and stored memory representations fixed. Our method improves retrieval across eight benchmarks and multiple model families without additional training. Query adaptation further increases the gains to 13.3 and 14.3 percentage points in average Recall@10 and NDCG@10 on Qwen3-Embedding-4B. These retrieval gains translate into higher question-answering accuracy on long-term memory benchmarks.
authors: Han Luo, Zhan Zhuang, Xu He, Jujia Zhao, Yu Li, Suqin Yuan, Dong Li, Lei Feng
bullets: Addresses the weakness of single-vector retrieval when relevance depends on small parts of a memory.
Matches each query token to candidate-memory tokens and aggregates scores with whole-memory similarity.
Requires no additional training; an optional low-rank query adapter adds supervised adaptation while keeping the encoder and stored memories fixed.
Improves retrieval across eight benchmarks and multiple model families; adaptation further raises Recall@10 and NDCG@10 on Qwen3-Embedding-4B.
Retrieval improvements also increase question-answering accuracy on long-term memory benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Token-level memory retrieval for long-term memory assistants; fits LLM memory subtopic.
papers.title: Beyond the Final Embedding: Retrieving Memories from Token-Level Evidence
papers.tldr: Token-level sparse matching complements whole-memory embeddings to retrieve locally relevant evidence more effectively, improving retrieval and long-term-memory QA.

papers.abstract: LLM-as-a-Service has become a dominant paradigm for accessing large language models without requiring local deployment. However, the process raises severe privacy concerns when user queries may include sensitive or confidential contexts. Differential privacy (DP) provides a principled approach to protecting such inputs, but existing DP inference methods are primarily designed for short- or moderate-context settings and struggle with million-token-scale inputs due to limited context capacity and severe utility degradation under DP perturbation. In this paper, we propose DP-MIND, a memory-guided framework that scales differentially private inference to million-token contexts. DP-MIND enables private long-context inference by locally perturbing the input and processing it chunk by chunk with a compact memory that preserves task-relevant information across the sequence. To make this memory robust to DP noise, we optimize the memory construction policy directly on perturbed inputs using reinforcement learning, guided by both final answer correctness and memory consistency. We further recover perturbation-corrupted answer spans through a local denoising module without exposing the original context to the external model. We provide theoretical privacy analysis of DP-MIND and further conduct extensive empirical analysis across multiple long-context benchmarks with context lengths up to the million-token scale, demonstrating that DP-MIND consistently outperforms existing DP and long-context inference baselines in both scalability and utility.
authors: Zhihao Liu, Yitian Cheng, Shuang Liu, Rui Wen, Yuke Hu, Zhan Qin
bullets: Addresses privacy and utility challenges in LLM-as-a-Service for sensitive, million-token inputs.
Processes perturbed inputs chunk by chunk while a compact memory preserves task-relevant information across the sequence.
Uses reinforcement learning to make memory construction robust to differential privacy noise, optimizing correctness and memory consistency.
Applies local denoising to recover perturbation-corrupted answer spans without revealing the original context to the external model.
Theoretical and empirical analyses across long-context benchmarks show improved scalability and utility over existing DP and long-context inference baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Memory-guided differentially private inference for million-token contexts, fitting long-context and LLM memory.
papers.title: DP-MIND: Differentially private memory-guided Long context Inference
papers.tldr: DP-MIND enables differentially private inference over million-token contexts by combining input perturbation, chunk-wise memory, reinforcement-learned memory construction, and local answer denoising.

papers.abstract: Corpus-level long-context reasoning requires agents to acquire and integrate evidence across document collections that exceed their context windows. Existing agent harnesses enable incremental access to these corpora, but acquired evidence and evolving conclusions often remain entangled in a growing interaction history. This implicit state management can lead to two coupled failure modes: unbounded exploration, where retrieval expands the interaction history without resolving decision-relevant information gaps, and evidence-state drift, where previously acquired evidence or subsequent corrections fail to inform the current conclusion. We present LongHarness, a model-agnostic harness that makes the interaction between acquired evidence and evolving conclusions explicit. Its core mechanism, Evidence-Conclusion Coevolution, uses unresolved conclusions to guide exploration toward missing information, while newly acquired evidence strengthens or revises the conclusions that directed the search. LongHarness couples this process with Evidence Lifecycle Management, which keeps accumulated evidence current and traceable throughout the interaction. Together, these mechanisms focus retrieval on remaining information needs and keep conclusions aligned with current evidence. We evaluate LongHarness on OfficeQA Pro V1 and V2, AA-LCR, and LongBench v2 using GLM-5.3-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash. Compared with direct reasoning using the same backbone, LongHarness improves GLM-5.3-Flash exact match on OfficeQA Pro from 15.8% to 60.2% on V1 and from 4.4% to 61.1% on V2. Against state-of-the-art agent harnesses, it surpasses Claude Code by 12.0 percentage points on V1 and Codex by 18.9 points on V2. With Qwen3.8-Flash, LongHarness reaches 61.7% on V1, outperforming Claude Code by 8.3 points and Codex by 12.0 points.
authors: Songtao Huang, Zhijie Zhong, Xiaohan He, Shuaiyu Zhang, Zhiyin Yu, Li Kang, Heng Zhou, Yutao Fan, Xiangchao Yan, Bo Zhang, Shiyang Feng
bullets: Targets unbounded exploration and evidence-state drift in corpus-level reasoning.
Uses Evidence–Conclusion Coevolution to direct retrieval toward unresolved information gaps and revise conclusions as evidence changes.
Adds Evidence Lifecycle Management to keep acquired evidence current and traceable.
Evaluated on OfficeQA Pro V1/V2, AA-LCR, and LongBench v2 with GLM-5.3-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash.
On OfficeQA Pro, improves GLM-5.3-Flash exact match from 15.8% to 60.2% on V1 and 4.4% to 61.1% on V2; it also outperforms cited agent harnesses.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic harness for corpus-level long-context reasoning with explicit evidence-conclusion coevolution, directly relevant to long-context and memory management.
papers.title: LongHarness: Advancing Agentic Reasoning over 100M-Token Corpora via Stateful Evidence Management
papers.tldr: LongHarness improves agentic reasoning over 100M-token corpora by explicitly coevolving conclusions with traceable evidence, substantially boosting long-context QA performance.

papers.abstract: Processing a long sequence does not guarantee that distant information remains usable. As context grows, a fixed-size memory must retain many associations, connect information across positions, and preserve relevant structure without being overwhelmed by everything it observes. These are distinct requirements: a memory may store more information without representing the relationships needed for retrieval, and it may transport those relationships without preserving the ones that matter. Thus, the challenge is not simply extending context length, but constructing a memory that remains usable as context grows. We study this problem in large-chunk test-time training (TTT) and identify two basic failures: single-step writes accumulate interference, limiting capacity, while self-associative writes cannot form cross-position bindings. We introduce Double-Take (DT), which repairs these failures with multi-step unpinned updates and cross-position mixing, and adds bidirectional change-sensitive writes for selective retention. Capacity alone leaves end-to-end recall at the $0.10$ chance floor; adding binding raises it to $0.92$. Trained only on $32\,\mathrm{kb}$ genomic contexts, DT reaches $0.927$ AUROC at $131\,\mathrm{kb}$ and $0.856$ near $1\,\mathrm{Mb}$, while transferring zero-shot from human to mouse. Together, these results identify capacity, binding, and selectivity as three requirements for usable long-range memory.
authors: Vakul Raghavan, Utkarsh Grover, Mingyang Mao, Chengwen Wang, Xiaomin Lin
bullets: The work argues that extending context is insufficient: memory must retain information, bind distant positions, and selectively preserve relevant structure.
It identifies interference from single-step writes and the inability of self-associative writes to form cross-position bindings.
Double-Take addresses these issues with multi-step unpinned updates, cross-position mixing, and bidirectional change-sensitive writes.
Adding binding improves end-to-end recall from the 0.10 chance floor to 0.92, while models trained on 32 kb genomic contexts generalize to 131 kb and nearly 1 Mb.
The method also transfers zero-shot from human to mouse, supporting the role of capacity, binding, and selectivity in long-range memory.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a novel mechanism (Double-Take) for long-context memory that addresses capacity, binding, and selectivity. This is directly relevant to LLM Memory and Long-Context Models.
papers.title: Double-Take: Improving Capacity, Binding, and Selectivity In Long-Context Within Bidirectional Memory
papers.tldr: Double-Take makes long-context memory usable by combining capacity, cross-position binding, and selective retention in bidirectional test-time training.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory has been widely adopted in LLM-based agents to support persistent interaction and personalized assistance. Long-term multi-party interactions, however, accumulate substantially more detailed information, with decisions repeatedly updated and states evolving across participants and interaction stages. Temporal structure is therefore crucial for tracing such memories: relevant information often appears densely within short intervals, while transitions among different states are anchored by a strict temporal order. Existing temporally aware memory frameworks primarily store time as metadata or use temporal signals to guide retrieval over preconstructed memory structures, without using temporal structure to both recover locally concentrated evidence and reconstruct its complete event progression. To address these limitations, we propose T-Mem, a temporal-structure-based memory framework that preserves interactions and organizes query-relevant evidence through two temporal mechanisms. Temporal Evidence Discovery exploits the local concentration of related messages to recover overlooked evidence, while Temporal Memory Structuring models state transitions and supporting relations over time and compresses low-information spans within the resulting forest. Evidence Forest Linearization then serializes the structured evidence for answer generation. Experiments on two long-term multi-party memory benchmarks demonstrate that T-Mem consistently outperforms competitive memory frameworks across LLMs, parameter settings, domains, and query types.
authors: Junyou Guo, Chongyang Tao, Yan He, Yong Wang, Shuai Ma
bullets: Addresses the challenge of tracking evolving decisions and participant states in detailed, long-term multi-party interactions.
Uses Temporal Evidence Discovery to recover relevant messages concentrated within short time intervals.
Builds a temporal evidence forest that models state transitions and supporting relations while compressing low-information spans.
Linearizes the structured evidence into a format suitable for answer generation.
Outperforms competing memory frameworks across two benchmarks, multiple LLMs, domains, settings, and query types.
papers.selection_reason: Temporal-structure-based long-term memory framework for LLM agents; directly fits persistent external memory for language models.
papers.title: Temporal Evidence Forests for Long-Horizon Multi-Party Conversational Memory
papers.tldr: T-Mem improves long-horizon multi-party conversational memory by discovering locally concentrated evidence and reconstructing its temporal progression for answer generation.

papers.abstract: We introduce iRAG, a human-in-the-loop decision-support system combining Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with Hybrid Decision-Making. Unlike conventional RAG systems, relying on static Knowledge Bases (KBs), our proposal addresses settings where the KB is initially empty and is progressively populated through human decisions. The system stores previous decisions as retrievable precedents and moves from silent observation to evidence-grounded contestation and, finally, to autonomous handling with abstention. Against an independent baseline, iRAG matches final-decision error under 10% drift without retrieval decay and reduces it under 40% drift across all configurations. Retrieval decay improves performance on changed knowledge while increasing error on stable knowledge, evidencing a stability--plasticity trade-off rather than a general advantage. Human oversight is an architectural provision of the workflow; its usability with real human users remains to be evaluated.
bullets: Addresses decision support when the initial knowledge base is empty and populated progressively through human decisions.
Stores prior decisions as retrievable precedents and transitions from observation to contestation to autonomous handling with abstention.
Matches an independent baseline under 10% knowledge drift and reduces error under 40% drift across configurations.
Retrieval decay helps with changed knowledge but harms performance on stable knowledge, revealing a stability–plasticity trade-off.
The workflow includes human oversight, but usability with real users has not yet been evaluated.
papers.selection_reason: Incremental RAG with dynamically populated external memory, relevant to LLM memory and online adaptation.
papers.title: Incremental Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Human-in-the-Loop Decision Support
papers.tldr: iRAG incrementally builds a retrieval base from human decisions to support increasingly autonomous, evidence-grounded decision-making under changing knowledge.

papers.abstract: Agentic large language models now tackle complex tasks, yet strategic reasoning over long horizons is under-studied: most agentic benchmarks are short and episodic, and performance on long tasks is hard to dissect into stored knowledge, reasoning and luck. We introduce SpireBench, in which models play the complete commercial deck-builder Slay the Spire (StS), where early decisions decide long-term success. Across 20 large language models (LLMs) at the game's highest difficulty, frontier models beat heuristic baselines and match the average human player but remain far behind experts. This gap widens as the run lengthens: the strongest models win the first act as often as experts, then fall behind. What separates strong models from weak is how well they play each fight; all of them misjudge risk over a run, preserving health rather than spending it to grow stronger. A comprehensive, self-consistent renaming of every game term shows that part of their performance rests on prior knowledge of the game, and models do not improve from the memories they write across runs, which are often wrong and overly cautious. Our harness is the first to give a model the complete original game, and we compare it with existing harnesses. Overall, SpireBench offers an unsaturated long-horizon benchmark with tools to locate where and why agents fail.
authors: Scott C. Lowe, Sander W. Keemink
bullets: Tests 20 LLMs at Slay the Spire’s highest difficulty against heuristic baselines and human performance.
Models win the first act about as often as experts, but their performance declines as runs become longer.
Stronger models distinguish themselves mainly through better fight-by-fight play, while all models misjudge long-term risk.
Agents tend to preserve health instead of spending it to become stronger, and written memories across runs are often incorrect, overly cautious, and unhelpful.
Renaming game terms shows that performance partly depends on prior game knowledge; the benchmark is designed to diagnose long-horizon failure modes.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark evaluating long-horizon agentic LLM play and memory written across runs; directly relevant to agent memory.
papers.title: SpireBench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Strategic Play of Agentic Models with Slay the Spire
papers.tldr: SpireBench evaluates long-horizon strategic reasoning by having LLM agents play the complete game Slay the Spire, revealing that frontier models match average humans early but remain well below experts over full runs.

papers.abstract: Persistent memory allows an LLM agent to carry experience across conversations, but it also turns a local reasoning mistake into a durable one. During deliberation, an agent may consider a plan, simulate a tool result, report another speaker's belief, and then reject all of them. If memory retains only the resulting sentences, those once-useful possibilities can later return as facts. The record is neither fabricated nor irrelevant; it has simply been detached from the context in which it was valid. We identify this missing context as \emph{discourse ownership}: the world, branch, or speaker that licenses a proposition. Our first finding is counterintuitive. Language models already carry a causally active signal for ownership, yet conventional memory interfaces discard it when they convert reasoning into records. We introduce CASK (Causally Anchored Scoping Keys), a commit rule that preserves this signal so that shared-world facts enter durable memory while provisional content remains available only within its original scope. Our second finding is that the most obvious way to preserve the signal---storing the discovered internal coordinates---is unreliable because equivalent representations need not keep the same coordinates. CASK instead preserves the stable relations that express ownership. Controlled long-conversation conflicts and tool-agent traces show that this design improves memory admission and prevents provisional content from contaminating later answers while complementing runtime provenance. The resulting commit boundary lets agents explore more possibilities without granting every intermediate sentence authority over future behavior.
bullets: Persistent memory can turn discarded plans, simulated tool results, or reported beliefs into misleading future facts when their context is lost.
The paper identifies this missing context as discourse ownership: which world, branch, or speaker licenses a proposition.
CASK preserves stable ownership relations rather than unreliable internal representation coordinates.
Controlled conflict and tool-agent traces show improved memory admission and reduced contamination from provisional content.
The approach complements runtime provenance and enables broader reasoning without granting every intermediate sentence durable authority.
papers.selection_reason: Scope-aware commit rules for persistent LLM memory; directly fits LLM memory.
papers.title: Whose Memory Is It? Scope-Aware Commit Rules for Long-Term LLM Memory
papers.tldr: CASK makes LLM long-term memory scope-aware, preserving only facts licensed by the correct world, reasoning branch, or speaker while keeping provisional content local.

papers.abstract: LLM agents rely on long-term memory to retain and reuse information when performing tasks over long horizons. Existing methods provide limited support for handling memories that become outdated as new observations or domain evidence arrive. Such outdated memories may remain semantically relevant, continue to affect dependent records, and retain value as historical evidence. This calls for two capabilities: dependency tracking to identify downstream effects and historical preservation to retain useful past records. We propose Provenance-Aware Cascading Memory Invalidation (PACMI), a framework that represents memories and new evidence in a provenance graph with typed dependency edges. PACMI assigns records to a four-state validity lattice, propagates validity changes to dependent memories, and uses the resulting states for retrieval and stale-premise detection. We also introduce a diagnostic benchmark with 100 cases and 300 queries across five domains. The evaluation separates node, context-, and answer-level performance. PACMI achieves the highest final-answer accuracy on this benchmark, and its paired difference from the strongest baseline is significant under an exact McNemar test. The premise checker achieves perfect precision, recall, and F 1 on the controlled query distribution. Cascading propagation primarily improves memorystate correctness: removing it increases final-answer errors from 3 to 11, but the paired difference does not reach the 0.05 significance threshold. Code and data will be made publicly available.
bullets: Addresses stale memories that remain relevant, influence dependent records, and may retain historical value.
Represents memories and new evidence in a provenance graph with typed dependencies and a four-state validity lattice.
Uses propagated validity for retrieval and detecting answers based on stale premises.
On a 100-case, 300-query benchmark across five domains, PACMI achieved the highest final-answer accuracy; its advantage over the strongest baseline was statistically significant.
Cascading propagation reduced final-answer errors from 11 to 3, though this difference was not statistically significant; the premise checker achieved perfect metrics on the controlled queries.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses long-term memory management and retrieval for LLM agents, fitting the LLM memory subtopic.
papers.title: PACMI: Provenance-Aware Cascading Memory Invalidation for Long-Term LLM Agents
papers.tldr: PACMI helps long-term LLM agents manage outdated memories by tracking provenance, cascading validity changes, and preserving historical evidence.

papers.abstract: Unlearning benchmarks such as TOFU and MUSE certify forgetting by reading the model's final answer, where a model that refuses to answer already counts as having forgotten. We show that this model-level certificate does not transfer once the model is deployed as an agent. We introduce K-Bench, a benchmark that scores LLM unlearning under agentic deployment. K-Bench inspects all six channels a ReAct agent exposes, including its chain-of-thought (CoT), tool calls and tool observations, and elicited summary. A query counts as leaked if the secret appears in any of them. Each experiment places the secret in exactly one of the agent's three sources (the weights, the prompt, or the retrieval store). The K-Score is computed separately for each source and credits forgetting only when the agent remains usable. Clearing the answer channel does not make the secret unrecoverable. On structured retrieval, the secret stays verbatim in the tool-observation channel and the aggregate leak rate is unchanged. When the secret lives in the prompt or the retrieval store, TOFU and MUSE report no leakage, while the deployed agent still leaks it on 22--86\% of queries. When the secret is in the weights, none of the twenty evaluated published methods demonstrably removes it, and only an input-corruption intervention reaches selective forgetting under the evaluated observer. The top-ranked method changes across base models. A refusal-tuning method resists the evaluated extraction without verified knowledge removal.
bullets: Evaluates leakage across six ReAct channels, including chain-of-thought, tool interactions, observations, and summaries.
Tests secrets stored separately in model weights, prompts, or retrieval stores, and credits forgetting only when the agent remains usable.
Secrets in prompts or retrieval stores leaked in 22–86% of agent queries despite TOFU and MUSE reporting no leakage.
For weight-stored secrets, none of 20 evaluated published methods demonstrably removed the knowledge; only input corruption achieved selective forgetting under the evaluated observer.
Refusal tuning resisted extraction but did not verify knowledge removal, and the top-ranked method varied by base model.
papers.selection_reason: Develops K-Bench to evaluate LLM unlearning in agentic deployments, highlighting the gap between model-level and agent-level forgetting.
papers.title: K-Bench: A Benchmark for LLM Unlearning in Agentic Deployments
papers.tldr: K-Bench shows that LLM unlearning verified at the answer level often fails when models are deployed as agents with multiple leakage channels.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents that reason over clinical records must track changes in a patient's state while preserving the history needed to understand them. Simply accumulating memories leaves it unclear which information still applies, whereas overwriting earlier memories can erase evidence needed to reconstruct treatment history and clinical trajectories. We introduce STAM, a state-transition-aware memory framework that records state changes as new clinical entries arrive. STAM combines semantic retrieval with typed clinical relations to identify affected memories, maintaining current information in Active and superseded or resolved information in History. At read time, a query-dependent gate selectively serves historical memory. Across four longitudinal clinical benchmarks, we evaluate STAM with downstream question answering, direct state-maintenance diagnostics, and comparisons at approximately matched context lengths.
bullets: Addresses the tension between accumulating memories and overwriting outdated clinical information.
Uses semantic retrieval and typed clinical relations to detect which memories are affected by new entries.
Separates current information into Active memory from superseded or resolved information in History.
Applies a query-dependent gate to selectively retrieve historical memory.
Evaluated on four longitudinal clinical benchmarks using question answering, state-maintenance diagnostics, and matched-context comparisons.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a state-transition-aware memory framework for LLM agents, directly relevant to persistent agent memory.
papers.title: Personalized State-Transition-Aware Memory for Clinical Agents
papers.tldr: STAM helps clinical LLM agents track evolving patient states while preserving relevant historical information.

papers.abstract: The evolution of Large Language Model agents from single-task execution to long-term autonomous operation highlights the critical challenge of transforming continuous experiences into reusable knowledge. To address this, we propose Hippocam, a hierarchical memory and continual learning architecture. Hippocam draws inspiration from two characteristics of human memory: cognitive processes selectively maintain information relevant to current goals, while long-term memories form gradually through repeated consolidation. Accordingly, Hippocam structures an agent's ongoing work as nested intents. The active context remains centered on the current intent, while completed intents are consolidated into the task-relevant outcomes and state needed for subsequent work, rather than carrying forward their full working details. Concurrently, a recursive prefix consolidation mechanism repeatedly consolidates earlier history, causing long-unused experiences to become increasingly abstract. Original interactions are preserved, allowing the agent to progressively recover finer-grained details through the hierarchy and stop once sufficient information is available. Crucially, when past experiences are recalled and reintegrated into active work, they undergo subsequent consolidation alongside new experiences, thereby being reinforced, supplemented, and updated. Through this memory dynamic of use and disuse, Hippocam connects working context, long-term memory, knowledge accumulation, and skill learning within a single continuously evolving experiential process. This enables agents to learn and evolve capabilities through their own experiences without parameter updates.
authors: Xiangyi Zeng, Baihang Liu, Xutong Wang, Ze Jin, Yunpeng Li, Qixu Liu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of turning continuous agent experiences into reusable knowledge for long-term autonomous operation.
Organizes work into nested intents, keeping active context focused on current goals and consolidating completed intents into task-relevant outcomes and state.
Uses recursive prefix consolidation to abstract older history while retaining original interactions for progressively finer-grained recall.
Recalled memories are reconsolidated with new experiences, allowing them to be reinforced, supplemented, and updated.
Supports capability and skill accumulation from experience without changing model parameters.
papers.selection_reason: Hierarchical memory and continual consolidation for LLM agents; directly fits LLM memory and continual learning.
papers.title: Use and Disuse: Intent-Structured Experience Consolidation for Memory and Learning in LLM Agents
papers.tldr: Hippocam gives LLM agents a hierarchical, continually consolidating memory that preserves useful experience while progressively abstracting disused details—without parameter updates.

papers.abstract: For persistent and personalized conversational agents, memory systems can enable them to remember, update, and reason over long histories by storing past interactions and retrieving relevant information. Existing memory systems typically follow two paradigms: flat-structured memory and graph-based memory. The former is lightweight but leaves event relations and state updates implicit, while the latter explicitly models memory structure but incurs additional construction cost and introduces irrelevant relations over long histories. To address these limitations, we propose QGMem, a novel memory construction and activation framework motivated by human memory, in which experience is organized into events and query-relevant events are modeled by graph as working memory. QGMem converts long dialogue histories into event-indexed atomic memory units that preserve individual experiences and consolidates related units into dynamic memory traces that retain state trajectories and current states. When a query arrives, hybrid memory retrieval gathers complementary candidate memories, and query-aware reranking activates the most relevant units as a compact working memory. To expose relational dependencies in the working memory and support conflict-aware reasoning, QGMem organizes the working memory as a local graph, which is then encoded as a graph token and provided to the LLM together with the textual working memory to improve evidence utilization during answer generation. Experiments across six benchmarks validate the framework and show consistent gains in retrieval, multi-hop evidence composition, conflict resolution, and ultra-long dialogue reasoning with compact contexts and moderate inference cost.
authors: Yichen Liu, Chunfeng Yuan, Haowei Liu, Wenjuan Li, Zefeng Lin, Bing Li, Xu Chen, Weiming Hu
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between lightweight flat memory and costly, noisy global graph memory.
Converts dialogue histories into atomic event memories and dynamic traces that preserve state changes and current states.
Uses hybrid retrieval and query-aware reranking to activate a compact working memory.
Encodes relationships among activated memories as a local graph token alongside text for conflict-aware reasoning.
Across six benchmarks, improves retrieval, multi-hop composition, conflict resolution, and ultra-long dialogue reasoning with moderate inference cost.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes persistent event-centric memory and retrieval for long-term conversational agents, fitting LLM memory.
papers.title: Event-Centric Memory with Query-Aware Graph Augmentation for Long-Term Conversational Agents
papers.tldr: QGMem builds event-centric, query-aware graph memories that retrieve compact, relevant evidence for more effective long-term conversational reasoning.

papers.abstract: Long-term personalization requires language models to use interaction history to track users' preferences across sessions. Parametric memory encodes this interaction history into model parameters or adapters, reducing the need to include it in the inference context. However, independent context compilation leaves cross-session integration unspecified, while recurrent updates can attenuate earlier evidence. To address these challenges, we propose Dual-Path Parametric Memory (DPPM). Its Evidence path directly pools representations of the interaction history to preserve earlier evidence, while its Delta path sequentially updates an associative state to capture changes. Fusing both outputs produces history-conditioned LoRA adapters that combine evidence accumulation with ordered revision. Across multiple backbones, DPPM outperforms the evaluated baselines, achieving 54.22% on PersonaMem-v2 and 86.79% on PrefEval. These results suggest that DPPM provides a simple and effective design choice for cross-session personalized parametric memory.
authors: Yuhao Chen, Shuochen Liu, Jiayao Shi, Jian Hong, Chen Cheng, Xinyun Ding, Tao Wang, Ya Li, Quan Liu, Tong Xu
bullets: Addresses weak cross-session integration in independent memory compilation and evidence attenuation in recurrent updates.
Uses an Evidence path to pool interaction-history representations and retain earlier information.
Uses a Delta path to sequentially update an associative state and capture preference changes.
Fuses both paths into history-conditioned LoRA adapters.
Outperforms evaluated baselines across multiple backbones, reaching 54.22% on PersonaMem-v2 and 86.79% on PrefEval.
papers.selection_reason: Parametric memory for cross-session personalization, directly relevant to LLM memory.
papers.title: DPPM: Dual-Path Parametric Memory for Personalized Language Models
papers.tldr: DPPM combines direct evidence pooling with sequential updates to preserve and revise user preferences across sessions in personalized language models.

papers.abstract: The genome holds the blueprint that governs the biological properties of the cell. Consequently, advancing our knowledge of genomic function is crucial both for a broader understanding of biology and for continued biomedical advances. The success of large language models on natural language and protein sequences has motivated similar efforts on genomic data. However, standard genomic language models (gLMs) often require extremely large computational resources and still fall behind traditional methods on some downstream tasks.
